q.v: An oncology researcher is evaluating the structure of cytarabine, an anticancer agent used to halt abnormal cell division. Chemical analysis confirms that the administered drug consists solely of a nitrogenous base covalently linked to a five-carbon sugar at the 1' position, lacking any negatively charged groups at the 5' position. Based on its structural components, how is this compound classified, and what must occur intracellularly before it can be directly incorporated into a growing nucleic acid polymer?
o: It is a nucleotide that must be deaminated by adenosine deaminase.
It is a nucleoside analog that must have phosphate groups added by nucleotide kinases.
It is a free purine base that must be attached to PRPP by APRT.
It is a deoxynucleotide that must have its 2' hydroxyl group restored by thioredoxin.
It is a pyrimidine ring precursor that must undergo ring closure via dihydroorotase.
q.p: Step 1 (Identify cytarabine as a nucleoside analog composed of a base and pentose sugar without a 5' phosphate group) -> Step 2 (Deduce that nucleotide kinases must add phosphate groups to convert the nucleoside into a nucleotide building block for DNA/RNA).

r.A: A molecule lacking a phosphate group is classified as a nucleoside rather than a nucleotide, and adenosine deaminase is involved in purine degradation rather than activating cytarabine.
r.C: Cytarabine already contains a pentose sugar attached to its base, whereas APRT salvages free adenine bases by attaching them to PRPP.
r.D: Cytarabine is a nucleoside lacking a phosphate group, and thioredoxin functions to help ribonucleotide reductase remove, rather than restore, a 2' hydroxyl group.
r.E: The aromatic base ring in cytarabine is already closed and attached to a sugar, unlike acyclic carbamoyl-aspartate intermediates acted upon by dihydroorotase.

q.s: Slide 4 (Overview), Slide 5 (Nucleoside - Nucleotide Component Parts), and Slide 23 (Stage 3: Formation of UTP, CTP, dTTP and dCTP)

q.v: In an in vitro metabolic labeling experiment, rapidly dividing human cells are cultured in media containing isotopically labeled amino acids to trace the de novo assembly of the two-ring purine nucleobase structure. The investigator specifically tracks the incorporation of the molecule that donates both carbon and nitrogen atoms to positions 4, 5, and 7 of the core ring, as well as the specific amino acid that later donates an amino group to convert the common precursor inosine monophosphate (IMP) into guanosine monophosphate (GMP). Which of the following pairs correctly identifies these two required substrates in respective order?
o: Aspartate and glycine
Glutamine and aspartate
Glycine and glutamine
Tetrahydrofolate and glutamine
Bicarbonate and aspartate
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that glycine donates the C4, C5, and N7 atoms to the purine ring during de novo synthesis) -> Step 2 (Determine that glutamine donates the amino group to convert IMP into GMP, whereas aspartate donates the amino group to make AMP).

r.A: Aspartate donates only N1 to the purine ring and the amino group to form AMP, while glycine contributes to the core ring rather than the conversion of IMP to GMP.
r.B: Glutamine donates only single nitrogen atoms (N3 and N9) to the core ring rather than the C4-C5-N7 backbone, and aspartate is used to synthesize AMP rather than GMP.
r.D: Tetrahydrofolate donates only single carbon atoms (C2 and C8 via formate) rather than a carbon-nitrogen backbone.
r.E: CO2/bicarbonate donates C6 and aspartate donates N1, neither of which provides the C4-C5-N7 atoms or the amino group for GMP synthesis.

q.s: Slide 6 (De Novo Nucleotide Synthesis) and Slide 8 (Purine Metabolism)

q.v: A researcher is studying a cultured hepatocyte cell line with a targeted genetic knockout of adenylosuccinate synthetase, completely blocking the conversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) into adenosine monophosphate (AMP). As intracellular AMP concentrations plummet while guanosine monophosphate (GMP) levels remain normal, how will the cells intrinsically attempt to regulate the de novo purine synthesis pathway?
o: High GMP levels will allosterically activate the conversion of IMP to GMP to compensate for total purine loss.
Low AMP levels will relieve negative feedback on the IMP-to-AMP branch, while GMP continues to inhibit its own synthesis from IMP.
Accumulated IMP will strongly activate glutamine PRPP aminotransferase to accelerate the first committed step.
Depleted AMP will directly inhibit PRPP synthase, halting the generation of PRPP from ribose-5-phosphate.
Excess GMP will be directly converted into AMP via a single-step transamination reaction catalyzed by APRT.
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that AMP and GMP synthesis from the common IMP precursor is regulated by independent negative feedback loops to balance the two nucleotides) -> Step 2 (Conclude that low AMP removes feedback inhibition on the IMP-to-AMP branch while normal/high GMP continues to inhibit the IMP-to-GMP branch).

r.A: High levels of GMP inhibit, rather than activate, the conversion of IMP to GMP through negative feedback.
r.C: IMP, along with AMP and GMP, acts as an allosteric inhibitor rather than an activator of glutamine PRPP aminotransferase.
r.D: Low AMP does not inhibit PRPP synthase; rather, decreased AMP reduces negative feedback on the pathway to promote AMP restoration.
r.E: APRT salvages free adenine with PRPP to form AMP and cannot interconvert GMP directly into AMP.

q.s: Slide 7 (Purine Nucleotide Biosynthesis) and Slide 9 (Purine Nucleotide Synthesis Is Regulated by GMP and AMP)

q.v: A 58-year-old man with a history of recurrent, painful inflammation of his first metatarsophalangeal joint is started on daily preventative therapy with allopurinol. Concurrent medications include low-dose aspirin for cardiovascular prophylaxis. Two weeks later, urine biochemical analysis shows a marked decrease in uric acid crystals and a compensatory rise in two other purine metabolites. Which of the following best describes the properties of these elevated urinary metabolites and the opposing effect his low-dose aspirin has on renal uric acid handling?
o: They are allantoin and inosine, which are less water soluble than uric acid; aspirin promotes renal uric acid excretion.
They are xanthine and hypoxanthine, which are more water soluble than uric acid; aspirin inhibits renal uric acid excretion.
They are guanine and adenine, which are more water soluble than uric acid; aspirin inhibits xanthine oxidase.
They are PRPP and ribose-5-phosphate, which crystallize easily; aspirin activates urate oxidase.
They are IMP and GMP, which are freely filtered; aspirin mimics probenecid by enhancing tubular urate secretion.
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, preventing the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid) -> Step 2 (Deduce that excreted xanthine and hypoxanthine are more water soluble than uric acid, while low-dose aspirin inhibits renal uric acid excretion).

r.A: Allantoin is produced by rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) rather than allopurinol, and low-dose aspirin inhibits rather than promotes uric acid excretion.
r.C: Xanthine oxidase acts on hypoxanthine and xanthine rather than adenine, and aspirin acts on renal excretion rather than xanthine oxidase.
r.D: PRPP and ribose-5-phosphate are intracellular synthesis precursors rather than excreted purine degradation products.
r.E: IMP and GMP are intracellular nucleotides, and low-dose aspirin opposes probenecid by inhibiting, rather than enhancing, renal uric acid excretion.

q.s: Slide 10 (Purine salvage pathway) and Slide 14 (Treatment: Target an Enzyme)

q.v: A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, excruciating pain, redness, and swelling of his right great toe. Joint aspiration reveals needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals that have been ingested by polymorphonuclear leukocytes. According to the pathophysiology of this condition, what is the immediate downstream cellular consequence of crystal ingestion by these immune cells?
o: Inhibition of the mitochondrial electron transport chain and arrest of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
Activation of the inflammasome, neutrophil NETosis, and formation of aggregated NETs with cytokine cleavage.
Depletion of intracellular PRPP pools leading to acute arrest of lymphocyte DNA replication.
Direct mechanical obstruction of the synovial lymphatics without cytokine mediator release.
Up-regulation of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase to salvage the ingested urate crystals.
q.p: Step 1 (Identify acute gout triggered by neutrophil ingestion of monosodium urate crystals) -> Step 2 (Connect crystal ingestion to activation of the inflammasome, neutrophil NETosis, and formation of AggNETs with cytokine cleavage).

r.A: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) is a mitochondrial enzyme involved in de novo pyrimidine synthesis, not neutrophil crystal response.
r.C: Depletion of PRPP pools or RNR inhibition affects DNA synthesis in dividing cells, whereas mature neutrophils respond to urate crystals via inflammatory cascades.
r.D: Monosodium urate crystals in joints actively trigger inflammatory mediators and cytokine cleavage rather than simple mechanical obstruction, which occurs in renal tubules during tumor lysis syndrome.
r.E: HGPRT salvages hypoxanthine and guanine, whereas uric acid is an end product of purine degradation that cannot be salvaged by HGPRT.

q.s: Slide 12 and Slide 13 (Acute Gout: Mechanisms of Inflammation in Gout)

q.v: A 14-year-old boy being treated with induction chemotherapy for high-grade lymphoma develops oliguria and rising serum creatinine resulting from mechanical obstruction of his renal tubules by precipitated crystals. To rapidly clear the offending metabolite without relying on xanthine oxidase inhibition, the oncology team administers an intravenous recombinant enzyme. What reaction is catalyzed by this therapeutic agent, and why does it resolve the tubular obstruction?
o: It converts hypoxanthine into IMP, trapping purines inside cells so they cannot be filtered by the kidney.
It converts uric acid into allantoin, which is a more soluble metabolite that is readily excreted.
It cleaves pyrimidine rings into beta-alanine and CO2, reducing the acid load in the renal tubules.
It phosphorylates adenosine into AMP, preventing the buildup of nephrotoxic deoxyadenosine.
It inhibits PRPP synthetase, immediately halting the release of DNA from lysing lymphoma cells.
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize tumor lysis syndrome causing acute renal failure via uric acid crystal obstruction of renal tubules) -> Step 2 (Identify rasburicase as a recombinant urate oxidase that converts uric acid into allantoin, a more water-soluble metabolite).

r.A: Converting hypoxanthine to IMP is performed intracellularly by HGPRT, which is not an intravenous recombinant enzyme used for tumor lysis syndrome.
r.C: Tumor lysis syndrome nephropathy is driven by purine degradation to uric acid rather than pyrimidine degradation.
r.D: Phosphorylating adenosine relates to purine salvage, whereas recombinant urate oxidase directly degrades uric acid.
r.E: Chemotherapy-induced cell lysis releases pre-existing cellular DNA; inhibiting de novo synthesis via PRPP synthetase does not clear released uric acid.

q.s: Slide 10 (Purine salvage pathway - Rasburicase note) and Slide 16 (Tumor Lysis Syndrome)

q.v: A biochemist is studying the multi-functional CAD enzyme complex and mitochondrial enzymes responsible for the early stages of de novo pyrimidine synthesis in human fibroblasts. In an experiment, she introduces a compound that selectively blocks the committed step of pyrimidine ring synthesis without affecting the initial rate-limiting generation of carbamoyl phosphate. Which specific enzymatic activity is being targeted, and where in the cell does the subsequent oxidation step that forms orotate take place?
o: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II; in the cytosol
Aspartate transcarbamoylase; in the mitochondria
Dihydroorotase; in the nucleus
UMP synthase; in the endoplasmic reticulum
CTP synthase; in the mitochondrial matrix
q.p: Step 1 (Distinguish the rate-limiting step catalyzed by CPS-II from the committed step of pyrimidine ring synthesis, which is the reaction of carbamoyl-P and aspartate catalyzed by aspartate transcarbamoylase) -> Step 2 (Identify that following ring closure by dihydroorotase, an additional step by DHODH in the mitochondria produces orotate).

r.A: CPS-II catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step that forms carbamoyl phosphate, rather than the committed step combining carbamoyl-P with aspartate.
r.C: Dihydroorotase catalyzes the third part of the CAD reaction (ring closure), and the subsequent oxidation by DHODH occurs in the mitochondria rather than the nucleus.
r.D: UMP synthase acts after orotate is formed to convert orotate to orotidylate and UMP, rather than catalyzing the committed step of ring synthesis.
r.E: CTP synthase acts much later in Stage 3 to aminate UTP into CTP using glutamine.

q.s: Slide 19 (Stage 1: Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthesis) and Slide 20 (Stage 2: Reactions in Pyrimidine Nucleotide Biosynthesis)

q.v: A 6-month-old infant presents with lethargy, poor feeding, and megaloblastic anemia. Urine analysis demonstrates markedly elevated levels of orotic acid. Before initiating oral uridine replacement therapy, the pediatrician orders a serum ammonia and blood urea nitrogen panel to rule out an alternative metabolic defect outside of the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway that also causes orotic aciduria. A deficiency in which alternative enzyme is the pediatrician evaluating, and how would oral uridine act if the defect is instead confirmed to be in UMP synthase?
o: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS-II); uridine activates dihydroorotase to clear orotic acid.
Ornithine transcarbamoylase 1 (OTC1); uridine is converted to UTP, which feedback-inhibits CPS-II to reduce orotic acid production.
Glucose-6-phosphatase; uridine shunts ribose-5-phosphate back into the pentose phosphate pathway.
Adenosine deaminase; uridine binds the S-site of ribonucleotide reductase to stimulate dATP synthesis.
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase; uridine provides the amino group needed to convert UTP to CTP.
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that orotic aciduria can occur either from UMP synthase deficiency or a defect in the urea cycle enzyme OTC1) -> Step 2 (Recognize that oral uridine treats UMP synthase deficiency by bypassing the block to form UMP/UTP, which inhibits CPS-II and inhibits orotic acid production).

r.A: A deficiency in CPS-II would prevent carbamoyl phosphate and orotic acid formation rather than cause orotic aciduria, and uridine inhibits rather than activates upstream synthesis.
r.C: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (Von Gierke disease) causes hyperuricemia and gout via the pentose phosphate shunt, not orotic aciduria.
r.D: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes SCID via dATP accumulation, and uridine does not stimulate dATP synthesis.
r.E: HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricemia, and glutamine—not uridine—donates the amino group to convert UTP to CTP.

q.s: Slide 19 (Stage 1: Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthesis) and Slide 21 (Orotic aciduria)

q.v: In a cell-free DNA replication assay, a molecular biologist measures the catalytic output of purified ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) holoenzyme as various nucleotides are added to the buffer. The buffer initially contains high levels of ATP, keeping the enzyme active. She then adds a high concentration of deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP), which binds with high affinity to the enzyme's substrate specificity site (S site). Which specific deoxyribonucleotide will the enzyme now preferentially synthesize, and what cofactor system is required to regenerate the active, reduced form of the enzyme during this reaction?
o: dATP; dihydrofolate reductase and 5,10-methylene-THF
dGTP; thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase using NADPH
dCTP; glutamine and 2 molecules of ATP
dUMP; xanthine oxidase and molecular oxygen
dTTP; PRPP synthetase and ribose-5-phosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Determine from RNR S-site rules that when dTTP binds the specificity site with high affinity, the enzyme is directed to make dGTP) -> Step 2 (Identify from the deoxynucleotide synthesis pathway that RNR requires reduced thioredoxin, which is regenerated from oxidized thioredoxin by thioredoxin reductase and NADPH).

r.A: dGTP binding to the S-site stimulates dATP production, whereas dTTP binding stimulates dGTP production; dihydrofolate reductase is used for thymidylate synthesis.
r.C: CTP and UTP (dCDP/dUDP) reduction is favored when ATP or dATP binds the S-site with medium affinity, and glutamine/ATP are used by CTP synthase.
r.D: dUMP is formed from UDP/dUDP or dCMP, and xanthine oxidase is a purine degradation enzyme.
r.E: dTTP is synthesized from dUMP via thymidylate synthase rather than directly by RNR, and dTTP binding to the S-site promotes dGTP synthesis.

q.s: Slide 4 (Overview: Deoxynucleotide Synthesis) and Slide 28 (Ribonucleotide Reductase: S Site)

q.v: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and a history of sickle cell disease is being evaluated for cytoreductive and disease-modifying therapies. Her physician reviews three pharmacological agents that disrupt DNA synthesis: Drug X directly inhibits the enzyme that reduces ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates; Drug Y inhibits the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate (THF) from dihydrofolate (DHF); and Drug Z irreversibly inhibits the enzyme that methylates dUMP using 5,10-methylene-THF. Which of the following correctly matches Drug X, Drug Y, and Drug Z?
o: Drug X: Methotrexate; Drug Y: 5-Fluorouracil; Drug Z: Hydroxyurea
Drug X: Hydroxyurea; Drug Y: Methotrexate; Drug Z: 5-Fluorouracil
Drug X: Cytarabine; Drug Y: Allopurinol; Drug Z: Probenecid
Drug X: 5-Fluorouracil; Drug Y: Hydroxyurea; Drug Z: Methotrexate
Drug X: Allopurinol; Drug Y: Rasburicase; Drug Z: Cytarabine
q.p: Step 1 (Match each enzymatic description to its target: RNR converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides; DHFR converts folate/DHF to THF; Thymidylate synthase converts dUMP to dTMP/dTTP using 5,10-THF) -> Step 2 (Link each enzyme to its specific inhibitor: Hydroxyurea inhibits RNR, Methotrexate inhibits DHFR, and 5-FU irreversibly inhibits Thymidylate synthase).

r.A: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase rather than RNR, 5-FU inhibits thymidylate synthase, and hydroxyurea inhibits RNR.
r.C: Allopurinol and probenecid are gout medications that do not target dihydrofolate reductase or thymidylate synthase.
r.D: 5-Fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthase rather than RNR, hydroxyurea inhibits RNR, and methotrexate inhibits DHFR.
r.E: Allopurinol and rasburicase act on purine degradation (uric acid) rather than RNR or DHFR.

q.s: Slide 22 (Stage 3: Formation of UTP, CTP, dTTP and dCTP) and Slide 31 (Drug Summary: Chemotherapy Involve DNA Synthesis)

q.v: Which of the following correctly pairs the enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step of de novo purine biosynthesis with its allosteric activator?
o: PRPP synthase / ribose-5-phosphate
Glutamine PRPP amidotransferase / PRPP
Glutamine PRPP amidotransferase / IMP
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II / ATP
Aspartate transcarbamoylase / carbamoyl phosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Ribose-5-phosphate is converted to PRPP by PRPP synthase) -> Step 2 (Glutamine PRPP amidotransferase catalyzes the first committed step of purine synthesis and is allosterically activated by PRPP and inhibited by IMP, AMP, and GMP)

r.A: PRPP synthase generates PRPP from ribose-5-phosphate, which precedes the committed step of de novo purine biosynthesis.
r.C: IMP, along with AMP and GMP, is an allosteric inhibitor rather than an activator of glutamine PRPP amidotransferase.
r.D: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS-II) catalyzes the rate-limiting step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis, not purine synthesis.
r.E: Aspartate transcarbamoylase catalyzes the committed step of pyrimidine ring synthesis, not purine synthesis.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 7: Purine Nucleotide Biosynthesis

q.v: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric neurology clinic for evaluation of severe developmental delay, hypotonia, and recurrent self-inflicted bite wounds on his fingers and lips. His mother notes gritty, orange-colored deposits in his diapers and states that her brother died in childhood with similar neurological symptoms. Laboratory evaluation reveals marked hyperuricemia. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern and the change in intracellular phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) levels in this patient's disorder?
o: Autosomal recessive / PRPP decreased
Autosomal recessive / PRPP increased
X-linked recessive / PRPP decreased
X-linked recessive / PRPP increased
Autosomal dominant / PRPP increased
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Lesch-Nyhan syndrome from self-mutilation, neurological disorder, and hyperuricemia due to HGPRT deficiency) -> Step 2 (Recognize X-linked recessive inheritance and that blocked salvage of hypoxanthine and guanine leads to accumulation of PRPP, driving de novo purine synthesis)

r.A: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner, and failure to consume PRPP in the salvage pathway causes PRPP levels to increase.
r.B: While intracellular PRPP levels are increased due to the block in the purine salvage pathway, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern.
r.C: Although Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder, the block in HGPRT prevents PRPP consumption in purine salvage, resulting in increased PRPP levels.
r.E: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern rather than an autosomal dominant pattern.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slide 16: Lesch-Nyhan Syndrome

q.v:
A 4-year-old girl is followed in the metabolic clinic for a glycogen storage disease caused by a deficiency in the enzyme that converts glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose. On physical examination, she has prominent hepatomegaly and a swollen, tender left ankle. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum glucose: 42 mg/dL
  Serum lactate: elevated
  Serum triglycerides: elevated
  Serum uric acid: 9.8 mg/dL
Increased synthesis of which of the following intermediates directly links her underlying enzymatic defect to the development of hyperuricemia?
o: Carbamoyl phosphate
Orotic acid
Ribose-5-phosphate
Deoxyadenosine triphosphate
Dihydrofolate
q.p: Step 1 (Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase in Von Gierke disease causes intracellular accumulation of glucose-6-phosphate) -> Step 2 (Excess glucose-6-phosphate is shunted into the pentose phosphate pathway, generating ribose-5-phosphate and PRPP, which drives excess purine synthesis and degradation to uric acid)

r.A: Carbamoyl phosphate is an intermediate in pyrimidine synthesis and the urea cycle, which are not driven by glucose-6-phosphate accumulation.
r.B: Orotic acid is an intermediate in de novo pyrimidine synthesis that accumulates in UMP synthase or OTC1 deficiency.
r.D: Deoxyadenosine triphosphate (dATP) accumulates in adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency and inhibits ribonucleotide reductase.
r.E: Dihydrofolate is an intermediate in folate metabolism targeted by methotrexate, unrelated to the pentose phosphate shunt in Von Gierke disease.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slide 15: Von Gierke Disease and Gout

q.v:
A 64-year-old woman with recently diagnosed high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma is admitted to the oncology ward for induction chemotherapy. Forty-eight hours after her first infusion, she develops flank pain, lethargy, and decreased urine output. Laboratory studies obtained before and after chemotherapy initiation are shown below:
  Pre-treatment serum uric acid: 4.5 mg/dL
  Post-treatment serum uric acid: 14.2 mg/dL
  Post-treatment serum creatinine: 3.1 mg/dL
  Urinalysis: numerous uric acid crystals
To prevent further mechanical obstruction of her renal tubules, the team considers two pharmacologic interventions: Drug X, which inhibits the synthesis of uric acid, and Drug Y, a recombinant enzyme that converts existing uric acid into allantoin. Which of the following correctly identifies the molecular target of Drug X and the identity of Drug Y?
o: HGPRT / Probenecid
Xanthine oxidase / Rasburicase
Ribonucleotide reductase / Allopurinol
Thymidylate synthase / Febuxostat
Adenosine deaminase / Hydroxyurea
q.p: Step 1 (Tumor lysis syndrome causes massive purine degradation to uric acid via xanthine oxidase, which is inhibited by allopurinol or febuxostat [Drug X]) -> Step 2 (Rasburicase [Drug Y] is a recombinant urate oxidase that converts uric acid into the more water-soluble metabolite allantoin)

r.A: HGPRT is a purine salvage enzyme rather than a target for reducing uric acid synthesis, and probenecid alters renal urate excretion rather than converting uric acid to allantoin.
r.C: Ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited by hydroxyurea for chemotherapy, and allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase rather than acting as a recombinant urate oxidase.
r.D: Thymidylate synthase is inhibited by 5-FU in cancer therapy, and febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor rather than a recombinant enzyme.
r.E: Adenosine deaminase is an enzyme in purine degradation/salvage, and hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 10, 14, and 16: Purine Salvage Pathway and Tumor Lysis Syndrome

q.v: Which of the following correctly contrasts the de novo synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides with the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides?
o: Pyrimidine synthesis builds the base directly on PRPP, whereas purine synthesis forms the free base before attaching PRPP.
Pyrimidine synthesis forms the six-membered ring as orotate before attaching PRPP, whereas purine synthesis builds the base on PRPP.
Pyrimidine synthesis uses glycine as a core ring precursor, whereas purine synthesis uses aspartate as its sole amino acid precursor.
Pyrimidine synthesis is regulated at the committed step by IMP, whereas purine synthesis is regulated by UTP.
Pyrimidine synthesis occurs entirely within the mitochondria, whereas purine synthesis occurs in the nucleus.
q.p: Step 1 (In de novo pyrimidine synthesis, the six-membered ring is synthesized first as orotate and then attached to PRPP by UMP synthase) -> Step 2 (In de novo purine synthesis, PRPP provides the foundation on which the purine ring is constructed starting with glutamine PRPP amidotransferase)

r.A: This statement reverses the two pathways; purines are assembled directly on the PRPP sugar, whereas the pyrimidine ring is synthesized before attachment to PRPP.
r.C: Glycine is used in purine synthesis, whereas aspartate is used in both purine and pyrimidine synthesis.
r.D: IMP, AMP, and GMP inhibit glutamine PRPP amidotransferase in purine synthesis, while UTP inhibits CPS-II in pyrimidine synthesis.
r.E: De novo pyrimidine synthesis is primarily cytosolic with one mitochondrial enzyme (DHODH), and purine synthesis occurs in the cytosol.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 7, 19, and 20: Reactions in Pyrimidine Nucleotide Biosynthesis

q.v:
A 10-month-old girl is brought to the clinic for evaluation of pallor, poor weight gain, and developmental delay. Her parents also report that she cries during urination and occasionally passes small, gritty stones in her diaper. Laboratory studies show:
  Hemoglobin: 7.8 g/dL
  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV): 118 fL
  Serum vitamin B12: normal
  Serum folate: normal
  Urine orotic acid: markedly elevated
The physician initiates daily oral supplementation with a specific nucleoside that bypasses the patient's enzymatic block, reverses her anemia, and inhibits further overproduction of orotic acid. Which of the following treatments was most likely prescribed, and which enzyme is inhibited by its downstream phosphorylated product?
o: Adenosine / Glutamine PRPP amidotransferase
Uridine / Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS-II)
Thymidine / Thymidylate synthase
Cytidine / Aspartate transcarbamoylase
Guanosine / Xanthine oxidase
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize hereditary orotic aciduria due to UMP synthase deficiency presenting with megaloblastic anemia and orotic acid bladder stones) -> Step 2 (Oral uridine is converted to UMP and UTP, which replenishes pyrimidines and feedback-inhibits CPS-II to reduce orotic acid production)

r.A: Adenosine is a purine nucleoside, and glutamine PRPP amidotransferase regulates purine synthesis rather than pyrimidine synthesis.
r.C: Thymidine only supplies dTTP and cannot replenish UTP or CTP pools needed for RNA synthesis and feedback inhibition of CPS-II.
r.D: Oral uridine is the standard treatment for orotic aciduria, and the rate-limiting enzyme inhibited by UTP in humans is CPS-II.
r.E: Guanosine is a purine nucleoside, and xanthine oxidase is involved in purine degradation rather than pyrimidine synthesis.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 19 and 21: Stage 1 Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthesis and Orotic Aciduria

q.v: A 59-year-old woman with metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma is receiving systemic chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). Within her tumor cells, 5-FU is converted into an active deoxynucleotide analog that irreversibly inhibits a target enzyme required for DNA synthesis. Inhibition of this target enzyme directly blocks a reaction that requires which of the following cofactors?
o: NADPH
Biotin
5,10-methylene tetrahydrofolate
10-formyl tetrahydrofolate
Pyridoxal phosphate
q.p: Step 1 (5-FU is converted to FdUMP, which irreversibly inhibits thymidylate synthase) -> Step 2 (Thymidylate synthase catalyzes the methylation of dUMP to dTMP, a reaction that requires 5,10-methylene THF as the one-carbon donor)

r.A: NADPH serves as the reducing agent for thioredoxin reductase to regenerate ribonucleotide reductase and dihydrofolate reductase, not directly for thymidylate synthase catalysis.
r.B: Biotin is a cofactor for carboxylation reactions and is not involved in the conversion of dUMP to dTMP.
r.D: 10-formyl tetrahydrofolate donates carbon atoms during de novo purine ring synthesis, whereas 5,10-methylene THF is required by thymidylate synthase.
r.E: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) is not the methyl donor cofactor for thymidylate synthase.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 22, 23, and 24: Stage 3 Formation of UTP, CTP, dTTP and dCTP

q.v: A 4-month-old girl is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with Pneumocystis pneumonia, persistent mucocutaneous candidiasis, and chronic diarrhea. Newborn screening and follow-up genetic testing confirm severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. Intracellular nucleotide profiling of her lymphocytes reveals a massive accumulation of deoxyadenosine triphosphate (dATP). Binding of excess dATP to which of the following sites is directly responsible for shutting down DNA replication in her lymphocytes?
o: Catalytic (C) site of ribonucleotide reductase
Specificity (S) site of ribonucleotide reductase
Activity (A) site of ribonucleotide reductase
Allosteric site of glutamine PRPP amidotransferase
Active site of thymidylate synthase
q.p: Step 1 (ADA deficiency prevents deamination of adenosine/deoxyadenosine, leading to intracellular buildup of dATP) -> Step 2 (High dATP binds to the lower-affinity Activity [A] site of ribonucleotide reductase, inactivating the enzyme and depleting dNTPs required for lymphocyte DNA replication)

r.A: The C site is the catalytic site where ribonucleotide substrates are reduced, not the allosteric activity-determining site where dATP binds to turn the enzyme off.
r.B: Binding of dATP (or ATP) to the S (specificity) site occurs with medium affinity and directs the enzyme to reduce CDP and UDP rather than inactivating the enzyme.
r.D: Glutamine PRPP amidotransferase is regulated by PRPP, IMP, AMP, and GMP, and is not the target of dATP toxicity in ADA-SCID.
r.E: Thymidylate synthase converts dUMP to dTMP and is inhibited by 5-FU, not by elevated dATP levels.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slides 27, 28, 29, and 30: Ribonucleotide Reductase A Site and ADA Deficiency

q.v:
A molecular biologist is investigating how ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) maintains a balanced pool of deoxyribonucleotides during S phase to minimize DNA replication errors. She measures the substrate preference of purified RNR holoenzyme when ATP is bound to the activity (A) site and different allosteric effectors are added to the specificity (S) site, as shown in the table below:
  Condition 1: dTTP bound at S site -> Primary product X (high affinity)
  Condition 2: dGTP bound at S site -> Primary product Y (high affinity)
Which of the following correctly identifies Primary product X and Primary product Y?
o: Product X: dATP / Product Y: dGTP
Product X: dGTP / Product Y: dATP
Product X: dCDP / Product Y: dUDP
Product X: dUDP / Product Y: dCDP
Product X: dTTP / Product Y: dCTP
q.p: Step 1 (When dTTP binds with high affinity to the S site of RNR, it promotes the synthesis of dGTP [Product X]) -> Step 2 (When dGTP accumulates and binds with high affinity to the S site of RNR, it promotes the synthesis of dATP [Product Y])

r.A: This option reverses the allosteric specificity rules; dTTP binding stimulates dGTP production, whereas dGTP binding stimulates dATP production.
r.C: Production of pyrimidine intermediates (CDP/UDP reduction) is stimulated when ATP or dATP binds to the S site with medium affinity.
r.D: Reduction of UDP and CDP is promoted by ATP or dATP binding to the S site, not by dTTP or dGTP binding.
r.E: RNR reduces ribonucleoside diphosphates rather than producing dTTP directly, and dTTP binding favors dGTP synthesis.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slide 28: Ribonucleotide Reductase S Site

q.v: A 28-year-old man newly diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is started on a multi-agent chemotherapy regimen that includes methotrexate and hydroxyurea. Both medications impair DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing leukemic blasts by depleting intracellular precursors. Which of the following correctly pairs the direct enzymatic target of methotrexate with the direct enzymatic target of hydroxyurea?
o: Thymidylate synthase / Dihydrofolate reductase
Dihydrofolate reductase / Ribonucleotide reductase
Ribonucleotide reductase / Thymidylate synthase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II / Xanthine oxidase
Glutamine PRPP amidotransferase / UMP synthase
q.p: Step 1 (Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase [DHFR], blocking the conversion of folate to DHF and DHF to THF) -> Step 2 (Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase [RNR], blocking the conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides)

r.A: Thymidylate synthase is the direct target of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), whereas dihydrofolate reductase is the target of methotrexate.
r.C: This option lists the target of hydroxyurea (ribonucleotide reductase) first and pairs it with the target of 5-FU (thymidylate synthase).
r.D: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II and xanthine oxidase are enzymes of pyrimidine synthesis and purine degradation, respectively, and are not targeted by methotrexate or hydroxyurea.
r.E: Neither glutamine PRPP amidotransferase nor UMP synthase is the direct target of methotrexate or hydroxyurea.

q.s: SLO 4 and SLO 5 / Slide 31: Drug Summary: Chemotherapy Involve DNA Synthesis

q.v: A researcher is characterizing a novel peptide hormone that regulates cellular metabolism. In vitro assays demonstrate that when the hormone binds to the extracellular domain of its cell-surface receptor, a stimulatory G protein (Gs) is activated, leading to the conversion of ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP) by adenylyl cyclase. The newly formed cAMP subsequently binds to the regulatory subunits of a cAMP-dependent kinase, releasing active catalytic subunits that phosphorylate specific protein substrates to elicit a cellular response. If an experimental compound is added to this system that specifically inhibits the enzyme responsible for removing phosphate groups from these phosphorylated protein substrates, which of the following enzymes is being directly targeted?
o: Adenylyl cyclase
Phosphodiesterase
Phosphatase
Receptor tyrosine kinase
cAMP-dependent protein kinase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the cAMP second messenger pathway components and the specific step of dephosphorylating substrate proteins: S~P -> S + Pi) -> Step 2 (Identify the enzyme mediating this specific regulatory step as phosphatase [P'ase]).

r.A: Adenylyl cyclase (AC) is the effector enzyme activated by Gs that catalyzes the conversion of ATP into cAMP, rather than modifying phosphorylated protein substrates.
r.B: Phosphodiesterases (PDE) terminate the second messenger signal by hydrolyzing cAMP into 5'-AMP, not by removing phosphate groups from downstream proteins.
r.D: Receptor tyrosine kinases phosphorylate tyrosine residues on target proteins and are part of a separate transmembrane signaling mechanism distinct from the Gs-cAMP pathway.
r.E: cAMP-dependent protein kinases use ATP to transfer phosphate groups onto protein substrates (S to S~P), which is the opposite action of the inhibited enzyme.

q.s: Slide 32: Example: cAMP Second Messenger Pathway

q.v: A pharmaceutical scientist is evaluating two distinct growth factors, Factor X and Factor Y, in an isolated cell culture system. Both factors are water-soluble ligands that bind to the extracellular domains of their respective transmembrane receptors and ultimately result in the phosphorylation of downstream cytoplasmic tyrosine residues (Y to Y-P). However, structural analysis reveals that Factor X binds to a transmembrane protein whose own cytoplasmic domain possesses intrinsic enzymatic activity, whereas Factor Y binds to a transmembrane receptor that lacks intrinsic enzymatic activity and instead relies on a separate, non-covalently bound cytoplasmic enzyme to phosphorylate the substrate. Which of the following best describes the signaling mechanism utilized by Factor Y?
o: Diffusion across the plasma membrane to bind an intracellular receptor
Activation of a receptor bound to a separate protein tyrosine kinase
Direct regulation of the opening of a transmembrane ion channel
Activation of a G protein that stimulates an intracellular effector enzyme
Stimulation of an intrinsic receptor cytoplasmic enzymatic domain
q.p: Step 1 (Differentiate between Transmembrane Signaling Mechanism 2 and Mechanism 3 based on whether the enzymatic activity is intrinsic to the receptor or on a separate bound protein) -> Step 2 (Identify Mechanism 3 as a transmembrane receptor bound to a separate protein tyrosine kinase).

r.A: Crossing the plasma membrane to act on an intracellular receptor (Mechanism 1) requires a lipid-soluble chemical signal, whereas Factor Y is water-soluble and binds an extracellular domain.
r.C: Direct regulation of an ion channel opening (Mechanism 4) involves ion flux across the membrane rather than direct tyrosine phosphorylation.
r.D: G-protein signaling (Mechanism 5) utilizes a G protein to link the receptor to an effector enzyme or ion channel to convert substrates to products, rather than directly activating a bound protein tyrosine kinase.
r.E: Stimulation of an intrinsic cytoplasmic enzymatic domain describes Mechanism 2 (used by Factor X), whereas Factor Y's receptor lacks intrinsic enzymatic activity.

q.s: Slides 30-31: 5 Basic Mechanisms of Transmembrane Signaling

q.v: During a preclinical pharmacology study, a student performs a radioligand binding assay using an idealized in vitro receptor preparation to determine the binding characteristics of a newly synthesized compound, Drug M. The student plots the ratio of receptor-bound drug to free drug (Bound / Free) on the y-axis against the concentration of receptor-bound drug (Drug Bound) on the x-axis, generating a linear Scatchard plot. The resulting line intersects the y-axis at 0.12 and intersects the x-axis at 8.0, with a calculated slope of -0.015. If the student wants to determine the total concentration of receptor sites (Bmax) and the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) from this plot, which of the following correctly pairs the graphical features with these two pharmacodynamic parameters?
o: The x-intercept represents Bmax, and the slope represents -1/Kd
The y-intercept represents 1/Bmax, and the x-intercept represents -1/Kd
The x-intercept represents Kd, and the y-intercept represents Bmax
The slope represents Kd/Bmax, and the y-intercept represents 1/Bmax
The y-intercept represents Bmax, and the slope represents -Kd
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the graph described as a Scatchard plot based on the axes: Bound/Free vs. Drug Bound) -> Step 2 (Apply the mathematical relationships of a Scatchard plot where the x-intercept equals Bmax and the slope equals -1/Kd).

r.B: A y-intercept of 1/Emax (or 1/Bmax) and an x-intercept of -1/Kd are the graphical properties of a double reciprocal plot (1/Effect vs. 1/[Drug]), not a Scatchard plot.
r.C: On a Scatchard plot, the x-intercept represents Bmax rather than Kd, and the y-intercept is Bound/Free at infinitely low bound drug, not Bmax.
r.D: A slope of Kd/Emax (or Km/Vmax) and a y-intercept of 1/Emax (or 1/Vmax) describe the Lineweaver-Burk double reciprocal plot, not a Scatchard transformation.
r.E: The y-intercept on a Scatchard plot represents the ratio of Bound/Free as bound drug approaches zero, whereas Bmax is found at the x-intercept and the slope is the negative reciprocal of Kd (-1/Kd).

q.s: Slide 38: More Fun Transformations (Reciprocal plot & Scatchard plot)

q.v: A researcher is studying the pharmacodynamics of an experimental agonist, Drug A, in an isolated tissue bath containing a fixed population of target receptors. When Drug A is tested alone, it achieves a maximal biological response (Emax) of 100 units with an EC50 of 2 nM. The researcher then washes out the tissue bath and pre-treats the preparation with a low concentration of an irreversible orthosteric antagonist, Drug B, which permanently inactivates a fraction of the receptors. When the concentration-effect curve for Drug A is repeated, the curve is shifted to the right with a new EC50 of 10 nM, but the maximal biological response remains completely unchanged at 100 units. However, when the tissue is pre-treated with a 10-fold higher concentration of Drug B, the maximal response to Drug A drops to 40 units. Which of the following best explains why the low concentration of Drug B failed to decrease the Emax of Drug A?
o: Drug B acts as a positive allosteric modulator at low concentrations before becoming an antagonist at high concentrations
The tissue preparation contains spare receptors in excess of the number required to produce a maximal biologic response
Drug A was able to competitively displace Drug B from the orthosteric binding sites when given at high concentrations
The equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) of Drug A is significantly higher than its EC50 in this tissue system
Drug B binds exclusively to the agonist-receptor complex rather than the free receptor at low concentrations
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that an irreversible antagonist shifted the agonist curve right without reducing Emax at low antagonist concentrations, but reduced Emax at higher concentrations) -> Step 2 (Conclude that spare receptors exist, meaning maximal biologic response occurs when the agonist occupies only a fraction of total receptors, leaving excess receptors available even after partial irreversible blockade).

r.A: Drug B is defined as an irreversible orthosteric antagonist, which inactivates agonist binding sites rather than allosterically enhancing receptor function.
r.C: Once an irreversible orthosteric antagonist binds to a receptor, competition stops and the agonist cannot replace or displace it regardless of how much agonist is added.
r.D: In a system with spare receptors, the EC50 (concentration needed for 50% maximal effect) is actually much less than the Kd (concentration needed to saturate 50% of receptor binding sites), not higher.
r.E: Binding exclusively to the receptor-ligand (or enzyme-substrate) complex defines an uncompetitive inhibitor, which decreases both Vmax (Emax) and Km (Kd) rather than preserving Emax via receptor reserve.

q.s: Slides 50-51: Detour: Need to Discuss Spare Receptors

q.v: A 68-year-old man is undergoing cardiovascular surgery and receives a high dose of intravenous heparin to prevent thrombosis during the procedure. Following the completion of the bypass, the anesthesiologist administers intravenous protamine to rapidly reverse the anticoagulant effects of heparin. Rather than binding to a cellular receptor to trigger an opposing physiological pathway, protamine carries a strong positive charge that causes it to bind directly to the negatively charged heparin molecules in the bloodstream, forming an inactive complex that cannot interact with coagulation factors. Which of the following mechanisms of antagonism is best illustrated by the interaction between protamine and heparin?
o: Pharmacokinetic antagonism
Physiologic antagonism
Allosteric antagonism
Chemical antagonism
Irreversible competitive antagonism
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that protamine neutralizes heparin by directly binding to the drug itself to form an inactive complex, reducing the concentration of active agonist without involving a receptor) -> Step 2 (Classify this specific non-receptor mechanism as chemical antagonism).

r.A: Pharmacokinetic antagonism occurs when one drug decreases the absorption or accelerates the metabolic elimination/excretion of another agent, rather than forming a direct molecular complex.
r.B: Physiologic antagonism occurs when two drugs produce opposite actions mediated through different cellular receptors and distinct physiologic pathways (e.g., one raising and one lowering blood pressure via separate receptors).
r.C: Allosteric antagonism involves an antagonist binding to a separate site on a target receptor to modify the receptor's conformation and decrease agonist binding or activation.
r.E: Irreversible competitive antagonism involves an antagonist binding permanently to the agonist's active binding site on a cellular receptor, whereas protamine binds directly to the heparin molecule itself.

q.s: Slide 70: Other Mechanisms of Antagonism

q.v: In a neuropharmacology laboratory, investigators are studying a cloned central nervous system receptor that exists in a dynamic equilibrium between an inactive, nonfunctional conformation (Ri) and an activated conformation (Ra). Even in the complete absence of any endogenous neurotransmitter or exogenous ligand, a small fraction of the receptor population naturally exists in the Ra isoform, producing a measurable baseline downstream signal known as constitutive activity. Four different ligands (Compounds 1, 2, 3, and 4) are tested independently in this system. Compound 1 has a much higher affinity for Ra than Ri. Compound 2 has an intermediate affinity for both Ra and Ri, favoring Ra slightly. Compound 3 has an equal affinity for both Ri and Ra. Compound 4 has a much higher affinity for Ri than Ra. If the investigators wish to maintain the exact baseline level of constitutive activity while blocking the effects of Compound 1, which compound should they select, and what is its classification?
o: Compound 2; Partial agonist
Compound 3; Conventional antagonist
Compound 4; Inverse agonist
Compound 3; Inverse agonist
Compound 4; Noncompetitive antagonist
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the two-state receptor model [Ri and Ra] where constitutive activity is produced by baseline Ra, and identify that preserving baseline constitutive activity requires keeping the Ri:Ra ratio unchanged) -> Step 2 (Select Compound 3, which has equal affinity for both Ri and Ra, and classify it as a conventional antagonist).

r.A: Compound 2 is a partial agonist with intermediate affinity for both forms that shifts the equilibrium toward Ra-Dpa complexes, which would increase receptor activity above the baseline constitutive level.
r.C: Compound 4 is an inverse agonist because its high affinity for Ri stabilizes the Ri-Di complex, shifting the equilibrium away from Ra and decreasing constitutive activity below baseline.
r.D: Although Compound 3 is the correct ligand, it acts as a conventional antagonist rather than an inverse agonist because it maintains the natural ratio of Ri and Ra instead of reducing constitutive activity.
r.E: Compound 4 acts as an inverse agonist that reduces constitutive activity by stabilizing Ri, rather than mantener baseline constitutive activity.

q.s: Slides 72-74: Receptor Model Continued & A model of drug-receptor interaction

q.v: A clinical pharmacologist is evaluating four different antihypertensive medications (Drugs A, B, C, and D) that all act as agonists at the same vascular smooth muscle receptor to lower systolic blood pressure. Graded dose-response curves are plotted on a semilog scale with log drug dose on the x-axis and blood pressure reduction (response) on the y-axis. Drug B achieves a maximal blood pressure reduction of 20 mmHg and has an ED50 of 0.5 mg. Drug A achieves a maximal reduction of 40 mmHg with an ED50 of 2 mg. Drug C achieves a maximal reduction of 40 mmHg with an ED50 of 15 mg. Drug D achieves a maximal reduction of 40 mmHg with an ED50 of 50 mg, and its curve rises from 0% to 100% response over a very narrow dose range (extremely steep slope) compared to the other three drugs. Based on this data, which of the following statements correctly identifies the most potent drug and the drug that would be the most difficult to safely titrate in a patient?
o: Most potent: Drug A; Most difficult to titrate: Drug B
Most potent: Drug B; Most difficult to titrate: Drug D
Most potent: Drug D; Most difficult to titrate: Drug D
Most potent: Drug B; Most difficult to titrate: Drug A
Most potent: Drug A; Most difficult to titrate: Drug C
q.p: Step 1 (Evaluate the four graded dose-response curves: Drug B is furthest to the left with the lowest ED50 despite a lower Emax, while Drug D has the steepest slope) -> Step 2 (Conclude that Drug B is the most potent because potency is determined solely by the lowest ED50/EC50, and Drug D is the most difficult to titrate because a steep slope means small dose adjustments cause dramatic changes in clinical response).

r.A: Drug A has high efficacy (40 mmHg reduction), but it is less potent than Drug B because its ED50 (2 mg) is higher than Drug B's ED50 (0.5 mg); furthermore, Drug B's shallow curve is easier to titrate than Drug D.
r.C: Drug D has the highest ED50 (50 mg), making it the least potent of the four drugs, even though its steep slope correctly makes it the most difficult to titrate.
r.D: While Drug B is correctly identified as the most potent, Drug A has a standard sigmoidal slope and is easier to titrate than Drug D, which exhibits a very steep dose-response curve.
r.E: Drug A is less potent than Drug B, and Drug C has a gradual slope similar to Drug A, making it much easier to titrate than Drug D.

q.s: Slides 76-78, 85, and 96: Potency and Efficacy & Practice Problems

q.v: A Phase II clinical trial is conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel antiarrhythmic agent in a population of 500 patients. The investigators construct quantal dose-effect plots by graphing the cumulative percentage of patients exhibiting the desired antiarrhythmic effect and the cumulative percentage of patients experiencing dose-limiting central nervous system toxicity against the log dose of the drug. Data analysis reveals that 50% of the patient population achieves the desired antiarrhythmic response at a dose of 4 mg, and 99% achieve the desired response at 10 mg. Conversely, 1% of the population experiences significant toxicity at 40 mg, and 50% of the population experiences toxicity at 120 mg. Based on these population-level findings, what is the Therapeutic Index (TI) of this medication, and what is its approximate Therapeutic Window?
o: Therapeutic Index: 30; Therapeutic Window: 4 mg to 40 mg
Therapeutic Index: 4; Therapeutic Window: 10 mg to 40 mg
Therapeutic Index: 30; Therapeutic Window: 10 mg to 120 mg
Therapeutic Index: 0.033; Therapeutic Window: 4 mg to 40 mg
Therapeutic Index: 12; Therapeutic Window: 4 mg to 120 mg
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the population-level parameters from the vignette: ED50 = 4 mg, TD50 = 120 mg, onset of effective response around ED50 [4 mg], and onset of significant toxicity at 40 mg) -> Step 2 (Calculate the Therapeutic Index as TD50 / ED50 = 120 / 4 = 30, and identify the Therapeutic Window as the range of doses producing a therapeutic effect without significant toxic effects, approximately 4 mg to 40 mg).

r.B: A value of 4 incorrectly calculates the ratio of the minimal toxic dose (40 mg) to the maximal effective dose (10 mg), rather than TD50 / ED50.
r.C: While the Therapeutic Index is correctly calculated as 30, extending the therapeutic window up to 120 mg (the TD50) is incorrect because half of the patients would experience significant toxicity at that dose.
r.D: A value of 0.033 incorrectly inverts the Therapeutic Index formula by dividing ED50 by TD50 (4 / 120) instead of dividing TD50 by ED50.
r.E: A Therapeutic Index of 12 incorrectly divides the TD50 (120 mg) by the 99% effective dose (10 mg), and a window up to 120 mg includes doses that cause toxicity in 50% of patients.

q.s: Slides 83-85 and 99: Quantal Dose-Effect Plot, Relating Toxic and Therapeutic Effects, & Practice Problems

q.v: A 52-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic with a resting heart rate of 95 beats/min. The physician initiates therapy with Drug D, an agonist that binds to a specific cardiac receptor (R) that normally interacts with an endogenous ligand (L) to slow the heart rate. Upon starting Drug D, the patient's heart rate successfully decreases to 85 beats/min. However, after several weeks of continuous daily administration, the patient's resting heart rate gradually rises back to 90 beats/min despite strict medication adherence. Frustrated by the diminished effect, the patient abruptly stops taking Drug D, and presents to the emergency department the next day with palpitations and a resting heart rate of 110 beats/min. Which of the following cellular mechanisms best explains why his heart rate rose to 110 beats/min (higher than his pre-treatment baseline of 95 beats/min) upon drug withdrawal?
o: Chronic agonist exposure caused receptor up-regulation, leading to excessive stimulation by endogenous ligand L
Chronic agonist exposure caused receptor down-regulation, leaving fewer receptors available for endogenous ligand L to hit
Drug D induced sensitization of the receptor, increasing the coupling efficiency of endogenous ligand L upon drug removal
Abrupt withdrawal of Drug D unmasked an idiosyncratic hyperreactive response to endogenous catecholamines
Drug D acted as a chemical antagonist that permanently complexed with and depleted endogenous ligand L
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that Drug D is a chronic agonist that lowers heart rate alongside natural ligand L, and that chronic agonist exposure leads to tolerance [HR rising from 85 to 90] via receptor down-regulation) -> Step 2 (Deduce that abrupt withdrawal of Drug D leaves the endogenous ligand L with fewer receptors to hit than before treatment started, resulting in a rebound tachycardia of 110 beats/min).

r.A: Receptor up-regulation (increasing the number of receptors) occurs in response to chronic exposure to antagonists, not agonists; furthermore, more receptors for L would lower the heart rate rather than raise it.
r.C: Sensitization (increased coupling efficiency) is a cellular adaptation to chronic antagonist exposure, whereas chronic agonist exposure causes desensitization (decreased coupling efficiency).
r.D: Idiosyncratic responses are infrequently observed reactions that often make no pharmacologic sense, whereas rebound tachycardia is a predictable consequence of receptor down-regulation.
r.E: Drug D is an agonist at receptor R rather than a chemical antagonist, and the rebound effect is caused by a decrease in receptor number (R R R R instead of R R R R R) rather than depletion of ligand L.

q.s: Slides 89-90: Mechanisms of Variation in Response & Simplified Example of Down Regulation and 'Rebound'

q.v: A 34-year-old woman is prescribed an oral antihistamine for seasonal allergic rhinitis. Two hours after taking her first standard dose, she experiences profound drowsiness and dry mouth. At her follow-up visit, she asks her physician why a medication designed to target histamine receptors in her nasal passages would cause these unwanted symptoms in other parts of her body. Based on the principles of pharmacodynamics, which of the following is the primary reason why medications commonly produce such adverse effects at therapeutic doses?
o: Most drugs are specific rather than selective, meaning they bind exclusively to a single receptor subtype that mutates across tissues
Unwanted effects are typically idiosyncratic reactions caused by genetic defects in downstream second messenger pathways
Drugs are selective rather than specific, and their target receptors are distributed across multiple organ systems rather than just one tissue
Therapeutic doses of agonists rapidly induce tachyphylaxis in non-target tissues, leading to paradoxical side effects
Most adverse effects are caused by pharmacokinetic antagonism between the active drug and endogenous hormones
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the pharmacodynamic principles governing drug-receptor interactions and adverse effects) -> Step 2 (Conclude that no drug has just one effect because drugs are only selective [not truly specific to a single receptor type] and the target receptors themselves are present in multiple organ systems and tissues, making unwanted effects an extension of the drug's normal pharmacologic action).

r.A: Drugs are described as selective rather than specific because they do not bind to just one single receptor type, and receptors do not mutate across tissues to cause standard side effects.
r.B: Idiosyncratic reactions are rare, unpredictable responses, whereas common adverse effects like drowsiness and dry mouth are direct, predictable pharmacologic actions of the drug.
r.D: Tachyphylaxis is a rapid desensitization (decreased effect) occurring with subsequent doses of a drug, which does not explain the immediate onset of off-target pharmacologic effects after a first dose.
r.E: Pharmacokinetic antagonism involves one drug altering the absorption or elimination of another agent, which is unrelated to a single drug binding receptors in multiple tissues.

q.s: Slide 91: Adverse Effects

q.v: A 28-year-old woman presents to the sleep clinic with severe daytime somnolence. She participates in a clinical trial for a novel wakefulness-promoting agent, Drug W. In vitro studies show that the target central nervous system receptor normally exhibits constitutive activity that promotes baseline sedation even in the absence of endogenous ligand. When Drug W binds to this receptor, it stabilizes the receptor in its inactive conformation (Ri) and produces wakefulness. Which of the following best classifies Drug W?
o: Competitive antagonist
Full agonist
Inverse agonist
Negative allosteric modulator
Partial agonist
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize a ligand that binds a receptor with constitutive activity and produces the opposite effect of an agonist by stabilizing the inactive Ri conformation) -> Step 2 (Classify the drug as an inverse agonist)

r.A: A competitive antagonist binds to both Ri and Ra in the same ratio as they occur naturally and maintains baseline constitutive activity without reducing it.
r.B: A full agonist has high affinity for the activated conformation (Ra) and increases receptor activity above baseline, which would cause further sedation.
r.D: A negative allosteric modulator binds to a separate site to decrease the affinity or efficacy of an agonist, rather than stabilizing the Ri isoform to reduce constitutive activity.
r.E: A partial agonist has intermediate affinity for both Ri and Ra and produces a submaximal agonist response (sedation) rather than the opposite physiological effect.

q.s: Objective 1 / Slides 71-74: Inverse Agonists and Receptor Model

q.v: A 62-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with severe postoperative pain and is placed on a high-dose intravenous infusion of a full mu-opioid receptor agonist, achieving maximal analgesia. A resident physician inadvertently orders an intravenous dose of Drug P, which is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor. Shortly after Drug P is administered, the patient reports a marked return of his severe pain. Which of the following best explains the decreased analgesia observed in this patient?
o: Acceleration of full agonist elimination
Competition with the full agonist for receptor occupancy
Formation of an inactive chemical complex in the plasma
Irreversible covalent modification of the receptor
Stabilization of the receptor exclusively in the inactive conformation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify co-administration of a partial agonist in the presence of a full agonist) -> Step 2 (Recognize that the partial agonist competes for receptor binding sites and lowers net response toward the partial agonist's lower Emax)

r.A: Accelerating the elimination of another drug is the mechanism of a pharmacokinetic antagonist, not a receptor partial agonist.
r.C: Forming a chemical complex to reduce drug concentration (such as protamine binding heparin) describes a chemical antagonist.
r.D: Irreversible covalent binding to the active site describes a classic noncompetitive (irreversible) antagonist rather than a partial agonist.
r.E: Stabilizing the receptor exclusively in the inactive conformation (Ri) to reduce constitutive activity is the mechanism of an inverse agonist.

q.s: Objective 6 / Slides 19, 68-69, 100: Partial Agonists

q.v: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after an intentional overdose of a toxin that acts as a classic (orthosteric) noncompetitive antagonist at vascular alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, resulting in severe hypotension. An intravenous infusion of an alpha-1 receptor full agonist is initiated and titrated to very high concentrations, yet the patient's blood pressure fails to reach the normal maximal response. Which of the following best describes the effect of this toxin on the agonist concentration-effect curve?
o: Decreased Emax and unchanged EC50
Decreased Emax and decreased EC50
Increased Emax and increased EC50
Unchanged Emax and decreased EC50
Unchanged Emax and increased EC50
q.p: Step 1 (Identify a classic orthosteric noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist) -> Step 2 (Determine its effect on the agonist concentration-effect curve: decreased Emax without changing EC50)

r.B: Decreased Emax and decreased EC50 (or Km) is characteristic of an uncompetitive enzyme inhibitor, whereas a noncompetitive antagonist does not decrease EC50.
r.C: An antagonist attenuates the effect of an agonist and never increases the maximal response (Emax).
r.D: Unchanged Emax and decreased EC50 (a leftward shift) represents positive allosteric modulation (potentiation), not antagonism.
r.E: Unchanged Emax and increased EC50 (a rightward shift) is the effect of a reversible competitive antagonist, which can be overcome by high agonist concentrations.

q.s: Objective 3 / Slides 47-49, 54: Non-competitive Antagonists

q.v: A 55-year-old woman with hypertension and a history of asthma is prescribed a beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist to control her blood pressure. After taking the medication consistently for six months, she runs out of her prescription while traveling and abruptly stops taking the drug. Two days later, she presents to the urgent care clinic with severe palpitations and a resting heart rate of 125 beats/min. Which of the following cellular changes most likely occurred during her six months of therapy to explain her current presentation?
o: Decreased coupling efficiency of the receptors
Decreased synthesis of endogenous norepinephrine
Down-regulation of beta-adrenergic receptors
Increased number of beta-adrenergic receptors
Rapid tachyphylaxis of downstream signaling pathways
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize abrupt withdrawal following chronic exposure to a receptor antagonist) -> Step 2 (Identify receptor up-regulation—increasing the number of receptors—as the adaptation to chronic antagonist exposure)

r.A: Decreased coupling efficiency (desensitization) occurs in response to chronic exposure to agonists, not antagonists.
r.B: Rebound tachycardia after antagonist withdrawal is driven by normal endogenous ligands acting on an increased number of receptors, not decreased ligand synthesis.
r.C: Down-regulation (decreasing the number of receptors) occurs in response to chronic exposure to agonists and explains tolerance.
r.E: Tachyphylaxis is a rapid desensitization that occurs with subsequent doses of an agonist, rather than a response to chronic antagonist therapy.

q.s: Objective 1 / Slide 89: Mechanisms of Variation in Response

q.v: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with acute status epilepticus. He is treated with an intravenous medication that binds to GABA-A receptors in the central nervous system and directly regulates the opening of a transmembrane chloride channel to rapidly hyperpolarize neurons. Which of the following transmembrane signaling mechanisms is utilized by this patient's medication?
o: Activation of a separate cytoplasmic protein tyrosine kinase
Activation of an intrinsic cytoplasmic enzymatic domain
Crossing the plasma membrane to bind an intracellular receptor
Direct regulation of an ion channel
Stimulation of a G-protein coupled effector enzyme
q.p: Step 1 (Identify a ligand that binds a transmembrane receptor and directly gates chloride ion flow) -> Step 2 (Match to Mechanism 4 of the 5 basic mechanisms of transmembrane signaling: direct regulation of an ion channel)

r.A: Binding an extracellular domain bound to a separate protein tyrosine kinase (Mechanism 3) is typical of cytokine signaling, not ion channels.
r.B: Binding an extracellular domain to activate an intrinsic cytoplasmic enzymatic domain (Mechanism 2) describes receptor tyrosine kinases like the insulin receptor.
r.C: Crossing the plasma membrane to act on an intracellular receptor (Mechanism 1) is the mechanism of lipid-soluble signals such as steroid hormones.
r.E: Binding a cell-surface receptor linked to an effector enzyme by a G protein (Mechanism 5) involves second messengers like cAMP rather than direct channel gating.

q.s: Objective 4 / Slides 30-31: 5 Basic Mechanisms of Transmembrane Signaling

q.v: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with severe respiratory depression after an overdose of fentanyl, a full agonist at the mu-opioid receptor. The physician administers intravenous naloxone, which binds reversibly to the exact same site on the mu-opioid receptor as fentanyl without activating it. Following naloxone administration, the patient's respiratory rate normalizes. If fentanyl were subsequently re-administered in progressively higher doses, how would the presence of naloxone affect the concentration-effect relationship of fentanyl?
o: It decreases the potency of fentanyl without changing its maximal efficacy
It decreases the maximal efficacy of fentanyl without changing its potency
It increases the affinity of fentanyl for the mu-opioid receptor
It irreversibly prevents fentanyl from binding to the mu-opioid receptor
It shifts the fentanyl concentration-effect curve to the left
q.p: Step 1 (Identify naloxone as a reversible competitive antagonist binding the orthosteric site) -> Step 2 (Determine its effect on the agonist: shifts EC50 to the right, which decreases agonist potency without changing maximal efficacy)

r.B: Decreasing maximal efficacy without changing potency (EC50) is the hallmark of a noncompetitive antagonist.
r.C: A competitive antagonist competes with the agonist for the binding site, increasing the apparent EC50 rather than increasing agonist affinity.
r.D: Naloxone binds reversibly to the agonist site, so its effects can be overcome by increasing the concentration of the agonist.
r.E: A competitive antagonist shifts the agonist concentration-effect curve to the right, whereas a leftward shift indicates increased potency or potentiation.

q.s: Objective 3 / Slides 44-45, 49: Competitive Antagonists

q.v: In an isolated tissue preparation, a pharmacology researcher observes that an agonist achieves 50% of its maximal biological effect (EC50) at a concentration of 2 nM, whereas radioligand binding assays show that a concentration of 100 nM is required to occupy 50% of the receptor binding sites (Kd). Which of the following best explains why the EC50 of this drug is substantially lower than its Kd?
o: Allosteric antagonism
Constitutive receptor activity
High equilibrium dissociation constant
Positive cooperativity of binding
Presence of spare receptors
q.p: Step 1 (Compare EC50 = 2 nM to Kd = 100 nM, noting EC50 is much less than Kd) -> Step 2 (Attribute this difference to the presence of spare receptors, where maximal biological response occurs without occupying all receptors)

r.A: Allosteric antagonism decreases the maximal effect of an agonist and does not allow half-maximal response at low receptor occupancy.
r.B: Constitutive activity refers to baseline receptor signaling in the absence of any ligand, not the difference between EC50 and Kd.
r.C: A high equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) simply means low receptor affinity, which by itself does not explain why EC50 is much lower than Kd.
r.D: Quantitative receptor binding models assume independent, non-cooperative binding sites rather than positive cooperativity.

q.s: Objective 2 / Slides 50-53: Spare Receptors

q.v: On a double-reciprocal plot of drug effect (1/E on the y-axis versus 1/[Drug] on the x-axis), which of the following parameters is represented by the y-intercept?
o: -1 / Kd
1 / Bmax
1 / Emax
Kd / Emax
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the double-reciprocal equation: 1/E = (Kd / Emax)(1/[D]) + 1/Emax) -> Step 2 (Identify the y-intercept as 1 / Emax, analogous to 1 / Vmax on a Lineweaver-Burk plot)

r.A: The value -1 / Kd represents the x-intercept on a double-reciprocal plot and the slope on a Scatchard plot.
r.B: Bmax is the total concentration of receptor sites, which is found at the x-intercept of a Scatchard plot (Bound/Free vs. Bound).
r.C: The reciprocal of EC50 (or Kd) is related to the x-intercept (-1/Kd), not the y-intercept.
r.E: The ratio Kd / Emax represents the slope of the line on a double-reciprocal plot, analogous to Km / Vmax on a Lineweaver-Burk plot.

q.s: Objective 2 / Slides 38, 40-41: More Fun Transformations and Analogies Between Receptors and Enzymes

q.v:
A pharmacology laboratory evaluates three experimental bronchodilators (Drug X, Drug Y, and Drug Z) that all act as agonists at the beta-2 adrenergic receptor. In vitro binding and graded concentration-effect studies yield the following data:
  Drug X: Kd = 10 nM, EC50 = 10 nM, Emax = 100%
  Drug Y: Kd = 1 nM, EC50 = 1 nM, Emax = 60%
  Drug Z: Kd = 100 nM, EC50 = 100 nM, Emax = 100%
Based on these data, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Drug X has a higher receptor affinity than Drug Y
Drug Y is a partial agonist with higher potency than Drug X
Drug Y has a higher maximal efficacy than Drug Z
Drug Z is a competitive antagonist of Drug X
Drug Z is more potent than Drug X
q.p: Step 1 (Compare Kd, EC50, and Emax across the three drugs: Drug Y has the lowest EC50 of 1 nM and a submaximal Emax of 60%) -> Step 2 (Conclude that Drug Y has the highest potency due to the lowest EC50, and is a partial agonist due to having a lower Emax than the full agonists)

r.A: Receptor affinity is inversely related to Kd; because Drug Y has a lower Kd (1 nM) than Drug X (10 nM), Drug Y has higher affinity.
r.C: Maximal efficacy is defined by Emax; Drug Y has a lower maximal efficacy (60%) than Drug Z (100%).
r.D: Drug Z achieves a 100% Emax when tested alone, which defines it as a full agonist rather than a competitive antagonist.
r.E: Potency is inversely related to EC50; because Drug Z has a higher EC50 (100 nM) than Drug X (10 nM), Drug Z is less potent.

q.s: Objectives 1, 2, 6 / Slides 35-36, 68, 76-78: Potency, Efficacy, Affinity, and Partial Agonists

q.v:
A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is being evaluated for oral anticoagulation therapy. Clinical population studies comparing two candidate anticoagulants, Drug M and Drug N, reveal the following quantal dose-effect parameters:
  Drug M: ED50 = 4 mg, TD50 = 12 mg, Minimum effective dose = 2 mg, Minimum toxic dose = 8 mg
  Drug N: ED50 = 10 mg, TD50 = 150 mg, Minimum effective dose = 5 mg, Minimum toxic dose = 100 mg
What are the Therapeutic Index (TI) and Therapeutic Window for Drug M?
o: TI = 0.33; Therapeutic Window = 4 mg to 12 mg
TI = 3; Therapeutic Window = 2 mg to 8 mg
TI = 3; Therapeutic Window = 4 mg to 12 mg
TI = 4; Therapeutic Window = 2 mg to 8 mg
TI = 15; Therapeutic Window = 5 mg to 100 mg
q.p: Step 1 (Calculate the Therapeutic Index for Drug M as TD50 / ED50 = 12 mg / 4 mg = 3) -> Step 2 (Determine the Therapeutic Window for Drug M as the range between the minimum effective dose and minimum toxic dose = 2 mg to 8 mg)

r.A: A TI of 0.33 incorrectly divides ED50 by TD50, and 4 mg to 12 mg represents the ED50 to TD50 range rather than the therapeutic window.
r.C: While the TI of 3 is correct, the therapeutic window is the dosage range between minimum effective and minimum toxic concentrations (2 mg to 8 mg), not ED50 to TD50.
r.D: A TI of 4 incorrectly divides the minimum toxic dose (8 mg) by the minimum effective dose (2 mg) instead of using TD50 / ED50.
r.E: A TI of 15 and a window of 5 mg to 100 mg correspond to the values for Drug N rather than Drug M.

q.s: Objective 5 / Slides 83-85, 99: Relating Toxic and Therapeutic Effects
