q.v: A 28-year-old man enrolled in a nutritional study consumes a diet heavily supplemented with high-fructose corn syrup (HFCS) for 4 weeks. Repeat laboratory testing demonstrates a marked elevation in serum triglyceride and lipid levels compared to baseline, and an endoscopic small-bowel biopsy reveals noticeably elongated intestinal villi. Which of the following intracellular changes within the intestinal villus cells directly promotes the survival of hypoxic cells to drive this structural adaptation?
o: Accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate favoring the monomeric form of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2)
Activation of the PKM2 tetramer by elevated galactose-1-phosphate
Inhibition of ketohexokinase (KHK) by excess cytoplasmic citrate
Direct conversion of fructose to glucose-6-phosphate at the apical brush border
Depletion of intracellular NADPH due to rapid reduction of fructose by aldose reductase
q.p: Step 1 (High dietary HFCS enters enterocytes via GLUT5 and is phosphorylated by KHK to fructose-1-phosphate) -> Step 2 (Fructose-1-phosphate promotes the PKM2 monomer over the PKM2 tetramer, activating pathways that aid the survival of hypoxic villus cells, leading to villi lengthening and increased nutrient uptake/blood lipid levels).

r.B: Fructose-1-phosphate transitions PKM2 toward its monomeric state rather than activating the tetrameric form, and galactose-1-phosphate is not involved in this pathway.
r.C: Ketohexokinase (KHK) actively phosphorylates fructose to fructose-1-phosphate in the villus cell rather than being inhibited by citrate.
r.D: In enterocytes, fructose is phosphorylated to fructose-1-phosphate by KHK rather than being directly converted to glucose-6-phosphate at the apical membrane.
r.E: Aldose reductase reduces glucose or galactose into sugar alcohols using NADPH, whereas intestinal villi lengthening is driven by KHK-mediated fructose-1-phosphate formation.

q.s: Slide 4: SLO 1 - Possible mechanism linking fructose consumption to increased nutrient uptake

q.v: A healthy 22-year-old woman consumes a small serving of fruit containing a low, moderate dose of fructose. Later that evening, she consumes a 64-ounce soda containing a very large dose of fructose. Compared to the low dose of fructose, which of the following best describes the fate and downstream lipid packaging of the high dose of fructose?
o: It is completely metabolized into glucose within enterocytes and exported via SGLT1
It overflows from the intestine to the liver via the portal blood, where excess carbons can be packaged into B100-VLDL
It is trapped inside intestinal enterocytes due to saturation of basolateral GLUT2 transporters
It bypasses intestinal GLUT5 transporters and is absorbed exclusively in the colon as short-chain fatty acids
It is preferentially converted into chylomicrons by hepatocytes after uptake via SGLT1
q.p: Step 1 (Moderate doses of fructose are mostly metabolized by intestinal enterocytes, whereas high doses exceed enterocyte capacity and overflow to the liver and colon) -> Step 2 (Hepatocytes take up the excess fructose via GLUT5 and GLUT2 and, if used to produce fat, package it into B100-VLDL rather than enterocyte-derived chylomicrons).

r.A: Low doses of fructose are metabolized by the intestine, whereas high doses overwhelm enterocyte metabolism and overflow to the liver and colon; additionally, SGLT1 transports glucose and galactose, not fructose.
r.C: During high-dose fructose consumption, excess fructose exits across the basal membrane into the capillary vessel and overflows to the liver and colon rather than becoming trapped.
r.D: High doses of fructose still utilize apical GLUT5 in enterocytes before overflowing to the capillary blood, liver, and colon.
r.E: Chylomicrons are produced by enterocytes, whereas the liver produces B100-VLDL following fructose uptake via GLUT5 and GLUT2.

q.s: Slide 5: SLO 1 - Low doses vs. High doses of fructose metabolism

q.v: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with lethargy, vomiting, and diaphoresis two hours after being fed a commercial baby food sweetened with sorbitol. Physical examination shows jaundice and hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation reveals severe hypoglycemia, lactic acidemia, hyperuricemia, and normal serum ketone levels. Deficiency of the enzyme responsible for this infant's condition directly prevents the cleavage of a phosphorylated intermediate into which of the following pairs of molecules?
o: UDP-glucose and glucose-1-phosphate
Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde
Fructose-6-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate
Acetaldehyde and acetic acid
q.p: Step 1 (Clinical presentation of hypoglycemia, lactic acidemia, hyperuricemia, and normal ketones after sorbitol/fructose ingestion indicates Hereditary Fructose Intolerance caused by Aldolase B deficiency) -> Step 2 (Aldolase B normally cleaves fructose-1-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate [DHAP] and glyceraldehyde).

r.A: UDP-glucose and glucose-1-phosphate are intermediates in the galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) pathway, which is defective in classic galactosemia.
r.C: Fructose-6-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate are upstream glycolytic intermediates bypassed during hepatic fructose metabolism.
r.D: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is formed downstream from glyceraldehyde and DHAP, rather than being cleaved directly from fructose-1-phosphate along with pyruvate.
r.E: Acetaldehyde and acetic acid are intermediates of ethanol metabolism, not fructose metabolism.

q.s: Slide 6 & Slide 18: SLO 1 - Fructose Metabolism Disorders (Hereditary Fructose Intolerance)

q.v: A 40-year-old man consumes a diet extremely high in sucrose and high-fructose corn syrup. Unlike hepatic glucose metabolism, which is tightly controlled by feedback inhibition at its rate-limiting steps, hepatic fructose metabolism enters glycolysis unchecked and floods the citric acid cycle. Which of the following intermediates is exported in excess from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm to serve as the direct precursor for acetyl-CoA and subsequent triacylglycerol (TAG) synthesis?
o: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
Fructose-1-phosphate
Citrate
Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP)
Galactitol
q.p: Step 1 (Fructose metabolism bypasses the highly regulated steps of glycolysis—glucokinase/hexokinase and PFK-1—entering as DHAP and glyceraldehyde to form glyceraldehyde-3-P, pyruvate, and mitochondrial acetyl-CoA) -> Step 2 (Excess citrate from the citric acid cycle is exported to the cytoplasm, where it is converted back to acetyl-CoA to synthesize fatty acids and TAG).

r.A: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is a cytoplasmic glycolytic intermediate that is bypassed by fructose-1-phosphate cleavage, not exported from the citric acid cycle.
r.B: Fructose-1-phosphate is formed in the cytoplasm by fructokinase and cleaved by aldolase B; it does not exit the mitochondria to form acetyl-CoA.
r.D: DHAP is a cytoplasmic cleavage product of fructose-1-phosphate that enters glycolysis, not a citric acid cycle intermediate exported to form cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA.
r.E: Galactitol is an osmotically active sugar alcohol formed from galactose by aldose reductase, unrelated to hepatic fatty acid synthesis.

q.s: Slide 4 & Slide 6: SLO 1 - Fructose Metabolism Disorders (Glycolysis bypass and excess citrate export)

q.v: A 24-year-old man from Northern Europe and his 24-year-old friend from East Asia both consume a large milkshake. Two hours later, one man remains completely asymptomatic, while the other develops severe abdominal cramps, bloating, flatulence, and watery diarrhea. Which of the following evolutionary genetic mechanisms best explains why the asymptomatic individual is able to tolerate this meal in adulthood?
o: Upregulation of basolateral GLUT5 transporters in the colon
Independent acquisition of mutations that maintain lactase expression after infancy
Constitutive suppression of intestinal SGLT1 cotransporters
Increased expression of hepatic galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT)
Adaptive deficiency of fructokinase (KHK) in small intestinal enterocytes
q.p: Step 1 (Adult-type lactose intolerance results from the normal reduction in lactase expression after infancy, causing unabsorbed lactose to induce osmotic water retention and bacterial fermentation) -> Step 2 (Some human populations independently acquired mutations that maintain lactase expression later in life, preventing symptoms after dairy intake).

r.A: GLUT5 is a fructose transporter, whereas lactose digestion requires brush-border lactase to cleave lactose into glucose and galactose.
r.C: SGLT1 is required for the apical absorption of galactose and glucose; suppressing it would worsen carbohydrate malabsorption rather than allow dairy tolerance.
r.D: GALT metabolizes galactose-1-phosphate intracellularly after absorption and has no role in cleaving luminal lactose in the intestine.
r.E: Fructokinase deficiency causes essential fructosuria and does not enable the digestion of dietary lactose.

q.s: Slide 8 & Slide 18: SLO 2 - Galactose Metabolism (Lactose Intolerance)

q.v: A 5-day-old breastfed neonate is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit with vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and failure to thrive. Ophthalmologic exam reveals bilateral lens opacities, and blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. Laboratory studies show hypoglycemia with normal serum ketone levels. A deficiency in the culprit enzyme blocks the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate into glucose-1-phosphate, a reaction that normally requires the recycling of UDP-galactose back into UDP-glucose via which of the following enzymes?
o: Aldose reductase
Galactokinase
4-Epimerase
Sorbitol dehydrogenase
Aldolase B
q.p: Step 1 (Neonatal vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, and E. coli sepsis in a breastfed infant indicate Classic Galactosemia due to galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase [GALT] deficiency) -> Step 2 (In the normal GALT pathway, galactose-1-phosphate reacts with UDP-glucose to form glucose-1-phosphate and UDP-galactose, which is regenerated into UDP-glucose by 4-epimerase).

r.A: Aldose reductase converts excess unphosphorylated galactose into galactitol, which causes cataracts, rather than interconverting UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose.
r.B: Galactokinase catalyzes the initial ATP-dependent phosphorylation of galactose to galactose-1-phosphate.
r.D: Sorbitol dehydrogenase converts sorbitol to fructose in the polyol pathway and plays no role in galactose metabolism.
r.E: Aldolase B cleaves fructose-1-phosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde in fructose metabolism.

q.s: Slide 8 & Slide 18: SLO 2 - Galactose Metabolism (Classic Galactosemia pathway)

q.v: A 62-year-old woman with a 15-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus undergoes a physiological study comparing intracellular metabolites across different tissues. Biopsies of her peripheral nerves and renal cortex demonstrate markedly elevated intracellular sorbitol concentrations and cellular swelling, whereas analysis of seminal vesicle tissue shows active conversion of glucose to sorbitol without toxic sorbitol accumulation. Which of the following best explains why seminal vesicles are spared from the osmotic swelling observed in her nerves and kidneys?
o: Seminal vesicles require insulin for glucose entry across the plasma membrane
Seminal vesicles lack aldose reductase and cannot reduce glucose
Seminal vesicles express sorbitol dehydrogenase, which oxidizes sorbitol to fructose using NAD+
Seminal vesicles rapidly phosphorylate sorbitol into sorbitol-1-phosphate via fructokinase
Seminal vesicles export sorbitol into the bloodstream via high-capacity GLUT2 transporters
q.p: Step 1 (In hyperglycemia, glucose enters insulin-independent tissues and is converted to sorbitol by aldose reductase using NADPH) -> Step 2 (Whereas lens, nerve, retina, and kidney cells have low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase [SD] leading to osmotic sorbitol accumulation, seminal vesicles possess SD, which uses NAD+ to convert sorbitol into fructose).

r.A: Seminal vesicles actively take up glucose and convert it to sorbitol and fructose to fuel sperm, rather than blocking glucose entry.
r.B: Seminal vesicles do possess aldose reductase to convert glucose into sorbitol as the first step in producing fructose.
r.D: Sorbitol is oxidized to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase, not phosphorylated by fructokinase.
r.E: Sorbitol does not pass freely out of cells; seminal vesicles prevent accumulation by oxidizing it to fructose via sorbitol dehydrogenase.

q.s: Slide 10 & Slide 11: SLO 3 - Effect of Hyperglycemia on Sorbitol Metabolism

q.v: In an experimental model of diabetic retinopathy and cataract formation, retinal and lens cells are incubated in a medium containing high concentrations of glucose. Intracellular tracking reveals a rapid influx of glucose without insulin stimulation, followed by the accumulation of an osmotically active molecule that cannot pass freely out of the cells, resulting in cellular influx of water. The enzymatic reaction that directly synthesizes this osmotically active molecule requires an adequate intracellular supply of which of the following cofactors?
o: NAD+
NADH + H+
ATP
NADPH + H+
UDP-glucose
q.p: Step 1 (In the lens and retina during hyperglycemia, insulin-independent glucose entry leads to sorbitol production via aldose reductase, causing osmotic water influx) -> Step 2 (The conversion of glucose to sorbitol by aldose reductase requires adequate supplies of NADPH + H+, which is oxidized to NADP+).

r.A: NAD+ is the cofactor required by sorbitol dehydrogenase to convert sorbitol to fructose, not by aldose reductase to synthesize sorbitol.
r.B: NADH + H+ is the product formed when sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidizes sorbitol to fructose.
r.C: ATP is required by kinases such as fructokinase and galactokinase, whereas aldose reductase utilizes NADPH + H+.
r.E: UDP-glucose is a nucleotide sugar cofactor used by galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase in galactose metabolism.

q.s: Slide 10, Slide 11, & Slide 12: SLO 3 - Effect of Hyperglycemia on Sorbitol Metabolism

q.v: A 26-year-old man experiences intense facial flushing, tachycardia, and nausea shortly after drinking a single glass of wine. A similar reaction occurs in a 50-year-old man who drinks beer while taking disulfiram for alcohol use disorder. Both individuals are experiencing the accumulation of a toxic, highly reactive electrophile due to reduced activity of an enzyme that is partially deficient in up to 35–40% of certain global populations. Which of the following reactions is directly catalyzed by the affected enzyme?
o: Conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde coupled with the reduction of NAD+
Conversion of acetaldehyde to acetate coupled with the reduction of NAD+
Conversion of acetic acid to acetyl-CoA coupled with the hydrolysis of ATP
Conversion of glycolic acid to glyoxylic acid using thiamine
Conversion of formic acid to carbon dioxide and water using folate
q.p: Step 1 (Both disulfiram treatment and the common genetic deficiency present in 35-40% of some populations impair aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing toxic acetaldehyde accumulation) -> Step 2 (Aldehyde dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetate while reducing NAD+ to NADH + H+).

r.A: The conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde is catalyzed by alcohol dehydrogenase (AldH), which is upstream of the enzyme inhibited by disulfiram.
r.C: The activation of acetic acid to acetyl-CoA occurs downstream of aldehyde dehydrogenase.
r.D: The metabolism of glycolic acid involves ethylene glycol detoxification pathways, not the oxidation of acetaldehyde by aldehyde dehydrogenase.
r.E: The folate-dependent conversion of formic acid to CO2 and H2O is the final detoxification step of methanol metabolism.

q.s: Slide 13 & Slide 14: SLO 4 - Ethanol Metabolism and Aldehyde Dehydrogenase

q.v: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after intentionally ingesting automotive antifreeze (ethylene glycol). Before alcohol dehydrogenase inhibition can be initiated, a portion of the ethylene glycol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase into glycolic acid, which is subsequently converted to glyoxylic acid. To shunt glyoxylic acid away from forming renal-toxic oxalic acid and instead promote its conversion into non-toxic metabolites such as glycine and alpha-hydroxy-beta-ketoadipate, which of the following pairs of vitamin cofactors is directly involved in this downstream detoxification pathway?
o: Folate and cobalamin
Thiamine and pyridoxine
Niacin and riboflavin
Biotin and pantothenic acid
Ascorbic acid and vitamin K
q.p: Step 1 (Ethylene glycol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase to glycolic acid and glyoxylic acid, which can form toxic oxalic acid) -> Step 2 (As shown in the ethylene glycol detoxification pathway, thiamine promotes the conversion of glycolic/glyoxylic intermediates to alpha-hydroxy-beta-ketoadipate, and pyridoxine promotes the conversion of glyoxylic acid to glycine).

r.A: Folate is used to detoxify formic acid into CO2 and H2O during methanol poisoning, not ethylene glycol poisoning.
r.C: Niacin (precursor to NAD+) drives the initial oxidation of ethylene glycol into toxic intermediates via alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases rather than shunting glyoxylic acid to glycine.
r.D: Biotin and pantothenic acid are not the vitamin cofactors utilized in the detoxification of glycolic and glyoxylic acid.
r.E: Ascorbic acid and vitamin K are not involved in the enzymatic shunting of glycolic acid or glyoxylic acid.

q.s: Slide 14: SLO 4 - Ethanol, methanol and ethylene glycol metabolism

q.v:
A 19-year-old woman presents for a routine college pre-admission physical examination. She feels completely healthy, exercises regularly, and has no medical complaints or history of liver disease. Routine urinalysis reveals the following:
  Urine pH: 6.0
  Urine protein: negative
  Urine glucose (glucose oxidase dipstick): negative
  Urine reducing substances: positive
  Urine ketones: negative
Which of the following is the primary biochemical cause of this patient's urinary finding?
o: Inability to phosphorylate fructose to fructose-1-phosphate
Inability to cleave fructose-1-phosphate into trioses
Inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate
Inability to phosphorylate galactose to galactose-1-phosphate
Inability to cleave lactose into glucose and galactose
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize asymptomatic positive urine reducing sugar with negative glucose dipstick as essential fructosuria) -> Step 2 (Identify the blocked reaction due to fructokinase deficiency: fructose to fructose-1-phosphate)

r.B: Inability to cleave fructose-1-phosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde occurs in aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance), which causes severe hypoglycemia, jaundice, and hepatomegaly rather than a benign asymptomatic state.
r.C: Inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate is caused by galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency (classic galactosemia), which presents in neonates with severe systemic disease.
r.D: Inability to phosphorylate galactose to galactose-1-phosphate occurs in galactokinase deficiency, which classically presents with bilateral cataracts in childhood due to galactitol accumulation.
r.E: Inability to cleave lactose into glucose and galactose is due to decreased lactase expression (lactose intolerance), which presents with osmotic diarrhea, gas, and bloating after dairy ingestion rather than fructosuria.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 6 (Fructose Metabolism Disorders) and Slide 18 (Summary Table)

q.v:
A 9-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with lethargy, vomiting, and irritability that began shortly after her parents introduced pureed fruits and sucrose-sweetened cereal into her diet. Physical examination reveals jaundice and hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum glucose: 34 mg/dL
  Serum lactic acid: elevated
  Serum uric acid: elevated
  Serum ketones: normal
Which of the following best explains the severe hypoglycemia observed in this patient?
o: Increased insulin secretion stimulated by accumulated fructose
Inhibition of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis due to phosphate trapping
Direct competitive inhibition of intestinal SGLT1 glucose transporters
Depletion of cytosolic NADPH required for hepatic glucose export
Shift of pyruvate to lactate driven by an elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize hereditary fructose intolerance from post-fruit/sucrose onset of hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, jaundice, lacticacidemia, hyperuricemia, and normal ketones) -> Step 2 (Connect accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate to phosphate trapping and ATP depletion -> inhibition of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis)

r.A: Fructose metabolism disorders do not cause hypoglycemia via hyperinsulinemia; rather, intracellular phosphate depletion impairs hepatic glucose production.
r.C: SGLT1 transports glucose and galactose across the intestinal brush border and is not competitively inhibited by intracellular fructose-1-phosphate accumulation.
r.D: NADPH is consumed by aldose reductase during sorbitol and galactitol synthesis, whereas the hypoglycemia in aldolase B deficiency is driven by trapping of inorganic phosphate and lack of ATP.
r.E: An elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio driving pyruvate to lactate is the mechanism by which ethanol metabolism inhibits gluconeogenesis, not the mechanism of hereditary fructose intolerance.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 6 (Fructose Metabolism Disorders) and Slide 7 (SLO1 Review)

q.v: Which of the following pairs of metabolites are produced directly by the aldolase B-catalyzed cleavage of fructose-1-phosphate in the liver?
o: Glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate
Dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde
Galactose-1-phosphate and glucose-1-phosphate
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
Pyruvate and acetyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the reaction catalyzed by aldolase B in hepatic fructose metabolism) -> Step 2 (Name the direct cleavage products of fructose-1-phosphate: DHAP and glyceraldehyde)

r.A: Glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate are early intermediates of glycolysis that are bypassed during hepatic fructose metabolism.
r.C: Galactose-1-phosphate and glucose-1-phosphate are intermediates in the galactose metabolism pathway interconverted by galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase.
r.D: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is cleaved by aldolase A in glycolysis, while glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is formed downstream after phosphorylation of glyceraldehyde or isomerization of DHAP.
r.E: Pyruvate and acetyl-CoA are formed far downstream of aldolase B at the end of glycolysis and via pyruvate dehydrogenase, respectively.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 6 (Fructose Metabolism Disorders) and Slide 18 (Summary Table)

q.v: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric ophthalmologist after his parents notice a white reflex in both eyes and difficulty tracking objects. Slit-lamp examination reveals bilateral cataracts. He has met all developmental milestones, has normal growth parameters, and has no history of vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, or bacterial infections. Accumulation of which of the following metabolites is directly responsible for his ocular finding?
o: Galactose-1-phosphate
Galactitol
Fructose-1-phosphate
Sorbitol
UDP-galactose
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize isolated bilateral cataracts without systemic liver disease or sepsis as galactokinase deficiency) -> Step 2 (Identify galactitol produced via aldose reductase as the osmotically active metabolite accumulating in the lens)

r.A: Galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency) and causes severe systemic toxicity including hepatomegaly, jaundice, and renal dysfunction, which are absent in this child.
r.C: Fructose-1-phosphate is the toxic intermediate that accumulates in hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency), causing hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia rather than cataracts.
r.D: Sorbitol is the sugar alcohol formed from excess glucose by aldose reductase that causes cataracts in patients with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, whereas galactitol is formed from galactose.
r.E: UDP-galactose is an intermediate in the GALT and 4-epimerase cycle of galactose metabolism and does not accumulate osmotically in the lens.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 8 (Galactose Metabolism) and Slide 18 (Summary Table)

q.v: A 6-day-old exclusively breastfed male infant is brought to the emergency department for poor feeding, persistent vomiting, and lethargy. Physical examination shows icteric sclerae, hepatomegaly, and early bilateral lens opacities. Which of the following pairs correctly matches the deficient enzyme with the accumulated toxic phosphorylated intermediate in this patient?
o: Aldolase B — Fructose-1-phosphate
Galactokinase — Galactose-1-phosphate
Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase — Galactose-1-phosphate
Fructokinase — Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
UDP-galactose 4-epimerase — Glucose-1-phosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose classic galactosemia in a breastfed neonate presenting with vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and cataracts) -> Step 2 (Match the condition to GALT deficiency and toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation)

r.A: Aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance) causes fructose-1-phosphate accumulation, but presents after weaning when fructose or sucrose is introduced, and does not cause cataracts.
r.B: Galactokinase deficiency blocks the conversion of galactose to galactose-1-phosphate, so galactose and galactitol accumulate rather than galactose-1-phosphate, causing isolated cataracts.
r.D: Fructokinase deficiency (essential fructosuria) blocks phosphorylation of fructose, resulting in benign urinary excretion of fructose without phosphorylated intermediate accumulation.
r.E: Glucose-1-phosphate is the downstream product formed by galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase for entry into glycolysis or glycogenesis, not a toxic accumulating substrate.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 8 (Galactose Metabolism) and Slide 18 (Summary Table)

q.v: A 29-year-old woman presents to the clinic with recurrent episodes of abdominal cramps, bloating, flatulence, and watery diarrhea that occur approximately one hour after consuming milk or ice cream. She had no difficulty consuming dairy products during infancy. Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism of her condition?
o: Normal age-related reduction in intestinal brush-border lactase expression
Deficiency of intestinal SGLT1 cotransporters preventing galactose uptake
Accumulation of toxic galactose-1-phosphate in small intestinal enterocytes
Overflow of excess dietary monosaccharides through basolateral GLUT5 transporters
Conversion of unabsorbed galactose into osmotically active galactitol in the colon
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize adult-onset abdominal cramps, bloating, gas, and diarrhea after dairy as primary lactase non-persistence / lactose intolerance) -> Step 2 (Identify the mechanism as the normal reduction in lactase expression after infancy leading to osmotic water retention and bacterial fermentation)

r.B: SGLT1 transports monosaccharides (glucose and galactose) into enterocytes, whereas lactose intolerance results from failure to cleave the disaccharide lactose prior to absorption.
r.C: Toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation occurs in classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency), an inborn error presenting in infancy with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and cataracts.
r.D: Overflow through GLUT5 transporters describes how high doses of dietary fructose exceed enterocyte capacity and spill over to the liver and colon.
r.E: Galactitol is formed intracellularly in the lens by aldose reductase in galactosemia and galactokinase deficiency; in lactose intolerance, unabsorbed lactose itself causes osmotic water retention and bacterial fermentation in the gut.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 8 (Galactose Metabolism) and Slide 18 (Summary Table)

q.v: A 58-year-old man with a 12-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with progressive bilateral vision loss from cataracts and numbness and tingling in both feet. His physician explains that chronic hyperglycemia leads to the intracellular accumulation of an osmotically active molecule in his lenses and peripheral nerves. Which of the following combinations of cofactors is required for the two sequential enzymatic steps that convert glucose into fructose via this pathway?
o: ATP in the first step; NAD+ in the second step
NADPH in the first step; NAD+ in the second step
NAD+ in the first step; NAD+ in the second step
NADH in the first step; NADPH in the second step
ATP in the first step; ADP in the second step
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the polyol/sorbitol pathway converting glucose -> sorbitol -> fructose in insulin-independent tissues) -> Step 2 (Identify the cofactor oxidized when aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol [NADPH] and when sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidizes sorbitol to fructose [NAD+])

r.A: Kinases such as fructokinase and galactokinase require ATP for phosphorylation, whereas aldose reductase catalyzes a reduction using NADPH without phosphorylating glucose.
r.C: Utilizing NAD+ in both sequential steps is characteristic of ethanol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase, not the sorbitol pathway.
r.D: Aldose reductase consumes NADPH (generating NADP+) to reduce glucose to sorbitol, and sorbitol dehydrogenase consumes NAD+ (generating NADH) to oxidize sorbitol to fructose.
r.E: The conversion of glucose to sorbitol and then to fructose is a two-step redox pathway (polyol pathway) that does not directly consume or generate ATP or ADP.

q.s: SLO 3, Slide 11 (Effect of Hyperglycemia on Sorbitol Metabolism) and Slide 12 (SLO3 Review)

q.v: In which of the following cells or tissues is sorbitol rapidly converted into fructose by high levels of sorbitol dehydrogenase to provide a metabolic energy source, rather than accumulating and causing osmotic cell swelling?
o: Seminal vesicles
Retinal cells
Peripheral nerve cells
Lens cells
Renal cells
q.p: Step 1 (Recall tissue differences in sorbitol dehydrogenase [SD] expression from the lecture diagram) -> Step 2 (Identify seminal vesicles as the tissue that expresses sorbitol dehydrogenase to convert sorbitol to fructose, unlike lens, retina, kidney, and nerve)

r.B: Retinal cells have low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase activity, leading to sorbitol accumulation and diabetic retinopathy during chronic hyperglycemia.
r.C: Peripheral nerve cells have low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase activity, causing osmotic sorbitol accumulation, cell swelling, and diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
r.D: Lens cells lack significant sorbitol dehydrogenase activity, causing intracellular sorbitol accumulation, water influx, and cataract formation in uncontrolled diabetes.
r.E: Kidney cells have low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase activity, contributing to osmotic damage and diabetic nephropathy.

q.s: SLO 3, Slide 11 (Effect of Hyperglycemia on Sorbitol Metabolism)

q.v:
A 48-year-old man with a history of chronic heavy alcohol use and poor nutritional intake is brought to the emergency department after being found confused and diaphoretic. He has not eaten solid food in 48 hours, though he has continued drinking vodka. Laboratory evaluation reveals:
  Serum glucose: 42 mg/dL
  Serum lactate: 5.8 mmol/L (elevated)
  Arterial pH: 7.28
  Blood ethanol: 240 mg/dL
The consumption of which cofactor during both enzymatic steps of ethanol metabolism is primarily responsible for his lactic acidosis and impaired gluconeogenesis?
o: NADP+
FAD
NAD+
NADPH
Thiamine pyrophosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize ethanol-induced fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis) -> Step 2 (Identify that both alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase consume NAD+ and produce NADH -> altered redox balance promotes lactic acidosis and inhibits gluconeogenesis)

r.A: NADP+ is generated when aldose reductase consumes NADPH during sorbitol synthesis and is not involved in the oxidation of ethanol.
r.B: FAD is a flavin cofactor used in other oxidative pathways such as the TCA cycle and beta-oxidation, whereas ethanol metabolism specifically utilizes two molecules of NAD+.
r.D: NADPH is consumed by aldose reductase in the polyol pathway; ethanol oxidation reduces NAD+ to NADH.
r.E: Although thiamine deficiency is common in patients with chronic alcohol use and thiamine is used in ethylene glycol detoxification, the direct redox shift causing lactic acidosis and impaired gluconeogenesis in ethanol metabolism is the consumption of two NAD+ molecules.

q.s: SLO 4, Slide 13 (Ethanol Metabolism) and Slide 15 (SLO4 Review)

q.v: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with confusion, flank pain, and rapid breathing several hours after drinking a sweet-tasting liquid from an unlabeled garage container. Intravenous ethanol is immediately administered to competitively inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase. Which of the following pairs of toxic organic acids corresponds to the metabolites that would otherwise accumulate from methanol versus ethylene glycol poisoning, respectively?
o: Acetic acid (from methanol) and formic acid (from ethylene glycol)
Formic acid (from methanol) and oxalic acid (from ethylene glycol)
Glycolic acid (from methanol) and formaldehyde (from ethylene glycol)
Acetaldehyde (from methanol) and acetic acid (from ethylene glycol)
Oxalic acid (from methanol) and acetic acid (from ethylene glycol)
q.p: Step 1 (Trace the alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase pathways for methanol and ethylene glycol on Slide 14) -> Step 2 (Match methanol to formaldehyde/formic acid and ethylene glycol to glycolic acid/oxalic acid)

r.A: Acetic acid is the intermediate produced from ethanol metabolism, whereas formic acid is produced from methanol, not ethylene glycol.
r.C: Glycolic acid is a toxic intermediate of ethylene glycol metabolism, while formaldehyde is the aldehyde intermediate of methanol metabolism.
r.D: Acetaldehyde and acetic acid are the sequential intermediates of ethanol metabolism, not methanol or ethylene glycol.
r.E: Oxalic acid is a toxic end-product of ethylene glycol metabolism, whereas methanol is metabolized to formaldehyde and formic acid.

q.s: SLO 4, Slide 14 (Ethanol, Methanol and Ethylene Glycol)

myLectures.name: Lymphoid Organs
myLectures.note: New lecture (Mullins, Mon Nov 2). Cards picked to match the slides, checked against your 19 Lymphoid Organs cards (see lymphoid_organs_card_check.csv). Every pick was rechecked against the slides; related B&B cards the lecture doesn't discuss (DiGeorge, SCID, AIRE, CD4/CD8 in the thymus, splenectomy vaccines, sickle cell autosplenectomy) were left out. Adds 3 cloze notes (deck: Mullins - Lymphoid Organs): MALT vs lymph node, the lymph route through a node, and white pulp surveillance of blood.

add.cloze: MALT samples antigens from {{c1::mucosal surfaces}}; unlike a lymph node, it lies {{c2::directly beneath the epithelium and lacks a complete capsule and afferent lymphatics}}
add.extra: Antigen crosses specialized epithelium (M cells) to follicles beneath the mucosa. Peyer patches are most prominent in the ileum; plasma cells support mucosal IgA responses.

add.cloze: Lymph flows through a lymph node: afferent lymphatic → {{c1::subcapsular sinus}} → {{c2::cortical (trabecular) sinuses}} → {{c3::medullary sinuses}} → efferent lymphatic
add.extra: Afferents enter the convex surface; the efferent exits at the hilum, where blood vessels and high endothelial venules enter. APCs sample the lymph along the route.

add.cloze: Splenic {{c2::white pulp}} performs {{c1::immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens}}
add.extra: White pulp = PALS (T cells around a central arteriole) + follicles (B cells). Red pulp = cords of Billroth + sinusoids: RBC quality control.

slides.name: MAD Lymphoid Organs 2026 FINAL With Quiz Questions.pdf

practice.name: Quiz_ CYK1_ Immune Organs.pdf

q.v: A 34-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 3-day history of worsening redness, warmth, and swelling over the dorsum of his right foot after stepping on a splinter while gardening. Physical examination reveals tender, erythematous skin over the foot and palpable, tender lymphadenopathy in the ipsilateral groin. Dendritic cells carrying bacterial antigens from the foot travel via afferent lymphatics to the draining lymph node. Which of the following sequences best traces the path of lymph through the sinuses of this regional lymph node before exiting at the hilum?
o: Medullary sinus -> trabecular sinus -> subcapsular sinus
Subcapsular sinus -> trabecular sinus -> medullary sinus
Trabecular sinus -> subcapsular sinus -> medullary sinus
Subcapsular sinus -> medullary sinus -> trabecular sinus
Medullary sinus -> subcapsular sinus -> trabecular sinus
q.p: Step 1 (Afferent lymphatics from the lower extremity enter the convex surface of an inguinal lymph node) -> Step 2 (Lymph flows sequentially through the subcapsular sinus, trabecular/cortical sinuses, and medullary sinuses before exiting via the efferent lymphatic at the hilum)

r.A: This sequence reverses the normal physiological direction of lymph flow, which enters at the convex surface and exits at the hilum.
r.C: Lymph from afferent vessels enters the subcapsular sinus directly beneath the capsule before reaching the trabecular sinuses.
r.D: Lymph must pass through the cortical/trabecular sinuses before reaching the deep medullary sinuses.
r.E: Medullary sinuses are the final sinus compartment prior to exiting via the efferent lymphatic at the hilum, not the entry point.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 13: Lymph node: follow the lymph

q.v: A 19-year-old woman presents to the student health clinic with a 4-day history of fever, sore throat, and malaise. Physical examination reveals pharyngeal erythema and tender, bilaterally enlarged cervical lymph nodes. A biopsy of one of the reactive lymph nodes demonstrates prominent proliferation of T lymphocytes interacting with antigen-presenting dendritic cells. In addition to these two cell types, which of the following anatomical structures is specifically located within this same compartment of the lymph node?
o: Germinal centers
Hassall corpuscles
Cords of Billroth
High endothelial venules
Splenic sinusoids
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the lymph node compartment containing T cells and dendritic cells as the paracortex) -> Step 2 (Associate the paracortex with its specialized vascular landmark, high endothelial venules, which allow circulating naive lymphocytes to enter from the blood)

r.A: Germinal centers appear after B-cell activation in the outer cortex of the lymph node, not the paracortex.
r.B: Hassall corpuscles are concentric epithelial structures found exclusively in the medulla of the thymus.
r.C: Cords of Billroth are located in the red pulp of the spleen and function in erythrocyte quality control.
r.E: Splenic sinusoids are vascular channels in the red pulp of the spleen that test erythrocyte deformability.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 14: Lymph node: place the cells

q.v: A 62-year-old man undergoes radical resection of a pelvic malignancy along with an extensive unilateral inguinal lymph node dissection. Two months after the operation, he returns to the clinic with persistent, non-tender swelling of his entire right lower extremity. Physical examination shows firm edema of the right leg without erythema or warmth. Obstruction of the lymphatic delivery network in this patient produces interstitial fluid accumulation with which of the following characteristics?
o: Protein-rich interstitial fluid
Lipid-depleted intracellular fluid
Hemosiderin-laden sinusoidal fluid
IgA-enriched mucosal fluid
Hemoglobin-rich intravascular fluid
q.p: Step 1 (Surgical removal of inguinal lymph nodes obstructs one-way lymphatic drainage from the lower extremity) -> Step 2 (Impaired clearance of excess interstitial fluid by blind-ended lymphatic capillaries results in protein-rich interstitial edema)

r.B: Lymphatic capillaries collect extracellular interstitial fluid rather than intracellular fluid.
r.C: Hemosiderin and iron recovery occur via macrophage-mediated erythrocyte clearance in the splenic red pulp, not peripheral lymphatics.
r.D: Mucosal IgA is secreted across exposed epithelia in MALT rather than accumulating in peripheral extremity interstitium.
r.E: Free hemoglobin in intravascular fluid is a feature of intravascular hemolysis, whereas lymphatic obstruction causes interstitial protein accumulation.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 12: Lymphatics: the delivery network & Slide 21: Checkpoint!

q.v: A 26-year-old man presents to the clinic with watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping several days after returning from a camping trip. Endoscopic biopsy of the terminal ileum demonstrates prominent lymphoid aggregates located directly beneath the exposed intestinal epithelium, characterized by organized B-cell follicles and interfollicular T-cell zones without a surrounding capsule or afferent lymphatic vessels. Plasma cells generated during an immune response in this tissue primarily support the production of which of the following effectors?
o: Secretory IgA across the mucosal epithelium
Complement proteins into the central arteriole
Self-MHC molecules for thymocyte positive selection
Iron-binding proteins within the cords of Billroth
Macrophage enzymes in the subcapsular sinus
q.p: Step 1 (Identify unencapsulated ileal lymphoid aggregates lacking afferent lymphatics as Peyer patches / MALT) -> Step 2 (Connect MALT antigen sampling via M cells to its key output, plasma cell production of mucosal secretory IgA)

r.B: A central arteriole surrounded by T cells (PALS) is the signature structure of splenic white pulp, not intestinal MALT.
r.C: Positive selection of thymocytes via self-MHC recognition occurs exclusively in the cortex of the thymus.
r.D: Iron recovery within the cords of Billroth is a function of the splenic red pulp during red blood cell turnover.
r.E: A subcapsular sinus receiving afferent lymph is a defining feature of an encapsulated lymph node, which is absent in MALT.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 23: MALT: immune surveillance at the border & Slide 32: Rapid recognition matrix

q.v: A 9-year-old boy with a congenital erythrocyte membrane defect undergoes evaluation for chronic anemia. In the spleen, his erythrocytes are released from the open circulation into the cords of Billroth and must deform to pass into the venous sinusoids. Because his red blood cells have reduced membrane flexibility, they fail this deformability test. Which of the following best describes the immediate fate of these rigid erythrocytes?
o: Transcytosis across specialized M cells into the lumen
Retention in the splenic cords and phagocytosis by macrophages
Transport out of the spleen via efferent subcapsular sinuses
Migration into the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath for apoptosis
Filtration through high endothelial venules into the paracortex
q.p: Step 1 (Blood enters the open circulation of the splenic red pulp and is released into the splenic cords of Billroth) -> Step 2 (Rigid or senescent erythrocytes cannot traverse the narrow slits between sinusoidal endothelial cells and are retained and phagocytosed by macrophages)

r.A: M cells transcytose luminal antigens across mucosal epithelia in MALT and do not transport erythrocytes in the spleen.
r.C: The spleen lacks subcapsular sinuses, which are anatomical landmarks of lymph nodes.
r.D: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) is the T-cell zone of the splenic white pulp and does not perform red blood cell quality control.
r.E: High endothelial venules are located in the paracortex of lymph nodes to facilitate lymphocyte entry, not erythrocyte filtration.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 25: Red pulp: a deformability test

q.v: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of high fever, chills, and confusion. Four years ago, she underwent an emergency splenectomy following a motor vehicle collision. Her temperature is 39.6 C (103.3 F), blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg, and heart rate is 128/min. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric intravenous antibiotics are initiated immediately. The rapid progression of systemic infection in this patient is most directly explained by impaired blood clearance of which of the following?
o: Intracellular viruses within respiratory epithelial cells
Unopsonized bacterial toxins in peripheral lymph
Opsonized encapsulated bacteria circulating in the blood
Luminal parasites attached to the ileal mucosa
Self-reactive T lymphocytes escaping the thymic medulla
q.p: Step 1 (History of splenectomy results in surgical asplenia and loss of splenic white and red pulp filtration) -> Step 2 (Asplenia causes loss of rapid defense against blood-borne, opsonized encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, and N. meningitidis)

r.A: Viral infections of the lung primarily drain to hilar and tracheobronchial lymph nodes rather than relying specifically on splenic clearance of encapsulated organisms.
r.B: Peripheral lymph is sampled and filtered by regional lymph nodes via afferent lymphatics, whereas the spleen samples blood.
r.D: Luminal intestinal pathogens are sampled across the epithelium by M cells in MALT (Peyer patches), not by the spleen.
r.E: Deletion of self-reactive T lymphocytes (central tolerance) occurs via negative selection in the thymic medulla.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 28: Asplenia: what function cannot be fully replaced?

q.v:
A 31-year-old man is evaluated at a primary care clinic for a routine physical examination. His medical history is notable for a laparotomy performed 5 years ago after a skiing accident. A complete blood count and peripheral blood smear are obtained:
  Hemoglobin: 14.2 g/dL
  Platelet count: 465,000/mm3
  Target cells: increased
  Erythrocyte inclusions: single, round, dark-purple cytoplasmic bodies
The erythrocyte inclusions observed on this patient's peripheral blood smear are composed of which of the following?
o: Denatured hemoglobin
Aggregated ribosomal RNA
DNA/nuclear remnants
Iron-containing granules
Immunoglobulin crystals
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize increased target cells, mild thrombocytosis from reduced platelet sequestration, and dark cytoplasmic RBC inclusions after abdominal surgery as post-splenectomy findings) -> Step 2 (Identify the inclusions as Howell-Jolly bodies, which are DNA/nuclear remnants normally removed by the splenic red pulp)

r.A: Denatured hemoglobin precipitates form Heinz bodies, whereas Howell-Jolly bodies represent nuclear DNA remnants.
r.B: Aggregated ribosomal RNA forms basophilic stippling rather than Howell-Jolly bodies.
r.D: Iron-containing granules within erythrocytes are Pappenheimer bodies, not Howell-Jolly bodies.
r.E: Immunoglobulins are secreted by plasma cells in the medullary cords of lymph nodes and MALT, not retained as nuclear remnants in erythrocytes.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 27: Checkpoint! & Slide 28: Asplenia: what function cannot be fully replaced?

q.v:
A pathologist is reviewing histologic tissue sections from four different lymphoid organs (Samples 1-4) obtained during an autopsy. The defining microscopic findings for each sample are summarized in the table below:
  Sample 1: Fibrous septa dividing tissue into lobules; dark cortex; pale medulla with concentric epithelial whorls; no B-cell follicles
  Sample 2: Outer capsule; subcapsular sinus; cortical B-cell follicles; paracortical high endothelial venules
  Sample 3: White-pulp follicles adjacent to a central arteriole surrounded by T cells; red-pulp sinusoids
  Sample 4: Subepithelial lymphoid follicles beneath an intestinal crypt; overlying M cells; no capsule
Which of the following correctly pairs the tissue sample with the primary material sampled by that organ?
o: Sample 1 - Blood-borne antigens
Sample 2 - Self-antigens and MHC
Sample 3 - Mucosal lumen antigens
Sample 4 - Peripheral interstitial lymph
Sample 1 - Self-antigens and MHC
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Sample 1 as the thymus by its lobules, dark cortex, pale medulla, Hassall corpuscles, and absence of follicles) -> Step 2 (Match the thymus to what it samples: self/MHC during T-cell development)

r.A: Sample 1 is the thymus, while blood-borne antigens are sampled by the spleen (Sample 3).
r.B: Sample 2 is a lymph node, which samples peripheral lymph entering via afferent lymphatics rather than conducting thymic self/MHC selection.
r.C: Sample 3 is the spleen, which samples blood; mucosal lumen antigens are sampled by MALT (Sample 4).
r.D: Sample 4 is MALT, which samples the mucosal lumen directly across specialized epithelium and lacks afferent lymphatics.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 11: One Map for the Whole System & Slide 32: Rapid recognition matrix

q.v: During T-cell maturation, bone marrow-derived precursors enter a primary lymphoid organ and migrate through distinct anatomical compartments where their T-cell receptors (TCRs) are tested. Which of the following correctly matches the anatomical compartment with the selection question asked and its immunological result?
o: Thymic cortex: Does the TCR bind self antigen too strongly? -> Central tolerance
Thymic medulla: Can the TCR recognize self MHC? -> MHC-restricted T cells
Thymic cortex: Can the TCR recognize self MHC? -> MHC-restricted T cells
Splenic white pulp: Does the TCR bind self antigen too strongly? -> Central tolerance
Lymph node paracortex: Can the TCR recognize self MHC? -> MHC-restricted T cells
q.p: Step 1 (Localize positive selection of immature thymocytes to the thymic cortex) -> Step 2 (Connect positive selection to the question 'Can the TCR recognize self MHC?', where survival yields MHC-restricted T cells)

r.A: Testing whether the TCR binds self antigen too strongly is negative selection, which occurs in the thymic medulla to produce central tolerance.
r.B: Positive selection for self-MHC recognition occurs in the thymic cortex, whereas the medulla performs negative selection.
r.D: The splenic white pulp is a secondary lymphoid compartment for blood surveillance, not a primary lymphoid site for T-cell selection.
r.E: The lymph node paracortex is the site where mature naive T cells encounter antigen presented by dendritic cells, not where thymic MHC restriction occurs.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 31: T-cell selection: two questions, two compartments

q.v: Which of the following anatomical features is shared by both mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) and the spleen?
o: Presence of Hassall corpuscles in the medulla
Absence of afferent lymphatic vessels
Absence of organized B-cell follicles
Presence of a central arteriole surrounded by T cells
Presence of a subcapsular sinus receiving lymph
q.p: Step 1 (Compare the structural landmarks of MALT and the spleen using the lymphoid organ map) -> Step 2 (Identify that both MALT and the spleen lack afferent lymphatic vessels, as MALT samples the mucosal lumen across epithelium and the spleen samples blood directly)

r.A: Hassall corpuscles are unique to the medulla of the thymus and are absent in both MALT and the spleen.
r.C: Both MALT and the spleen contain organized B-cell follicles; the thymus is the lymphoid organ that lacks follicles.
r.D: A central arteriole surrounded by a periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) is the signature structure of the spleen and is not found in MALT.
r.E: A subcapsular sinus receiving lymph from afferent vessels is a defining feature of lymph nodes, not MALT or the spleen.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 11: One Map for the Whole System

q.v: A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 5-day history of dry cough, fever, and shortness of breath. Chest radiograph reveals diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates consistent with a viral infection of the lung. During the immune response, antigen-bearing dendritic cells travel via lymphatic vessels from the pulmonary parenchyma to the regional draining lymph nodes. Which of the following lymph node groups is the primary site of initial antigen arrival in this patient?
o: Axillary nodes
Cervical nodes
Hilar and tracheobronchial nodes
Inguinal nodes
Mesenteric nodes
q.p: Step 1 (Identify pulmonary viral infection draining via regional lymphatics) -> Step 2 (Localize drainage of lung parenchyma to hilar/tracheobronchial lymph nodes)

r.A: Axillary lymph nodes receive lymphatic drainage from the upper extremities and breast, such as from an infected cut on the hand.
r.B: Cervical lymph nodes filter lymph draining from the head and neck region rather than the lower respiratory tract.
r.D: Inguinal lymph nodes receive lymph from the lower extremities, such as in a patient with cellulitis of the foot.
r.E: Mesenteric lymph nodes drain the gastrointestinal tract rather than the pulmonary parenchyma.

q.s: Slide 16, Reactive node: predict the enlarged compartment (LO3)

q.v: A 41-year-old man presents to the primary care clinic with a 1-week history of a painful, purulent skin laceration on his right palm sustained while repairing a metal fence. Physical examination reveals tender right axillary lymphadenopathy. Within the enlarged lymph nodes, activated B lymphocytes have differentiated into antibody-secreting plasma cells to export immunoglobulins into the efferent lymph. In which of the following anatomical compartments of the lymph node do these plasma cells predominantly reside?
o: Cortical follicles
Medullary cords
Medullary sinuses
Paracortex
Subcapsular sinus
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize antibody-secreting plasma cells in a reactive lymph node) -> Step 2 (Localize resident plasma cells to the medullary cords)

r.A: Cortical follicles are B-cell zones where germinal centers appear after activation, prior to plasma cell migration to the medulla.
r.C: Medullary sinuses contain macrophages and draining lymph en route to the efferent lymphatic vessel, rather than resident plasma cells.
r.D: The paracortex is the T-cell zone populated by T lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and high endothelial venules.
r.E: The subcapsular sinus is the initial space that receives incoming lymph from afferent lymphatic vessels on the convex surface.

q.s: Slide 14, Lymph node: place the cells (LO2)

q.v: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician for a routine checkup. He recently recovered from an acute viral gastroenteritis. During the infection, luminal viral antigens in the distal small intestine were transported across the specialized epithelium of Peyer patches by M cells and presented to underlying lymphocytes, resulting in plasma cell differentiation. Which of the following is the primary immunologic output of this specific lymphoid tissue?
o: Activated T cells and IgG in efferent lymph
Clearance of opsonized bacteria from blood
Mature naive MHC-restricted T cells
Mechanical filtration of rigid erythrocytes
Secretory IgA across the mucosal epithelium
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Peyer patches in the ileum as MALT activated via M-cell transcytosis) -> Step 2 (Connect MALT plasma cell function to mucosal secretory IgA responses)

r.A: Export of activated lymphocytes and antibody into efferent lymph is the key output of encapsulated lymph nodes.
r.B: Clearance of blood-borne opsonized encapsulated bacteria is a primary immune function of the spleen.
r.C: Production of mature naive MHC-restricted T cells is the primary output of the thymus.
r.D: Mechanical filtration and removal of rigid or senescent erythrocytes is performed by the splenic red pulp.

q.s: Slide 23, MALT: immune surveillance at the border; Slide 32, Rapid recognition matrix (LO4)

q.v: A 54-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with high fever, rigors, and hypotension due to bacteremia from an indwelling central venous catheter. As blood-borne bacterial antigens circulate through the spleen, they are captured and presented to T lymphocytes to initiate a systemic adaptive immune response. In which of the following splenic structures are these T lymphocytes primarily organized?
o: Cords of Billroth
Germinal centers
Marginal zone follicles
Periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS)
Venous sinusoids
q.p: Step 1 (Identify blood-borne antigen surveillance in the splenic white pulp) -> Step 2 (Localize splenic T cells to the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath around the central arteriole)

r.A: The cords of Billroth are located in the red pulp and function in macrophage-mediated erythrocyte quality control.
r.B: Germinal centers within white-pulp follicles are B-cell compartments rather than the primary T-cell zone.
r.C: Follicles adjacent to the central arteriole in the white pulp are composed of B lymphocytes.
r.E: Venous sinusoids are red pulp vascular channels with narrow endothelial slits that test erythrocyte deformability.

q.s: Slide 24, Spleen: two pulps, two jobs; Slide 32, Rapid recognition matrix (LO2)

q.v: A 4-month-old infant is evaluated in the immunology clinic for recurrent opportunistic infections. Diagnostic imaging reveals absence of the anterior mediastinal lymphoepithelial organ normally responsible for T-cell maturation. In a healthy infant, bone marrow-derived thymocyte precursors enter this organ and migrate to the medulla after successfully recognizing self-MHC in the cortex. Which of the following events normally occurs in the medullary compartment of this organ?
o: Apoptosis of cells that bind self-antigen too strongly
Apoptosis of cells unable to recognize self-MHC
Differentiation of B cells into IgA-secreting plasma cells
Filtration of incoming lymph through trabecular sinuses
Transcytosis of luminal antigens across M cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the thymus and its medullary compartment) -> Step 2 (Connect the thymic medulla to negative selection via apoptosis of strongly self-reactive T cells to establish central tolerance)

r.B: Apoptosis of thymocytes whose TCRs fail to recognize self-MHC occurs during positive selection in the thymic cortex.
r.C: Differentiation of B cells into IgA-secreting plasma cells occurs in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT).
r.D: Filtration of lymph through subcapsular, trabecular, and medullary sinuses occurs in lymph nodes.
r.E: Transcytosis of luminal antigens by M cells occurs across the specialized epithelium of MALT.

q.s: Slide 31, T-cell selection: two questions, two compartments (LO4)

q.v: A 68-year-old man undergoes a thoracic surgical procedure during which a small biopsy of normal anterior mediastinal tissue is obtained. Histologic examination reveals a bilobed organ divided into lobules by fibrous septa, with each lobule containing a dark outer cortex, a pale inner medulla with Hassall corpuscles, and abundant interspersed adipose tissue. Which of the following best explains the presence of increased adipose tissue in this patient's biopsy?
o: Accumulation of chylomicrons from intestinal lymphatics
Chronic obstruction of efferent lymphatic vessels
Compensatory hyperplasia of splenic red pulp cords
Infiltration by lipid-laden macrophages during positive selection
Normal age-related involution occurring after puberty
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize thymus histology by lobules, dark cortex, pale medulla, and Hassall corpuscles) -> Step 2 (Identify adipose replacement as normal post-pubertal thymic involution)

r.A: The thymus has no afferent lymphatics and does not sample intestinal lymph or chylomicrons.
r.B: Obstruction of lymphatic vessels causes protein-rich interstitial edema (lymphedema) in peripheral tissues, not thymic adiposity.
r.C: Splenic red pulp cords filter erythrocytes from the blood and are unrelated to mediastinal thymic architecture.
r.D: Positive selection involves thymocyte TCR interaction with self-MHC in the cortex, not lipid-laden macrophage infiltration.

q.s: Slide 29, Thymus: recognize the lymphoepithelial organ (LO1)

q.v:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of abrupt-onset fever, chills, and malaise. Three years ago, she underwent an emergency splenectomy following blunt abdominal trauma. Her vital signs are: temperature 39.4 C (102.9 F), heart rate 118/min, and blood pressure 96/60 mm Hg. Laboratory studies and peripheral blood smear examination are obtained:
  White blood cell count: 16,500/mm3
  Platelet count: 480,000/mm3
  Peripheral blood smear: basophilic nuclear remnants inside erythrocytes; increased target cells
Blood cultures are drawn and empiric intravenous antibiotics are initiated immediately. This patient is at greatest risk for rapidly progressive bloodstream infection caused by which of the following groups of pathogens?
o: Cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Varicella-zoster virus
Enterobius vermicularis, Giardia lamblia, and Cryptosporidium
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Listeria, and Candida albicans
Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Pseudomonas
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret post-splenectomy hematologic findings: Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, and thrombocytosis from reduced platelet sequestration) -> Step 2 (Predict susceptibility to opsonized encapsulated bacteria: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, and N. meningitidis)

r.A: Defense against herpesviruses is primarily mediated by T lymphocytes rather than splenic clearance of opsonized blood-borne organisms.
r.B: Luminal intestinal parasites are surveyed at the mucosal border by MALT rather than cleared from the blood by the spleen.
r.C: Intracellular bacteria and fungi are primarily controlled by T-cell-mediated immunity, which is impaired in thymic dysfunction.
r.D: Asplenia specifically impairs rapid clearance of opsonized encapsulated bacteria from the blood rather than non-encapsulated pyogenic bacteria.

q.s: Slide 27, Checkpoint; Slide 28, Asplenia: what function cannot be fully replaced? (LO5)

q.v:
An immunologist is studying the trafficking of fluid, antigens, and lymphocytes across different compartments of a peripheral lymph node. Fluid samples and tissue biopsies are collected from five distinct anatomical locations (Locations 1-5) within the node and analyzed:
  Location 1: Enters at the convex surface; contains valves and drains interstitial fluid from tissue
  Location 2: Directly beneath the capsule; receives incoming fluid from Location 1
  Location 3: Deep to the cortex; contains high endothelial venules, dendritic cells, and T cells
  Location 4: Outer region containing B-cell follicles with active germinal centers
  Location 5: Exits at the concave hilum; carries exported antibodies and draining lymph
Based on these findings, which of the following correctly identifies the anatomical structure where circulating naive T lymphocytes exit the bloodstream to enter the lymph node parenchyma?
o: Location 1
Location 2
Location 3
Location 4
Location 5
q.p: Step 1 (Match Location 3 to the paracortex based on T cells, dendritic cells, and high endothelial venules) -> Step 2 (Identify high endothelial venules in the paracortex as the entry route for blood-borne naive lymphocytes)

r.A: Location 1 describes afferent lymphatic vessels, which deliver tissue lymph and migrating dendritic cells rather than blood-borne lymphocytes.
r.B: Location 2 describes the subcapsular sinus, which receives lymph from afferent lymphatics rather than blood from the circulation.
r.D: Location 4 describes the cortex, which houses B-cell follicles and germinal centers rather than the high endothelial venules of the paracortex.
r.E: Location 5 describes the efferent lymphatic vessel at the hilum, which exports lymph and antibodies out of the node.

q.s: Slide 13, Lymph node: follow the lymph; Slide 14, Lymph node: place the cells (LO3)

q.v: Which of the following structural features facilitates the entry of excess interstitial fluid and proteins into blind-ended lymphatic capillaries within peripheral tissues?
o: Active pumping by smooth muscle in the capillary wall
Continuous tight junctions between endothelial cells
Fenestrated endothelium with a thick basement membrane
Overlapping endothelial cells and an incomplete basement membrane
Transcytosis across specialized microfold (M) epithelial cells
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the structural architecture of blind-ended lymphatic capillaries) -> Step 2 (Connect overlapping endothelial cells and an incomplete basement membrane to fluid entry)

r.A: Lymphatic vessels have no central pump and rely on skeletal muscle contraction and respiratory movement to propel lymph.
r.B: Continuous tight junctions would block fluid entry, whereas overlapping endothelial cells create openings that favor interstitial fluid entry.
r.C: Lymphatic capillaries possess an incomplete basement membrane rather than a thick basement membrane.
r.E: Transcytosis by M cells is the mechanism for antigen transport across the mucosal epithelium in MALT, not fluid entry into lymphatics.

q.s: Slide 12, Lymphatics: the delivery network (LO1)

q.v: In the architectural organization of lymphoid organs, which of the following correctly pairs a primary or secondary lymphoid organ with the absence of B-cell follicles?
o: Lymph node
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)
Peyer patches of the ileum
Spleen
Thymus
q.p: Step 1 (Compare the B-cell and T-cell compartments across the four major lymphoid organs) -> Step 2 (Identify the thymus as the primary T-cell organ that lacks B-cell follicles)

r.A: The lymph node contains organized B-cell follicles and germinal centers within its outer cortex.
r.B: MALT contains organized B-cell follicles positioned directly beneath the exposed mucosal epithelium.
r.C: Peyer patches are prominent MALT aggregates in the ileum that contain subepithelial B-cell follicles.
r.D: The spleen contains B-cell follicles located adjacent to the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath within the white pulp.

q.s: Slide 11, One Map for the Whole System; Slide 32, Rapid recognition matrix (LO1, LO2)

Adds 10 cloze notes (deck: Fuerst - Lipoproteins). B&B has no cards on Tangier disease, Lp(a) or saturated fat and LDL clearance.

add.cloze: Apo{{c1::E}} mediates hepatic uptake of chylomicron remnants by {{c2::receptor-mediated endocytosis}}
add.extra: Remnant receptors on the liver include the LDL receptor. Chylomicrons get ApoE (and ApoC-II) from HDL in the blood.

add.cloze: The primary structural apolipoprotein required for synthesis and secretion of VLDL by the liver is {{c1::ApoB-100}}
add.extra: The ApoB gene encodes both B-48 (intestine, chylomicrons) and B-100 (liver, VLDL/IDL/LDL); RNA editing in enterocytes creates a stop codon → shorter B-48.

add.cloze: Statins {{c1::competitively}} inhibit HMG-CoA reductase
add.extra: Lowering hepatocyte cholesterol then increases LDL receptor expression and LDL clearance.

add.cloze: Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa) is caused by mutations in the {{c1::LDL receptor}} pathway (most in the LDL-binding domain). Normally, after LDL is delivered to the endosome, the LDL receptor is {{c2::recycled back to the plasma membrane}}
add.extra: LDLR life cycle: synthesis → transport → LDL binding → clustering in clathrin-coated pits → recycling; mutations can hit any step.

add.cloze: When intracellular cholesterol is high: {{c1::ACAT is activated}} to store cholesterol as esters, and {{c2::HMG-CoA reductase activity and LDL receptor synthesis}} are downregulated
add.extra: Mevalonate also feeds back to inhibit HMG-CoA reductase.

add.cloze: A lipoprotein has a hydrophobic core of {{c1::triglycerides and cholesteryl esters}} and an amphipathic outer monolayer of {{c2::phospholipids and unesterified cholesterol}} (plus apolipoproteins)
Glycerol released from chylomicron triglycerides is converted to glycerol 3-phosphate in the liver by {{c1::glycerol kinase}}
add.extra: Adipocytes lack glycerol kinase, so glycerol goes to the liver (e.g., for gluconeogenesis).

add.cloze: Deficiency of Apo{{c1::C-II}} (or of lipoprotein lipase) prevents clearance of triglycerides in lipoproteins from the blood → hypertriglyceridemia
add.extra: ApoC-II is the cofactor that activates LPL on capillary endothelium (bound to heparan sulfate proteoglycan).

add.cloze: De novo cholesterol synthesis is activated in the {{c1::well-fed state, when insulin signaling dominates}}
The amino acid {{c1::leucine}} can serve as a precursor for the HMG-CoA reductase pathway
add.extra: Leucine is purely ketogenic; its breakdown yields acetyl-CoA and HMG-CoA.
