q.v: A 52-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use presents to the clinic with weight loss and foul-smelling, greasy stools that float in the toilet bowl. Imaging of the abdomen reveals pancreatic calcifications consistent with chronic pancreatitis. Which of the following enzyme and cofactor pairs is normally required in the intestinal lumen to complete the hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids?
o: Lingual lipase and bile salts
Gastric lipase and ApoB-48
Pancreatic lipase and colipase
Lipoprotein lipase and ApoC-II
Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase and ApoA-I
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize fat malabsorption due to pancreatic insufficiency) -> Step 2 (Identify pancreatic lipase and colipase as the enzyme-cofactor pair that binds bile salt micelles to complete intestinal triglyceride hydrolysis)

r.A: Lingual lipase partially hydrolyzes dietary triglycerides early in digestion and does not require bile salts to complete intestinal hydrolysis.
r.B: Gastric lipase partially hydrolyzes dietary triglycerides in the stomach, whereas ApoB-48 is required later for chylomicron secretion from enterocytes.
r.D: Lipoprotein lipase and its cofactor ApoC-II hydrolyze triglycerides within circulating chylomicrons and VLDL at the capillary endothelium, not in the intestinal lumen.
r.E: Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) and its activator ApoA-I esterify cholesterol on HDL particles in the plasma during reverse cholesterol transport.

q.s: SLO1 / Slide 8: Dietary Triglyceride Is Hydrolyzed to Monoglycerides/Free Fatty Acids for Intestinal Absorption

q.v: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for poor weight gain, abdominal distension, and chronic fatty diarrhea since birth. Blood samples drawn both fasting and two hours after feeding show a complete absence of chylomicrons in the plasma. A small bowel biopsy demonstrates enterocytes distended with re-esterified triglycerides that cannot be exported into the intestinal lacteals. Which of the following apolipoproteins is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: ApoA-I
ApoB-48
ApoB-100
ApoC-II
ApoE
q.p: Step 1 (Identify failure of enterocytes to secrete nascent chylomicrons into lacteals) -> Step 2 (Link chylomicron assembly and secretion from intestinal mucosal cells to ApoB-48)

r.A: ApoA-I is synthesized by hepatocytes and enterocytes to activate LCAT on HDL particles, not to secrete chylomicrons.
r.C: ApoB-100 is synthesized by hepatocytes for the release of nascent VLDL from the liver, whereas enterocytes require ApoB-48.
r.D: ApoC-II is acquired in the circulation from HDL to activate capillary lipoprotein lipase, after chylomicrons have already been secreted.
r.E: ApoE is acquired from HDL in the circulation to mediate receptor-mediated endocytosis of chylomicron remnants by the liver.

q.s: SLO1 / Slide 9: Intestinal Mucosal Cells Package The Dietary Lipid into Chylomicrons

q.v:
A 19-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain radiating to her back. She has had two similar episodes over the past three years. A blood sample drawn after a meal appears milky and turbid. Laboratory studies show:
  Total cholesterol: 185 mg/dL
  Triglycerides: 2,400 mg/dL
  LDL cholesterol: 90 mg/dL
  HDL cholesterol: 42 mg/dL
Assays of capillary endothelial lipoprotein lipase show normal enzyme protein levels, but the enzyme fails to hydrolyze chylomicron triglycerides until normal donor HDL is added to the sample. Which of the following apolipoproteins is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: ApoA-I
ApoB-48
ApoB-100
ApoC-II
ApoD
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab panel showing severe postprandial hypertriglyceridemia and milky plasma corrected by HDL addition) -> Step 2 (Identify ApoC-II as the apolipoprotein transferred from HDL that activates lipoprotein lipase)

r.A: ApoA-I activates LCAT on HDL particles to esterify cholesterol and does not activate lipoprotein lipase.
r.B: ApoB-48 is required for enterocyte secretion of nascent chylomicrons, so its deficiency would cause low plasma triglycerides rather than chylomicron accumulation.
r.C: ApoB-100 is the structural apolipoprotein of hepatic VLDL and LDL and does not serve as the cofactor for lipoprotein lipase.
r.E: ApoD is associated with cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP) on HDL particles rather than lipoprotein lipase activation.

q.s: SLO1 / Slide 11: How Are Chylomicrons Used As A Source of Energy?

q.v: During the fasting state, hepatocytes package endogenous triglycerides into nascent VLDL particles and secrete them into the bloodstream. As VLDL circulates through peripheral capillaries, lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes its core triglycerides, converting the particle into IDL and eventually LDL. Which of the following apolipoproteins is synthesized by hepatocytes to mediate nascent VLDL release and remains on the resulting LDL particle to bind the hepatic LDL receptor?
o: ApoB-100
ApoA-I
ApoB-48
ApoC-II
ApoD
q.p: Step 1 (Trace hepatic VLDL secretion and its conversion to LDL) -> Step 2 (Identify ApoB-100 as the hepatocyte-derived protein required for VLDL release and LDLR binding)

r.B: ApoA-I is associated with HDL particles and functions to activate lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT).
r.C: ApoB-48 is produced in the gut for chylomicron release and is not present on hepatic VLDL or LDL particles.
r.D: ApoC-II is temporarily exchanged between HDL and VLDL to activate lipoprotein lipase and does not mediate LDL receptor binding.
r.E: ApoD is associated with HDL and cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP) rather than VLDL secretion or LDL receptor binding.

q.s: SLO2 / Slide 13: VLDL Metabolism and the Formation of LDL

q.v:
A 26-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with progressive numbness and weakness in his hands and feet. Physical examination reveals enlarged, yellow-orange tonsils, mild corneal clouding, and hepatosplenomegaly. A fasting lipid panel shows:
  Total cholesterol: 65 mg/dL
  Triglycerides: 210 mg/dL
  LDL cholesterol: 45 mg/dL
  HDL cholesterol: 2 mg/dL
Which of the following physiological processes is most directly impaired as a consequence of this patient's near absence of HDL particles?
o: Hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides in the intestinal lumen
Secretion of nascent chylomicrons into the intestinal lacteals
Export of endogenous triglycerides from the liver as VLDL
Reverse cholesterol transport from peripheral tissues to the liver
Conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate in the endoplasmic reticulum
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Tangier disease from yellow-orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly, neuropathy, and near-absent HDL) -> Step 2 (Connect near absence of HDL to impaired reverse cholesterol transport)

r.A: Intestinal triglyceride hydrolysis is mediated by pancreatic lipase, colipase, and bile salts, which are unaffected in Tangier disease.
r.B: Secretion of nascent chylomicrons into lacteals requires intestinal ApoB-48 rather than HDL particles.
r.C: Export of endogenous triglycerides from the liver is carried out by ApoB-100-containing VLDL particles.
r.E: Conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate is the rate-limiting step of de novo cholesterol synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum.

q.s: SLO2 / Slide 19: Reverse Cholesterol Transport by HDL

q.v: A 48-year-old man with no history of smoking, hypertension, or diabetes undergoes a coronary CT angiogram after experiencing exertional chest pain, which reveals severe coronary atherosclerosis and a partially occlusive thrombus. His routine fasting lipid panel is unremarkable, so his cardiologist orders a specialized test that need only be measured once in a patient's lifetime because its levels are genetically determined. The test reveals a markedly elevated level of an LDL particle with an attached apolipoprotein that mimics plasminogen. Which of the following particles was elevated in this patient?
o: Nascent chylomicron
Chylomicron remnant
VLDL
Lp(a)
Pre-beta HDL
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize an atherogenic and thrombogenic LDL variant measured once due to genetic determination) -> Step 2 (Identify Lp(a) as LDL with Apo(a) attached that mimics plasminogen and blocks clot breakdown)

r.A: Nascent chylomicrons contain ApoB-48 and transport dietary triglycerides from the intestine after meals.
r.B: Chylomicron remnants are cleared by hepatic ApoE receptors and do not contain Apo(a) or mimic plasminogen.
r.C: VLDL transports endogenous triglycerides from the liver and varies with diet and metabolic state rather than being measured once in a lifetime.
r.E: Pre-beta HDL participates in reverse cholesterol transport by acquiring free cholesterol from peripheral cells.

q.s: SLO2 / Slide 17: Lipoproteins Transport Lipids between The Tissues

q.v: Which of the following enzymes is an integral membrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum that uses NADPH to catalyze the rate-limiting step of de novo cholesterol synthesis?
o: Thiolase
HMG-CoA synthase
HMG-CoA reductase
Acyl-CoA cholesterol acyltransferase
Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the rate-limiting step of de novo cholesterol synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum) -> Step 2 (Select HMG-CoA reductase as the NADPH-dependent enzyme converting HMG-CoA to mevalonate)

r.A: Thiolase condenses two molecules of acetyl-CoA to form acetoacetyl-CoA early in the pathway and is not rate-limiting.
r.B: HMG-CoA synthase converts acetoacetyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA into HMG-CoA prior to the rate-limiting step.
r.D: Acyl-CoA cholesterol acyltransferase esterifies excess intracellular free cholesterol for storage when cellular cholesterol levels rise.
r.E: Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) operates in the plasma on HDL particles to esterify cholesterol derived from phosphatidylcholine.

q.s: SLO3 / Slide 21: Stages in Cholesterol Synthesis & Slide 23: HMG-CoA Reductase

q.v: A hepatocyte is exposed to high concentrations of circulating LDL, leading to rapid receptor-mediated endocytosis and a significant rise in intracellular free cholesterol levels. Which of the following coordinated regulatory changes will occur inside this hepatocyte in response to the elevated intracellular cholesterol?
o: HMG-CoA reductase inhibited / ACAT activated / LDL receptor synthesis inhibited
HMG-CoA reductase activated / ACAT inhibited / LDL receptor synthesis activated
HMG-CoA reductase inhibited / ACAT inhibited / LDL receptor synthesis activated
HMG-CoA reductase activated / ACAT activated / LDL receptor synthesis inhibited
HMG-CoA reductase inhibited / ACAT activated / LDL receptor synthesis activated
q.p: Step 1 (Determine the cellular state: rising intracellular free cholesterol) -> Step 2 (Apply the three regulatory responses: inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, activate acyl-CoA cholesterol acyltransferase, and inhibit LDL receptor synthesis)

r.B: This pattern describes the opposite response (seen when intracellular cholesterol is low), whereas high intracellular cholesterol suppresses both synthesis and uptake.
r.C: High intracellular cholesterol activates ACAT to store cholesterol esters and inhibits LDL receptor synthesis to prevent further cholesterol uptake.
r.D: Rising intracellular cholesterol inhibits, rather than activates, HMG-CoA reductase via negative feedback.
r.E: Rising intracellular cholesterol inhibits LDL receptor synthesis so the cell stops importing additional LDL from the plasma.

q.s: SLO3 / Slide 22: Cholesterol Directly Regulates Genes in Its Own Metabolism

q.v:
A 12-year-old boy is evaluated in the lipid clinic after developing firm, nodular swellings over both Achilles tendons and yellow plaques on his knees and elbows. Both of his parents have a history of hypercholesterolemia treated with statins. A fasting lipid panel is obtained:
  Total cholesterol: 690 mg/dL
  VLDL cholesterol: 20 mg/dL
  LDL cholesterol: 635 mg/dL
  HDL cholesterol: 35 mg/dL
  Triglycerides: 105 mg/dL
Genetic sequencing of the defective receptor in this patient is most likely to identify a mutation in which of the following functional domains?
o: Signal sequence domain
LDL ligand binding domain
EGF precursor homology domain
O-linked sugars domain
Cytoplasmic domain
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia from tendon xanthomas in adolescence and LDL > 600 mg/dL) -> Step 2 (Identify the LDL ligand binding domain as the site where most LDLR mutations reside)

r.A: Mutations in the signal sequence domain (Exon 1) are much less frequent than those in the ligand binding domain.
r.C: Although mutations can occur in the EGF precursor homology domain, the highest concentration of FH mutations resides in the LDL binding domain.
r.D: Very few mutations in familial hypercholesterolemia occur in the O-linked sugars domain (Exon 15).
r.E: Mutations in the cytoplasmic domain are rare compared with mutations in the LDL ligand binding domain.

q.s: SLO4 / Slide 30: Familial Hypercholesterolemia & Slide 32: Most Mutations Reside in the LDL Binding Domain of the Receptor

q.v: A 49-year-old woman with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia continues to have an elevated serum LDL cholesterol of 195 mg/dL despite maximally tolerated lovastatin therapy and dietary saturated fat restriction. Her physician adds a monoclonal antibody medication that increases the number of functional LDL receptors on the hepatocyte surface by preventing their normal intracellular degradation. Which of the following is the molecular target of this new medication?
o: HMG-CoA reductase
PCSK9
Intestinal bile acids
Cholesterol ester transfer protein
Pancreatic colipase
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize an add-on LDL-lowering therapy that blocks degradation of hepatic LDL receptors) -> Step 2 (Identify PCSK9 as the protein that normally degrades LDL receptors and is targeted by inhibitors to increase LDLR number)

r.A: HMG-CoA reductase is the target of statins like lovastatin, which block cholesterol production rather than directly preventing receptor degradation.
r.C: Bile salt binding resins bind intestinal bile acids to deplete hepatic cholesterol, rather than directly blocking the protein that degrades LDL receptors.
r.D: Cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP) transfers cholesterol esters from HDL to LDL and is not the target that degrades hepatic LDL receptors.
r.E: Pancreatic colipase assists pancreatic lipase in intestinal triglyceride digestion and does not regulate hepatic LDL receptor degradation.

q.s: SLO4 / Slide 33: Multiple Therapies Lower LDL Cholesterol: Increase LDLR Number and LDL Uptake

q.v: A 64-year-old woman presents to the gastroenterology clinic with progressive weight loss, bloating, and bulky, greasy stools six months after undergoing surgical resection of her terminal ileum for severe Crohn disease. Her physician explains that the surgery disrupted the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts, impairing the formation of mixed micelles in the small intestinal lumen. Which of the following enzymes requires colipase to bind to these bile salt micelles and complete the luminal hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids?
o: Gastric lipase
Lingual lipase
Lipoprotein lipase
Pancreatic lipase
Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase
q.p: Step 1 (Terminal ileal resection depletes bile salts needed to form nascent bile salt micelles with dietary lipids) -> Step 2 (Pancreatic lipase and its cofactor colipase bind to bile salt micelles to complete hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides to monoglycerides and free fatty acids)

r.A: Gastric lipase only partially hydrolyzes dietary triglycerides in the stomach prior to bile salt micelle formation in the small intestine.
r.B: Lingual lipase initiates partial hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides in the mouth and stomach rather than completing hydrolysis on bile salt micelles.
r.C: Lipoprotein lipase is anchored to capillary endothelial cells and hydrolyzes triglycerides within circulating chylomicrons and VLDL when activated by Apo C-II.
r.E: Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase is activated by Apo A-1 on HDL particles to esterify free cholesterol during reverse cholesterol transport.

q.s: SLO1, Slide 8: Dietary Triglyceride Is Hydrolyzed to Monoglycerides/Free Fatty Acids for Intestinal Absorption

q.v:
A 31-year-old man participates in a clinical nutrition study evaluating postprandial lipid trafficking. Two hours after he consumes a meal rich in butter and eggs, blood samples are drawn from both the superior mesenteric vein (portal circulation) and the radial artery (systemic circulation). Laboratory analysis of the lipid particles entering his systemic circulation is performed:
  Plasma appearance: turbid and milky
  Predominant lipoprotein particle: nascent chylomicrons
  Required structural apolipoprotein: Apo B-48
By which of the following anatomical pathways did these newly synthesized lipoprotein particles directly exit the intestinal mucosa before entering the systemic bloodstream?
o: Hepatic portal vein
Intestinal lacteals
Biliary canaliculi
Capillary fenestrations
Clathrin-coated pits
q.p: Step 1 (Enterocytes re-esterify free fatty acids and monoglycerides into triglycerides and package them with Apo B-48 into nascent chylomicrons) -> Step 2 (Chylomicrons are secreted into intestinal lacteals of the lymphatic system before entering the systemic bloodstream)

r.A: Water-soluble nutrients and short-chain molecules enter the hepatic portal vein, whereas chylomicrons bypass the portal vein by entering the lymphatics.
r.C: Biliary canaliculi transport bile acids and cholesterol from hepatocytes into the biliary tree for secretion into the intestine.
r.D: Capillary fenestrations in the intestinal villi absorb non-lipid nutrients, while large chylomicron particles require lymphatic lacteals for export.
r.E: Clathrin-coated pits mediate the receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL particles into target cells rather than the secretion of chylomicrons.

q.s: SLO1, Slide 9: Intestinal Mucosal Cells Package The Dietary Lipid into Chylomicrons

q.v: A 54-year-old man presents for a routine checkup and is found to have elevated triglycerides and cholesterol on a non-fasting lipid panel. His physician explains that after peripheral capillary lipoprotein lipase removes triglycerides from dietary chylomicrons and hepatic VLDL, the resulting remnant particles must be cleared from the circulation by hepatocytes. Which of the following apolipoproteins, acquired in the bloodstream from HDL particles, is required for the receptor-mediated endocytosis of chylomicron remnants by the liver?
o: Apo A-1
Apo B-48
Apo C-II
Apo D
Apo E
q.p: Step 1 (Nascent chylomicrons acquire Apo C-II and Apo E from HDL in the circulation and undergo triglyceride hydrolysis by lipoprotein lipase) -> Step 2 (Chylomicron remnants retain Apo E, which mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis by hepatic Apo E receptors and LDLR)

r.A: Apo A-1 is synthesized by hepatocytes and enterocytes to activate lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) on HDL particles.
r.B: Apo B-48 is required for the assembly and secretion of nascent chylomicrons from enterocytes, but it does not bind hepatic remnant receptors.
r.C: Apo C-II functions as the essential cofactor that activates capillary lipoprotein lipase to cleave triglycerides from chylomicrons and VLDL.
r.D: Apo D is associated with cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP) on HDL particles rather than mediating remnant endocytosis.

q.s: SLO1 / SLO2, Slide 10: Chylomicron Metabolism & Slide 16: Apolipoproteins Impart Functions/Signals on the Lipoprotein

q.v: Both Apo B-48 and Apo B-100 are encoded by the same ApoB gene. Which of the following correctly pairs the site of synthesis and the primary lipoprotein particle associated with each of these apolipoproteins?
o: Apo B-48: hepatocyte / VLDL; Apo B-100: enterocyte / chylomicron
Apo B-48: enterocyte / chylomicron; Apo B-100: hepatocyte / VLDL
Apo B-48: enterocyte / HDL; Apo B-100: hepatocyte / chylomicron
Apo B-48: hepatocyte / LDL; Apo B-100: enterocyte / VLDL
Apo B-48: adipocyte / chylomicron; Apo B-100: hepatocyte / HDL
q.p: Step 1 (The single ApoB gene is expressed in both intestinal enterocytes and hepatic parenchymal cells) -> Step 2 (Enterocytes produce Apo B-48 for nascent chylomicron release, whereas hepatocytes produce Apo B-100 for VLDL secretion, which remains on IDL and LDL)

r.A: This reverses the tissues and lipoproteins; Apo B-48 is made in the gut for chylomicrons and Apo B-100 is made in the liver for VLDL.
r.C: HDL particles contain Apo A-1, Apo C-II, Apo D, and Apo E rather than Apo B-48, and chylomicrons are made in the gut rather than the liver.
r.D: LDL contains Apo B-100 derived from hepatic VLDL metabolism, whereas VLDL is never synthesized by intestinal enterocytes.
r.E: Adipocytes store triglycerides and take up free fatty acids, but they do not synthesize Apo B-48 or secrete chylomicrons.

q.s: SLO2, Slide 13: VLDL Metabolism and the Formation of LDL & Slide 16: Apolipoproteins Impart Functions/Signals on the Lipoprotein

q.v: During reverse cholesterol transport, nascent HDL particles collect unesterified cholesterol from peripheral tissues and convert it into cholesteryl esters via lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). Which of the following proteins, associated with Apo D on mature HDL particles, subsequently transfers these cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL, IDL, and LDL particles?
o: Acyl-CoA cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT)
Cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP)
3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) synthase
Lipoprotein lipase (LPL)
Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9)
q.p: Step 1 (Apo A-1 activates LCAT on HDL to convert phosphatidylcholine and free cholesterol into hydrophobic cholesteryl esters) -> Step 2 (Cholesterol ester transfer protein [CETP], associated with Apo D, transfers cholesteryl esters from mature HDL to VLDL, IDL, and LDL)

r.A: Acyl-CoA cholesterol acyltransferase is an intracellular enzyme activated when cytosolic cholesterol rises to esterify cholesterol for cellular storage.
r.C: HMG-CoA synthase is an intracellular enzyme in the de novo cholesterol synthesis pathway that condenses acetoacetyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA.
r.D: Lipoprotein lipase is an endothelial enzyme activated by Apo C-II that hydrolyzes triglycerides in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL.
r.E: PCSK9 is a secreted protein that binds to and degrades hepatic LDL receptors rather than transferring cholesteryl esters between lipoproteins.

q.s: SLO2, Slide 15: HDL Metabolism, Slide 16 & Slide 18: Reverse Cholesterol Transport by HDL

q.v: A 58-year-old man is started on lovastatin after a routine lipid panel shows an elevated LDL cholesterol of 175 mg/dL. His physician explains that lovastatin competitively inhibits the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo cholesterol biosynthesis because the drug's chemical structure closely resembles the reaction's product, which also serves as the natural negative feedback inhibitor of this enzyme. Which of the following compounds is the immediate product of this rate-limiting reaction?
o: Acetoacetyl-CoA
Acetyl-CoA
HMG-CoA
Mevalonate
Squalene
q.p: Step 1 (HMG-CoA reductase uses 2 NADPH to catalyze the rate-limiting conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane) -> Step 2 (Mevalonate inhibits HMG-CoA reductase via negative feedback, and lovastatin structurally mimics mevalonate to inhibit the enzyme)

r.A: Acetoacetyl-CoA is formed early in the pathway by the condensation of two acetyl-CoA molecules via thiolase prior to HMG-CoA formation.
r.B: Acetyl-CoA is the initial two-carbon starting substrate for de novo cholesterol synthesis rather than the product of HMG-CoA reductase.
r.C: HMG-CoA is the immediate substrate of HMG-CoA reductase, synthesized from acetoacetyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA by HMG-CoA synthase.
r.E: Squalene is a downstream 30-carbon intermediate formed later in cholesterol synthesis from polymerization of activated isoprene units.

q.s: SLO3, Slide 21: Stages in Cholesterol Synthesis & Slide 23: HMG-CoA Reductase

q.v: A 42-year-old woman comes to the preventive cardiology clinic seeking dietary advice after her fasting lipid panel shows elevated total and LDL cholesterol. She reports cooking daily with coconut oil and consuming large amounts of full-fat dairy and tropical fats. The physician counsels her that certain dietary saturated fatty acids raise plasma LDL cholesterol by reducing hepatic LDL receptor activity, whereas shorter-chain saturated fatty acids have no effect on LDL clearance. Based on the carbon chain lengths of saturated fatty acids, which of the following pairs has the greatest effect on reducing LDL receptor activity?
o: C8 and C10
C10 and C12
C14 and C16
C16 and C18
C8 and C18
q.p: Step 1 (Dietary saturated fatty acids differ by carbon chain length in their effect on hepatic LDL receptor activity) -> Step 2 (C14 and C16 saturated fats reduce LDLR activity the most [C14~C16 >= C12 >>> C18], whereas C8 and C10 produce no change)

r.A: Medium-chain saturated fatty acids with 8 and 10 carbons (C8 and C10) produce no change in hepatic LDL receptor activity or LDL clearance.
r.B: C10 causes no change in LDL clearance, and while C12 may reduce LDL clearance, it also increases HDL and is less potent than C14 and C16.
r.D: Although C16 strongly reduces LDL receptor activity, C18 (stearic acid) has a much weaker effect (C14~C16 >= C12 >>> C18).
r.E: Neither C8 (no change) nor C18 (minimal effect compared to C14 and C16) is a primary driver of saturated fat-induced LDLR reduction.

q.s: SLO3, Slide 24: Saturated fat and LDL Clearance

q.v: A 61-year-old man who died of an acute myocardial infarction undergoes autopsy. Histologic examination of the left anterior descending coronary artery reveals a thickened intima containing a necrotic lipid core covered by a thin fibrous cap and numerous lipid-laden foam cells. Which of the following cell types migrates across the damaged endothelium into the tunica intima and engulfs excess LDL to form these foam cells?
o: Endothelial cells
Hepatocytes
Monocytes / macrophages
Platelets
Smooth muscle cells
q.p: Step 1 (Endothelial damage allows circulating LDL and monocytes to migrate across the endothelium into the arterial intima via VCAM-1) -> Step 2 (Monocytes differentiate into macrophages in the intima and ingest excess cholesterol-rich LDL to become foam cells, forming fatty streaks and atheromas)

r.A: Endothelial cells line the vessel lumen and undergo damage that initiates plaque formation, but they do not differentiate into intimal foam cells.
r.B: Hepatocytes internalize LDL from the circulation via LDLR to regulate systemic cholesterol levels rather than migrating into arterial walls.
r.D: Platelets adhere to ruptured plaques to form an occlusive arterial thrombus, but they are not the precursor cells of intimal foam cells.
r.E: Smooth muscle cells are recruited by cytokines from the media to form the fibrous cap over the plaque rather than differentiating into macrophage foam cells.

q.s: SLO4, Slide 28: Atherosclerosis: Applications of Enzyme Inhibition & Slide 29: Development of Atherosclerosis

q.v:
A 34-year-old man with a family history of premature coronary artery disease presents for evaluation of hypercholesterolemia and Achilles tendon xanthomas. Molecular analysis of his cultured fibroblasts is performed to determine the specific functional defect in his LDL receptor life cycle:
  LDL receptor protein synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum: normal
  LDL receptor transport through the Golgi to the cell surface: normal
  Clustering of LDL receptors in clathrin-coated pits: normal
  Endosomal recycling of LDL receptors to the plasma membrane: normal
  Surface binding of Apo B-100-containing LDL particles: markedly decreased
A mutation in which of the following exons or regions of the LDL receptor gene most likely accounts for the most common class of defect seen in this patient?
o: Exon 1 (signal sequence)
Exons 2 to 6 (ligand binding domain)
Exons 7 to 14 (EGF precursor homology domain)
Exon 15 (O-linked sugars domain)
Exons 16 to 17 (membrane-spanning domain)
q.p: Step 1 (Familial hypercholesterolemia can result from mutations affecting LDLR synthesis, transport, LDL binding, clustering in coated pits, or recycling) -> Step 2 (The patient has defective LDL binding with normal synthesis, transport, clustering, and recycling; most FH mutations reside in the LDL ligand-binding domain encoded by exons 2 to 6)

r.A: Mutations in the promoter or exon 1 signal sequence impair initial synthesis and translocation of the receptor into the endoplasmic reticulum.
r.C: The EGF precursor homology domain (exons 7 to 14) is required for acid-dependent dissociation of LDL in the endosome and receptor recycling.
r.D: Exon 15 encodes the O-linked sugar domain near the extracellular surface and has very few documented familial hypercholesterolemia mutations.
r.E: Exons 16 and 17 encode the hydrophobic membrane-spanning domain that anchors the receptor in the plasma membrane rather than binding LDL.

q.s: SLO4, Slide 31: Mutations in Familial Hypercholesterolemia & Slide 32: Most Mutations Reside in the LDL Binding Domain of the Receptor

q.v: A 56-year-old woman with hypercholesterolemia develops severe muscle aches after starting lovastatin and is switched to a bile salt binding resin. After eight weeks of therapy, her serum LDL cholesterol has decreased by 20%. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which bile salt binding resins lower plasma LDL cholesterol?
o: Activation of LCAT on circulating nascent HDL particles
Depletion of hepatic bile acids, driving conversion of hepatic cholesterol to bile acids and upregulating LDL receptors
Direct competitive inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum
Inhibition of intestinal pancreatic lipase and colipase activity in the duodenum
Prevention of PCSK9-mediated degradation of LDL receptors in hepatocyte lysosomes
q.p: Step 1 (Bile salt binding resins prevent intestinal reabsorption of bile acids, causing hepatic bile acid depletion and diverting intracellular hepatic cholesterol into bile acid synthesis) -> Step 2 (Lowered intracellular hepatic cholesterol stimulates synthesis and surface expression of LDL receptors, increasing hepatic uptake of plasma LDL)

r.A: LCAT is activated by Apo A-1 on HDL particles to esterify free cholesterol and is not the target of bile salt binding resins.
r.C: Direct competitive inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase in the endoplasmic reticulum is the mechanism of statin medications such as lovastatin.
r.D: Inhibition of pancreatic lipase impairs dietary triglyceride hydrolysis in the intestinal lumen rather than depleting hepatic bile acids to upregulate LDLR.
r.E: Preventing the degradation of hepatic LDL receptors is the mechanism of action of monoclonal PCSK9 inhibitors rather than bile acid resins.

q.s: SLO4, Slide 33: Multiple Therapies Lower LDL Cholesterol: Increase LDLR Number and LDL Uptake

Picks limited to what the slides discuss; related B&B cards the lecture doesn't cover (primary carnitine deficiency, MCAD inheritance/treatment, ketone urine tests, aspirin dosing/toxicity, PGs in the kidney/uterus/ductus, celecoxib sulfa) were left out. Adds 7 cloze notes (deck: Fuerst - Lipid Metabolism).

add.cloze: Glucagon and epinephrine activate hormone-sensitive lipase through {{c1::cAMP → protein kinase A phosphorylation}}
add.extra: Counterregulatory hormones: epinephrine, glucagon, cortisol, GH. Cortisol and GH act by a different, slower mechanism. Insulin opposes HSL.

add.cloze: Free fatty acids released from adipose tissue travel in the blood bound to {{c1::albumin}}
add.extra: Glycerol leaves the adipocyte through an aquaporin and goes to the liver for gluconeogenesis.

add.cloze: {{c1::HMG-CoA synthase}} is the rate-limiting enzyme of ketone body synthesis; ketone and cholesterol synthesis share the intermediate {{c2::HMG-CoA}}
add.extra: Mitochondrial HMG-CoA → ketones; cytosolic HMG-CoA → mevalonate (HMG-CoA reductase) → cholesterol.

add.cloze: The liver cannot use the ketone bodies it makes because it lacks {{c1::succinyl-CoA transferase (SCOT, thiophorase)}}
add.extra: SCOT transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA to acetoacetate in extrahepatic tissues. SCOT deficiency → ketoacidosis during fasting.

add.cloze: {{c1::Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)}} is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo fatty acid synthesis; it is activated by {{c2::insulin}} (and citrate) and inhibited by {{c3::glucagon, via cAMP-driven phosphorylation}}
add.extra: ACC needs biotin and ATP. Its product malonyl-CoA blocks CPT-I, so fatty acids are not oxidized while being made.

add.cloze: The glycerol backbone for both triglyceride and phospholipid synthesis comes from {{c1::glycerol-3-phosphate}}
add.extra: G3P comes from glucose metabolism (DHAP). Phosphatidic acid → DAG → TAG or phosphatidylcholine.

add.cloze: Phospholipase A2 is activated by a rise in cytosolic {{c1::Ca2+}}
add.extra: Receptor → G protein → PLC → IP3 → Ca2+ release from ER → PLA2 releases arachidonic acid from C-2 of membrane phospholipids. Cortisol (glucocorticoids) inhibit PLA2.

q.v: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with severe diaphoresis, palpitations, and anxiety during an acute stress response. Serum testing shows markedly elevated epinephrine levels, which stimulate the breakdown of stored triglycerides in his adipose tissue. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which epinephrine activates the key enzyme in this pathway?
o: Increased cAMP and activation of protein kinase A, which phosphorylates hormone-sensitive lipase
Increased cAMP and activation of protein kinase A, which dephosphorylates hormone-sensitive lipase
Decreased cAMP and inhibition of protein kinase A, which phosphorylates hormone-sensitive lipase
Release of IP3 and increased intracellular calcium, which phosphorylates hormone-sensitive lipase
Direct binding to a nuclear receptor to upregulate the transcription of hormone-sensitive lipase
q.p: Epinephrine/Glucagon receptor binding -> Increased cAMP + Protein Kinase A activation -> Phosphorylation of Hormone Sensitive Lipase (HSL -> HSL-P) -> Triglyceride breakdown into glycerol and free fatty acids

r.B: Hormone-sensitive lipase is activated by phosphorylation, whereas dephosphorylation inactivates the enzyme.
r.C: Counterregulatory hormones like glucagon and epinephrine increase cAMP and activate protein kinase A rather than inhibiting them.
r.D: IP3 and intracellular calcium mediate the activation of phospholipase A2 in eicosanoid synthesis, not hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes.
r.E: While cortisol and growth hormone act over a longer time frame via a different mechanism, epinephrine and glucagon rapidly activate hormone-sensitive lipase via cAMP and protein kinase A.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 9: Breakdown: Counterregulatory Hormones Stimulates Triglyceride Breakdown in the Adipocyte

q.v:
A 9-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with lethargy, vomiting, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure after a 14-hour overnight fast caused by a viral gastroenteritis. Physical examination shows mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show:
  Blood glucose: 38 mg/dL (normal: 70-110 mg/dL)
  Serum ketone bodies: undetectable (normal: 0.5-1.5 mmol/L)
  Plasma free carnitine: 30 µmol/L (normal: 25-50 µmol/L)
  Plasma C6 acylcarnitine: 0.14 µmol/L (normal: 0.02-0.15 µmol/L)
  Plasma C8 acylcarnitine: 1.8 µmol/L (normal: 0.01-0.10 µmol/L)
  Plasma C10 acylcarnitine: 1.4 µmol/L (normal: 0.01-0.08 µmol/L)
  Plasma C16 acylcarnitine: 0.04 µmol/L (normal: 0.01-0.10 µmol/L)
Which of the following cofactors is directly reduced by the enzyme that is deficient in this patient?
o: NAD+
NADP+
FAD
Biotin
Cobalamin
q.p: Fasting -> Mobilization of fatty acids -> Defect in Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase (MCAD) -> Accumulation of C6-C10 acylcarnitines & failure to reduce FAD to FADH2 in step 1 of beta-oxidation

r.A: NAD+ is reduced to NADH later in beta-oxidation by beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, not during the initial step catalyzed by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
r.B: NADPH is oxidized to NADP+ during the reduction steps of de novo fatty acid synthesis, not generated during mitochondrial beta-oxidation.
r.D: Biotin (vitamin B7) is a cofactor required for carboxylation reactions such as acetyl-CoA carboxylase and propionyl-CoA carboxylase.
r.E: Cobalamin (vitamin B12) is required for the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA during odd-chain fatty acid metabolism.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 12-13: Fatty Acid Beta-Oxidation Gives Us Acetyl-CoA

q.v: A 19-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with progressive muscle cramping, weakness, and dark urine following a 10-mile hike. A muscle biopsy reveals decreased activity of the enzyme located on the inner mitochondrial membrane that transfers long-chain fatty acids from acylcarnitine back to Coenzyme A in the mitochondrial matrix. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT-I)
Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase
Carnitine acyltransferase II (CAT-II)
Acyl-CoA synthetase
Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (VLCAD)
q.p: Cytosolic acyl-CoA -> CAT-I forms acylcarnitine -> Translocase moves acylcarnitine into matrix -> CAT-II transfers fatty acyl group back to CoA to reform acyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix

r.A: Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT-I) is located on the outer mitochondrial membrane and swaps CoA for carnitine to allow entry into the intermembrane space.
r.B: Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase is the transporter that shuttles acylcarnitine across the inner mitochondrial membrane in exchange for free carnitine, without catalyzing the transfer to CoA.
r.D: Acyl-CoA synthetase conjugates free fatty acids to CoA in the cytosol prior to their interaction with the carnitine shuttle.
r.E: Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (VLCAD) catalyzes the first oxidation step of beta-oxidation rather than regenerating acyl-CoA from acylcarnitine.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slide 11: Carnitine Shuttle Brings The Fatty Acids Across the Inner Mitochondrial Membrane for Beta-Oxidation

q.v: Which of the following fatty acids is initially oxidized in the peroxisome, generating acetyl-CoA and hydrogen peroxide, until it is shortened enough to move into the mitochondrion?
o: Propionic acid (3:0)
Caproic acid (6:0)
Lauric acid (12:0)
Palmitic acid (16:0)
Hexacosanoic acid (26:0)
q.p: Very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA = C22+, e.g., 26:0 hexacosanoic acid) -> Beta-oxidation in peroxisome (produces acetyl-CoA and H2O2) -> Shortened to medium/short-chain fatty acids -> Diffuses/transported to mitochondria

r.A: Propionic acid (3:0) is a 3-carbon short-chain odd-chain fatty acid metabolized in the mitochondria via propionyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA.
r.B: Caproic acid (6:0) is a short/medium-chain fatty acid that can diffuse directly into the mitochondria without requiring peroxisomal chain shortening.
r.C: Lauric acid (12:0) is a medium-chain fatty acid (C6-C12) that is oxidized directly inside the mitochondria.
r.D: Palmitic acid (16:0) is a long-chain fatty acid (C13-C21) that enters the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle for beta-oxidation.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 4 & 15: Short Chain and VLCFAs

q.v:
A 14-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with tachypnea, vomiting, and lethargy after refusing solid food for 18 hours during an ear infection. Her parents report a similar episode at 8 months of age. Laboratory studies obtained at 18 hours of fasting show:
  Blood glucose: 78 mg/dL (normal: 70-110 mg/dL)
  Arterial pH: 7.18 (normal: 7.35-7.45)
  Total blood ketone bodies: 8.5 mM (normal at 18 hr fast: 1.0-3.0 mM)
  Plasma acylcarnitine profile: normal
Genetic testing confirms a deficiency in the enzyme required by extrahepatic tissues to catabolize acetoacetate. Which of the following reactions is directly catalyzed by the deficient enzyme?
o: Conversion of acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA to HMG-CoA
Cleavage of HMG-CoA to acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA
Transfer of CoA from succinyl-CoA to acetoacetate to form acetoacetyl-CoA
Cleavage of acetoacetyl-CoA to two molecules of acetyl-CoA
Oxidation of D-beta-hydroxybutyrate to acetoacetate
q.p: Fasting -> Hepatic ketone synthesis -> Extrahepatic uptake of acetoacetate -> Succinyl-CoA transferase (SCOT) transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA to acetoacetate -> Forms acetoacetyl-CoA and succinate

r.A: The condensation of acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA is catalyzed by HMG-CoA synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis in the liver.
r.B: The cleavage of HMG-CoA to produce acetoacetate is part of hepatic ketone body synthesis, which would cause hypoketotic hypoglycemia if deficient.
r.D: The cleavage of acetoacetyl-CoA into two acetyl-CoA molecules is catalyzed by thiolase downstream of the SCOT reaction.
r.E: The reversible interconversion of beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate utilizes NAD+/NADH and occurs prior to the activation step by SCOT.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 19-20: Ketone Body Utilization By The Tissues and SCOT

q.v: Which of the following is true regarding the synthesis and utilization of ketone bodies during a prolonged fast?
o: Ketone synthesis and cholesterol synthesis share malonyl-CoA as a common intermediate
A high hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio favors the conversion of acetoacetate to beta-hydroxybutyrate
Succinyl-CoA transferase is highly expressed in hepatocytes to provide ATP for gluconeogenesis
The brain immediately utilizes ketone bodies for 70-80% of its energy needs within 2 hours of fasting
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic ketone body production
q.p: Prolonged fasting -> High beta-oxidation in liver -> High hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio -> Drives conversion of acetoacetate to beta-hydroxybutyrate for export to bloodstream

r.A: Ketone body synthesis and cholesterol synthesis share HMG-CoA, not malonyl-CoA, as a common intermediate.
r.C: Succinyl-CoA transferase (SCOT) is lacking in the liver, preventing hepatocytes from catabolizing the ketone bodies they produce.
r.D: The brain must adapt to fasting before it can use ketone bodies to meet 70-80% of its energy needs.
r.E: HMG-CoA synthase is the rate-limiting enzyme in ketone body synthesis, whereas acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in de novo fatty acid synthesis.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 17-19: Ketone Body Synthesis By The Liver

q.v: A 32-year-old man eats a high-carbohydrate meal, resulting in an elevated serum insulin-to-glucagon ratio. In his hepatocytes, citrate is transported from the mitochondrial matrix into the cytoplasm, where it is cleaved into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. The resulting cytoplasmic oxaloacetate is subsequently reduced to malate, which is then oxidized and decarboxylated to pyruvate before returning to the mitochondrion. Which of the following molecules generated by this cytoplasmic conversion of malate to pyruvate is directly required by fatty acid synthase?
o: NADH
NADPH
FADH2
Biotin
Carnitine
q.p: Cytoplasmic Citrate -> Acetyl-CoA + Oxaloacetate -> Oxaloacetate reduced to Malate -> Malate oxidized to Pyruvate + CO2 (generates NADPH) -> NADPH used in Reduction steps of Fatty Acid Synthase

r.A: NADH is oxidized to NAD+ during the reduction of cytoplasmic oxaloacetate to malate, whereas fatty acid synthase specifically requires NADPH.
r.C: FADH2 is produced during mitochondrial beta-oxidation and is not used as the reducing equivalent for fatty acid synthase.
r.D: Biotin is a vitamin cofactor required by acetyl-CoA carboxylase to form malonyl-CoA, and is not synthesized by the malate-to-pyruvate reaction.
r.E: Carnitine is used to shuttle long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria for beta-oxidation, a process that is inhibited by malonyl-CoA during fatty acid synthesis.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 23-25: Fatty Acid Synthesis: Making 16 Carbon Fatty Acids

q.v: A 40-year-old woman is consuming a high-calorie diet rich in simple sugars. In her adipocytes, glucose enters the cells via GLUT4 transporters to support triglyceride storage. Before three fatty acyl groups can be esterified to form a triglyceride globule coated with perilipin, glucose must be converted into which of the following immediate 3-carbon backbone substrates?
o: Oxaloacetate
Malonyl-CoA
Citrate
Glycerol-3-phosphate
Acetoacetate
q.p: Insulin stimulation -> Glucose uptake via GLUT4 -> Glycolysis produces Glycerol-3-phosphate (G-3-P) -> 3 fatty acids linked to G-3-P -> Triglyceride globule coated with perilipin

r.A: Oxaloacetate is a 4-carbon TCA cycle intermediate involved in the citrate shuttle, not the 3-carbon backbone of triglycerides.
r.B: Malonyl-CoA is the 3-carbon donor that adds 2-carbon units to the growing fatty acid chain on fatty acid synthase, not the glycerol backbone.
r.C: Citrate is a 6-carbon TCA cycle intermediate that shuttles acetyl-CoA equivalents into the cytoplasm for de novo fatty acid synthesis.
r.E: Acetoacetate is a 4-carbon ketone body synthesized in the liver during fasting, not a substrate for adipocyte triglyceride esterification.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slide 29: Triglyceride Synthesis

q.v: A 64-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease and peptic ulcer disease presents to the clinic for management of osteoarthritis knee pain. To avoid worsening his gastric ulcers, the physician prescribes celecoxib rather than daily aspirin. Compared to celecoxib, how does aspirin inhibit cyclooxygenase to prevent thromboxane A2 synthesis in platelets?
o: Reversibly binds to COX-2 only without affecting COX-1
Irreversibly acetylates a serine residue in the active site of both COX-1 and COX-2
Inhibits phospholipase A2 by preventing calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum
Blocks 5-lipoxygenase to shunt arachidonic acid toward lipoxin synthesis
Antagonizes the G-protein-coupled thromboxane receptor on the platelet membrane
q.p: Aspirin -> Irreversibly acetylates serine 530 in the catalytic site of COX-1 and COX-2 -> Blocks arachidonic acid access -> Cuts off substrate flow to thromboxane synthase -> Decreased platelet aggregation

r.A: Celecoxib is a selective COX-2 inhibitor that spares COX-1, whereas aspirin inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2.
r.C: Inhibition of phospholipase A2 is the mechanism of corticosteroids (cortisone), whereas calcium stimulates phospholipase A2.
r.D: Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase rather than 5-lipoxygenase, which actually increases leukotriene production by shunting arachidonic acid into the lipoxygenase pathway.
r.E: Aspirin prevents the synthesis of thromboxane A2 by inhibiting COX, rather than blocking the downstream thromboxane receptor on platelets.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slides 37-38: Aspirin Covalently Inhibits Cyclooxygenase

q.v: A 19-year-old woman with a history of moderate persistent asthma presents to the urgent care clinic with acute wheezing, shortness of breath, and airway mucosal edema after exposure to an allergen. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows a marked infiltration of eosinophils, neutrophils, and mast cells releasing eicosanoids. Activation of the leukotriene receptor on airway smooth muscle cells triggers contraction through which of the following intracellular signaling pathways?
o: Activation of adenylyl cyclase, increased cAMP, and activation of protein kinase A
Activation of phospholipase C, release of IP3 from PIP2, and calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum
Inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1, decreased prostaglandin E2, and decreased intracellular calcium
Direct phosphorylation of hormone-sensitive lipase and release of free fatty acids
Acetylation of serine 530 on phospholipase A2 and release of arachidonic acid
q.p: Leukotriene binds LT Receptor on smooth muscle -> Activates PLC -> Releases IP3 from PIP2 -> IP3 binds ER to release Ca++ -> Calcium activates contractile proteins -> Smooth muscle contraction

r.A: The cAMP and protein kinase A pathway mediates glucagon and epinephrine signaling in adipocytes, not leukotriene-induced smooth muscle contraction.
r.C: Inhibition of COX-1 increases leukotriene synthesis upstream, whereas leukotriene receptor signaling acts by increasing intracellular calcium via IP3.
r.D: Hormone-sensitive lipase hydrolyzes stored triglycerides in adipocytes during fasting and plays no role in airway smooth muscle contraction.
r.E: Acetylation of serine 530 is the mechanism by which aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase, not a signaling step of the leukotriene receptor.

q.s: SLO 6 / Slides 39-40: Asthma Involves Inappropriate Leukotriene Synthesis and Action

q.v: A 52-year-old woman undergoes a 16-hour pre-operative fast prior to an elective cholecystectomy. During this period of fasting, rising glucagon levels bind to receptors on her adipocytes and stimulate the phosphorylation of hormone-sensitive lipase via cAMP and protein kinase A. The resulting free fatty acids are released from the adipocytes to serve as an energy source for peripheral tissues. Which of the following proteins is required to transport these released fatty acids through the bloodstream?
o: Albumin
Perilipin
Carnitine
Citrate
Succinyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Counterregulatory hormones like glucagon activate hormone-sensitive lipase via cAMP and Protein Kinase A to hydrolyze stored triglycerides into glycerol and free fatty acids) -> Step 2 (Free fatty acids exit the adipocyte and bind to serum albumin for transport in the blood)

r.B: Perilipin is a protein acquired by triglyceride globules for intracellular lipid storage within the adipocyte, not for bloodstream transport.
r.C: Carnitine is used by the carnitine shuttle to transport long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane, not through the plasma.
r.D: Citrate is used to shuttle acetyl groups from the mitochondrial matrix into the cytoplasm for de novo fatty acid synthesis.
r.E: Succinyl-CoA serves as a CoA donor during ketone body utilization in extrahepatic tissues and as a TCA cycle intermediate.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 9: Breakdown: Counterregulatory Hormones Stimulates Triglyceride Breakdown in the Adipocyte

q.v:
A 4-month-old girl is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of poor feeding, lethargy, and hypotonia after a night of poor oral intake. Her newborn screen had been flagged for an abnormality in the metabolism of odd-chain fatty acids. Laboratory studies obtained in the emergency department show:
  Blood glucose: 52 mg/dL
  Arterial pH: 7.22
  Plasma propionyl-CoA derivatives: markedly elevated
  Urine methylmalonic acid: normal
Deficiency of which of the following vitamin cofactors would result in this biochemical profile?
o: Cobalamin (B12)
Biotin (B7)
Riboflavin (B2)
Niacin (B3)
Thiamine (B1)
q.p: Step 1 (Odd-chain fatty acids undergo mitochondrial beta-oxidation until a 3-carbon propionyl-CoA residue remains) -> Step 2 (Conversion of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA requires biotin [B7]; a defect here elevates propionyl-CoA without elevating methylmalonic acid)

r.A: Cobalamin (B12) is required to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, so its deficiency causes elevated methylmalonic acid in addition to propionyl-CoA.
r.C: Riboflavin (B2) is the precursor for FAD used by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in standard beta-oxidation rather than the carboxylation of propionyl-CoA.
r.D: Niacin (B3) is the precursor for NAD+ used by beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase in beta-oxidation rather than propionyl-CoA carboxylation.
r.E: Thiamine (B1) is a cofactor for dehydrogenases in carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism, not for the conversion of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slide 15: Short Chain and VLCFAs / Odd Chain FAs

q.v:
A 7-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with vomiting, lethargy, and a generalized seizure after a 12-hour fast due to acute otitis media. Laboratory evaluation reveals:
  Blood glucose: 38 mg/dL (normal: 70-110 mg/dL)
  Serum ketone bodies: undetectable (normal: 0.5-1.5 mmol/L)
  Plasma C6 acylcarnitine: 0.14 µmol/L (normal: 0.02-0.15 µmol/L)
  Plasma C8 acylcarnitine: 1.8 µmol/L (normal: 0.01-0.10 µmol/L)
  Plasma C10 acylcarnitine: 1.4 µmol/L (normal: 0.01-0.08 µmol/L)
  Plasma C16 acylcarnitine: 0.04 µmol/L (normal: 0.01-0.10 µmol/L)
The enzyme deficient in this patient normally catalyzes a reaction that directly reduces which of the following cofactors?
o: NAD+ to NADH
NADP+ to NADPH
FAD to FADH2
O2 to H2O2
CoA-SH to Acetyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Identify MCAD deficiency from hypoketotic hypoglycemia and elevated C8/C10 medium-chain acylcarnitines) -> Step 2 (Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase catalyzes the first step of mitochondrial beta-oxidation, transferring electrons to FAD to produce FADH2)

r.A: NAD+ is reduced to NADH later in beta-oxidation by beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, not by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
r.B: NADPH is oxidized to NADP+ during the reduction steps of de novo fatty acid synthesis by fatty acid synthase.
r.D: Reduction of O2 to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) occurs during the peroxisomal beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, not mitochondrial MCAD activity.
r.E: CoA-SH is used in the final thiolytic cleavage step by acyl-CoA acetyl-transferase to release acetyl-CoA, not in the initial dehydrogenation step.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 12-13: Fatty Acid Beta-Oxidation Gives Us Acetyl-CoA

q.v:
A 2-year-old boy is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with rapid breathing and lethargy following a 16-hour fast during a stomach virus. Serial blood samples taken during the fast are compared against normal age-matched fasting reference ranges:
  8 hours fasting total ketone bodies: 2.8 mM (normal: <0.5 mM)
  14 hours fasting total ketone bodies: 4.5 mM (normal: 0.5-1.5 mM)
  20 hours fasting total ketone bodies: 9.8 mM (normal: 1.5-3.0 mM)
  Blood glucose at 20 hours: 78 mg/dL
  Arterial pH at 20 hours: 7.18
Which of the following enzyme deficiencies best explains these laboratory findings?
o: Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT-I)
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD)
HMG-CoA synthase
Succinyl-CoA transferase (SCOT)
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the fasting data showing severe ketoacidosis with persistently and massively elevated total ketone bodies during fasting) -> Step 2 (Link inability of peripheral tissues to break down ketone bodies for energy to Succinyl-CoA Transferase [SCOT] deficiency)

r.A: Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT-I) deficiency impairs long-chain fatty acid entry into mitochondria, resulting in hypoketotic hypoglycemia rather than ketoacidosis.
r.B: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency impairs beta-oxidation and ketone synthesis, causing low or absent ketone bodies during fasting.
r.C: HMG-CoA synthase is the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic ketone body synthesis, so its deficiency would prevent ketone body formation.
r.E: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) is the rate-limiting enzyme for de novo fatty acid synthesis in the fed state and is normally inhibited during fasting.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 19-20: Succinyl-Co-A Transferase (SCOT) Deficiency Leads to Ketoacidosis

q.v: During prolonged fasting, hepatocytes convert excess acetyl-CoA derived from beta-oxidation into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. Which of the following intermediates is shared between hepatic ketone body synthesis and cholesterol synthesis?
o: Malonyl-CoA
HMG-CoA
Succinyl-CoA
Propionyl-CoA
Phosphatidic acid
q.p: Step 1 (During ketogenesis in the liver, acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA are condensed by HMG-CoA synthase to form HMG-CoA) -> Step 2 (Recognize that HMG-CoA is the shared intermediate used in both ketone body synthesis and cholesterol synthesis)

r.A: Malonyl-CoA is the committed intermediate in de novo fatty acid synthesis and an inhibitor of the carnitine shuttle, not an intermediate in ketogenesis.
r.C: Succinyl-CoA is a TCA cycle intermediate used by SCOT in extrahepatic tissues to catabolize acetoacetate, not to synthesize ketones or cholesterol.
r.D: Propionyl-CoA is the 3-carbon product of odd-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation that enters the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA.
r.E: Phosphatidic acid is the 3-carbon glycerol-phosphate backbone with two esterified fatty acids used to synthesize triglycerides and phospholipids.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slide 18: Ketone Body Synthesis By The Liver

q.v: A 24-year-old woman eats a carbohydrate-rich meal, stimulating insulin release and hepatic de novo synthesis of 16-carbon palmitate. During this process, citrate is transported out of the mitochondrion into the cytoplasm and cleaved into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. The cytoplasmic oxaloacetate is subsequently reduced to malate and then oxidized to pyruvate. Which of the following required cofactors for fatty acid synthase is directly generated by this cytoplasmic conversion of malate to pyruvate?
o: Biotin
FADH2
NADH
NADPH
ATP
q.p: Step 1 (Cytoplasmic oxaloacetate derived from citrate cleavage is reduced to malate and then oxidized and decarboxylated to pyruvate) -> Step 2 (The oxidation of malate to pyruvate generates NADPH, which is required for the priming and reduction steps of Fatty Acid Synthase)

r.A: Biotin is a vitamin cofactor required by acetyl-CoA carboxylase to bind CO2, and is not synthesized by the malate-to-pyruvate reaction.
r.B: FADH2 is generated inside the mitochondrial matrix during beta-oxidation and the TCA cycle, not during cytoplasmic malate oxidation.
r.C: NADH is oxidized to NAD+ when oxaloacetate is reduced to malate in the cytoplasm, rather than being generated during the conversion of malate to pyruvate.
r.E: ATP is consumed by citrate cleavage and acetyl-CoA carboxylase during fatty acid synthesis, rather than being produced by malate decarboxylation.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 23-25: Fatty Acid Synthesis: Making 16 Carbon Fatty Acids

q.v: Following de novo synthesis of palmitate (16:0) by fatty acid synthase in the cytoplasm, cells can further modify the fatty acid into longer or unsaturated species such as stearate (18:0) and oleate (18:1). In which of the following cellular compartments do fatty acid elongation and desaturation take place?
o: Mitochondrial matrix
Peroxisome
Endoplasmic reticulum
Cytoplasm
Intermembrane space
q.p: Step 1 (Fatty acid synthase in the cytoplasm produces the 16-carbon saturated fatty acid palmitate) -> Step 2 (Further elongation and desaturation of palmitate into longer and unsaturated fatty acids occur in the endoplasmic reticulum)

r.A: The mitochondrial matrix is the site of beta-oxidation of short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids and ketogenesis.
r.B: The peroxisome is the site of beta-oxidation of very-long-chain and branched-chain fatty acids.
r.D: The cytoplasm is the site of de novo palmitate (16:0) synthesis by fatty acid synthase, prior to elongation and desaturation.
r.E: The mitochondrial intermembrane space is where acyl-CoA is converted to acyl-carnitine by CAT-I during the carnitine shuttle.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slide 27: Elongation and Desaturation

q.v: A 34-year-old man is recovering from a minor skin laceration, and platelets are actively aggregating at the site of vascular injury to form a primary hemostatic plug. During this process, activated platelets release thromboxane A2, which binds to receptors on neighboring platelets and activates phospholipase C (PLC) to cleave PIP2 into IP3. The resulting IP3-mediated increase in intracellular calcium directly promotes platelet aggregation by inducing which of the following changes?
o: Inhibition of phospholipase A2
Fibrinogen receptor exposure
Acetylation of cyclooxygenase-1
Activation of 5-lipoxygenase
Degradation of membrane phosphatidic acid
q.p: Step 1 (Thromboxane acts on platelets via PLC and IP3 release from PIP2 to increase intracellular calcium) -> Step 2 (Increased intracellular calcium permits cytoskeletal rearrangements, fibrinogen receptor exposure, and alpha granule release to drive platelet aggregation)

r.A: Intracellular calcium binds to and activates phospholipase A2 to release arachidonic acid; cortisone inhibits phospholipase A2.
r.C: Acetylation of a serine residue in the active site of cyclooxygenase is the pharmacological mechanism of aspirin, not an endogenous effect of calcium.
r.D: 5-lipoxygenase converts arachidonic acid into 5-HPETE and leukotrienes in inflammatory cells to mediate vasoconstriction and bronchoconstriction.
r.E: Phosphatidic acid is dephosphorylated to diacylglycerol (DAG) during complex lipid and phospholipid synthesis in the fed state.

q.s: SLO 5 & 6 / Slide 37: Thromboxane and Platelet Interactions

q.v: A 62-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction takes a daily low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events. Aspirin reduces thrombus formation by cutting off the flow of prostaglandin precursors to thromboxane synthase in platelets. Which of the following best describes the molecular mechanism by which aspirin inhibits its target enzyme?
o: Reversible competitive binding to the COX-2 active site
Irreversible acetylation of a serine residue in the COX active site
Inhibition of calcium binding to phospholipase A2
Blockade of IP3-mediated calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum
Allosteric inhibition of thromboxane synthase
q.p: Step 1 (Aspirin targets both COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes in the arachidonic acid pathway) -> Step 2 (It transfers an acetyl group onto serine 530 in the cyclooxygenase active site, irreversibly blocking arachidonic acid access)

r.A: Selective reversible binding to COX-2 only is the mechanism of coxib drugs like celecoxib and rofecoxib, whereas aspirin irreversibly inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2.
r.C: Inhibition of phospholipase A2 is the mechanism of action of corticosteroids like cortisone, whereas calcium stimulates phospholipase A2.
r.D: IP3-mediated calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum is the downstream signaling pathway of thromboxane and leukotriene receptors, not the target of aspirin.
r.E: Aspirin does not directly inhibit thromboxane synthase; instead, it inhibits upstream cyclooxygenase to cut off substrate flow to thromboxane synthase.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slides 37-38: Aspirin Covalently Inhibits Cyclooxygenase

q.v: A 29-year-old woman presents to the clinic with resolving acute bacterial pneumonia. Over the past week, neutrophil infiltration and vascular permeability in her lungs were driven by arachidonic acid metabolites produced by polymorphonuclear leukocytes, macrophages, and mast cells. As the infection clears, her inflammatory cells shift toward producing a specific class of lipoxygenase-derived eicosanoids whose primary physiological role is to terminate the inflammatory response. Which of the following mediators is responsible for this resolution phase?
o: Prostaglandins
Thromboxanes
Leukotrienes
Lipoxins
Phosphatidylcholines
q.p: Step 1 (Arachidonic acid is metabolized via lipoxygenase pathways in inflammatory cells into HPETEs and HETEs) -> Step 2 (Lipoxins are synthesized from these intermediates by inflammatory cells specifically to terminate inflammation)

r.A: Prostaglandins are produced by most cells via cyclooxygenase and promote vascular permeability, pain, and fever rather than terminating inflammation.
r.B: Thromboxanes are produced by platelets and macrophages via cyclooxygenase and promote vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation.
r.C: Leukotrienes are produced by inflammatory cells via 5-lipoxygenase and promote vasoconstriction, vascular permeability, leukocyte attraction, and bronchoconstriction.
r.E: Phosphatidylcholines are structural membrane phospholipids that store arachidonic acid until it is cleaved by phospholipase A2.

q.s: SLO 5 & 6 / Slides 33-34: Eicosanoids: Lipid Mediators in the Progression of the Inflammatory Response

myLectures.name: The Science of the Mediterranean Diet
myLectures.note: Weinberg, Tue Nov 3. Checked against your 23 Mediterranean Diet cards (see mediterranean_diet_card_check.csv). B&B barely covers this lecture: only essential fatty acids, fish oil lowering TGs, vitamin E and antioxidant vitamins, and oxidized LDL. So 11 cloze notes come from your cards (deck: Weinberg - The Science of the Mediterranean Diet). Ezetimibe/NPC1L1 cards were left out because the lecture covers phytosterols, not the drug.
myLectures.deck: Weinberg - The Science of the Mediterranean Diet

add.cloze: The Mediterranean diet is roughly {{c1::20% protein, 45% carbohydrate and 35% fat}}; its main plant-based proteins are {{c2::beans, peas and lentils}}
add.extra: Other components: whole grains, fresh vegetables, fruit, fish and shellfish, cheese and yogurt, olive oil and olives, nuts and seeds, moderate red wine.

add.cloze: PREDIMED compared a low-fat control diet with two Mediterranean diet arms: one supplemented with {{c1::extra virgin olive oil}} and one with {{c2::mixed tree nuts}}; a significant reduction in cardiovascular events appeared after only {{c3::1 year}}
add.extra: PREDIMED, N Engl J Med 2018 (primary prevention). Med Diet benefits were first described by Ancel Keys in the Seven Countries Study (1957).

add.cloze: The CORDIOPREV trial (2022) found a 26% reduction in major cardiovascular events with the Mediterranean diet in people with {{c1::established cardiovascular disease}} (secondary prevention)
Plant isomers of cholesterol are called {{c1::phytosterols}}. β-sitosterol {{c2::competes with cholesterol for the NPC1L1 transporter}}, competitively inhibiting intestinal cholesterol absorption
add.extra: Cholesterol absorption ~50% vs β-sitosterol <1%: NPC1L1 takes up all sterols, and ABC-G5/G8 selectively pumps phytosterols back out of the enterocyte.

add.cloze: Less dietary cholesterol reaching the liver (in chylomicrons) leads to upregulation of hepatic {{c1::LDL receptors}}, lowering plasma LDL
add.extra: More phytosterols + less dietary cholesterol lowers plasma LDL by ~30% (lecture).

add.cloze: Adding plant sterols to margarine can lower LDL by about {{c1::15%}}

DHA makes up about {{c1::50%}} of retinal phospholipids (and ~30% of brain phospholipids); increased {{c2::fish intake (DHA/EPA)}} is linked to neuroprotection and neonatal visual and brain development
add.extra: ALA (18:3 ω-3) is the essential precursor of the longer ω-3s; EPA (20:5) is a prostanoid precursor; DHA is 22:6.

add.cloze: Omega-3 fatty acids compete with {{c1::arachidonic acid}} (ω-6) for cyclooxygenase; shifting prostanoid synthesis toward ω-3 derivatives reduces {{c2::inflammation}}
add.extra: ω-6 (arachidonic acid) → inflammatory prostanoids; ω-3 (EPA, DHA) → non-inflammatory prostanoids.

add.cloze: The antiarrhythmic effect of omega-3 fatty acids is attributed to {{c1::stabilization of the cardiac membrane}}
add.extra: Other ω-3 cardiovascular effects: ↓ VLDL synthesis and plasma TGs, ↓ blood pressure, ↓ platelet aggregation.

add.cloze: Replacing saturated fat with monounsaturated fat {{c1::decreases}} the LDL/HDL ratio; MUFAs are better than PUFAs for vascular health because they {{c2::resist free-radical lipoxidation}}
add.extra: SFA: ↓ LDL uptake (LDL receptors) and ↑ VLDL secretion → ↑ plasma LDL. MUFA: ↑ LDL uptake and ↓ VLDL secretion → ↓ LDL and TG. Oleic acid = 18:1.

add.cloze: Antioxidant sources in the Mediterranean diet: extra virgin olive oil → {{c1::polyphenols}}; red wine → {{c2::resveratrol}}; leafy greens (kale, spinach) → {{c3::vitamin E and carotenoids}}. These phytochemical antioxidants prevent the formation of {{c4::atherogenic advanced oxidation products}}
add.extra: Antioxidants arrest the free-radical peroxidation chain reaction of unsaturated fatty acids in membranes and limit the inflammatory response to oxidative damage. Others: flavonoids, vitamin C, β-carotene, lycopene.
