q.v: A 42-year-old woman presents for a routine wellness visit and asks for nutritional advice. She recently switched to a strict plant-based diet that excludes all fish and animal products, and she wants to ensure she is consuming all essential fatty acids. To meet her requirement for both essential omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids, her diet must include sources of which of the following pairs of compounds?
o: Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid
Oleic acid and stearic acid
Eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid
Stearic acid and linoleic acid
Oleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid
q.p: Step 1 (Identify dietary essential fatty acids from polyunsaturated fatty acid classes) -> Step 2 (Match omega-6 linoleic acid [18:2w6] and omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid [18:3w3])

r.B: Oleic acid (18:1w9) is a monounsaturated fatty acid and stearic acid (18:0) is a saturated fatty acid, neither of which is classified as an essential fatty acid.
r.C: Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) are longer-chain omega-3 fatty acids that can be synthesized from the essential precursor alpha-linolenic acid.
r.D: Stearic acid is a long-chain saturated fatty acid found in animal fats and is not an essential dietary fatty acid.
r.E: Oleic acid is a monounsaturated omega-9 fatty acid abundant in olive oil and avocados, not an essential polyunsaturated fatty acid.

q.s: Objective 1 / Slide 4: Dietary Fatty Acids

q.v:
A 54-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic for follow-up of hyperlipidemia. Six months ago, he replaced the butter and lard in his diet with another cooking fat. Repeat fasting lipid panel and lipoprotein analysis today compared to baseline show:
  Plasma LDL cholesterol: markedly decreased
  Plasma HDL cholesterol: unchanged
  Plasma triglycerides: unchanged
  Lipoprotein susceptibility to free-radical oxidation: increased
Which of the following dietary fats did this patient most likely add to his diet?
o: Olive oil
Corn oil
Coconut oil
Flaxseed oil
Partially hydrogenated vegetable oil
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze lipid panel changes: marked decrease in LDL, unchanged HDL and triglycerides, high oxidation susceptibility) -> Step 2 (Match to polyunsaturated omega-6 fatty acids found in corn and seed oils)

r.A: Olive oil is rich in monounsaturated fatty acids, which decrease LDL, increase HDL, decrease triglycerides, and have low susceptibility to oxidation.
r.C: Coconut oil contains saturated fatty acids, which increase both LDL and HDL while having low susceptibility to oxidation.
r.D: Flaxseed oil is rich in omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, which have no effect on LDL, increase HDL, and markedly decrease triglycerides.
r.E: Partially hydrogenated oils contain trans fatty acids, which markedly increase LDL, decrease HDL, and increase triglycerides.

q.s: Objective 1 & 4 / Slide 4: Dietary Fatty Acids & Slide 14: Monounsaturated Fats

q.v: Which of the following combinations of dietary modifications is specifically recommended to lower plasma VLDL levels?
o: Decreased total calories and increased omega-3 fatty acids
Increased total fat and moderate alcohol consumption
Decreased dietary cholesterol and decreased saturated fat
Increased saturated fat and decreased monounsaturated fat
Decreased omega-3 fatty acids and increased total fat
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the target lipoprotein as VLDL) -> Step 2 (Match VLDL reduction to decreased total caloric intake and increased omega-3 fatty acid consumption)

r.B: Increasing total fat and adding moderate alcohol consumption is the dietary modification that increases plasma HDL levels.
r.C: Decreasing dietary cholesterol and saturated fat while increasing monounsaturated or polyunsaturated fat is the primary strategy to lower plasma LDL levels.
r.D: Increasing saturated fat intake raises plasma LDL levels rather than lowering VLDL levels.
r.E: Decreasing total fat is used to reduce chylomicrons, whereas decreasing omega-3 fatty acids would worsen VLDL and triglyceride levels.

q.s: Objective 1 / Slide 5: Plasma Lipoproteins

q.v: A 61-year-old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and dyslipidemia enrolls in a clinical study evaluating dietary interventions for primary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). She is assigned to a traditional Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra virgin olive oil or mixed nuts, while a control group follows a standard low-fat diet. Based on the results of the landmark PREDIMED trial, after what minimum duration of dietary adherence is a statistically significant reduction in cumulative cardiovascular events first observed in the Mediterranean diet groups compared to the control group?
o: 1 month
6 months
1 year
3 years
5 years
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the PREDIMED trial cumulative cardiovascular event curves for EVOO and nut supplementation) -> Step 2 (Identify that significant event reduction occurred after 1 year)

r.A: One month is too short; the cumulative incidence curves in the PREDIMED trial barely begin to diverge at this early time point.
r.B: Although the event curves begin separating within the first year, a statistically significant reduction was specifically noted at the 1-year mark.
r.D: Significant cardiovascular protection is already well established before 3 years of adherence to the Mediterranean diet.
r.E: Five years represents the total follow-up duration of the trial graph, not the earliest point at which significant event reduction occurred.

q.s: Objective 2 & 3 / Slide 6: Mediterranean Diet (PREDIMED Study)

q.v: A 49-year-old man with elevated LDL cholesterol begins a diet rich in fresh vegetables, whole grains, and nuts, substantially increasing his daily intake of beta-sitosterol. Although beta-sitosterol and dietary cholesterol both enter intestinal enterocytes via the same brush-border transporter, less than 1% of ingested beta-sitosterol is absorbed into the systemic circulation compared to approximately 50% of dietary cholesterol. Activity of which of the following proteins is directly responsible for keeping net intestinal beta-sitosterol absorption below 1%?
o: ABC-G5/G8
NPC1L1
ACAT
HMG-CoA reductase
7-alpha-hydroxylase
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that both cholesterol and phytosterols enter enterocytes via NPC1L1) -> Step 2 (Identify ABC-G5/G8 as the transporter that selectively exports phytosterols back into the intestinal lumen)

r.B: NPC1L1 transports all sterols into the enterocyte from the intestinal lumen and does not selectively export phytosterols.
r.C: ACAT esterifies free cholesterol into cholesterol esters inside cells and is not an apical efflux transporter for phytosterols.
r.D: HMG-CoA reductase is the hepatic enzyme responsible for endogenous cholesterol synthesis.
r.E: 7-alpha-hydroxylase is the hepatic enzyme that converts free cholesterol into bile acids.

q.s: Objective 4 / Slide 9 & 10: Phytosterols

q.v: A 57-year-old woman with hypercholesterolemia is counseled to adopt a Mediterranean diet. She eliminates red meat and dairy from her diet and replaces them with vegetables, legumes, whole grains, and nuts, thereby reducing her dietary cholesterol intake and increasing her phytosterol intake. Which of the following sequences of changes in intestinal cholesterol transport and hepatic LDL receptor expression best explains the resulting 30% reduction in her plasma LDL levels?
o: Decreased chylomicron cholesterol delivery to the liver and increased hepatic LDL receptors
Increased chylomicron cholesterol delivery to the liver and increased hepatic LDL receptors
Decreased chylomicron cholesterol delivery to the liver and decreased hepatic LDL receptors
Increased enterocyte NPC1L1 cholesterol uptake and decreased hepatic LDL receptors
Decreased enterocyte ABC-G5/G8 phytosterol efflux and decreased hepatic LDL receptors
q.p: Step 1 (Phytosterols competitively inhibit intestinal cholesterol absorption via NPC1L1, reducing chylomicron cholesterol transport to the liver) -> Step 2 (Reduced hepatic cholesterol uptake upregulates hepatic LDL receptors, clearing plasma LDL)

r.B: Phytosterols competitively inhibit intestinal cholesterol absorption, which decreases rather than increases chylomicron cholesterol delivery to the liver.
r.C: When less dietary cholesterol reaches the liver, the hepatocyte compensates by upregulating, not downregulating, LDL receptor expression.
r.D: Phytosterols compete with cholesterol at NPC1L1 to decrease cholesterol uptake and ultimately increase hepatic LDL receptor expression.
r.E: ABC-G5/G8 actively exports phytosterols back into the gut lumen, and phytosterol ingestion leads to increased hepatic LDL receptor expression.

q.s: Objective 4 / Slide 9 & 10: Phytosterols Lower Plasma LDL Levels

q.v: A 52-year-old man transitions from a diet high in butter and animal fats to a Mediterranean diet in which extra virgin olive oil and avocados are his primary sources of fat. Compared to long-chain saturated fatty acids, how does oleic acid (18:1w9) alter hepatic enzyme activity to shrink the hepatic free cholesterol regulatory pool and lower plasma LDL levels?
o: Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase and stimulates ACAT
Stimulates HMG-CoA reductase and inhibits ACAT
Stimulates both HMG-CoA reductase and ACAT
Inhibits both HMG-CoA reductase and 7-alpha-hydroxylase
Stimulates 7-alpha-hydroxylase and inhibits LDL receptor expression
q.p: Step 1 (Identify oleic acid as a monounsaturated fatty acid acting on the liver) -> Step 2 (MUFAs inhibit HMG-CoA reductase to decrease cholesterol synthesis and stimulate ACAT to increase cholesterol ester storage, shrinking the free cholesterol pool)

r.B: Stimulating HMG-CoA reductase and inhibiting ACAT is the exact mechanism of saturated fatty acids, which expands the free cholesterol pool and raises plasma LDL.
r.C: Monounsaturated fatty acids inhibit HMG-CoA reductase rather than stimulating it, thereby reducing endogenous hepatic cholesterol synthesis.
r.D: Inhibiting ACAT would prevent free cholesterol from being stored as cholesterol esters, which is an effect of saturated fatty acids rather than monounsaturated fatty acids.
r.E: Shrinking the hepatic free cholesterol regulatory pool via monounsaturated fats increases, rather than inhibits, hepatic LDL receptor expression.

q.s: Objective 4 / Slide 13 & 14: Monounsaturated Fats

q.v:
A 64-year-old man with hypertriglyceridemia and Rheumatoid Arthritis increases his intake of salmon, mackerel, and sardines to four servings per week as part of a Mediterranean diet. Laboratory studies three months later show:
  Plasma triglycerides: 115 mg/dL (baseline: 260 mg/dL)
  Platelet aggregation: decreased
  Joint pain and swelling: improved
In addition to decreasing hepatic VLDL synthesis, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, C20:5w3) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, C22:6w3) produce these clinical benefits by inhibiting the conversion of which of the following compounds into inflammatory prostanoids?
o: Arachidonic acid (20:4)
Oleic acid (18:1)
Alpha-linolenic acid (18:3)
Stearic acid (18:0)
Beta-sitosterol
q.p: Step 1 (Identify EPA and DHA as omega-3 fatty acids from fatty fish) -> Step 2 (EPA and DHA inhibit the conversion of omega-6 arachidonic acid [20:4] into inflammatory prostanoids while promoting non-inflammatory prostanoids)

r.B: Oleic acid (18:1) is an omega-9 monounsaturated fatty acid that regulates hepatic cholesterol metabolism and is not the precursor for inflammatory prostanoids.
r.C: Alpha-linolenic acid (18:3) is the essential omega-3 precursor that is converted into EPA and DHA, which generate non-inflammatory prostanoids.
r.D: Stearic acid (18:0) is a saturated fatty acid and does not serve as a substrate for prostanoid synthesis.
r.E: Beta-sitosterol is a plant sterol that inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption and is not involved in eicosanoid synthesis.

q.s: Objective 4 / Slide 16: Omega-3 Fatty Acids

q.v: Which of the following omega-3 fatty acids makes up approximately 30% of brain phospholipids and 50% of retinal phospholipids and is critical for neonatal visual and brain development?
o: Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA)
Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA)
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)
Linoleic acid (LA)
Arachidonic acid (AA)
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the structural roles of the three major omega-3 fatty acids) -> Step 2 (Identify DHA [C22:6w3] as the specific fatty acid comprising 30% of brain and 50% of retinal phospholipids)

r.A: Alpha-linolenic acid (C18:3w3) is an essential dietary fatty acid that serves as the metabolic precursor for longer-chain omega-3 fatty acids.
r.B: Eicosapentaenoic acid (C20:5w3) primarily serves as a direct precursor for non-inflammatory prostanoid synthesis and an inhibitor of inflammatory prostanoid synthesis.
r.D: Linoleic acid (18:2w6) is an essential omega-6 fatty acid found in corn and seed oils, not an omega-3 structural component of the retina and brain.
r.E: Arachidonic acid (20:4w6) is an omega-6 fatty acid derived from linoleic acid that serves as the precursor for inflammatory prostanoids.

q.s: Objective 4 / Slide 16: Omega-3 Fatty Acids

q.v: A 68-year-old man with a history of transient ischemic attacks is advised to adopt a Mediterranean diet rich in blueberries, red wine, extra virgin olive oil, nuts, citrus fruits, and dark leafy greens (kale, spinach, and collards). These foods provide high levels of flavonoids, resveratrol, polyphenols, tocopherol (vitamin E), ascorbic acid (vitamin C), and carotenoids (beta-carotene and lycopene). By donating a hydrogen atom to lipid peroxyl radicals, these phytochemicals directly arrest free-radical chain reactions in cell membranes affecting which of the following classes of molecules?
o: Polyunsaturated fatty acids
Saturated fatty acids
Phytosterols
Bile acids
Glycogen
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the dietary compounds as phytochemical antioxidants) -> Step 2 (Antioxidants donate a hydrogen atom to arrest the free-radical peroxidation chain reaction of polyunsaturated fatty acids in membranes)

r.B: Saturated fatty acids lack double bonds and have low susceptibility to free-radical oxidation.
r.C: Phytosterols act in the intestinal lumen to competitively inhibit cholesterol absorption rather than undergoing free-radical peroxidation chain reactions in membranes.
r.D: Bile acids are synthesized from hepatic free cholesterol for biliary excretion and are not the membrane targets of lipid peroxidation chain reactions.
r.E: Glycogen is a carbohydrate storage polymer and is not involved in membrane lipid peroxidation.

q.s: Objective 2 & 4 / Slide 18, 19 & 24: Phytochemical Anti-Oxidants & The Digest

q.v: A 46-year-old man presents to the preventive cardiology clinic with a family history of premature coronary artery disease. His baseline fasting lipid panel shows a low plasma HDL cholesterol level of 32 mg/dL, while his LDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels are within normal limits. He asks which specific dietary modifications would most directly increase his plasma HDL levels. According to the lecture's nutritional guidelines for improving plasma lipoprotein levels, which of the following dietary changes is most appropriate to increase his HDL?
o: Increased total fat intake and moderate alcohol consumption
Decreased total fat intake and avoidance of alcohol
Decreased total caloric intake and decreased total fat intake
Increased dietary cholesterol intake and decreased total fat intake
Decreased monounsaturated fat intake and decreased total caloric intake
q.p: Step 1 (Identify goal of raising plasma HDL levels to reduce ASCVD risk) -> Step 2 (Match HDL improvement to increased total fat intake and moderate alcohol consumption on the Plasma Lipoproteins chart)

r.B: Decreased total fat intake is recommended to lower chylomicron levels rather than to raise HDL levels.
r.C: Decreasing total calories is a primary dietary strategy used to reduce plasma VLDL levels, not to increase HDL.
r.D: Increasing dietary cholesterol raises plasma LDL levels and increases atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk.
r.E: Monounsaturated fats should be increased rather than decreased to improve HDL and lower LDL levels.

q.s: Slide 5: Plasma Lipoproteins / Objective 1: Flash review of lipoproteins and fatty acids

q.v: A 53-year-old woman presents for a routine health maintenance exam and asks for dietary advice to lower her cardiovascular risk. She currently cooks exclusively with butter and lard and wants to switch to a plant-based oil rich in an 18-carbon fatty acid containing a single double bond at the omega-9 position. Which of the following foods is a primary dietary source of this specific fatty acid in the Mediterranean diet?
o: Coconut oil
Corn oil
Flaxseed oil
Avocados
Fatty fish
q.p: Step 1 (Identify 18:1 omega-9 fatty acid as oleic acid, a monounsaturated fatty acid) -> Step 2 (Match oleic acid/MUFA to its primary dietary sources: olive oil and avocados)

r.A: Coconut oil is a tropical oil composed primarily of medium- and long-chain saturated fatty acids with no double bonds.
r.B: Corn oil is primarily a source of linoleic acid (18:2 omega-6), a polyunsaturated fatty acid.
r.C: Flaxseed oil is rich in alpha-linolenic acid (18:3 omega-3), an essential polyunsaturated fatty acid.
r.E: Fatty fish are rich in long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids such as EPA (20:5 omega-3) and DHA (22:6 omega-3).

q.s: Slide 4: Dietary Fatty Acids / Objective 2: Understand the dietary features and lipid components in the Mediterranean Diet

q.v: A 67-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia enrolls in a randomized clinical trial modeled after the PREDIMED study. He has no prior history of myocardial infarction or stroke. He is assigned to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra virgin olive oil, while a control group is assigned to a standard control diet. Based on the results of the PREDIMED trial, what is the earliest time point at which a statistically significant reduction in cumulative cardiovascular events is observed in the Mediterranean diet group compared to the control group?
o: 1 year
2 years
3 years
4 years
5 years
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the PREDIMED study design evaluating Mediterranean diet with EVOO or nuts vs. control diet) -> Step 2 (Identify from the cumulative incidence curve that a significant reduction in CV events occurs after only 1 year)

r.B: The divergence in cumulative cardiovascular events becomes statistically significant prior to the 2-year mark.
r.C: By 3 years, the event curves continue to separate, but significant benefit was already established at 1 year.
r.D: Four years represents late follow-up in the trial rather than the earliest point of significant event reduction.
r.E: Five years was the total duration of the plotted trial follow-up, not the earliest time point of significant benefit.

q.s: Slide 6: Mediterranean Diet (PREDIMED Study) / Objective 3: Understand that clinical trials have proven the Med Diet useful for 1° and 2° prevention of ASCVD

q.v: A 48-year-old woman adopts a traditional Mediterranean diet to reduce her risk of chronic disease. She eliminates red meat and processed foods and begins eating meals centered around whole grains, fresh vegetables, fruit, olive oil, and moderate amounts of red wine. To ensure adequate protein intake while adhering strictly to traditional Mediterranean diet components, which of the following combinations of foods should she include in her diet?
o: Fish, shellfish, beans, peas, lentils, nuts, seeds, cheese, and yogurt
Beef, pork, poultry, butter, and tropical oils
Corn oil, seed oils, beef, and whole milk
Soy protein isolates,butter, lard, and egg whites
Pork, lamb, coconut oil, andrefined grains
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the four major macronutrient categories of the Mediterranean diet: proteins, carbohydrates, fats, and alcohol) -> Step 2 (Select the specific protein sources taught: fish & shellfish, beans/peas/lentils, nuts & seeds, and cheese & yogurt)

r.B: Red meat, butter, and tropical oils are sources of saturated fats that are reduced or avoided in the Mediterranean diet.
r.C: Corn oil, seed oils, and beef are typical of a Western diet rather than protein sources in the Mediterranean diet.
r.D: Butter and lard are animal fats high in long-chain saturated fatty acids, not Mediterranean diet protein components.
r.E: Red meats like pork and tropical oils like coconut oil are not featured components of the Mediterranean diet.

q.s: Slide 7: Mediterranean Diet Components / Objective 2: Understand the dietary features and lipid components in the Mediterranean Diet

q.v: Which of the following membrane proteins is located at the enterocyte brush border and transports both dietary cholesterol and plant-derived beta-sitosterol from the intestinal lumen into the enterocyte?
o: HMG-CoA reductase
7-alpha-hydroxylase
NPC1L1
ABCG5/G8
ACAT
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the mechanism of intestinal sterol uptake at the enterocyte brush border) -> Step 2 (Identify NPC1L1 as the non-selective sterol transporter that mediates uptake of both cholesterol and phytosterols)

r.A: HMG-CoA reductase is the hepatic enzyme responsible for de novo cholesterol synthesis.
r.B: 7-alpha-hydroxylase is the hepatic enzyme that converts free cholesterol into bile acids.
r.D: ABCG5/G8 is the enterocyte transporter that selectively exports phytosterols back into the intestinal lumen.
r.E: ACAT is an intracellular hepatic enzyme that esterifies free cholesterol into cholesterol esters.

q.s: Slide 9: Phytosterols / Objective 4: Understand the biochemical and metabolic properties of components in the Med Diet

q.v: A 59-year-old man presents for evaluation of elevated LDL cholesterol. His dietary history reveals daily consumption of butter, cheese, and fatty cuts of beef. His physician explains that the long-chain saturated fatty acids in these foods alter hepatic cholesterol metabolism to raise plasma LDL levels. Compared to monounsaturated fatty acids, how do dietary saturated fatty acids regulate hepatic HMG-CoA reductase and acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT) to expand the hepatic free cholesterol regulatory pool?
o: Stimulate HMG-CoA reductase / inhibit ACAT
Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase / stimulate ACAT
Stimulate HMG-CoA reductase / stimulate ACAT
Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase / inhibit ACAT
Stimulate 7-alpha-hydroxylase / stimulate LDL receptor expression
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that dietary saturated fatty acids expand the hepatic free cholesterol regulatory pool, decreasing LDL uptake and increasing VLDL secretion) -> Step 2 (Identify from the hepatic metabolism diagram that SFA stimulates (+) HMG-CoA reductase and inhibits (-) ACAT)

r.B: Inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase and stimulating ACAT is the beneficial hepatic mechanism of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), not saturated fatty acids.
r.C: Saturated fatty acids inhibit rather than stimulate ACAT, reducing the conversion of free cholesterol into stored cholesterol esters.
r.D: Saturated fatty acids stimulate rather than inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, increasing hepatic cholesterol synthesis.
r.E: Expansion of the free cholesterol pool by saturated fatty acids downregulates hepatic LDL receptor expression.

q.s: Slides 13-14: Monounsaturated Fats (Hepatic Cholesterol Metabolism) / Objective 4: Understand the biochemical and metabolic properties of components in the Med Diet

q.v:
A nutritional study compares the fasting lipid panels and lipoprotein oxidation profiles of five patient cohorts, each consuming a diet enriched in a different class of fatty acids. The results relative to baseline are shown in the table below:
  Cohort 1: LDL ↑↑ / HDL ↓ / Triglycerides ↑ / Oxidation susceptibility: Low
  Cohort 2: LDL ↑ / HDL ↑ / Triglycerides ↔ / Oxidation susceptibility: Low
  Cohort 3: LDL ↓ / HDL ↑ / Triglycerides ↓ / Oxidation susceptibility: Low
  Cohort 4: LDL ↓↓ / HDL ↔ / Triglycerides ↔ / Oxidation susceptibility: High
  Cohort 5: LDL ↔ / HDL ↑ / Triglycerides ↓↓ / Oxidation susceptibility: High
Based on these data, which cohort was assigned to a diet enriched in corn and seed oils?
o: Cohort 1
Cohort 2
Cohort 3
Cohort 4
Cohort 5
q.p: Step 1 (Identify corn and seed oils as dietary sources of omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids) -> Step 2 (Match omega-6 PUFAs on the Fatty Acid Effects table to markedly decreased LDL, unchanged HDL and triglycerides, and high susceptibility to oxidation)

r.A: Cohort 1 shows the lipid profile of trans fatty acids, which raise LDL and triglycerides while lowering HDL.
r.B: Cohort 2 shows the lipid profile of saturated fatty acids, which raise both LDL and HDL without changing triglycerides.
r.C: Cohort 3 shows the lipid profile of monounsaturated fatty acids (such as olive oil), which lower LDL and triglycerides, raise HDL, and have low oxidation susceptibility.
r.E: Cohort 5 shows the lipid profile of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (such as fatty fish), which markedly lower triglycerides and raise HDL.

q.s: Slides 4 & 14: Dietary Fatty Acids and Fatty Acid Effects on Plasma Lipids / Objective 1 & 4

q.v: A 38-year-old woman with an autoimmune inflammatory joint disorder increases her intake of walnuts, flaxseed oil, and salmon as part of a Mediterranean diet. She wants to understand how the omega-3 fatty acids in these foods reduce systemic inflammation. In the prostanoid synthesis pathway, which 20-carbon omega-3 fatty acid directly inhibits the conversion of arachidonic acid (20:4 omega-6) into inflammatory prostanoids while serving as a precursor for non-inflammatory prostanoids?
o: Oleic acid
Linoleic acid
Alpha-linolenic acid
Eicosapentaenoic acid
Docosahexaenoic acid
q.p: Step 1 (Trace the omega-3 pathway from alpha-linolenic acid [18:3] to eicosapentaenoic acid [EPA, 20:5]) -> Step 2 (Identify EPA as the direct precursor for prostanoid synthesis that inhibits arachidonic acid conversion to inflammatory prostanoids)

r.A: Oleic acid (18:1 omega-9) is a monounsaturated fatty acid that regulates hepatic cholesterol metabolism rather than eicosanoid synthesis.
r.B: Linoleic acid (18:2 omega-6) is an omega-6 precursor that is converted into arachidonic acid to produce inflammatory prostanoids.
r.C: Alpha-linolenic acid (18:3 omega-3) is an 18-carbon essential fatty acid that must first be elongated and desaturated to EPA before entering prostanoid synthesis.
r.E: Docosahexaenoic acid (22:6 omega-3) is a 22-carbon fatty acid derived from EPA that primarily comprises brain and retinal phospholipids.

q.s: Slide 16: Omega-3 Fatty Acids / Objective 4: Understand the biochemical and metabolic properties of components in the Med Diet

q.v: A biochemical assay evaluates the free radical peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids in cellular membranes. An initiator radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from a membrane polyunsaturated fatty acid, and reaction with molecular oxygen (O2) generates lipid peroxyl radicals and atherogenic oxidation products in a self-propagating chain reaction. Which of the following pairs of phytochemical antioxidants found in dark leafy greens (such as kale, spinach, and collards) directly arrests this free radical chain reaction?
o: Beta-sitosterol and oleic acid
Eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid
Vitamin E (tocopherol) and carotenoids (beta-carotene, lycopene)
Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid
Chylomicrons and high-density lipoproteins
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the free radical peroxidation chain reaction in membrane PUFAs that is arrested by antioxidants) -> Step 2 (Match leafy greens [kale, spinach, collards] on The Digest table to their specific antioxidants: Vitamin E and carotenoids)

r.A: Beta-sitosterol inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption and oleic acid alters hepatic lipoprotein metabolism; neither is an antioxidant vitamin or carotenoid from leafy greens.
r.B: EPA and DHA are long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids from fish that regulate prostanoid synthesis and are themselves highly susceptible to oxidation.
r.D: Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are essential polyunsaturated fatty acids that serve as substrates for peroxidation rather than chain-breaking antioxidants.
r.E: Chylomicrons and HDL are plasma lipoprotein particles that transport lipids in the circulation rather than phytochemical antioxidants.

q.s: Slides 18 & 24: Phytochemical Anti-Oxidants and The Digest / Objective 4: Understand the biochemical and metabolic properties of components in the Med Diet

q.v: Which of the following correctly pairs a Mediterranean diet modification with its primary physiological effect and clinical impact as summarized in the lecture's Digest table?
o: Decreased dairy and increased olive oil -> decreased intestinal cholesterol absorption -> cardioprotective and neuroprotective
Increased fish and nuts -> decreased LDL synthesis and increased HDL synthesis -> decreased LDL/HDL ratio
Decreased red meat and increased vegetables/whole grains -> decreased inflammatory prostanoid synthesis -> decreased risk for degenerative diseases
Increased fruits and red wine -> increased polyphenols, flavonoids, and resveratrol -> decreased risk for degenerative diseases
Increased leafy greens -> increased phytosterol intake -> decreased plasma LDL and ASCVD risk
q.p: Step 1 (Consult The Digest summary table matching dietary features to altered components, physiological effects, and clinical impact) -> Step 2 (Verify that increased fruits and red wine provide polyphenols, flavonoids, and resveratrol, which act as antioxidants to decrease the risk for degenerative diseases)

r.A: Decreased dairy and increased olive oil decreases LDL synthesis and increases HDL synthesis to lower the LDL/HDL ratio, whereas decreased cholesterol absorption is caused by phytosterols.
r.B: Increased fish and nuts increases omega-3 fatty acid and vitamin E intake to decrease inflammatory prostanoid synthesis and provide cardioprotective/neuroprotective effects.
r.C: Decreased red meat and increased vegetables and whole grains decreases cholesterol intake and increases phytosterol intake, which inhibits cholesterol absorption and lowers plasma LDL.
r.E: Increased leafy greens provides vitamin E and carotenoids that act as antioxidants to reduce degenerative disease risk.

q.s: Slide 24: The Digest / Objective 2 & 4

Karyotype, nondisjunction, mosaicism, Robertsonian, CATCH-22 and 7q deletion cards are already in Cytogenetics and DNA Repair.

add.cloze: In trisomy 21, overexpression of the {{c1::APP (amyloid precursor protein)}} gene on chromosome 21 contributes to {{c2::early-onset Alzheimer disease}}
add.extra: Lecture: ~10% by age 50, ~75% by age 60

add.cloze: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) classically has {{c1::postaxial}} polydactyly
add.extra: Postaxial = extra digit on the ulnar/fibular (pinky) side. Other T13 features: cutis aplasia, holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, microphthalmia

add.cloze: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the {{c1::most common sex chromosome aneuploidy in males}} and presents after puberty with {{c2::small, firm testes}}
add.extra: ~1 in 500-1000 males; testicular fibrosis → hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and infertility

add.cloze: The psychiatric disorder significantly more common in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is {{c1::schizophrenia}}
add.extra: Lecture: ~25% of adults; also autism (~20% of children), ADHD, anxiety

add.cloze: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) can cause {{c1::hypercalcemia}}
add.extra: Idiopathic; B&B attributes it to increased sensitivity to vitamin D. Hypothyroidism also occurs

q.v: A 1-day-old male infant in the neonatal intensive care unit is evaluated for bilious emesis. Physical examination reveals microcephaly, generalized hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a protruding tongue, and a single transverse palmar crease. An abdominal radiograph shows a distended stomach and proximal duodenum with an absence of distal intestinal gas, consistent with duodenal atresia. Which of the following hematologic conditions is this patient at greatest increased risk of developing during childhood?
o: Megakaryoblastic leukemia
Primary mediastinal germ cell tumor
Severe T-cell immunodeficiency
Breast carcinoma
Idiopathic hypercalcemia
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize clinical features of Down syndrome / Trisomy 21 including hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, single palmar crease, and duodenal atresia) -> Step 2 (Identify the specific associated hematologic malignancy, megakaryoblastic leukemia, which requires yearly CBC screening)

r.B: Primary mediastinal germ cell tumors occur at an increased rate (1%) in adults with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).
r.C: Immune deficiency due to thymic hypoplasia or aplasia is a hallmark feature of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome).
r.D: Adults with Klinefelter syndrome have an increased risk (3%) of developing breast carcinoma.
r.E: Idiopathic hypercalcemia is an endocrine abnormality classically associated with Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion).

q.s: SLO 1 & 4; Slides 5, 9, 10: Trisomy 21 Common Features, Gastrointestinal, and Hematologic

q.v: A 2-hour-old female newborn is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to apneic episodes and seizures. Physical examination reveals microcephaly, microphthalmia, a bilateral cleft lip and palate, a small punched-out scalp defect at the vertex, and an extra digit on the ulnar aspect of both hands. A brain MRI demonstrates failure of the forebrain to separate into right and left hemispheres. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Down syndrome
Patau syndrome
Edwards syndrome
Cri-du-chat syndrome
Williams syndrome
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the constellation of cutis aplasia, microphthalmia, cleft lip/palate, postaxial polydactyly, and holoprosencephaly) -> Step 2 (Connect these classic clinical findings to Trisomy 13, also known as Patau syndrome)

r.A: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) presents with hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, and single palmar creases rather than holoprosencephaly or cutis aplasia.
r.C: Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18) presents with hypertonia, overlapping fingers, and rocker bottom feet.
r.D: Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) presents with a high-pitched cat-like cry, hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, and downturned mouth.
r.E: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) presents with stellate irides, wide mouth, and supravalvular aortic stenosis.

q.s: SLO 1; Slides 23, 24, 27: Trisomy 13, Trisomy 13 Common Features, and Holoprosencephaly

q.v: A 3-day-old male infant born small for gestational age is evaluated in the nursery for poor feeding and seizures. Physical examination demonstrates microcephaly, microphthalmia, low-set and malformed ears, and generalized hypertonia. His hands are clenched with the index and fifth fingers overlapping the third and fourth fingers, and his feet have prominent heels with convex soles. Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most likely present in this infant?
o: Trisomy 13
Monosomy X
Trisomy 18
Deletion of 5p
Trisomy 21
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize prenatal growth deficiency, hypertonia, overlapping fingers, and rocker bottom feet) -> Step 2 (Identify the underlying chromosomal abnormality as Trisomy 18 / Edwards syndrome)

r.A: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) is characterized by midline defects such as cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly, cutis aplasia, and postaxial polydactyly.
r.B: Monosomy X (Turner syndrome) occurs in females and presents with lymphedema of the hands and feet, webbed neck, and coarctation of the aorta.
r.D: Deletion of 5p (Cri-du-chat syndrome) presents with hypotonia, a high-pitched cry, and microcephaly rather than hypertonia and overlapping fingers.
r.E: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) presents with generalized hypotonia, single transverse palmar creases, and a sandal toe gap deformity.

q.s: SLO 1; Slides 28, 29: Trisomy 18 and Trisomy 18 Common Features

q.v: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric endocrinology clinic for evaluation of short stature. She is below the 3rd percentile for height and has not developed breast buds or begun menstruating. Physical examination shows a webbed neck, down-slanting palpebral fissures, a high-arched palate, and a broad chest with widely spaced nipples. A renal ultrasound reveals a horseshoe kidney, and karyotype analysis confirms 45,X. Which of the following is true regarding the medical management of this patient?
o: Growth hormone therapy must be delayed until after the onset of puberty
Estrogen replacement therapy will restore normal fertility and ovarian function
Growth hormone therapy can increase final adult height if given prior to puberty
Testosterone replacement therapy is indicated to promote linear bone growth
Annual complete blood counts are required to screen for megakaryoblastic leukemia
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose Turner syndrome from short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, webbed neck, shield chest, and horseshoe kidney) -> Step 2 (Recall treatment guidelines: growth hormone therapy increases final adult height if given prior to puberty, while estrogen helps develop secondary sex characteristics but does not affect fertility)

r.A: Growth hormone therapy must be administered prior to the onset of puberty to effectively increase final adult height.
r.B: Estrogen replacement therapy helps girls with Turner syndrome develop female secondary sex characteristics, but it does not affect fertility.
r.D: Testosterone replacement therapy is used at the time of puberty in males with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), not in females with Turner syndrome.
r.E: Annual CBC screening for leukemia is part of the management guidelines for Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), not Turner syndrome.

q.s: SLO 2 & 4; Slides 32, 33, 35, 36: Turner Syndrome, Gonadal Dysgenesis, and Treatment

q.v: A 28-year-old man presents to the fertility clinic with his partner after 18 months of inability to conceive. He notes that he has always been taller than his peers and has never needed to shave his face regularly. Physical examination reveals a tall, long-limbed man with bilateral gynecomastia, sparse axillary and pubic hair, and small, firm testes. Which of the following genetic mechanisms best explains this patient's tall stature and long limbs?
o: Overexpression of the APP gene
An extra copy of the SHOX gene
Paternal deletion on chromosome 15q11-q13
Maternal meiosis error involving chromosome 21
Microdeletion on chromosome 7q11.23
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Klinefelter syndrome / 47,XXY from male infertility, tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, and reduced body hair) -> Step 2 (Attribute the tall stature and longer limbs to the extra copy of the SHOX gene located on the sex chromosomes)

r.A: Overexpression of the APP (amyloid precursor protein) gene on chromosome 21 is responsible for the increased incidence of early-onset Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome.
r.C: A paternal deletion on chromosome 15q11-q13 causes Prader-Willi syndrome, which presents with hypotonia in infancy followed by hyperphagia and obesity.
r.D: Maternal meiosis errors involving chromosome 21 cause free Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), which is associated with short stature rather than tall stature.
r.E: A microdeletion on chromosome 7q11.23 causes Williams syndrome, which is associated with short stature and failure to thrive.

q.s: SLO 2; Slides 37, 38, 39: Klinefelter Syndrome

q.v:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents due to excessive weight gain and behavioral challenges. As an infant, he had severe hypotonia and poor feeding requiring nasogastric tube supplementation, as well as global developmental delay. Over the past 3 years, he has developed an insatiable appetite, frequently sneaking food from the pantry and eating from the garbage can. Physical examination reveals a BMI at the 99th percentile, almond-shaped eyes, and small hands and feet. Genetic testing is ordered: 
  Chromosome 15q11-q13 FISH: normal (no deletion detected)
  Methylation analysis of 15q11-q13: abnormal (only methylated maternal alleles present)
  Microsatellite DNA analysis: both copies of chromosome 15 inherited from the mother
Which of the following genetic mechanisms is the cause of this patient's condition?
o: Paternal uniparental disomy
Maternal uniparental disomy
Point mutation in the UBE3A gene
Balanced Robertsonian translocation
Somatic mosaicism
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Prader-Willi syndrome from infantile hypotonia/feeding issues followed by childhood hyperphagia, obesity, almond-shaped eyes, and small hands/feet) -> Step 2 (Interpret the lab panel showing two maternal copies of chromosome 15 and no active paternal copy as maternal uniparental disomy, which accounts for 25% of PWS cases)

r.A: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 results in no active maternal copy of UBE3A, causing Angelman syndrome rather than Prader-Willi syndrome.
r.C: Mutations in the maternally expressed UBE3A gene cause Angelman syndrome (accounting for 11% of cases).
r.D: Balanced Robertsonian translocations involve fusion of acrocentric chromosomes and are associated with familial Down syndrome or Trisomy 13, not imprinting disorders in a patient with two intact maternal copies.
r.E: Somatic mosaicism refers to two or more populations of cells with different genotypes in one individual, whereas this patient uniformly inherited both copies of chromosome 15 from his mother.

q.s: SLO 3 & 6; Slides 63, 71, 72, 73: Prader-Willi Syndrome and Imprinting

q.v: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the neurology clinic for evaluation of poorly controlled seizures and severe developmental delay. Her head circumference was normal at birth, but she now exhibits microcephaly. She has not developed any spoken language. During the examination, she has a wide-based, ataxic gait with upheld, flexed arms, coarse tremors, and frequent unprovoked bursts of laughter. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is the most common cause of this patient's disorder?
o: Deletion on the paternal copy of 15q11-q13
Deletion on the maternal copy of 15q11-q13
Deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5
Deletion on chromosome 22q11.2
Deletion on chromosome 7q11.23
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Angelman syndrome from postnatal microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, absent speech, seizures, ataxia with upheld arms, and unprovoked laughter) -> Step 2 (Determine that a deletion on the maternal copy of chromosome 15q11-q13 is the most common genetic etiology, accounting for 70-75% of cases)

r.A: A deletion on the paternal copy of 15q11-q13 causes Prader-Willi syndrome because the maternal copy of the PWS region (MAGEL2) is silenced by imprinting.
r.C: A deletion on the short arm (p-arm) of chromosome 5 causes Cri-du-chat syndrome, characterized by a cat-like cry in infancy.
r.D: A deletion on chromosome 22q11.2 causes DiGeorge/Velocardiofacial syndrome, presenting with conotruncal cardiac defects, hypocalcemia, and cleft palate.
r.E: A deletion on chromosome 7q11.23 causes Williams syndrome, in which patients have strong verbal and language skills rather than absent speech.

q.s: SLO 3 & 6; Slides 67, 68, 71, 72, 73: Angelman Syndrome and Imprinting

q.v: A 22-year-old man with a history of repaired Tetralogy of Fallot and a cleft palate is brought to the psychiatric clinic due to auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions, and social withdrawal over the past 8 months. His medical records indicate that he had neonatal hypocalcemic seizures, recurrent sinopulmonary infections in childhood due to T-cell lymphopenia, and mild learning disabilities in school (IQ of 72). His current presentation is a known adult-onset complication of which of the following chromosomal disorders?
o: Williams syndrome
Cri-du-chat syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome
22q11.2 deletion syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome
q.p: Step 1 (Connect conotruncal heart defect [Tetralogy of Fallot], cleft palate, neonatal hypocalcemia, immune deficiency, and mild intellectual disability to CATCH 22) -> Step 2 (Recognize that schizophrenia occurs in 25% of adults with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome)

r.A: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia, and an overly friendly personality rather than Tetralogy of Fallot, hypocalcemia, and schizophrenia.
r.B: Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) is associated with moderate-to-severe intellectual disability, hyperactivity/aggression, and patent ductus arteriosus.
r.C: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) presents with tall stature, hypogonadism, and infertility, without conotruncal heart defects or hypocalcemia.
r.E: Prader-Willi syndrome (paternal 15q11-q13 deficiency) presents with infantile hypotonia and childhood hyperphagia/obesity rather than CATCH 22 features.

q.s: SLO 3 & 4; Slides 47, 48, 49: 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome and Cardiac Defects in 22q11.2 Deletion syndrome

q.v:
A 6-month-old girl is evaluated in the genetics clinic for developmental delay and dysmorphic features. In the newborn nursery, she was noted to have low birth weight, hypotonia, and a distinctive, high-pitched cry resembling a kitten, which is now beginning to resolve. Physical examination reveals microcephaly, hypertelorism with epicanthal folds, a broad nasal bridge, a shortened philtrum, a downturned mouth, and low-set ears with preauricular tags. Cardiac auscultation reveals a continuous machine-like murmur, and an echocardiogram confirms a patent ductus arteriosus. Laboratory and cytogenetic studies are performed:
  Serum calcium: 9.4 mg/dL (normal)
  Thyroid-stimulating hormone: 2.1 mIU/L (normal)
  Chromosomal microarray: terminal deletion detected
On which of the following chromosome regions is this patient's deletion located?
o: 5p
Xq
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Cri-du-chat syndrome from the resolving cat-like cry caused by laryngeal structural differences, microcephaly, hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, downturned mouth, low-set ears with preauricular tags, and PDA) -> Step 2 (Map Cri-du-chat syndrome to a deletion on the p-arm of chromosome 5 [5p-])

r.B: Deletions on 7q11.23 cause Williams syndrome, which features stellate irides, wide mouth, supravalvular aortic stenosis, and hypercalcemia.
r.C: Deletions on 15q11-q13 cause either Prader-Willi syndrome or Angelman syndrome depending on the parent of origin.
r.D: Deletions on 22q11.2 cause DiGeorge syndrome, which is associated with hypocalcemia and conotruncal cardiac defects such as VSD or Tetralogy of Fallot.
r.E: Abnormalities of Xq (such as isochromosome Xq) are associated with Turner syndrome, which presents with short stature, webbed neck, and coarctation of the aorta.

q.s: SLO 3 & 4; Slides 58, 59, 61: Cri-du-chat Syndrome, Facial Features in Cri-du-chat syndrome, and Common Features

q.v: Which of the following statements best describes the clinical features and management of an individual diagnosed with mosaic Trisomy 21?
o: The percentage of trisomic cells in the peripheral blood directly predicts the severity of intellectual disability
Affected individuals always exhibit a milder phenotype than those with free Trisomy 21
Patients should be managed and screened according to standard Down syndrome clinical guidelines
Mosaicism accounts for approximately 25% of all live-born cases of Down syndrome
The condition results from the fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes prior to fertilization
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the definition and clinical implications of mosaic Trisomy 21) -> Step 2 (Identify that although features range from minimal to very severe with no direct correlation to blood mosaicism percentage, patients are treated following typical Down syndrome guidelines)

r.A: There is no direct correlation between the percentage of mosaicism seen in peripheral blood and the clinical severity of features.
r.B: Clinical features in mosaic Trisomy 21 can range from minimal to very severe, rather than always being mild.
r.D: Mosaic Trisomy 21 accounts for only about 1% of cases of Trisomy 21, while free Trisomy 21 accounts for 95% and Robertsonian translocations account for 4%.
r.E: Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes describes a Robertsonian translocation, whereas mosaicism arises from a post-zygotic mutation/nondisjunction in a single fertilized egg.

q.s: SLO 5; Slides 20, 21: Mosaic Trisomy 21 and Mosaicism

q.v: A 2-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician for a routine well-child checkup. In the newborn period, he was noted to have generalized hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, single transverse palmar creases, and a sandal toe gap deformity. He underwent surgical repair of an atrioventricular septal defect at 4 months of age. His parents report that he is currently doing well and receiving early intervention therapies. A screening complete blood count (CBC) is ordered at this visit. Which of the following hematologic conditions is this patient at specifically increased risk of developing compared to the general population?
o: Megakaryoblastic leukemia
Primary mediastinal germ cell tumor
Severe T-cell immunodeficiency
Burkitt lymphoma
Aplastic anemia
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize clinical features and AV canal defect as Trisomy 21 / Down syndrome) -> Step 2 (Identify the specific hematologic malignancy risk as megakaryoblastic leukemia, a rare type of AML screened for with yearly CBCs)

r.B: Primary mediastinal germ cell tumors are associated with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), not Down syndrome.
r.C: Immune deficiency due to thymic hypoplasia or aplasia is a hallmark feature of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
r.D: Burkitt lymphoma is not specifically associated with Trisomy 21 in the lecture material.
r.E: Aplastic anemia is not the hematologic condition screened for with yearly CBCs in patients with Trisomy 21.

q.s: SLO 1 & 4 / Slide 10: Hematologic (Trisomy 21)

q.v: A 1-day-old female infant is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for respiratory distress and poor feeding. Prenatal ultrasound had shown intrauterine growth restriction. On physical examination, the infant's weight, length, and head circumference are all below the 3rd percentile. She has microphthalmia, low-set and malformed ears, and generalized hypertonia. Examination of the extremities reveals a distinctive clenching of the hands with the index and fifth fingers overlapping the third and fourth fingers, as well as convex soles of the feet. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Patau syndrome
Down syndrome
Turner syndrome
Cri-du-chat syndrome
Edwards syndrome
q.p: Step 1 (Identify prenatal/postnatal growth deficiency, hypertonia, overlapping fingers, and rocker bottom feet) -> Step 2 (Match clinical features to Trisomy 18 / Edwards syndrome)

r.A: Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13) typically presents with midline defects such as cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly, cutis aplasia, and postaxial polydactyly.
r.B: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) presents with generalized hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, single palmar creases, and a sandal toe gap.
r.C: Turner syndrome (45,X) in a newborn typically presents with lymphedema of the hands and feet, a webbed neck, and coarctation of the aorta.
r.D: Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p-) presents with a characteristic high-pitched cat-like cry, hypotonia, microcephaly, and hypertelorism.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slides 28-29: Trisomy 18 Common Features

q.v: A 2-day-old female newborn is evaluated in the nursery for marked swelling of the dorsum of her hands and feet. Prenatal ultrasound at 14 weeks gestation had demonstrated increased nuchal translucency and a cystic hygroma. Physical examination reveals a wide chest with widely spaced nipples, redundant nuchal skin, low-set ears, and down-slanting palpebral fissures. Which of the following renal anomalies is most likely to be found on abdominal ultrasound in this patient?
o: Polycystic kidney disease
Renal cell carcinoma
Horseshoe kidney
Medullary sponge kidney
Bladder exstrophy
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize cystic hygroma, dorsal lymphedema of hands/feet, shield chest, and webbed neck as Turner syndrome) -> Step 2 (Identify horseshoe kidney or pelvic kidney as the associated renal anomaly)

r.A: Polycystic kidney disease is not a characteristic renal anomaly associated with Turner syndrome.
r.B: Renal cell carcinoma is not a congenital renal malformation associated with Turner syndrome.
r.D: Medullary sponge kidney is not associated with Turner syndrome on the lecture slides.
r.E: Bladder exstrophy is not a feature of Turner syndrome, which is instead associated with horseshoe or pelvic kidneys.

q.s: SLO 2 & 4 / Slides 32-33: Turner Syndrome

q.v: A 19-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a pre-college physical examination. He has no acute complaints, though his mother notes he had mild delays in speech and motor milestones as a young child. On physical examination, he is 193 cm (6 ft 4 in) tall with disproportionately long arms and legs. He has sparse facial and axillary hair, bilateral gynecomastia, and small testes. Which of the following best explains the mechanism responsible for this patient's tall stature and long limbs?
o: Overexpression of the APP gene
Deficiency of growth hormone receptor degradation
Uniparental disomy of chromosome 15
Extra copy of the SHOX gene
Deletion of the elastin gene region
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize tall stature, long limbs, gynecomastia, small testes, and reduced body hair as Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY) -> Step 2 (Identify the extra copy of the SHOX gene on the extra X chromosome as the cause of tall stature and longer limbs)

r.A: Overexpression of the APP (amyloid precursor protein) gene on chromosome 21 explains the increased risk of Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome.
r.B: Growth hormone receptor degradation is not the mechanism of tall stature in Klinefelter syndrome.
r.C: Uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 is a genetic mechanism seen in Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes, not Klinefelter syndrome.
r.E: Microdeletion on 7q11.23 causes Williams syndrome, which is associated with short stature rather than tall stature.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 38-39: Klinefelter Syndrome

q.v: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic by her parents for a developmental evaluation. Her parents note that she is extremely outgoing, has no fear of strangers, and frequently engages adults at the grocery store in long conversations. Despite her strong verbal and language skills, she has global developmental delay and mild intellectual disability. In infancy, she was evaluated for failure to thrive. Physical examination reveals short stature, periorbital fullness, a wide mouth with widely spaced teeth, large earlobes, and a lacy, star-like pattern in her irides. Laboratory evaluation ordered at this visit is most likely to reveal which of the following endocrine abnormalities?
o: Hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia
Hyperglycemia and ketonuria
Hypercalcemia and hypothyroidism
Elevated testosterone and low LH
Adrenal insufficiency and hyponatremia
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize 'cocktail party' personality, stellate irides, wide mouth, and history of failure to thrive as Williams syndrome) -> Step 2 (Identify idiopathic hypercalcemia and hypothyroidism as the associated endocrine problems)

r.A: Hypocalcemia due to hypoparathyroidism is a classic feature of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome), whereas Williams syndrome is associated with hypercalcemia.
r.B: Hyperglycemia and ketonuria are not the characteristic endocrine abnormalities of Williams syndrome.
r.D: Abnormalities in sex hormones and gonadotropins are features of sex chromosome disorders like Turner or Klinefelter syndrome, not Williams syndrome.
r.E: Adrenal insufficiency is not a characteristic endocrine feature of Williams syndrome.

q.s: SLO 3 & 4 / Slides 53 & 55: Williams Syndrome

q.v: A 3-day-old male infant in the newborn nursery is evaluated for feeding difficulties and a distinctive, high-pitched cry that sounds like a meowing kitten. He was born at term with a birth weight below the 5th percentile. Physical examination reveals microcephaly, generalized hypotonia, hypertelorism with epicanthal folds, a broad nasal bridge, a downturned mouth, and low-set ears with preauricular tags. Cardiac auscultation reveals a continuous machine-like murmur. Which of the following statements best describes the natural history of this patient's characteristic vocal finding?
o: It is caused by laryngeal structure differences and typically resolves in infancy or early childhood
It is caused by vocal cord paralysis and requires tracheostomy in adolescence
It is caused by hypocalcemic laryngospasm and resolves with calcium supplementation
It is caused by progressive bulbar neurodegeneration and worsens throughout childhood
It is caused by a vascular ring compressing the trachea and requires surgical division
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize cat-like cry, microcephaly, hypertelorism, hypotonia, and PDA in a newborn as Cri-du-chat syndrome / 5p-) -> Step 2 (Identify that the cry is caused by differences in the structure of the larynx and typically resolves in infancy or early childhood)

r.B: The cry in Cri-du-chat syndrome is due to structural laryngeal differences and resolves spontaneously rather than requiring a tracheostomy.
r.C: Hypocalcemia is a feature of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, not Cri-du-chat syndrome.
r.D: The high-pitched cry in Cri-du-chat syndrome typically resolves in infancy or early childhood rather than worsening progressively.
r.E: The characteristic cry is due to intrinsic differences in larynx structure, not extrinsic compression by a vascular ring.

q.s: SLO 3 & 4 / Slides 58-61: Cri-du-chat Syndrome

q.v: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated in the genetics clinic for global developmental delay, mild intellectual disability, and rapid weight gain due to an insatiable appetite. In infancy, he had severe hypotonia and poor feeding. Physical examination reveals obesity, almond-shaped eyes, and small hands and feet. High-resolution chromosome analysis and methylation studies confirm that both of his copies of chromosome 15 were inherited from his mother, with no paternal copy present. Which of the following best describes why this genetic finding results in his clinical condition?
o: The maternal copy of the UBE3A gene on chromosome 15 is normally silenced by imprinting
The maternal copy of the MAGEL2 gene on chromosome 15 is normally silenced by imprinting
The presence of two maternal chromosomes causes a toxic double dosage of active 15q11-q13 genes
The maternal chromosomes undergo random X-inactivation in hypothalamic neurons
The paternal copy of chromosome 15 is required to prevent monosomy rescue in somatic cells
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize infantile hypotonia/feeding issues followed by childhood hyperphagia/obesity, almond-shaped eyes, and small hands/feet as Prader-Willi syndrome caused by maternal UPD 15) -> Step 2 (Recall that mom's copy of the Prader-Willi gene MAGEL2 is normally imprinted/methylated/silenced, so having no paternal copy leaves the patient with no active copy of the gene)

r.A: The paternal copy, not the maternal copy, of the Angelman syndrome gene (UBE3A) is normally imprinted (silenced).
r.C: Prader-Willi syndrome in maternal UPD results from the absence of the normally active paternal gene copy, not from overexpression of maternal genes.
r.D: X-inactivation applies to X chromosomes, whereas chromosome 15 is an autosome regulated by parent-of-origin genomic imprinting.
r.E: The pathology of maternal UPD 15 is specifically due to the lack of the active paternal allele of imprinted genes like MAGEL2 in the 15q11-q13 region.

q.s: SLO 3 & 6 / Slides 63, 70-73: Prader-Willi Syndrome & Imprinting

q.v:
A healthy 29-year-old man and his 27-year-old wife present for preconception genetic counseling because the man's sister has Down syndrome. Karyotype analysis performed on the couple reveals the following results:
  Wife: 46,XX
  Husband: 45,XY,rob(14;21)
Based on these findings, what is the approximate risk for this couple to have a live-born offspring with an unbalanced chromosomal translocation resulting in Down syndrome?
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the husband's karyotype as a male balanced carrier of a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21 and 14) -> Step 2 (Apply the parent-of-origin risk rule from the lecture: risk for unbalanced offspring is 0.5-2.5% if the father carries the balanced translocation)

r.B: A 10% to 15% risk applies when the mother, rather than the father, carries the balanced Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21.
r.C: A 25% risk is characteristic of autosomal recessive inheritance, not a paternal balanced Robertsonian translocation.
r.D: A 50% risk is characteristic of autosomal dominant inheritance, not a Robertsonian translocation carrier.
r.E: A 100% risk of Down syndrome in viable pregnancies would only occur if a parent carried a balanced 21;21 translocation, such as 45,XY,t(21q21q).

q.s: SLO 1 / Slides 16-18: Robertsonian Translocation

q.v:
Two patients with severe neurodevelopmental disorders undergo molecular cytogenetic testing of the 15q11-q13 region. The results are shown in the table below:
  Patient 1: Deletion of 15q11-q13 on the paternally derived chromosome 15
  Patient 2: Mutation of the maternal UBE3A gene on 15q11-q13
Which of the following clinical findings is most likely to be seen in Patient 2, as opposed to Patient 1?
o: Almond-shaped eyes and small hands and feet
Hyperphagia and severe childhood obesity
Ataxia, absence of speech, and unprovoked bursts of laughter
Supravalvular aortic stenosis and stellate irides
Thymic hypoplasia and hypocalcemic seizures
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the genetic data: Patient 1 has a paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causing Prader-Willi syndrome, whereas Patient 2 has a maternal UBE3A mutation causing Angelman syndrome) -> Step 2 (Identify the clinical features of Angelman syndrome: ataxia, no speech, and unprovoked bursts of laughter / 'Happy Puppet')

r.A: Almond-shaped eyes and small hands and feet are characteristic features of Prader-Willi syndrome (Patient 1), not Angelman syndrome (Patient 2).
r.B: Hyperphagia and childhood obesity are features of Prader-Willi syndrome (Patient 1), not Angelman syndrome (Patient 2).
r.D: Supravalvular aortic stenosis and stellate irides are features of Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion).
r.E: Thymic hypoplasia and hypocalcemia are features of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome).

q.s: SLO 3, 4 & 6 / Slides 63, 67-68, 71-73: Angelman Syndrome & Imprinting

q.v: Which of the following statements is true regarding the clinical features and reproductive health of individuals with Turner syndrome?
o: Approximately 90% of affected individuals have a non-mosaic 45,X karyotype
Estrogen replacement therapy initiates female secondary sex characteristics and restores fertility
Growth hormone therapy must be initiated after the completion of puberty to maximize adult height
Affected females are at increased risk for X-linked recessive disorders due to the loss of an X chromosome
Ovarian involution occurs in late adulthood, resulting in normal spontaneous menses during adolescence
q.p: Step 1 (Evaluate statements regarding Turner syndrome genetics, clinical features, and treatment) -> Step 2 (Identify that loss of the second X chromosome leaves females hemizygous and at risk for X-linked recessive disorders)

r.A: Approximately 50% (not 90%) of individuals with Turner syndrome have a 45,X karyotype, while the remainder have mosaicism or a structural X aberration.
r.B: Estrogen replacement therapy helps girls with Turner syndrome develop secondary sex characteristics, but it does not affect fertility.
r.C: Growth hormone therapy can help increase final adult height in Turner syndrome, but it must be administered prior to the onset of puberty.
r.E: In Turner syndrome, the ovaries involute early in life leading to premature ovarian failure, so girls typically do not have spontaneous menses.

q.s: SLO 2, 4 & 5 / Slides 31, 35-36: Turner Syndrome

myLectures.name: Introduction to Immunology
myLectures.note: New lecture (Mullins, Mon Nov 2). Cards picked to match the slides, checked against your 40 Intro to Immunology cards (see intro_immunology_card_check.csv). This lecture is mostly framework (danger model, the five stages, localization), which B&B doesn't teach as such, so 14 cloze notes come from your cards (deck: Mullins - Introduction to Immunology). Picks include what the picture-only slides show (innate cell types and complement, HLA-A/B/C vs DP/DQ/DR, beta2-microglobulin, invariant chain/MHC II loading, Langerhans cells carrying antigen to naive T cells, plasma cells in bone marrow). Left out: TLR4/CD14, MHC I on all nucleated cells, perforin/granzyme, Th subsets beyond Th1, IgG in the secondary response.

add.cloze: The central tension an effective immune system must manage: {{c1::eliminate threats while limiting unacceptable injury to host tissues}}
add.extra: Lecture: an effective system must be powerful, targeted, localized and self-limited. The same mechanisms that protect can cause collateral injury, autoimmunity, allergy or immunopathology.

add.cloze: Defining immunity only as recognition of non-self is limited: foreignness alone does not decide whether a response is needed; {{c1::danger, tissue injury and context}} also shape activation. Besides microbes, dangers include {{c2::tissue injury, irritants/toxins, cellular stress, and cancers (from infection or mutation)}}
add.extra: Lecture framing: "strangers" vs "dangers".

add.cloze: Stages of an immune response: (1) Detect: {{c1::barriers fail; innate sensors recognize microbial patterns or tissue injury}}. (2) Rapid local response: {{c2::pre-formed innate cells and molecules recognize and try to contain the danger}}. (3) Decide + amplify: {{c3::costimulation and cytokines determine whether rare antigen-specific lymphocytes activate and expand}}. (4) Localize + eliminate: {{c4::effectors reach the relevant tissue and remove the threat while limiting damage}}. (5) Resolve + remember: {{c5::the response contracts and selected lymphocytes persist as memory}}
add.extra: Stages 1-2 are innate; 3-5 are adaptive. Fire analogy: fire door (barrier), smoke detector (sensor), sprinkler (innate), fire department (adaptive).

add.cloze: Examples of innate barriers: {{c1::skin, mucociliary escalator, saliva, urinary mucous membranes, tears, and stomach acid}}
add.extra: Barriers prevent colonization and invasion from becoming disease.

add.cloze: Pattern-recognition receptors detect {{c1::conserved microbial structures and products}} and also {{c2::altered self, cellular stress and damage-associated signals}}; this is why a sterile needle puncture can still cause inflammation
add.extra: After bacteria enter a dirty cut, innate cells detect both microbial patterns and tissue-damage signals. In a sterile injury, damaged host cells release danger signals that activate innate cells without microbes.

add.cloze: Innate effectors are {{c1::already available}}, so innate immunity responds in minutes to hours; on first exposure adaptive immunity takes {{c2::days}} because {{c3::rare antigen-specific clones must be activated and expanded}}
On repeat exposure (e.g., after vaccination or infection), adaptive responses are {{c1::faster and larger}} because of memory, whereas innate responses are {{c2::broadly similar}}
add.extra: Lecture: primary vs memory responses, "why to get your flu shot".

add.cloze: An antigen is {{c1::a molecular structure specifically bound by an antibody/B-cell receptor, or recognized by a T-cell receptor as peptide-HLA}}. Antigen alone does not activate adaptive immunity: {{c2::antigen + danger = adaptive activation}}, because danger signals activate APCs and induce costimulation
add.extra: Antigen provides specificity; danger provides context.

add.cloze: HLA stands for {{c1::human leukocyte antigen}}, the human form of the {{c2::major histocompatibility complex (MHC)}}
add.extra: HLA molecules bind peptide fragments and display them for T cells: "Here's what I found. Should we respond?"

add.cloze: Signal 3 in naive T-cell activation is {{c1::cytokines}}, which shape clonal expansion and functional differentiation
add.extra: Signal 1: TCR recognizes peptide-HLA. Signal 2: costimulation (APC encountered danger and is licensed). Without signal 2 → anergy.

add.cloze: Clonal {{c1::selection}}: antigen activates lymphocytes bearing pre-existing receptors of the right specificity (antigen does not design the receptor). Clonal {{c2::expansion}}: the activated lymphocyte proliferates into many effector cells, some of which persist as memory
The adaptive effector that most directly eliminates a virus-infected host cell is {{c1::a CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocyte}} recognizing viral peptide presented by {{c2::HLA class I}}
add.extra: CD4 T cells see HLA class II and coordinate other leukocytes.

add.cloze: Humoral immunity (plasma cells secreting antibody) is best suited to {{c1::extracellular targets and toxins}}
add.extra: Antibodies recruit complement and Fc-receptor-bearing cells. Cell-mediated immunity: T cells recognize peptide-HLA on cells.

add.cloze: Localization: antigen is captured in tissue → carried to the {{c1::draining lymph node}} → specific lymphocytes activate and expand → enter the blood → {{c2::home back to the infected tissue}}. This matters because effectors must reach {{c3::the correct tissue to eliminate the threat while limiting systemic damage}}
add.extra: Tissue → lymph node → circulation → tissue.
