q.v: A 54-year-old man presents to the clinic with severe pain, redness, and swelling in his right great toe that began acutely overnight. Joint fluid aspiration reveals needle-shaped uric acid crystals, and Gram stain and culture are negative for microorganisms. Despite the absence of an infectious pathogen, large numbers of activated innate immune cells are present in the synovial fluid. Which of the following best explains the initiation of the inflammatory response in this patient?
o: Innate sensors recognize cellular stress and damage-associated signals
B-cell receptors bind directly to soluble uric acid crystals
Naive T cells recognize uric acid presented on HLA Class I molecules
Antibodies opsonize host cells injured by crystal deposition
Memory T cells undergo rapid clonal expansion in the joint space
q.p: Tissue injury and uric acid crystal deposition (Danger signal) -> Innate pattern-recognition receptors sense damage-associated signals -> Initiation of sterile innate inflammatory response

r.B: B-cell receptors are part of the adaptive immune system and recognize specific antigens rather than initiating acute sterile innate inflammation.
r.C: HLA Class I molecules bind and display peptide fragments rather than non-peptide uric acid crystals.
r.D: Antibody production is an adaptive humoral response that requires days to develop and does not initiate immediate sterile crystal inflammation.
r.E: Memory T-cell expansion is an adaptive mechanism requiring prior exposure to a specific peptide-HLA complex.

q.s: LO1 / Slides 8, 34-35, 41: A foundational principle for understanding (It's all about danger) & How the innate system detects a problem

q.v: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with fever, chills, and hypotension 6 hours after developing a severe urinary tract infection. Blood cultures grow a motile, flagellated Gram-negative rod. Resident macrophages and dendritic cells in her tissues rapidly detected the organism's surface lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and flagellin to trigger an early inflammatory alarm. Which of the following receptor pairs on her innate immune cells most likely mediated this recognition?
o: TLR2 and TLR3
TLR4 and TLR5
TLR7 and TLR8
TLR9 and NLR1
CD28 and CD80
q.p: Invasion by flagellated Gram-negative bacteria -> Innate pattern-recognition receptors TLR4 (binds LPS) and TLR5 (binds flagellin) detect conserved structures -> Rapid innate alarm

r.A: TLR2 recognizes peptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acid, and zymosan, while TLR3 recognizes viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA).
r.C: TLR7 and TLR8 recognize viral single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) rather than bacterial surface structures.
r.D: TLR9 recognizes unmethylated CpG motifs of DNA, and NLR1 recognizes specific peptidoglycan fragments.
r.E: CD28 and CD80 are costimulatory molecules involved in Signal 2 of T-cell activation, not innate pattern-recognition receptors.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 42: How the innate system detects a problem (Pattern recognition receptor table)

q.v: Which of the following pairs of characteristics best distinguishes the innate immune response from the adaptive immune response during a primary infection?
o: Innate: days to respond / Adaptive: minutes to hours to respond
Innate: recognizes peptide-HLA complexes / Adaptive: recognizes conserved microbial patterns
Innate: effectors already available / Adaptive: rare clones must expand
Innate: faster, larger secondary response / Adaptive: broadly similar repeat response
Innate: high antigen specificity / Adaptive: broad pattern recognition
q.p: Pathogen breaches barrier -> Pre-formed innate effectors act immediately -> Rare antigen-specific adaptive lymphocytes undergo clonal expansion over days

r.A: Innate immunity responds within minutes to hours, whereas adaptive immunity typically requires days on first exposure.
r.B: Innate immunity recognizes conserved microbial patterns, whereas adaptive T cells recognize specific peptide-HLA complexes.
r.D: Innate immunity mounts a broadly similar response upon repeat exposure, whereas adaptive immunity mounts a faster, larger secondary response.
r.E: Innate immunity relies on broad pattern recognition, whereas adaptive immunity is characterized by high antigen specificity.

q.s: LO2 / Slides 36-40: Innate and adaptive immunity (Use four dimensions to distinguish them)

q.v: A 28-year-old man steps on a rusty nail that punctures the skin of his foot, introducing extracellular bacteria into the subcutaneous tissue. Within hours, local innate sensors detect the microbes and recruit phagocytes to contain the infection. Meanwhile, dendritic cells capture bacterial antigens in the foot and become activated by local danger signals. Which of the following is the next key step required to bridge this local innate response to an effective adaptive response at the wound site?
o: Dendritic cells migrate to the draining lymph node, activate specific lymphocytes, which then exit into circulation and home to the tissue
Naive T cells circulate directly into the foot tissue, bind free bacterial antigens, and undergo clonal expansion locally
Dendritic cells differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells within the subcutaneous tissue
Activated neutrophils migrate from the foot to the draining lymph node to undergo clonal selection
Memory B cells in the bloodstream engulf the dendritic cells and transport them to the bone marrow
q.p: Antigen capture in tissue -> Migration of dendritic cells to draining lymph node -> Clonal activation and expansion of lymphocytes -> Exit into circulation -> Homing of effectors back to infected tissue

r.B: Naive T cells are activated by peptide-HLA complexes in the draining lymph node rather than by free antigen in peripheral tissue.
r.C: B cells, not dendritic cells, differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
r.D: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes recruited to the tissue to eliminate pathogens and do not undergo clonal selection in lymph nodes.
r.E: Memory B cells do not engulf dendritic cells; dendritic cells present antigen to lymphocytes in secondary lymphoid organs.

q.s: LO3 / Slides 45, 54-57: Localization: responders must reach the right place

q.v: Which of the following molecular interactions provides the second signal (Signal 2) that indicates an antigen-presenting cell has encountered danger and is licensed to activate a naive T cell?
o: T-cell receptor binding to a peptide-HLA Class II complex
CD28 on the T cell binding to CD80/CD86 (B7) on the antigen-presenting cell
IL-2 and IL-12 binding to cytokine receptors on the T cell
TLR4 on the macrophage binding to bacterial lipopolysaccharide
CD8 on the cytotoxic T cell binding to an HLA Class I heavy chain
q.p: APC encounters danger signals -> Upregulation of CD80/CD86 (B7) -> Engagement of CD28 on naive T cell (Signal 2) -> Licensing of T-cell activation

r.A: Recognition of a specific peptide displayed by an HLA molecule via the T-cell receptor represents Signal 1.
r.C: Cytokines binding to cytokine receptors represent Signal 3, which shapes expansion and functional differentiation.
r.D: TLR4 binding to lipopolysaccharide is an innate pattern-recognition event rather than a T-cell costimulatory signal.
r.E: CD8 binding to HLA Class I is part of antigen recognition (Signal 1) rather than costimulation (Signal 2).

q.s: LO3 / Slides 47-48: Antigen presentation and multi-signal activation

q.v: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of fever, myalgias, and a nonproductive cough. Nasopharyngeal swab confirms an acute viral infection of the respiratory epithelium. Inside the infected epithelial cells, viral proteins are synthesized in the cytosol and processed by the proteasome into peptide fragments. Which of the following mechanisms is most directly responsible for displaying these endogenous viral peptides on the epithelial cell surface and eliminating the infected cell?
o: Presentation on HLA Class I molecules to CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes
Presentation on HLA Class II molecules to CD4 helper T lymphocytes
Presentation on HLA Class I molecules to B lymphocytes
Direct binding of intact cytosolic viral proteins by secreted antibodies
Presentation on HLA Class II molecules to natural killer cells
q.p: Viral replication in cytosol -> Endogenous antigen processing via proteasome -> Peptide loaded onto HLA Class I -> Recognition by CD8 cytotoxic T cell -> Elimination of infected cell

r.B: HLA Class II molecules primarily present exogenous antigens processed in endosomes to CD4 helper T cells.
r.C: B lymphocytes recognize intact antigens via B-cell receptors and do not recognize peptides bound to HLA Class I.
r.D: Secreted antibodies function in humoral immunity against extracellular targets and toxins and cannot access intact cytosolic proteins inside live cells.
r.E: Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes and do not recognize viral peptides presented on HLA Class II molecules.

q.s: LO4 / Slides 45-46, 51-53: Antigen presentation & HLA: Displaying Antigens to T Cells

q.v: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with a painful, erythematous skin abscess on his forearm. Culture of the purulent drainage grows an extracellular bacterium that produces a soluble exotoxin. Which of the following adaptive immune mechanisms is best suited to neutralize the soluble toxin and recruit complement and Fc-receptor-bearing cells to clear the extracellular bacteria?
o: Differentiation of B cells into plasma cells that secrete antibodies
Direct lysis of extracellular bacteria by CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognizing HLA Class I
Endogenous processing of the toxin via the proteasome and TAP1/TAP2 transporters
Intracellular autophagy mediated by cytosolic NOD-like receptors
Induction of T-cell anergy through presentation of toxin without costimulation
q.p: Extracellular bacteria and toxins -> Humoral immunity engaged -> B cells differentiate into plasma cells -> Secreted antibodies bind targets and recruit complement and Fc-receptor-bearing cells

r.B: CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognize peptide-HLA Class I on infected host cells and do not directly lyse cell-free bacteria.
r.C: Proteasome and TAP processing is the endogenous pathway for intracellular antigens presented on HLA Class I.
r.D: Autophagy and NOD-like receptor sensing are innate intracellular defense mechanisms rather than adaptive humoral mechanisms.
r.E: T-cell anergy results in lymphocyte unresponsiveness rather than protective clearance of an extracellular pathogen.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 53: Humoral and cell-mediated immunity

q.v:
A 26-year-old medical student is exposed to a patient with active influenza. The student received the seasonal influenza vaccine 3 months ago, while her roommate, who was also exposed at the same time, has never been vaccinated or infected with this influenza strain. Serial blood samples are collected from both individuals to measure the kinetics of their immune responses:

Student (Previously Vaccinated):
  Time to detectable antigen-specific lymphocytes: 1-2 days
  Peak antibody titer: 1:1,280

Roommate (Unvaccinated):
  Time to detectable antigen-specific lymphocytes: 7-10 days
  Peak antibody titer: 1:80

Which of the following best explains the kinetic and magnitude differences observed in the vaccinated student's lab profile?
o: Rapid recognition and robust expansion by preexisting antigen-specific memory B and T cells
Upregulation of Toll-like receptor affinity on resident tissue macrophages
Continuous secretion of high-titer antibodies by innate dendritic cells
Permanent disruption of epithelial barriers allowing faster antigen entry
Bypass of HLA presentation requirements by naive CD4 and CD8 T cells
q.p: Prior vaccination -> Persistence of long-lived memory B and T cells -> Re-exposure to same antigen -> Rapid activation and high-magnitude secondary expansion

r.B: Innate pattern-recognition receptors such as TLRs have fixed specificity and yield a broadly similar response upon repeat exposure.
r.C: Antibodies are secreted by B-cell-derived plasma cells, not by innate dendritic cells.
r.D: Barrier disruption facilitates infection rather than protective immunity, and vaccination does not damage epithelial barriers.
r.E: T cells always require peptide presentation on HLA molecules and cannot bypass this requirement.

q.s: LO2, LO3 / Slides 40, 55, 58: Primary vs memory responses

q.v:
An 8-month-old boy is evaluated for recurrent sinopulmonary infections. To assess his lymphocyte repertoire and activation capacity, peripheral blood mononuclear cells are isolated and incubated with a novel viral peptide and antigen-presenting cells under two experimental conditions:

Condition 1 (APCs expressing peptide-HLA + costimulatory B7 + IL-12):
  Antigen-specific T-cell count at Day 0: 10 cells/well
  Antigen-specific T-cell count at Day 5: 50,000 cells/well

Condition 2 (Resting APCs expressing peptide-HLA only, without danger signals):
  Antigen-specific T-cell count at Day 0: 10 cells/well
  Antigen-specific T-cell count at Day 5: 10 cells/well (unresponsive to subsequent stimulation)

Which of the following best accounts for the laboratory findings in Condition 2?
o: TCR recognition of peptide-HLA without Signal 2 induces T-cell anergy
Absence of Signal 3 causes naive T cells to transdifferentiate into B cells
Resting APCs degrade the T-cell receptors via the proteasome
Lack of costimulation triggers immediate antibody secretion instead of proliferation
Naive T cells cannot bind peptide-HLA complexes unless IL-12 is present first
q.p: Naive T cell recognizes peptide-HLA (Signal 1) on resting APC -> Absence of danger context and costimulation (Signal 2) -> Induction of anergy (unresponsiveness) and failure of clonal expansion

r.B: T cells are lineage-committed lymphocytes and do not transdifferentiate into B cells.
r.C: The proteasome degrades endogenous intracellular proteins within the APC for HLA Class I presentation, not surface TCRs on T cells.
r.D: T cells do not secrete antibodies; humoral antibody production is a function of B-cell-derived plasma cells.
r.E: Naive T cells can bind peptide-HLA via their TCR (Signal 1) independently of Signal 3 cytokines, though full activation requires all three signals.

q.s: LO5 / Slides 43, 47-50: Antigen presentation and multi-signal activation & Clonal selection and expansion

q.v: A 42-year-old woman is receiving experimental therapy for an autoimmune disorder. The therapeutic agent selectively blocks the interaction between costimulatory ligands on tissue dendritic cells and their corresponding receptors on naive T cells within draining lymph nodes, while leaving epithelial barriers and innate pattern-recognition receptors completely intact. If this patient sustains a minor skin abrasion contaminated with novel bacteria, which of the following outcomes is most likely?
o: Normal local innate inflammation will occur, but antigen-specific T-cell clonal expansion will be impaired
Innate phagocytes will fail to detect bacterial lipopolysaccharide and peptidoglycan at the wound site
Epithelial barriers across the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts will immediately break down
Preexisting innate complement proteins will be unable to opsonize bacteria in the tissue
Dendritic cells will be unable to capture bacterial antigens or migrate to the draining lymph node
q.p: Skin abrasion with bacteria -> Intact innate sensors trigger local inflammation -> Blockade of costimulation (Signal 2) in lymph node -> Failure to decide/amplify rare antigen-specific T-cell clones

r.B: Innate recognition of microbial patterns via PRRs (such as TLRs and NLRs) does not depend on T-cell costimulatory signals.
r.C: Anatomic and chemical barriers function prior to immune activation and are unaffected by T-cell costimulation blockade.
r.D: Innate effectors such as complement are pre-formed and operate independently of adaptive T-cell costimulation.
r.E: Antigen capture and dendritic cell migration occur upstream of T-cell costimulation in the immune response sequence.

q.s: LO5 / Slides 14-18, 43, 47, 59: The Immune System (Decide + amplify) & Summary

q.v: A 67-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 4-day history of dysuria, urinary urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. She has a history of severe gastroesophageal reflux disease and Sjögren syndrome, which causes chronic dry eyes and dry mouth. Physical examination reveals suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites. Disruption of which of the following innate immune barriers most directly contributed to the development of this patient's acute infection?
o: Skin
Mucociliary escalator
Saliva
Urinary mucous membranes
Stomach acid
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize acute urinary tract infection from dysuria, urgency, and positive urinalysis) -> Step 2 (Identify urinary mucous membranes as the local innate barrier preventing colonization and invasion in the urinary tract)

r.A: The skin is an external physical barrier that prevents microbial invasion from cutaneous injuries rather than urinary tract colonization.
r.B: The mucociliary escalator is an innate barrier of the respiratory tract that clears inhaled microbes and mucus.
r.C: Saliva is an innate barrier of the oral cavity that protects against oral colonization, which is impaired in Sjögren syndrome but does not directly cause a urinary tract infection.
r.E: Stomach acid is a chemical barrier of the gastrointestinal tract that eliminates ingested pathogens.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 24-27: Checkpoint! & Are you in danger? (Innate immune barriers)

q.v: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with fever, irritability, and a petechial rash. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis confirms bacterial meningitis, and PCR identifies an infection with a DNA virus and bacteria containing unmethylated CpG-motifs of DNA. Macrophages and dendritic cells in the central nervous system detect these unmethylated CpG-motifs to initiate an innate alarm. Which of the following pattern-recognition receptors is directly responsible for recognizing this specific microbial structure?
o: TLR2
TLR3
TLR4
TLR9
NLR2
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the microbial target molecule as unmethylated CpG-motifs of DNA from bacteria and DNA viruses) -> Step 2 (Match unmethylated CpG-motifs of DNA to its specific pattern-recognition receptor, TLR9)

r.A: TLR2 recognizes peptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acid, lipoarabinomannan, and zymosan from Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi.
r.B: TLR3 recognizes double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) produced by viruses.
r.C: TLR4 recognizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from Gram-negative bacteria.
r.E: NLR2 recognizes muramyl dipeptide derived from bacterial peptidoglycan.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 42: How the innate system detects a problem (Pattern-recognition receptor table)

q.v:
A 24-year-old man lacerates his leg while hiking in the woods, introducing soil bacteria into the subcutaneous tissue for the first time. Within 2 hours, local innate sensors detect the bacteria and initiate an inflammatory response. However, a measurable adaptive response takes 7 days to develop. Laboratory evaluation of his immune response over time shows:
  Time 0 to 6 hours: High neutrophil and macrophage activity; undetectable antigen-specific T cells
  Day 1: Dendritic cell migration to draining lymph nodes; rare naive T-cell clones present
  Day 7: Markedly elevated numbers of antigen-specific effector T cells at the wound site
Which of the following best explains the delay in the appearance of the effector cells seen on Day 7?
o: Innate effectors must undergo gene rearrangement before recognizing conserved microbial patterns
Rare antigen-specific lymphocyte clones must undergo selection and clonal expansion
Pre-formed adaptive effector cells are sequestered in the bone marrow until innate immunity fails
Dendritic cells cannot capture antigen in peripheral tissues until antibodies are produced
HLA molecules are only synthesized by antigen-presenting cells after 5 days of inflammation
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the timeline data showing immediate innate activity within hours versus adaptive T-cell appearance at Day 7) -> Step 2 (Attribute the multi-day delay of the primary adaptive response to the need for rare antigen-specific clones to expand)

r.A: Innate immune cells use pre-formed pattern-recognition receptors that are already available and do not undergo gene rearrangement.
r.C: Adaptive effector cells are not pre-formed prior to a primary infection; they must be generated via proliferation and differentiation of rare naive clones.
r.D: Dendritic cells capture antigen at the site of infection early in the response and migrate to the draining lymph node to initiate adaptive immunity.
r.E: HLA molecules are constitutively expressed on antigen-presenting cells and present peptides to T cells early in the activation sequence.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 37-40 & 48: Innate and adaptive immunity (Scale and Timing) & Clonal selection and expansion

q.v: A 45-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of a painful, red, swollen lesion on his left hand after being bitten by a stray cat. A biopsy of the infected skin shows numerous extracellular bacteria being engulfed by neutrophils and macrophages, while immature dendritic cells are actively capturing bacterial antigens and entering afferent lymphatic vessels. According to the normal sequence of an immune response, which of the following events must occur next for effector T cells to reach the infected hand?
o: Direct migration of naive T cells from the thymus into the infected skin
Activation and clonal expansion of antigen-specific lymphocytes in the draining lymph node
Immediate differentiation of tissue macrophages into antibody-secreting plasma cells
Secretion of antibodies by naive T cells inside the afferent lymphatic vessels
Contraction of the lymphocyte pool to establish long-lived immunologic memory
q.p: Step 1 (Trace the localization sequence from antigen capture in tissue and migration via afferent lymphatics) -> Step 2 (Identify the next step in the draining lymph node: activation and clonal expansion of antigen-specific lymphocytes before exiting into circulation)

r.A: Naive T cells are activated by mature dendritic cells in the draining lymph node before homing to infected peripheral tissues as effector cells.
r.C: B cells, rather than macrophages, differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
r.D: B-lineage plasma cells secrete antibodies, whereas T cells mediate cell-mediated immunity via TCR recognition of peptide-HLA complexes.
r.E: Resolution and memory formation occur at the end of the immune response after effectors have localized to the tissue and eliminated the pathogen.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 54-55: Localization: responders must reach the right place & A typical immune response

q.v: Following antigen capture in an infected peripheral tissue, mature dendritic cells migrate to the T-cell zone of the draining lymph node to initiate an adaptive immune response. Which of the following best describes the specific role of Signal 3 during the multi-signal activation of a naive T cell?
o: Recognition of a specific peptide fragment displayed in the groove of an HLA molecule
Binding of CD80/CD86 on the dendritic cell to CD28 on the naive T cell
Licensing of the antigen-presenting cell by conserved microbial danger signals
Cytokine signaling that shapes T-cell expansion and functional differentiation
Homing of antibody-producing plasma cells to the bone marrow and mucosal sites
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the three-signal model of naive T-cell activation by an antigen-presenting cell) -> Step 2 (Identify Signal 3 as cytokine signaling, such as IL-2 and IL-12, which shapes clonal expansion and functional differentiation)

r.A: TCR recognition of a specific peptide displayed by an HLA molecule represents Signal 1 of T-cell activation.
r.B: The interaction between CD80/CD86 and CD28 provides costimulation, which is Signal 2 of T-cell activation.
r.C: Danger signals license the antigen-presenting cell to express costimulatory molecules (Signal 2), rather than acting directly as Signal 3.
r.E: Homing of plasma cells to the bone marrow or mucosal sites occurs during the localization and effector phase after B-cell activation.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 47-48: Antigen presentation and multi-signal activation & Clonal selection and expansion

q.v: A 31-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of fever, pharyngeal erythema, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Throat culture grows an extracellular bacterium. In the patient's draining cervical lymph nodes, dendritic cells internalize the extracellular bacteria into endosomes, degrade the bacterial proteins, and load the resulting peptide fragments onto surface display molecules to activate helper T cells. Which of the following pairs correctly matches the antigen-presenting molecule and the T-cell subset involved in this exogenous antigen processing pathway?
o: HLA Class I and CD4 T cells
HLA Class I and CD8 T cells
HLA Class II and CD4 T cells
HLA Class II and CD8 T cells
B-cell receptor and CD4 T cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the pathway as exogenous antigen processing of an extracellular bacterium within endosomes) -> Step 2 (Match exogenous peptide display to HLA Class II molecules, which present peptides primarily to CD4 helper T cells)

r.A: HLA Class I molecules present endogenous cytoplasmic peptides primarily to CD8 T cells, not CD4 T cells.
r.B: HLA Class I and CD8 T cells mediate the endogenous antigen processing pathway used to detect intracellular pathogens such as viruses.
r.D: HLA Class II molecules are recognized by CD4 helper T cells rather than CD8 cytotoxic T cells.
r.E: The B-cell receptor binds intact antigen directly on B cells and does not display processed peptides to T-cell receptors.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 45-46 & 53: Antigen presentation & HLA: Displaying Antigens to T Cells

q.v: Which of the following is a primary function of CD4 T cells in coordinating cell-mediated and humoral immunity after recognizing peptide-HLA complexes?
o: Differentiating directly into plasma cells that secrete antigen-specific antibodies
Binding conserved microbial patterns via surface Toll-like receptors
Forming pores in the membranes of extracellular bacteria via the complement cascade
Activating and coordinating other leukocytes and providing help for B-cell activation
Directly lysing virus-infected epithelial cells that display peptides on HLA Class I
q.p: Step 1 (Distinguish the effector roles of T-cell subsets in cell-mediated and humoral immunity) -> Step 2 (Identify CD4 helper T cells as the subset that activates and coordinates other leukocytes and provides help for B-cell activation)

r.A: B lymphocytes, rather than CD4 T cells, differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
r.B: Innate immune cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils use Toll-like receptors to bind conserved microbial patterns.
r.C: Complement proteins, which are innate effector molecules that can be recruited by antibodies, form membrane pores in microbes.
r.E: CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognize peptides on HLA Class I and directly kill virus-infected cells.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 53 & 55: Humoral and cell-mediated immunity & A typical immune response

q.v:
A 10-year-old girl is enrolled in a clinical study evaluating the immune response to a two-dose viral vaccine given at Day 0 and Day 60. Blood samples are collected after each dose to measure the relative number of virus-specific lymphocytes and serum antibody titers:
  Day 0 (Dose 1): Baseline
  Day 3: Virus-specific T cells undetectable; antibody titer undetectable
  Day 10: Virus-specific T cells 100 units; antibody titer 40 units
  Day 60 (Dose 2): Virus-specific T cells 20 units; antibody titer 15 units
  Day 63: Virus-specific T cells 850 units; antibody titer 600 units
Which of the following best explains the rapid increase in effector T cells and antibodies observed just 3 days after the second dose (Day 63) compared to the first dose (Day 3)?
o: Upregulation of Toll-like receptors on tissue-resident macrophages
Rapid recognition and activation of pre-existing long-lived memory B and T cells
Delayed migration of immature dendritic cells from the skin to the lymph node
De novo generation of diverse naive T-cell receptor repertoires in the bone marrow
Loss of epithelial barrier integrity at the injection site during the second dose
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the lab table showing a slow, lower-magnitude primary response peaking around Day 10 versus a rapid, high-magnitude secondary response within 3 days of re-exposure) -> Step 2 (Attribute the faster, larger secondary response to the persistence and rapid reactivation of memory B and T cells)

r.A: Innate immune cells such as macrophages produce a broadly similar response upon repeat exposure and do not account for antigen-specific memory.
r.C: Delayed dendritic cell migration would slow the immune response rather than produce a rapid secondary peak within 3 days.
r.D: Naive T-cell receptor diversity is generated prior to antigen exposure, whereas the secondary response relies on already-selected memory clones.
r.E: Barrier disruption initiates local innate detection in both doses but does not explain the accelerated expansion of antigen-specific lymphocytes.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 40, 55, & 58: Innate and adaptive immunity (Repeat exposure) & Primary vs memory responses

q.v: A 50-year-old man is recovering from a severe viral pneumonia that began 2 weeks ago. Repeat chest radiograph shows clearing of the pulmonary infiltrates, and viral PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab is now negative. In his lung tissue and draining lymph nodes, the vast majority of virus-specific effector lymphocytes are undergoing contraction, while a small subset persists as long-lived memory cells. Which of the following best explains the physiological importance of this resolution phase?
o: It allows innate pattern-recognition receptors to mutate and increase their affinity for the virus
It prevents ongoing collateral tissue injury and immunopathology once the threat is eliminated
It converts surviving memory T cells back into naive T cells with new antigen specificities
It ensures that all self-reactive T cells receive strong costimulation from tissue dendritic cells
It degrades all circulating antibodies so that humoral immunity is reset to baseline
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the patient's stage in the immune response as the resolution and memory phase following pathogen clearance) -> Step 2 (Connect contraction/resolution to the core principle that immune responses must be self-limited to prevent collateral tissue injury and immunopathology)

r.A: Innate pattern-recognition receptors are germline-encoded to bind conserved patterns and do not mutate to increase affinity.
r.C: Surviving memory T cells retain their original antigen specificity to provide faster protection upon re-exposure.
r.D: Costimulation of self-reactive T cells would promote autoimmunity rather than resolution and immune control.
r.E: Long-lived memory B cells and plasma cells continue to maintain protective antibody levels after the acute infection resolves.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 1, 3, 16, & 59: Why do we need an Immune System? & The Immune System (Resolve + remember)

q.v: A 29-year-old woman is evaluated for a newly diagnosed solid tumor of the breast. Histologic examination of the tumor biopsy shows malignant epithelial cells that have accumulated multiple somatic mutations, along with a dense infiltrate of host dendritic cells, macrophages, and T lymphocytes surrounding necrotic tumor cells. No bacterial, viral, or fungal organisms are present in the tissue. Which of the following best explains how the immune system initiates a response against this sterile tumor?
o: Innate sensors recognize altered self, cellular stress, and damage-associated signals released by tumor cells
Antibodies only bind to intact extracellular bacteria and cannot recognize transformed host cells
Naive T cells directly bind to intact, unprocessed DNA mutations inside the nucleus of tumor cells
Innate immunity can only be activated by foreign microbial structures such as lipopolysaccharide
Normal host cells lack HLA Class I molecules, allowing CD8 T cells to kill them indiscriminately
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize a sterile malignancy causing cellular stress and tissue necrosis without microbial infection) -> Step 2 (Apply the Danger hypothesis: innate pattern-recognition receptors sense altered self, cellular stress, and damage-associated signals from cancers to initiate an immune response)

r.B: The immune system is capable of recognizing and removing transformed (cancerous) cells in addition to microbes.
r.C: T-cell receptors cannot bind intact intracellular DNA; they only recognize processed peptide fragments displayed on cell-surface HLA molecules.
r.D: According to the danger model, innate sensors detect non-infectious dangers such as injuries, toxins, and cancers in addition to microbial strangers.
r.E: Normal nucleated host cells express HLA Class I molecules, which display intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells for targeted surveillance.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 3, 8, & 41: Why do we need an Immune System?, A foundational principle (Dangers), & How the innate system detects a problem

myLectures.name: Danger Signals and Antigens
myLectures.note: Mullins, Tue Nov 3 (slides are titled 'Danger Signal and Antigens'). Cards picked to match the slides and their figures, checked against your 34 cards (see danger_signals_card_check.csv). PAMP/PRR, innate-vs-adaptive and TCR cards are already in Introduction to Immunology, so they aren't repeated here. Adds 9 cloze notes (deck: Mullins - Danger Signals and Antigens). Left out: Gram stain and cell-wall details, prion disease, specific viruses, endotoxin structure, haptens/epitopes.

add.cloze: A {{c1::pathogen}} is an agent capable of causing disease in a susceptible host, whereas {{c2::microorganism (microbe)}} is a broad term for microscopic biological entities that does not imply disease
add.extra: Not every microbe causes disease, and not every infectious agent is cellular.

add.cloze: Infectious-agent classes: prokaryotic = bacteria; eukaryotic = {{c1::fungi, protozoa and helminths}}; non-cellular = {{c2::viruses and prions}}. Viruses replicate {{c3::using host-cell machinery}}; prions are {{c4::infectious misfolded proteins}}
add.extra: Prokaryotes: no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, cell wall present, binary fission. Eukaryotes: nucleus and organelles, cell division / complex life cycles.

add.cloze: Whether infection produces disease depends on {{c1::agent}} factors, {{c2::host}} factors and {{c3::contextual}} factors
add.extra: Agent: virulence factors, inoculum, tissue tropism, replication strategy. Host: barrier integrity, immune status, age, genetics, prior immunity. Context: portal of entry, tissue environment, microbiota, exposure conditions.

add.cloze: PAMP sources: unmethylated CpG DNA comes from {{c1::bacteria and some viruses}}; double-stranded RNA from {{c2::viral replication}}; fungal glycans (mannans, β-glucans) from {{c3::fungal cell walls}}
add.extra: Other PAMPs: LPS (Gram-negative outer membrane, TLR4), peptidoglycan (Gram-positive, TLR2), flagellin (bacterial flagella, TLR5).

add.cloze: Three advantages of recognizing conserved microbial patterns: {{c1::efficiency}} (a limited receptor set surveys many pathogens), {{c2::speed}} (immediate response) and {{c3::reliability}} (essential microbial structures are hard to discard)

An immunologic antigen is {{c1::a molecular structure recognized specifically by the adaptive immune system}}; pathogen-derived antigens include {{c2::proteins/peptides, polysaccharides, lipids and other complex molecules}}
add.extra: Antigens are both inducers and targets of adaptive responses. A capsid antigen from one virus generally differs from the matching antigen of a related virus.

add.cloze: A B cell recognizes {{c1::intact (native) antigen}} directly through its {{c2::B-cell receptor (membrane-bound antibody)}}
add.extra: T cells recognize only short peptides (~8-20 amino acids) bound to HLA (MHC) on antigen-presenting cells.

add.cloze: PRRs are {{c1::germline-encoded and pattern-focused}}, whereas BCRs and TCRs are {{c2::highly diverse and antigen-specific}}

Innate PAMP recognition answers "{{c1::Is a microbe present?}}"; adaptive antigen recognition answers "{{c2::Which specific target is present?}}". A PAMP is not the same as an antigen: PAMPs are {{c3::conserved patterns recognized by innate PRRs}}, antigens are {{c4::specific structures recognized by B- or T-cell receptors}}
add.extra: PAMPs are shared across many microbes; antigens are often unique to a pathogen or strain. Lecture: "All PAMPs are antigens, but not all antigens are PAMPs."

q.v: A 34-year-old woman presents to the clinic with watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping after returning from a camping trip where she drank untreated stream water. Stool examination reveals a microscopic infectious agent that possesses a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Which of the following classes of infectious agents is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
o: Bacteria
Protozoa
Viruses
Prions
Bacteriophages
q.p: Step 1 (Identify cellular organization with nucleus and membrane-bound organelles as eukaryotic) -> Step 2 (Match eukaryotic organization to protozoa, fungi, or helminths)

r.A: Bacteria are prokaryotic organisms that lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
r.C: Viruses are non-cellular infectious agents that do not have a nucleus or organelles and require host-cell machinery for replication.
r.D: Prions are non-cellular, protein-based infectious agents without nucleic acids or cellular organelles.
r.E: Bacteriophages are acellular viruses that infect bacteria and lack cellular organization.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 4-5: Medically important classes of infectious agents

q.v:
A 68-year-old man is hospitalized with fever and a productive cough. Sputum samples are analyzed to characterize the causative pathogen, yielding the following structural profile:
  Nucleus: Absent
  Membrane-bound organelles: Absent
  Cell wall: Present
  Replication strategy: Binary fission
Which of the following best classifies the biological organization of this pathogen?
o: Prokaryotic
Eukaryotic
Unicellular parasitic
Acellular viral
Protein-based non-cellular
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze lab profile showing absence of nucleus/organelles, presence of cell wall, and binary fission) -> Step 2 (Classify the agent as a prokaryote/bacterium)

r.B: Eukaryotic pathogens such as fungi, protozoa, and helminths possess a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
r.C: Unicellular parasites (protozoa) are eukaryotes that divide via eukaryotic cell division and complex life cycles rather than binary fission without a nucleus.
r.D: Acellular viral agents lack a cell wall and require host-cell machinery for replication.
r.E: Protein-based non-cellular agents (prions) lack a cell wall and do not replicate via binary fission.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 5: Medically important classes of infectious agents

q.v: A 24-year-old man is exposed to a respiratory virus after his roommate develops a severe cough. Although the virus is detected on his nasal swab, the man remains completely asymptomatic. The physician notes that the patient received a vaccine against this virus six months ago and has intact mucosal surfaces. In the host-agent-environment framework of infectious disease, which of the following pairs of factors best accounts for the absence of clinical disease in this patient?
o: Virulence factors and inoculum size
Tissue tropism and replication strategy
Barrier integrity and prior immunity
Portal of entry and microbiota
Tissue environment and exposure conditions
q.p: Step 1 (Identify intact mucosa as barrier integrity and vaccination as prior immunity) -> Step 2 (Classify both as host factors that prevent infection from progressing to clinical disease)

r.A: Virulence factors and inoculum size are properties of the infectious agent rather than the host.
r.B: Tissue tropism and replication strategy are characteristics of the infectious agent rather than the host.
r.D: Portal of entry and microbiota are contextual environmental factors rather than intrinsic host defense attributes described here.
r.E: Tissue environment and exposure conditions represent the context of the infection rather than the patient's barrier and immune status.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 6: Infection does not automatically equal disease

q.v: Which of the following best describes the relationship between pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and immunologic antigens?
o: All antigens are PAMPs, but not all PAMPs are antigens
All PAMPs are antigens, but not all antigens are PAMPs
PAMPs are recognized only by B cells, whereas antigens are recognized by macrophages
PAMPs are unique to individual viral strains, whereas antigens are shared across classes
PAMPs require MHC presentation, whereas antigens bind exclusively to Toll-like receptors
q.p: Step 1 (Compare the definitions of PAMPs as conserved microbial structures and antigens as any molecule recognized by adaptive receptors) -> Step 2 (Conclude that conserved PAMPs can also be recognized as antigens, but many unique antigens are not conserved PAMPs)

r.A: Many pathogen-specific antigens are unique to a single strain and do not function as conserved PAMPs for innate receptors.
r.C: PAMPs are recognized by innate pattern-recognition receptors on cells like macrophages, whereas antigens are recognized by B-cell and T-cell receptors.
r.D: PAMPs are conserved across many microbes, whereas antigens are often unique to a specific pathogen or strain.
r.E: Peptide antigens require MHC presentation for T-cell recognition, whereas PAMPs bind directly to pattern-recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 13: A PAMP is not the same as an antigen

q.v: A 45-year-old man develops redness, warmth, and swelling around a forearm laceration sustained while working in a garden. Within hours of the injury, tissue-resident innate immune cells detect conserved microbial structures and initiate an inflammatory alarm. Which of the following receptor types directly mediates this rapid recognition?
o: B-cell receptors
T-cell receptors
Toll-like receptors
MHC class I molecules
Secreted immunoglobulins
q.p: Step 1 (Identify rapid detection of conserved microbial structures as innate PAMP recognition) -> Step 2 (Match PAMP detection to germline-encoded pattern-recognition receptors, including Toll-like receptors)

r.A: B-cell receptors are adaptive immune receptors that recognize specific intact antigens rather than broad conserved danger signals.
r.B: T-cell receptors are adaptive immune receptors that recognize specific peptide antigens displayed by MHC molecules.
r.D: MHC molecules display processed peptide antigens to T cells rather than acting as innate signaling receptors for conserved PAMPs.
r.E: Secreted immunoglobulins (antibodies) are adaptive effectors produced by B cells that target specific antigens.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 8: Danger signals: pathogen-associated molecular patterns

q.v: A 52-year-old woman with an indwelling urinary catheter develops fever and flank pain. Urine culture grows a motile, Gram-negative rod that propels itself using surface appendages. Innate immune cells in the urinary tract detect both the outer membrane of this bacterium and the protein subunit of its locomotor appendages. Which of the following pairs of pathogen-associated molecular patterns is being recognized in this patient?
o: Lipopolysaccharide and flagellin
Fungal glycans and double-stranded RNA
CpG DNA and fungal glycans
Double-stranded RNA and lipopolysaccharide
Flagellin and fungal glycans
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the Gram-negative outer membrane component as LPS and the bacterial flagella component as flagellin) -> Step 2 (Combine both PAMPs as the innate signals detected during infection)

r.B: Fungal glycans are found in fungal cell walls and double-stranded RNA is a hallmark of viral replication, neither of which applies to a Gram-negative bacterium.
r.C: Fungal glycans are characteristic of fungal cell walls rather than the outer membrane or flagella of Gram-negative bacteria.
r.D: Double-stranded RNA is produced during viral replication rather than serving as the protein subunit of bacterial flagella.
r.E: Fungal glycans are derived from fungal cell walls rather than the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 10: Common examples of pathogen-associated molecular patterns

q.v: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and cough due to an acute respiratory infection. Inside his infected airway epithelial cells, the pathogen synthesizes double-stranded RNA intermediates to replicate its genome, while also displaying a strain-specific outer capsid protein. How do the boy's innate and adaptive immune systems classify these two pathogen-derived molecules?
o: Double-stranded RNA as a PAMP / capsid protein as an antigen
Double-stranded RNA as an antigen / capsid protein as a PRR
Double-stranded RNA as a PRR / capsid protein as a PAMP
Double-stranded RNA as an MHC molecule / capsid protein as a TLR
Double-stranded RNA as a B-cell receptor / capsid protein as a T-cell receptor
q.p: Step 1 (Identify viral double-stranded RNA replication intermediates as a conserved PAMP) -> Step 2 (Identify the strain-specific viral capsid protein as an immunologic antigen recognized by adaptive immunity)

r.B: The viral capsid protein is a pathogen-derived molecule (antigen), not a host pattern-recognition receptor (PRR).
r.C: Double-stranded RNA is a microbial danger signal (PAMP) rather than a host receptor, and the unique capsid protein functions as a specific antigen rather than a conserved PAMP.
r.D: MHC molecules and TLRs are host immune proteins, not viral structures.
r.E: B-cell and T-cell receptors are host adaptive lymphocyte receptors, not viral nucleic acids or capsid proteins.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 10 & 12: Common examples of PAMPs & Immunologic antigens

q.v: Which of the following accurately contrasts antigen recognition by B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes?
o: B cells bind peptides on MHC, whereas T cells bind intact surface antigens
B cells bind intact structures directly, whereas T cells recognize peptides displayed by MHC
B cells recognize only lipid PAMPs, whereas T cells recognize only fungal glycans
B cells use Toll-like receptors for specificity, whereas T cells use germline-encoded PRRs
B cells respond exclusively to prokaryotic cells, whereas T cells respond exclusively to viruses
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the structural requirement for B-cell receptor binding as intact molecular structures) -> Step 2 (Contrast with T-cell receptor binding, which requires processed peptide antigens presented on MHC)

r.A: This reverses the recognition mechanisms; B cells bind intact antigens directly, while T cells require MHC peptide presentation.
r.C: Both B and T cells recognize specific antigens rather than exclusively recognizing conserved PAMPs like fungal glycans.
r.D: Toll-like receptors and PRRs are innate receptors; B and T cells use highly diverse B-cell and T-cell receptors for antigen specificity.
r.E: Both B cells and T cells can participate in adaptive immune responses against a wide variety of prokaryotic, eukaryotic, and viral pathogens.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 14: B-cell and T-cell antigen recognition

q.v:
A research laboratory compares two distinct immune recognition pathways activated during a bacterial infection in a 40-year-old patient. The characteristics of each pathway are summarized below:
  Pathway 1: Detects motifs shared across many microbes; rapid and broad response; no immunologic memory.
  Pathway 2: Distinguishes molecular features unique to a single bacterial strain; specific response; generates long-lasting memory.
Which of the following receptor pairs mediates Pathway 1 and Pathway 2, respectively?
o: B-cell receptors and Toll-like receptors
T-cell receptors and B-cell receptors
Pattern-recognition receptors and T-cell receptors
MHC molecules and pattern-recognition receptors
Secreted antibodies and MHC molecules
q.p: Step 1 (Match Pathway 1's broad, rapid detection of shared motifs to innate pattern-recognition receptors) -> Step 2 (Match Pathway 2's strain-specific recognition and memory to adaptive B-cell or T-cell receptors)

r.A: B-cell receptors mediate specific adaptive recognition (Pathway 2), whereas Toll-like receptors mediate broad innate detection (Pathway 1).
r.B: Both T-cell and B-cell receptors mediate specific adaptive immunity (Pathway 2) rather than broad innate pattern detection.
r.D: MHC molecules present peptides to T cells rather than functioning as the broad innate receptors of Pathway 1, and PRRs do not generate adaptive memory in Pathway 2.
r.E: Secreted antibodies are adaptive effectors and MHC molecules are antigen-presenting proteins; neither serves as the innate pattern-recognition receptor for Pathway 1.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 15: PAMPs and antigens answer different questions

q.v: A 19-year-old woman receives an intramuscular booster vaccine containing a purified bacterial surface protein. Over the next two weeks, her immune system coordinates an integrated response that leads to durable, pathogen-specific protection. Which of the following sequences best represents how innate and adaptive immunity work together to establish this protection?
o: Broad innate detection -> antigen presentation -> precise adaptive targeting
Precise adaptive targeting -> PAMP synthesis -> broad innate detection
B-cell memory generation -> PRR downregulation -> innate inflammation
T-cell peptide binding -> intact antigen shedding -> TLR degradation
Antibody secretion -> binary fission -> germline receptor mutation
q.p: Step 1 (Innate PRRs broadly detect danger signals and activate antigen-presenting cells) -> Step 2 (Antigen presentation activates B and T lymphocytes for precise adaptive targeting and memory)

r.B: Innate detection precedes and activates adaptive targeting, and host cells do not synthesize microbial PAMPs.
r.C: Innate detection and inflammation occur initially to promote antigen presentation before B-cell memory is established.
r.D: Antigen processing and presentation precede T-cell peptide binding, and TLR degradation is not the mechanism of adaptive activation.
r.E: Binary fission is a prokaryotic replication strategy, and germline-encoded innate receptors do not undergo mutation after antibody secretion.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 1 & 16: Innate and adaptive immunity work together

q.v: A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with intense perianal itching that is worse at night. She works at a daycare center where several children have had similar symptoms. A tape test of the perianal skin reveals oval eggs of a multicellular parasite that undergoes a complex life cycle and possesses a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Which of the following best classifies this infectious agent and its cellular organization?
o: Prokaryote / Bacteria
Eukaryote / Helminth
Eukaryote / Protozoa
Non-cellular / Virus
Non-cellular / Prion
q.p: Step 1 (Identify multicellular parasite with nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, and complex life cycle) -> Step 2 (Classify as Eukaryotic Helminth)

r.A: Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotic organisms that lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
r.C: Protozoa are eukaryotic parasites, but they are unicellular organisms rather than multicellular worms.
r.D: Viruses are non-cellular infectious agents that lack organelles and require host-cell machinery for replication.
r.E: Prions are non-cellular, protein-based infectious agents that lack nucleic acids and cellular structures.

q.s: LO1, Slide 4-5: Medically important classes of infectious agents

q.v:
A 62-year-old man is evaluated for rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus. Brain biopsy reveals spongiform changes caused by an infectious agent that lacks nucleic acids and does not use host-cell machinery for genetic replication. Structural analysis of the isolated pathogen yields the following profile:
  Nucleus: Not applicable
  Membrane-bound organelles: Not applicable
  Cell wall: Not applicable
  Composition: Protein-based
Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
o: Bacterium
Fungus
Helminth
Prion
Virus
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret structural profile showing a non-cellular, protein-based agent) -> Step 2 (Identify the agent as a prion)

r.A: Bacteria are cellular prokaryotic organisms that possess a cell wall and replicate by binary fission.
r.B: Fungi are cellular eukaryotic organisms that possess a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
r.C: Helminths are multicellular eukaryotic organisms that possess a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
r.E: Viruses are non-cellular agents, but they contain genetic material and require host-cell machinery for replication.

q.s: LO1/LO2, Slide 4-5: Medically important classes of infectious agents

q.v: A 41-year-old man suffers a deep puncture wound to his foot while stepping on a rusty nail in a barnyard. Emergency department physicians note that whether this bacterial exposure progresses to clinical disease depends on the interaction among the agent, the host, and the context of the infection. In evaluating the context of this patient's exposure, which of the following pairs of factors best represents contextual determinants of disease?
o: Virulence factors and inoculum size
Tissue tropism and replication strategy
Barrier integrity and immune status
Patient age and prior immunity
Portal of entry and tissue environment
q.p: Step 1 (Distinguish agent, host, and contextual determinants of infection) -> Step 2 (Identify portal of entry and tissue environment as contextual factors)

r.A: Virulence factors and inoculum size are intrinsic properties of the infectious agent rather than the exposure context.
r.B: Tissue tropism and replication strategy are characteristics of the infectious agent itself.
r.C: Barrier integrity and immune status are host factors that influence susceptibility to disease.
r.D: Patient age and prior immunity are host-specific determinants rather than contextual environmental factors.

q.s: LO2, Slide 6: Infection does not automatically equal disease

q.v: Which of the following best explains why the innate immune system can rapidly survey and detect a vast diversity of microbial pathogens using only a limited repertoire of receptor families?
o: Receptors undergo somatic rearrangement after microbial exposure
One receptor detects a conserved motif shared across many microbes
Receptors bind only to peptides displayed on host MHC molecules
Each receptor is strictly specific to a single pathogen strain
Receptors are Newly synthesized only after adaptive T-cell activation
q.p: Step 1 (Recall that innate immunity uses germline-encoded PRRs) -> Step 2 (Recognize that a single PRR detects conserved PAMPs shared across many different microbes)

r.A: Innate pattern-recognition receptors are germline-encoded and do not undergo somatic rearrangement.
r.C: Recognition of peptides displayed on MHC molecules is a feature of adaptive T-cell receptors, not innate PRRs.
r.D: Strain-specific molecular recognition is a property of adaptive B-cell and T-cell receptors rather than innate PRRs.
r.E: Innate receptors are pre-formed and germline-encoded, allowing rapid detection prior to adaptive lymphocyte activation.

q.s: LO3, Slide 7-9: Danger signals: pathogen-associated molecular patterns

q.v: A 58-year-old man hospitalized in the intensive care unit with neutropenia develops a high fever and hypotension. Blood cultures grow a yeast that possesses a rigid cell wall rich in complex carbohydrates. Tissue-resident macrophages detect these conserved cell-wall structures via germline-encoded pattern-recognition receptors, triggering an immediate inflammatory response. Which of the following pathogen-associated molecular patterns is most likely initiating this patient's innate immune response?
o: CpG DNA
Double-stranded RNA
Flagellin
Fungal glycans
Lipopolysaccharide
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the pathogen as a fungus/yeast with a carbohydrate-rich cell wall) -> Step 2 (Match fungal cell walls to the representative PAMP, fungal glycans)

r.A: CpG DNA is a conserved nucleic acid motif characteristic of bacteria and some viruses.
r.B: Double-stranded RNA is a conserved nucleic acid intermediate produced during viral replication.
r.C: Flagellin is a conserved protein PAMP derived from bacterial flagella.
r.E: Lipopolysaccharide is a conserved structural component found in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.

q.s: LO4, Slide 10: Common examples of pathogen-associated molecular patterns

q.v: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever, chills, and hypotension 12 hours after undergoing a transrectal prostate biopsy. Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. Innate immune cells rapidly detect a conserved glycolipid component of the bacterial outer membrane, triggering robust cytokine release. Which of the following molecules is serving as the primary danger signal in this patient?
o: Capsid-derived peptide
CpG DNA
Fungal glycan
Lipopolysaccharide
Viral double-stranded RNA
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize E. coli as a Gram-negative bacterium with an outer membrane) -> Step 2 (Identify lipopolysaccharide as the outer membrane PAMP)

r.A: A capsid-derived peptide is a virus-specific adaptive antigen rather than a Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane PAMP.
r.B: CpG DNA is an intracellular nucleic acid PAMP, not a glycolipid component of the Gram-negative outer membrane.
r.C: Fungal glycans are conserved carbohydrate PAMPs located in fungal cell walls.
r.E: Viral double-stranded RNA is a nucleic acid PAMP generated during viral replication.

q.s: LO4, Slide 10: Common examples of pathogen-associated molecular patterns

q.v:
An immunology laboratory isolates two distinct microbial molecules from a patient with a systemic bacterial infection and evaluates how the host immune system recognizes them. The experimental findings are summarized below:
  Molecule X: Conserved across multiple bacterial genera; binds Toll-like receptors on macrophages; induces rapid cytokine release within 2 hours
  Molecule Y: Unique to this specific bacterial strain; binds surface immunoglobulin on a single B-cell clone; induces long-lived memory cells
Based on these findings, which of the following correctly classifies Molecule X and Molecule Y?
o: Molecule X: Capsid antigen / Molecule Y: Pattern-recognition receptor
Molecule X: Immunologic antigen only / Molecule Y: Pathogen-associated molecular pattern
Molecule X: MHC-restricted peptide / Molecule Y: Toll-like receptor ligand
Molecule X: Pathogen-associated molecular pattern / Molecule Y: Strain-specific antigen
Molecule X: T-cell receptor ligand / Molecule Y: Germline-encoded danger signal
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze data showing Molecule X is conserved and binds TLRs while Molecule Y is strain-specific and binds BCRs) -> Step 2 (Classify Molecule X as a PAMP and Molecule Y as a strain-specific antigen)

r.A: Molecule X is a conserved microbial ligand rather than a capsid antigen, and Molecule Y is a microbial antigen rather than a host receptor.
r.B: Molecule X functions as a conserved PAMP for innate immunity, whereas Molecule Y functions as a unique antigen for adaptive immunity.
r.C: Molecule X binds directly to Toll-like receptors rather than MHC, and Molecule Y binds B-cell receptors rather than Toll-like receptors.
r.E: Molecule X activates innate Toll-like receptors rather than T-cell receptors, and Molecule Y is an adaptive antigen rather than a germline danger signal.

q.s: LO3/LO5, Slide 13 & 15: PAMPs and antigens answer different questions

q.v: A 14-year-old girl recovers from an acute upper respiratory infection caused by rhinovirus serotype 16. Two months later, she is exposed to rhinovirus serotype 1B, a closely related virus, and develops another clinical cold. Laboratory analysis shows that antibodies generated during her first infection fail to bind the outer protein shell of the second virus. Which of the following best explains why her prior adaptive immune response did not protect her against the second virus?
o: Adaptive immune receptors fail to generate immunologic memory to viral proteins
B-cell receptors recognize only conserved structures shared across all viral serotypes
Capsid-derived antigens differ in molecular structure between closely related viruses
Capsid proteins cannot be recognized as antigens until converted into fungal glycans
Toll-like receptors prevent B cells from binding intact viral surface proteins
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that adaptive immunity targets unique molecular features with high specificity) -> Step 2 (Conclude that capsid-derived antigens differ between closely related viruses)

r.A: Adaptive recognition of viral protein antigens readily supports the generation of immunologic memory.
r.B: B-cell receptors distinguish unique, pathogen-specific molecular features rather than only conserved structures.
r.D: Viral capsid proteins are directly recognized as protein antigens by the adaptive immune system without conversion to glycans.
r.E: Innate Toll-like receptor activation promotes rather than prevents adaptive immune responses, and B cells bind intact antigens directly.

q.s: LO4/LO5, Slide 11-12: Immunologic antigens: specific targets

q.v: A 7-year-old boy receives a routine subunit vaccine containing a purified bacterial toxoid protein. In his draining lymph nodes, naive B lymphocytes and naive T lymphocytes both participate in generating a durable adaptive immune response against this protein antigen. Which of the following mechanisms is required for the boy's T lymphocytes to recognize this vaccine antigen?
o: Direct binding of intact toxoid protein by Toll-like receptors
Direct crosslinking of surface immunoglobulin by intact toxoid
Processing of the toxoid and presentation of peptides by MHC
Recognition of conserved bacterial flagellin motifs on the toxoid
Uncoating of viral double-stranded RNA inside host cytoplasm
q.p: Step 1 (Differentiate T-cell antigen recognition from B-cell antigen recognition) -> Step 2 (Identify that T cells require antigen processing and peptide display by MHC/HLA)

r.A: Toll-like receptors are innate pattern-recognition receptors, whereas T lymphocytes use T-cell receptors to recognize MHC-bound peptides.
r.B: Direct binding to intact protein antigen via surface immunoglobulin describes B-cell recognition rather than T-cell recognition.
r.D: T-cell receptors recognize specific processed peptide antigens presented by MHC, not conserved PAMPs like flagellin.
r.E: The vaccine contains a purified bacterial protein antigen, not a replicating virus producing double-stranded RNA.

q.s: LO4/LO5, Slide 14: B-cell and T-cell antigen recognition

q.v: Which of the following statements accurately compares the fundamental questions answered by innate pattern recognition versus adaptive antigen recognition during a microbial infection?
o: Innate asks whether the host has prior memory; adaptive asks whether barriers are intact
Innate asks which specific strain is present; adaptive asks whether a microbe is present
Innate asks whether a microbe is present; adaptive asks which specific target is present
Innate asks whether MHC is expressed; adaptive asks whether Toll-like receptors are active
Innate asks whether prions are replicating; adaptive asks whether binary fission is occurring
q.p: Step 1 (Contrast broad innate surveillance with precise adaptive targeting) -> Step 2 (Match innate to 'Is a microbe present?' and adaptive to 'Which specific target is present?')

r.A: Immunologic memory is a hallmark of adaptive immunity, whereas innate immunity provides rapid initial detection regardless of prior exposure.
r.B: This reverses the two systems; innate immunity detects shared microbial presence, while adaptive immunity identifies the specific pathogen or strain.
r.D: MHC presentation is required for adaptive T-cell recognition, whereas Toll-like receptors mediate innate pattern recognition.
r.E: Neither prions nor binary fission define the core recognition questions of innate versus adaptive immunity.

q.s: LO5, Slide 15: PAMPs and antigens answer different questions

myLectures.name: Pharmacokinetics
myLectures.note: Beardsley, Wed Nov 4. Cards picked to match the slides and the PK practice problems, checked against your 48 Pharmacokinetics cards (see pharmacokinetics_card_check.csv). Ion-trapping cards are already in pH, Acid-Base and Buffers. Left out: renal clearance (renal block), antiarrhythmic/glaucoma/clinical-trial 'phase' cards, prodrug examples the lecture doesn't name, NAT2 acetylators. Adds 21 cloze notes (deck: Beardsley - Pharmacokinetics), including your calculation cards.

add.cloze: Pharmacokinetics is {{c1::absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME)}} of drugs: how the body affects the drug
add.extra: Pharmacodynamics is how the drug affects the body.

add.cloze: The {{c1::uncharged (non-ionized)}} form of a drug crosses membranes by passive diffusion more readily. Most absorption of both weak acids and weak bases still occurs in the {{c2::small intestine}}, because its {{c3::very large surface area and more permeable membranes}} compensate even for ionized drug
add.extra: Weak acids are un-ionized in acidic environments; weak bases are ionized there. At pH = pKa, ionized = un-ionized.

add.cloze: Bioavailability (F) is {{c1::the fraction of unchanged drug that reaches the systemic circulation}}; for IV administration F = {{c2::1 (100%)}}
add.extra: F = AUC oral / AUC IV (equal doses). Typical F: IM/SC 75-100%, oral 5-<100%, rectal 30-<100%, transdermal 80-100%.

add.cloze: Morphine needs a much larger oral than IV dose because {{c1::extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism}} leaves an oral bioavailability of only about {{c2::30%}}
add.extra: First-pass loss: P-glycoprotein pumping back into the gut lumen, gut-wall enzymes, liver enzymes, biliary excretion. Propranolol is the lecture example of a big oral-vs-IV difference.

add.cloze: Grapefruit juice {{c1::inhibits intestinal CYP enzymes (CYP3A4) and P-glycoprotein}}, {{c2::increasing}} the oral bioavailability of many drugs (e.g., atorvastatin)
add.extra: Active components: furanocoumarins.

add.cloze: Serum drug levels should be drawn {{c1::after the distribution phase}} (after the initial rapid fall in plasma concentration)
add.extra: Levels drawn during distribution overestimate concentration and throw off Vd and clearance calculations. Most IV drugs are also given slowly so the early peak isn't toxic.

add.cloze: For a highly albumin-bound drug, low serum albumin {{c1::increases}} the Vd. Digoxin has a very high Vd because of {{c2::extensive binding to cardiac and skeletal muscle}}
add.extra: Tissue binding/distribution raises Vd; plasma protein binding lowers it.

add.cloze: Steady state is reached when {{c1::the rate of drug administration equals the rate of elimination}}. Average Css = {{c2::(F × dose) / (CL × dosing interval)}}; for a constant IV infusion, Css = {{c3::infusion rate / CL}}
add.extra: Equivalent: maintenance dose = (Css × CL × τ) / F.

add.cloze: Reduced renal or hepatic function {{c1::lowers clearance and raises Css}} at the same dosing rate, so if clearance falls 50% the maintenance dose should be {{c2::cut by 50%}}. Because half-life lengthens, the time to reach steady state {{c3::increases}}
add.extra: The loading dose is unchanged; only the maintenance dose depends on elimination.

add.cloze: Phase II metabolism is {{c1::conjugation}} (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glycine or glutathione conjugation). A prodrug is {{c2::an inactive compound activated by metabolism}}. A CYP inhibitor {{c3::raises levels and toxicity of an active drug}} but lowers the active metabolite of a prodrug
add.extra: Phase I: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis (CYP450). Example: etravirine (CYP2C19 inhibitor) decreases clopidogrel activation; cobicistat (CYP3A4 inhibitor) raises atorvastatin.

add.cloze: With zero-order (capacity-limited) elimination, as serum concentration rises {{c1::the elimination rate plateaus, so the drug accumulates rapidly and causes toxicity}}
add.extra: Lecture: a 40% dose increase is fine for valproate (first order) but dangerous for phenytoin (capacity-limited).

add.cloze: A larger Vd {{c1::lengthens}} the half-life, because t½ = {{c2::0.7 × Vd / CL}}
add.extra: More drug in tissues returns to plasma slowly.

add.cloze: A loading dose is given to {{c1::reach the target plasma concentration quickly}}; it {{c2::does not change}} the time to reach steady state, which depends only on half-life
add.extra: Loading dose = (Cp × Vd) / F. "Filling the tank" doesn't depend on how fast it drains.

add.cloze: The maintenance dose is determined by {{c1::clearance}}: MD = {{c2::(Css × CL × τ) / F}}. If oral F = 0.5, the oral dose must be {{c3::doubled}} vs IV. As the dosing interval lengthens, the dose per interval must {{c4::increase}} to keep the same average Css
add.extra: Lecture form: MD rate = (Cp × CL) / f. Dividing a daily dose more often reduces peak-trough variability.

add.cloze: A 100 mg IV bolus gives C0 = 2 mg/L, so Vd = {{c1::50 L}}
add.extra: Vd = dose / C0.

add.cloze: Oral loading dose with Vd = 40 L, target 2 mg/L and F = 0.5: {{c1::160 mg}}
Maintenance dose per 12 h with Css = 2 mg/L, CL = 4 L/hr and F = 0.5: {{c1::192 mg}}
A constant IV infusion of 12 mg/hr with CL = 6 L/hr gives Css = {{c1::2 mg/L}}
add.extra: Css = infusion rate / CL.

add.cloze: With Vd = 42 L and CL = 6 L/hr, t½ ≈ {{c1::4.9 hours}}
add.extra: t½ = 0.7 × Vd / CL = 0.7 × 42 / 6. (Vd/CL alone = 7 h is the mean residence time, not the half-life.)

add.cloze: If clearance falls by 50% and the infusion rate is unchanged, the steady-state concentration {{c1::doubles}}
add.extra: Css = infusion rate / CL.

add.cloze: A drug with t½ = 7 h is ~97% eliminated about {{c1::35 hours}} after stopping
