q.v:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with generalised tonic-clonic seizures. She is administered an intravenous loading dose of an anticonvulsant, and her seizures initially stop. Thirty minutes later, she begins having seizures again. Her weight is 50 kg, and the medication has a volume of distribution of 0.8 L/kg. Laboratory studies show:
  Current serum drug concentration: 6 mcg/mL
  Target serum drug concentration: 16 mcg/mL
Which of the following is the most appropriate additional intravenous dose to administer to this patient?
o: 160 mg
240 mg
400 mg
640 mg
800 mg
q.p: Step 1 (Calculate total Vd = 0.8 L/kg * 50 kg = 40 L and desired change in Cp = 16 mg/L - 6 mg/L = 10 mg/L) -> Step 2 (Calculate additional IV dose = Vd * change in Cp = 40 L * 10 mg/L = 400 mg)

r.A: This value is calculated by using a change in concentration of 4 mcg/mL instead of the required 10 mcg/mL difference.
r.B: This dose represents the amount of drug already present in the body (6 mg/L * 40 L) rather than the additional amount needed.
r.D: This would be the total loading dose needed if the patient had a starting serum drug concentration of zero (16 mg/L * 40 L).
r.E: This dose is double the required additional amount and would result in a toxic serum concentration of 26 mcg/mL.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 56: Incorporating Bioavailability into Dosing Equations & Slide 95: Practice Problem #5

q.v:
A 58-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit for severe sepsis and is started on a continuous intravenous infusion of a new antimicrobial agent. The medication follows first-order elimination kinetics. Pharmacokinetic parameters for this patient are:
  Volume of distribution (Vd): 30 L
  Clearance (CL): 3 L/hr
  Oral bioavailability (f): 0.5
Approximately how long will it take for the serum concentration of this medication to reach 87.5% of its steady-state concentration?
o: 7 hours
14 hours
21 hours
28 hours
35 hours
q.p: Step 1 (Calculate half-life = [0.7 * 30 L] / 3 L/hr = 7 hours, ignoring oral f for IV infusion) -> Step 2 (Recognize that 87.5% of steady state is achieved after 3 half-lives = 3 * 7 hours = 21 hours)

r.A: One half-life (7 hours) corresponds to the time required to achieve 50% of the steady-state concentration.
r.B: Two half-lives (14 hours) corresponds to the time required to achieve 75% of the steady-state concentration.
r.D: Four half-lives (28 hours) corresponds to the time required to achieve approximately 94% of the steady-state concentration.
r.E: Five half-lives (35 hours) corresponds to the time required to achieve 97% of the steady-state concentration.

q.s: SLO 1 & SLO 2 / Slide 25: Half-Life & Slide 27: A few more steady-state comments

q.v:
A 48-year-old man receives a one-time 800 mg intravenous push of an experimental analgesic in the postanesthesia care unit. Assume the medication undergoes rapid distribution. Serial serum drug concentrations are obtained:
  5 minutes post-dose: 40 mcg/mL
  2 hours post-dose: 35 mcg/mL
  4 hours post-dose: 30 mcg/mL
  6 hours post-dose: 25 mcg/mL
Assuming elimination characteristics do not change, what is the volume of distribution of this drug, and approximately how much longer after the 6-hour lab draw will it take for the drug to be completely eliminated from the body?
o: 20 L and 10 hours
20 L and 20 hours
20 L and 30 hours
40 L and 10 hours
40 L and 25 hours
q.p: Step 1 (Calculate Vd = Dose / initial Cp = 800 mg / 40 mg/L = 20 L) -> Step 2 (Recognize zero-order elimination at a constant rate of 5 mcg/mL every 2 hours [2.5 mcg/mL/hr], requiring 25 / 2.5 = 10 more hours to reach 0 mcg/mL)

r.B: This correctly calculates Vd as 20 L, but incorrectly multiplies the remaining 5 intervals by 4 hours instead of 2 hours.
r.C: This correctly calculates Vd as 20 L, but falsely applies the 5 half-lives rule (5 * 6 hours) to a drug undergoing zero-order elimination.
r.D: This correctly calculates the remaining elimination time as 10 hours, but miscalculates Vd by dividing 800 mg by 20 instead of 40 mg/L.
r.E: This miscalculates both the volume of distribution and the zero-order elimination rate.

q.s: SLO 1 & SLO 3 / Slide 22: First-Order vs. Zero-Order Elimination & Slide 89: Practice Problem #2

q.v: A 62-year-old woman with a history of deep vein thrombosis is stably anticoagulated on a daily oral dose of warfarin. She is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and is started on a multi-drug regimen that includes rifampin. One week later, her anticoagulation effect is markedly subtherapeutic. Which of the following best explains the decreased efficacy of warfarin in this patient?
o: Inhibition of intestinal P-glycoprotein efflux transporters
Inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
Induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
Displacement of warfarin from serum albumin binding sites
Decreased passive diffusion across the small intestinal mucosa
q.p: Step 1 (Identify warfarin as a common CYP450 substrate and rifampin as a CYP450 inducer) -> Step 2 (Recognize that CYP450 induction increases hepatic metabolism of the active substrate, decreasing plasma warfarin concentrations)

r.A: Inhibition of intestinal P-glycoprotein pumps increases oral absorption and bioavailability, which would elevate drug concentrations.
r.B: Inhibition of cytochrome P450 enzymes decreases metabolism of active substrates, leading to increased drug concentrations and toxicity.
r.D: Displacing a drug from serum albumin affects the volume of distribution and unbound fraction rather than causing rifampin-mediated metabolic clearance.
r.E: Rifampin reduces plasma concentrations of coadministered substrates by inducing Phase I hepatic enzymes, not by altering mucosal diffusion.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slide 71: Cytochrome P-450 Interactions & Slide 78: Common Drugs Involved in Drug Interactions

q.v: A 55-year-old man with HIV and coronary artery disease undergoes percutaneous coronary intervention with stent placement and is started on clopidogrel. His antiretroviral regimen includes etravirine. Two weeks later, he presents with acute stent thrombosis due to inadequate antiplatelet activity. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the failure of clopidogrel therapy in this patient?
o: Increased renal excretion of the active drug via urine alkalization
Accelerated inactivation of the parent drug via CYP3A4 induction
Impaired conversion of the prodrug to its active metabolite via CYP2C19 inhibition
Decreased oral bioavailability due to chelation in the stomach
Enhanced biliary excretion via P-glycoprotein activation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify clopidogrel as a prodrug activated by CYP2C19 and etravirine as a CYP2C19 inhibitor) -> Step 2 (Recognize that inhibiting CYP2C19 prevents conversion of the prodrug into its active antiplatelet metabolite)

r.A: Urine alkalization traps weak acids in the renal tubules and is not the mechanism of interaction between etravirine and clopidogrel.
r.B: Clopidogrel is an inactive prodrug that requires enzymatic activation rather than an active parent drug that is inactivated by CYP3A4 induction.
r.D: Etravirine interacts with clopidogrel at the level of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, not by binding the drug in the gastrointestinal lumen.
r.E: P-glycoprotein efflux lowers bioavailability of high first-pass drugs, whereas etravirine specifically inhibits CYP2C19-mediated prodrug activation.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slide 65: Metabolism & Slide 75: Impact on Pro-Drugs That Need to Be Activated

q.v: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with agitation, tachycardia, and hypertension after ingesting a large quantity of methamphetamine, a weak base that undergoes significant renal excretion. Which of the following interventions would most effectively increase the renal elimination of this drug, and what is the physical state of the trapped drug in the urine?
o: Administer ammonium chloride / ionized and hydrophilic
Administer ammonium chloride / un-ionized and lipophilic
Administer sodium bicarbonate / ionized and hydrophilic
Administer sodium bicarbonate / un-ionized and lipophilic
Administer sodium bicarbonate / equal proportions of ionized and un-ionized
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize methamphetamine as a weak base that requires urine acidification with ammonium chloride or ascorbic acid to enhance excretion) -> Step 2 (Determine that a weak base in an acidic environment becomes ionized [charged] and hydrophilic, preventing reabsorption)

r.B: Although ammonium chloride is used to acidify the urine, the un-ionized and lipophilic form diffuses freely back across the membrane into the blood.
r.C: Sodium bicarbonate alkalizes the urine, which is used to trap weak acids rather than weak bases like methamphetamine.
r.D: Alkalizing the urine with sodium bicarbonate shifts a weak base toward its un-ionized, lipophilic form, increasing tubular reabsorption into the blood.
r.E: Equal proportions of ionized and un-ionized drug occur only when the urine pH equals the pKa, which does not maximize ion trapping.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slide 38: Passive Diffusion & Slide 83: Using pH changes to trap a drug in the urine

q.v:
A 60-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ascites is admitted to the hospital and started on a medication that is normally highly bound to serum albumin. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum albumin: 1.8 g/dL (normal: 4.0 g/dL)
Compared to a patient with a normal serum albumin concentration, how will this patient's apparent volume of distribution (Vd) for this medication most likely change?
o: Decrease because more drug remains confined to the plasma compartment
Decrease because hepatic first-pass metabolism is reduced
Remain unchanged because Vd depends only on total drug clearance
Increase because a larger fraction of unbound drug distributes into peripheral tissues
Increase because renal tubular secretion of the protein-drug complex is enhanced
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that hypoalbuminemia [1.8 g/dL vs normal 4.0 g/dL] decreases plasma protein binding of highly albumin-bound drugs) -> Step 2 (Conclude that lower plasma concentration and greater distribution of free drug into tissues increases the apparent Vd)

r.A: Increased binding to serum proteins keeps drug in the plasma and decreases Vd, whereas low albumin reduces plasma retention.
r.B: First-pass metabolism affects oral bioavailability (f) rather than the apparent volume of distribution.
r.C: Volume of distribution and clearance are independent pharmacokinetic parameters.
r.E: Apparent Vd is determined by the ratio of total drug in the body to plasma concentration after distribution, not by renal secretion of protein complexes.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slide 18: Volume of Distribution & Slide 33: Relationship of serum albumin and VD

q.v:
A 42-year-old woman with chronic neuropathic pain is started on an oral medication given as 300 mg every 8 hours. The medication follows first-order elimination kinetics. Her pharmacokinetic parameters are:
  Volume of distribution (Vd): 20 L
  Clearance (CL): 5 L/hr
  Oral bioavailability (f): 0.8
Which of the following is the expected average steady-state serum concentration (Css) of this medication?
o: 4.8 mg/L
6.0 mg/L
7.5 mg/L
q.p: Step 1 (Calculate the hourly maintenance dose rate = 300 mg / 8 hours = 37.5 mg/hr) -> Step 2 (Rearrange MD = [Cp * CL] / f to solve for Cp = [MD * f] / CL = [37.5 mg/hr * 0.8] / 5 L/hr = 6.0 mg/L)

r.A: This value results from multiplying by bioavailability twice instead of once.
r.C: This value fails to account for the oral bioavailability of 0.8 (37.5 mg/hr divided by 5 L/hr = 7.5 mg/L).
r.D: This value results from using Vd (20 L) instead of clearance in the maintenance dose equation.
r.E: This value results from dividing the 300 mg dose by Vd (20 L) without accounting for dosing interval, clearance, or bioavailability.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 56: Incorporating Bioavailability into Dosing Equations & Slide 91: Practice Problem #3

q.v: In a laboratory experiment, four weak acid medications with different pKa values are tested for their ability to passively diffuse across the blood-brain barrier from plasma at a physiological pH of 7.4. Which of the following weak acid medications will have the greatest proportion in the uncharged, lipophilic form at pH 7.4?
o: Drug V (pKa = 3.4)
Drug W (pKa = 5.4)
Drug X (pKa = 7.4)
Drug Y (pKa = 8.4)
Drug Z (pKa = 9.4)
q.p: Step 1 (Apply the Henderson-Hasselbalch principle for weak acids: subtract pKa from solution pH [pH - pKa]) -> Step 2 (Select the weak acid where pH - pKa is most negative [7.4 - 9.4 = -2.0], indicating the drug is predominantly un-ionized and lipophilic)

r.A: At pH 7.4, a weak acid with a pKa of 3.4 has a pH - pKa of +4.0, meaning it is almost entirely ionized and hydrophilic.
r.B: At pH 7.4, a weak acid with a pKa of 5.4 has a pH - pKa of +2.0, meaning it is predominantly in the charged conjugate base form.
r.C: When the environmental pH equals the drug's pKa (7.4), the proportions of ionized and un-ionized drug are equal (50% each).
r.D: Although Drug Y is mostly uncharged at pH 7.4 (pH - pKa = -1.0), it has a smaller un-ionized proportion than a weak acid with a pKa of 9.4.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slide 38: Passive Diffusion & Slide 39: Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation

q.v: Which of the following terms specifically describes the study of how a single genetic marker influences interindividual variability in drug metabolism and treatment outcomes, rather than the collective influence of variability across the entire genome?
o: Pharmacokinetics
Pharmacodynamics
Pharmacogenetics
Pharmacogenomics
Bioavailability
q.p: Step 1 (Distinguish genetic influences on drug response from general ADME parameters) -> Step 2 (Identify pharmacogenetics as the effects of a single genetic marker, whereas pharmacogenomics refers to collective variability across the genome)

r.A: Pharmacokinetics describes how the body affects a drug through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, regardless of genetics.
r.B: Pharmacodynamics describes the biochemical and physiological effects of drugs on the body rather than single-gene metabolic variations.
r.D: Pharmacogenomics is broader in context and refers to the collective influence of variability across the entire genome to modulate drug response.
r.E: Bioavailability is the fraction of unchanged drug that reaches the systemic circulation following administration by any route.

q.s: SLO 6 / Slide 81: Genetic Variations in Metabolism

q.v:
A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is scheduled for an elective colon resection. He takes an oral anticoagulant that follows first-order elimination kinetics. Pharmacokinetic parameters for the medication are:
  Volume of distribution: 40 L
  Clearance: 2.8 L/hr
  Oral bioavailability: 0.8
If the medication is discontinued now, approximately how long will it take for 97% of the drug to be eliminated from his body?
o: 10 hours
20 hours
30 hours
40 hours
50 hours
q.p: Calculate half-life using t1/2 = (0.7 x Vd) / CL = (0.7 x 40) / 2.8 = 10 hours -> Multiply half-life by 5 to find time for 97% elimination (5 x 10 hours = 50 hours).

r.A: Ten hours represents only 1 half-life, at which point only 50% of the drug has been eliminated from the body.
r.B: Twenty hours represents 2 half-lives, at which point 75% of the drug has been eliminated from the body.
r.C: Thirty hours represents 3 half-lives, at which point 87.5% of the drug has been eliminated from the body.
r.D: Forty hours represents 4 half-lives, at which point approximately 94% of the drug has been eliminated from the body.

q.s: Objectives 1 & 2; Slides 25, 26, 30 (Half-Life and Steady State Concentrations)

q.v:
A 52-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is admitted to the hospital for an acute flare and is started on a continuous intravenous infusion of an immunosuppressive agent. The medication follows first-order elimination kinetics. Pharmacokinetic parameters for this drug are:
  Volume of distribution: 30 L
  Clearance: 3.5 L/hr
  Target steady-state concentration: 8 mcg/mL
Approximately how many hours after initiating the infusion will the patient's plasma concentration reach 75% of the target steady-state concentration?
o: 3 hours
6 hours
12 hours
18 hours
30 hours
q.p: Calculate half-life using t1/2 = (0.7 x 30 L) / 3.5 L/hr = 6 hours -> Recognize that reaching 75% of steady state requires 2 half-lives (2 x 6 hours = 12 hours).

r.A: Three hours represents half of one half-life, which is insufficient to reach 50% of the steady-state concentration.
r.B: Six hours represents 1 half-life, which is the time required to achieve 50% of the steady-state concentration.
r.D: Eighteen hours represents 3 half-lives, which is the time required to achieve 87.5% of the steady-state concentration.
r.E: Thirty hours represents 5 half-lives, which is the time required to achieve 97% of the steady-state concentration.

q.s: Objective 2; Slides 25, 27, 86 (Steady State Comments and Half-Life)

q.v: A 74-year-old man is hospitalized with sepsis and hypokalemia. His serum potassium is 3.3 mEq/L (normal: 3.5-5.5 mEq/L). An intravenous dose of 20 mEq of potassium chloride is ordered, and it is inadvertently administered as a rapid intravenous push over 2 minutes rather than infused over 2 hours. Immediately following the injection, the patient develops a fatal cardiac arrhythmia. Which of the following pharmacokinetic principles best explains this adverse outcome?
o: Saturation of hepatic first-pass metabolism
Instantaneous toxic peak plasma concentration prior to tissue distribution
Displacement of endogenous electrolytes from serum albumin
Conversion from first-order to zero-order renal elimination
Inhibition of P-glycoprotein reverse transporters
q.p: Rapid IV push bypasses the infusion dilution period -> Drug instantly reaches an extremely high plasma peak before the distribution phase allows uptake into peripheral tissues -> Toxic concentration at cardiac tissues causes arrest.

r.A: Intravenous administration completely bypasses the gastrointestinal tract and hepatic first-pass metabolism.
r.C: Potassium is an electrolyte that does not bind extensively to serum albumin to cause displacement toxicity.
r.D: The acute lethality of an intravenous bolus occurs immediately due to lacking time for distribution, not changes in renal elimination kinetics.
r.E: P-glycoprotein transporters pump drugs back into the gut lumen and do not mediate acute toxicity from an intravenous push.

q.s: Objective 5; Slides 5, 14, 60, 63 (IV Administration Terms and Clinical Impact of Distribution Phase)

q.v: A 36-year-old woman is being treated with a daily oral medication that has a narrow therapeutic index. She experiences intermittent toxicity shortly after taking her dose, followed by subtherapeutic symptoms late in the day. Her physician decides to keep the total daily dose the same, but divides it to be administered orally every 8 hours. Assuming first-order kinetics and unchanged bioavailability, which of the following pharmacokinetic parameters will decrease as a result of this dosing change?
o: Total drug clearance
Volume of distribution
Elimination half-life
Peak-to-trough concentration variability
Time required to reach steady state
q.p: Dividing a total daily dose into smaller, more frequent doses (every 8 hours vs. once daily) -> Reduces the magnitude of peak and minimum plasma levels -> Decreases concentration variability across the dosing interval.

r.A: Total clearance is an intrinsic pharmacokinetic parameter determined by organ function and is unaffected by the dosing interval for first-order drugs.
r.B: Volume of distribution depends on tissue and protein binding characteristics rather than the frequency of administration.
r.C: Elimination half-life is determined by volume of distribution and clearance, neither of which changes with dosing frequency.
r.E: The time to reach steady state depends solely on the drug's half-life (taking 4 to 5 half-lives) and is independent of dosing frequency.

q.s: Objective 2; Slide 32 (Dosing Interval vs. Concentration Variability)

q.v: A 50-year-old man with hyperlipidemia and HIV is stably managed on oral atorvastatin. His antiretroviral regimen is modified to include cobicistat. Two weeks later, he presents to the clinic with severe, diffuse muscle pain and weakness. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the interaction between these two medications?
o: Induction of CYP3A4 leading to toxic metabolite accumulation
Inhibition of CYP3A4 leading to increased active atorvastatin concentrations
Inhibition of CYP2C19 preventing prodrug activation of atorvastatin
Induction of P-glycoprotein increasing intestinal drug absorption
Competition for Phase II glucuronidation pathways in the liver
q.p: Cobicistat is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor -> Atorvastatin is an active drug that is a CYP3A4 substrate -> Inhibition decreases conversion to metabolites, increasing active atorvastatin plasma concentrations and causing toxicity.

r.A: Cobicistat is an enzyme inhibitor rather than an inducer, and atorvastatin toxicity is caused by the parent active component.
r.C: Inhibition of CYP2C19 prevents the activation of the prodrug clopidogrel by etravirine, whereas atorvastatin is administered in an active form.
r.D: Inducing P-glycoprotein reverse transporters would pump more drug back into the gut lumen and decrease absorption.
r.E: The interaction between cobicistat and atorvastatin occurs via Phase I cytochrome P450 oxidation (CYP3A4), not Phase II glucuronidation.

q.s: Objective 4; Slides 71, 73, 74 (Cytochrome P-450 Interactions: Cobicistat + Atorvastatin)

q.v: A 34-year-old woman with a seizure disorder is stably treated with oral phenytoin. She develops peptic ulcer disease and begins taking an over-the-counter medication for heartburn. One week later, she presents to the emergency department with nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech, and her serum phenytoin concentration is found to be markedly elevated. Which of the following medications did she most likely start taking?
o: Carbamazepine
Cimetidine
Griseofulvin
Phenobarbital
St. John's wort
q.p: Cimetidine is a cytochrome P450 inhibitor ('Magic Rack') used for acid suppression -> Phenytoin is a CYP450 substrate -> Inhibition decreases phenytoin metabolism, leading to elevated serum concentrations and toxicity.

r.A: Carbamazepine is a CYP450 inducer that would accelerate phenytoin metabolism and decrease its serum concentration.
r.C: Griseofulvin is an antifungal agent that induces CYP450 enzymes, which would decrease serum concentrations of CYP substrates.
r.D: Phenobarbital is a CYP450 inducer that increases the metabolism of co-administered CYP substrates.
r.E: St. John's wort is an herbal supplement that induces CYP450 enzymes, reducing the plasma levels of substrate medications.

q.s: Objective 4; Slides 71, 78, 79 (Common Drugs Involved in Drug Interactions)

q.v: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after ingesting an overdose of a weak acid medication with a pKa of 4.4. To enhance renal excretion of the medication, intravenous sodium bicarbonate is administered to alkalinize the urine to a pH of 7.4. Which of the following best explains why this intervention increases elimination of the drug?
o: The unionized form of the drug is actively secreted into the renal tubule
The drug becomes predominantly uncharged and lipophilic in the renal tubule
The drug becomes predominantly ionized and hydrophilic, preventing tubular reabsorption
Alkalinization saturates facilitated passive diffusion carriers in the collecting duct
Sodium bicarbonate induces renal Phase I hydrolysis of the weak acid
q.p: Urine pH (7.4) is much higher than the weak acid pKa (4.4) -> According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch principle, the weak acid becomes predominantly ionized (charged) -> Ionized form is hydrophilic and cannot passively diffuse back across tubular membranes ('ion trapping').

r.A: Passive diffusion across tubular membranes, rather than active secretion of the unionized form, governs pH-dependent ion trapping.
r.B: A weak acid is predominantly uncharged and lipophilic only when placed in an acidic environment where pH is less than pKa.
r.D: Ion trapping relies on preventing simple passive diffusion across lipid membranes rather than saturating protein carriers.
r.E: Sodium bicarbonate alters the luminal pH to change the drug's ionization state, not to induce metabolic enzymes.

q.s: Objective 5; Slides 38, 39, 83 (Passive Diffusion, Henderson-Hasselbalch, and Urine Trapping)

q.v:
A 64-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and atrial fibrillation is being evaluated for a new oral antiarrhythmic medication. During clinical trials, a 100 mg dose of the drug was administered both orally and intravenously to healthy volunteers, and serial plasma concentrations were measured over 48 hours:
  Dose (IV): 100 mg
  AUC (IV): 400 mg*hr/L
  Dose (oral): 100 mg
  AUC (oral): 160 mg*hr/L
  Clearance: 0.25 L/hr
Based on these data, what is the oral bioavailability (f) of this medication?
q.p: Recall that for equal doses of a first-order drug, oral bioavailability f = AUC(oral) / AUC(IV) -> Divide 160 mg*hr/L by 400 mg*hr/L = 0.40.

r.A: A value of 0.20 would result from dividing the oral AUC by twice the IV AUC.
r.B: A value of 0.25 confuses the drug's clearance rate (0.25 L/hr) with its bioavailability fraction.
r.D: A value of 0.60 represents the fraction of the oral dose lost to incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism (1 - 0.40).
r.E: A value of 0.80 would correspond to an oral AUC of 320 mg*hr/L rather than 160 mg*hr/L.

q.s: Objective 1; Slide 54 (Bioavailability)

q.v: Which of the following characteristics best describes drug transport across biological membranes via facilitated passive diffusion?
o: Requires direct cellular energy expenditure in the form of ATP
Transports drug molecules against an electrochemical or concentration gradient
Involves the engulfment of extracellular fluid droplets by the cell membrane
Depends on a selective carrier protein and moves down a concentration gradient
Occurs exclusively for small, lipophilic, unionized molecules without a carrier
q.p: Facilitated passive diffusion -> Involves formation of a selective carrier-substrate complex -> Proceeds down a concentration gradient without requiring energy expenditure.

r.A: Energy expenditure is required for active transport and pinocytosis, whereas facilitated passive diffusion requires no energy.
r.B: Transport against a concentration gradient is a feature of active transport and cannot occur via facilitated passive diffusion.
r.C: Engulfment of fluids or particles by a cell describes pinocytosis, not facilitated diffusion.
r.E: Movement of lipophilic, unionized molecules directly through the membrane without a carrier describes simple passive diffusion.

q.s: Objective 5; Slides 37, 41, 42, 43 (How Drugs Cross Membranes: Facilitated Passive Diffusion)

q.v: During hepatic biotransformation, a medication undergoes a chemical reaction that unmasks a sulfhydryl (-SH) functional group on the parent molecule prior to any conjugation. Which of the following metabolic classifications and specific reaction types best describes this process?
o: Phase I hydrolysis
Phase I methylation
Phase II sulfation
Phase II acetylation
Phase II glutathione conjugation
q.p: Unmasking or introducing a functional group (-OH, -NH2, -SH) is the definition of a Phase I reaction -> Phase I reactions consist of oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis.

r.B: Methylation is a Phase II conjugation reaction, not a Phase I reaction.
r.C: Sulfation is a Phase II reaction that conjugates a molecule with sulfuric acid to make it very polar.
r.D: Acetylation is a Phase II reaction that conjugates a drug with acetic acid rather than unmasking a functional group.
r.E: Glutathione conjugation is a Phase II reaction, whereas unmasking a sulfhydryl group is a Phase I transformation.

q.s: Objective 5; Slides 65, 67 (Metabolism: Phase I and II Reactions)

add.cloze: Innate immunity buys {{c1::time}} until adaptive immunity responds
add.extra: It also limits spread and shapes adaptive immunity.

add.cloze: Too little innate activation permits microbial {{c1::spread}}; too much causes tissue {{c2::injury}}
Innate defense layers: barriers, resident {{c1::sentinels}}, recruited cells, soluble mediators, and {{c2::resolution}}
Epithelial barriers work by mechanical removal, chemical inhibition, and resident {{c1::microbiota}}
Burns, indwelling devices, and mucosal injury raise infection risk by breaking {{c1::barriers}}
PRRs recognize conserved microbial patterns and signals of cell {{c1::damage}}
{{c1::DAMPs}} are molecules released by injured cells that activate innate sensors
add.extra: Damage-associated molecular patterns

add.cloze: PRR {{c1::location}} gives context: a molecule normal in one compartment can signal infection in another
add.extra: Surface, endosome, or cytosol

add.cloze: PRR activation makes macrophages release inflammatory {{c1::cytokines}} and chemokines
add.extra: Also enhanced phagocytosis, endothelial activation, and leukocyte recruitment

add.cloze: Phagolysosomes kill microbes with acid, lysosomal enzymes, ROS, and {{c1::NO}}
add.extra: NO = nitric oxide

add.cloze: Neutrophils can trap microbes in extracellular traps called {{c1::NETs}}
add.extra: They also kill by phagocytosis, granule contents, and ROS

add.cloze: Neutrophil recruitment: rolling → activation → firm {{c1::adhesion}} → transmigration → {{c2::chemotaxis}}
{{c1::Chemokines}} switch leukocyte integrins to a high-affinity state
Defective β2 integrins (CD18) impair firm {{c1::adhesion}} of neutrophils
add.extra: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency; rolling (selectins) is spared

add.cloze: NK cells kill when {{c1::activating}} signals outweigh inhibitory signals
add.extra: HLA class I gives the main inhibitory signal

add.cloze: NK cells perform ADCC by binding antibody-coated targets with {{c1::CD16}}
{{c1::Chemokines}} are cytokines that direct cell migration along concentration gradients
Type I interferons create an {{c1::antiviral}} state in cells
TNF activates {{c1::endothelium}}, recruits leukocytes, and amplifies inflammation
Low CH50 with normal AH50 suggests a {{c1::classical}} pathway defect
add.extra: Normal CH50 + low AH50 → alternative pathway

add.cloze: Recurrent Neisseria with low CH50 and low AH50 suggests a {{c1::terminal}} complement defect

q.v: A 42-year-old man is hospitalized in the burn unit after sustaining severe thermal injuries over 30% of his body surface area. Several days into his admission, he develops a secondary bacterial skin infection at the burn sites. Loss of which of the following protective factors most directly contributed to barrier failure at the injured tissue site?
o: Tears, lysozyme, and IgA
Flow, lactoferrin, and IgA
Salt, lysozyme, and fatty acids
Enzymes and pH 1–2
Mucus movement by cilia
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize thermal burn as loss of the skin barrier) -> Step 2 (Identify salt, lysozyme, and fatty acids from sweat and sebaceous glands as the key protective factors of skin)

r.A: Tears, lysozyme, and IgA are protective secretions produced by lacrimal glands in the eyes.
r.B: Flow, lactoferrin, lysozyme, and IgA are protective factors produced by salivary glands in the mouth.
r.D: Enzymes and an acidic pH of 1–2 are protective factors of gastric secretions in the stomach.
r.E: Movement of mucus by cilia is a mechanical barrier found in the respiratory tract (bronchi), not the skin.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 6: Barrier secretions

q.v: A 26-year-old woman presents to the clinic with fever, myalgias, and a nonproductive cough. A nasopharyngeal swab confirms an acute respiratory viral infection. Within infected respiratory epithelial cells, viral RNA has accumulated in the cytoplasm. Which of the following receptors is most likely responsible for detecting this intracellular viral nucleic acid?
o: Cell-surface lectin receptor
Cytosolic RIG-like receptor
Cytosolic NOD-like receptor
Cell-surface Toll-like receptor
Cell-surface scavenger receptor
q.p: Step 1 (Localize viral RNA to the cytosol of infected cells) -> Step 2 (Match cytosolic viral RNA detection to RIG-like receptors)

r.A: Cell-surface lectin receptors recognize extracellular microbial polysaccharides on the plasma membrane.
r.C: Cytosolic NOD-like receptors recognize bacterial peptidoglycans and products of damaged cells rather than viral RNA.
r.D: Cell-surface Toll-like receptors sample extracellular microbial structures on the plasma membrane.
r.E: Cell-surface scavenger receptors bind microbes on the plasma membrane to facilitate phagocytosis, not cytosolic viral RNA detection.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 10: Pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs, TLRs)

q.v: Which of the following events is directly triggered by pattern-recognition receptor (PRR) signaling in an immature dendritic cell residing in the epidermis?
o: Release of cytotoxic granules to lyse adjacent cells
Formation of extracellular traps to immobilize microbes
Maturation and migration to a draining lymph node
Cleavage of C3 into C3a and C3b on the cell surface
Spontaneous down-regulation of HLA class I molecules
q.p: Step 1 (Identify immature dendritic cells as tissue-resident cells that sample local material with low T-cell stimulatory capacity) -> Step 2 (Recognize that PRR danger signaling induces maturation and migration via afferent lymphatics to the lymph node to present antigen and provide costimulation to T cells)

r.A: Releasing cytotoxic granules to kill target cells is an effector function of NK cells, not dendritic cells.
r.B: Forming extracellular traps (NETs) is a microbial killing mechanism used by neutrophils.
r.D: Cleavage of C3 into C3a and C3b is mediated by C3 convertase in the complement cascade.
r.E: Down-regulation of HLA class I is an immune evasion mechanism used by virus-infected or tumor cells, not a normal maturation response of dendritic cells.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 17: Innate Functions 5: Dendritic cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity

q.v:
A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent bacterial skin and respiratory infections. Physical examination of an infected skin site shows erythema and warmth, but a complete absence of pus. Laboratory studies show:
  White blood cell count: 28,000/mm³ (markedly elevated neutrophils)
  Flow cytometry of neutrophils: absent β2 integrins
Which of the following steps in leukocyte recruitment is most directly impaired in this patient?
o: Selectin-mediated rolling
Chemokine-induced integrin activation
Stable adhesion to endothelium
Phagolysosome fusion
Reactive oxygen species generation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify β2 integrin deficiency with neutrophilia and absent pus) -> Step 2 (Determine that high-affinity integrins bind endothelial integrin ligands to mediate stable/firm adhesion)

r.A: Rolling along the endothelium is mediated by selectins binding to selectin ligands prior to integrin engagement.
r.B: Integrin activation is driven by chemokines binding to chemokine receptors on the leukocyte surface, which precedes stable adhesion.
r.D: Phagolysosome fusion is an intracellular step of phagocytosis that occurs after leukocytes have already migrated into tissues.
r.E: Reactive oxygen species generation is an intracellular killing mechanism mediated by phagocyte oxidase, not a step in endothelial recruitment.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 14: Checkpoint! (Neutrophil recruitment)

q.v: A 54-year-old man with severe rheumatoid arthritis is started on infliximab, a monoclonal antibody that neutralizes TNF activity. Three months later, he experiences significant improvement in joint pain and swelling, but he is hospitalized with a severe pulmonary infection caused by an intracellular bacterium. Interference with which of the following protective functions best explains his increased susceptibility to infection?
o: Endothelial activation and leukocyte recruitment
Establishing a cellular antiviral state
Inhibition of inflammatory tissue injury
Acceleration of bone marrow neutrophil production
Spontaneous C3 activation on microbial surfaces
q.p: Step 1 (Identify infliximab as an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody) -> Step 2 (Recognize that neutralizing TNF blocks endothelial activation, leukocyte recruitment, and inflammatory signaling, increasing infection susceptibility)

r.B: Establishing an antiviral state is the primary function of type I interferons, not TNF.
r.C: Inhibiting inflammatory activation to limit tissue injury is the function of regulatory cytokines like IL-10, whereas TNF amplifies inflammation.
r.D: Accelerating neutrophil production in the bone marrow is the function of G-CSF.
r.E: Spontaneous C3 activation on microbial surfaces initiates the alternative complement pathway independently of TNF.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 22: Clinical application (Anti-TNF therapy)

q.v: A 35-year-old woman presents with a painful, erythematous skin abscess on her forearm. Tissue macrophages at the site of infection have engulfed the invading bacteria into phagosomes, which subsequently fused with lysosomes. Which of the following sets of effectors directly mediates microbial killing and digestion within this intracellular compartment?
o: C5b, C6, C7, C8, and C9
Perforin and cytotoxic granules
Lysosomal enzymes, reactive oxygen species, and nitric oxide
TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and CXCL8
Properdin, Factor B, and Factor D
q.p: Step 1 (Follow the 4 steps of phagocytosis to phagolysosome fusion) -> Step 2 (Identify lysosomal enzymes, phagocyte oxidase-derived ROS, and iNOS-derived nitric oxide as the intracellular killing mechanisms)

r.A: C5b–C9 assemble on microbial surfaces to form the extracellular membrane attack complex (MAC).
r.B: Cytotoxic granules are used by NK cells to kill virus-infected or tumor cells, not by macrophages inside phagolysosomes.
r.D: TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and CXCL8 are secreted cytokines and chemokines that coordinate inflammation and recruitment rather than directly digesting microbes in phagolysosomes.
r.E: Properdin, Factor B, and Factor D are plasma proteins that form and stabilize the alternative pathway C3 convertase.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 12: Phagocytosis

q.v: A 61-year-old man is found to have a malignant solid tumor. Biopsy and flow cytometry of the tumor cells reveal that they express surface activating ligands, but HLA class I expression is markedly reduced compared to adjacent normal tissue. How will natural killer (NK) cells most likely respond upon encountering these tumor cells?
o: Spare the tumor cells because rearranged antigen receptors are absent
Spare the tumor cells because inhibitory receptor signaling dominates
Kill the tumor cells because activating receptor signaling dominates
Kill the tumor cells by assembling the C5b–C9 membrane attack complex
Spare the tumor cells and migrate to the lymph node to present antigen
q.p: Step 1 (Note reduced HLA class I expression and presence of activating ligands on the tumor cell) -> Step 2 (Predict that loss of the HLA class I inhibitory 'self' signal allows activating signals to dominate, resulting in NK-cell activation and target cell killing)

r.A: NK cells do not use rearranged T-cell or B-cell antigen receptors; they rely on germline-encoded activating and inhibitory receptors.
r.B: Inhibitory signaling dominates only when HLA class I is normally expressed, which spares healthy cells.
r.D: NK cells kill target cells using cytotoxic granules and IFN-γ production, whereas the C5b–C9 membrane attack complex is part of the soluble complement cascade.
r.E: Migrating to lymph nodes to present antigen to naive T cells is the role of dendritic cells, not NK cells.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 16: Innate Functions 4: NK cells killing unwanted cells

q.v: Which of the following complement components is required to form the C3 convertase in both the classical and lectin pathways, while leaving the alternative pathway intact if deficient?
o: C1q
C2
Factor B
Properdin
C8
q.p: Step 1 (Compare the C3 convertase composition of the classical/lectin pathways [C4b2a] versus the alternative pathway [C3bBb]) -> Step 2 (Identify C2 as the shared component of the classical and lectin C3 convertases)

r.A: C1q initiates only the classical pathway by binding antigen-antibody complexes; the lectin pathway uses MBL instead.
r.C: Factor B participates exclusively in the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb).
r.D: Properdin stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb) and is not used in the classical or lectin pathways.
r.E: C8 is a terminal complement component (C5b–C9) shared by all three pathways downstream of C5 convertase.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 29: Clinical case: recurrent encapsulated bacterial infection & Slide 32: Complement: key takeaways

q.v:
A 19-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, and a petechial rash. Cerebrospinal fluid cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis. His medical history is significant for two prior episodes of meningococcal meningitis during adolescence. Laboratory evaluation shows:
  Serum IgG, IgM, and IgA: normal
  CH50: undetectable
  AH50: undetectable
  Serum C3: normal
  Serum C4: normal
Deficiency of which of the following complement proteins best explains this patient's laboratory profile and clinical presentation?
o: C1q
C2
Mannose-binding lectin (MBL)
Factor D
C7
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret low CH50 and low AH50 with normal C3/C4 as a shared terminal pathway defect) -> Step 2 (Connect recurrent invasive Neisseria infection to impaired assembly of the C5b–C9 membrane attack complex, such as C7 deficiency)

r.A: C1q deficiency impairs only the classical pathway, which would cause a low CH50 with a normal AH50.
r.B: C2 deficiency impairs the classical and lectin pathways while sparing the alternative pathway, resulting in a normal AH50.
r.C: Mannose-binding lectin (MBL) initiates the lectin pathway and does not cause both CH50 and AH50 to be undetectable.
r.D: Factor D deficiency impairs only the alternative pathway, resulting in a normal CH50 and a low AH50.

q.s: LO5 / Slides 26–27, 30–31: Complement testing: use the pattern

q.v:
A 3-year-old girl is evaluated in the immunology clinic after recovering from her second episode of invasive bacterial sepsis. Functional complement screening assays are performed to localize her defect:
  CH50: normal
  AH50: markedly reduced
  Serum C3: normal
Based on this testing pattern, which of the following processes is most likely impaired in this patient?
o: C1q binding to antigen-bound IgM or IgG
Cleavage of C4 and C2 by MASP-1 and MASP-2
Stabilization of the C3bBb convertase by properdin
Assembly of the C5b–C9 pore on microbial membranes
Opsonization of microbes by C3b following classical activation
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret normal CH50 and low AH50 as an isolated alternative pathway component defect) -> Step 2 (Identify properdin stabilization of the alternative C3 convertase C3bBb, along with Factors B and D, as specific to the alternative pathway)

r.A: C1q binding to antigen-antibody complexes initiates the classical pathway, which is intact given the normal CH50.
r.B: MASP-mediated cleavage of C4 and C2 occurs in the lectin pathway; C4 and C2 defects would also reduce CH50.
r.D: Impaired assembly of the C5b–C9 membrane attack complex affects the shared terminal pathway and would reduce both CH50 and AH50.
r.E: Classical pathway activation and C3 levels are normal in this patient, so C3b opsonization via the classical pathway remains intact.

q.s: LO5 / Slides 30–32: Complement testing: use the pattern & Complement: key takeaways

q.v: A 68-year-old woman with Sjögren syndrome presents to the dental clinic with severe dry mouth and multiple new dental caries. Physical examination shows parched oral mucosa and a lack of pooled saliva in the floor of the mouth. Which of the following combinations of protective factors is normally provided by the secretions that are deficient in this patient?
o: Flow, enzymes, lysozyme, lactoferrin, and IgA
Salt, lysozyme, and fatty acids
Enzymes and a pH of 1–2
Tears, lysozyme, and IgA
Cerumen and antibacterial cryptidins
q.p: Step 1 (Identify salivary gland dysfunction causing dry mouth) -> Step 2 (Match salivary gland secretions to flow, enzymes, lysozyme, lactoferrin, and IgA)

r.B: Salt, lysozyme, and fatty acids are the key protective factors provided by sweat and sebaceous glands on the skin.
r.C: Enzymes combined with a highly acidic pH of 1–2 are characteristic of gastric secretions in the stomach.
r.D: Tears, lysozyme, and IgA represent the protective secretions produced by the lacrimal glands in the eyes.
r.E: Cerumen is secreted by sebaceous glands in the ears, whereas cryptidins are antibacterial peptides found in the intestine.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 6: Barrier secretions

q.v: A 30-year-old man develops a localized bacterial infection in the subcutaneous tissue of his hand after a rose thorn puncture. Resident tissue macrophages engulf the bacteria into phagosomes, where microbial degradation exposes bacterial DNA and RNA within the vesicular compartment. Which of the following pattern-recognition receptors is properly positioned to sample these internalized microbial nucleic acids?
o: Cell surface lectin receptors
Endosomal Toll-like receptors
Cytosolic NOD-like receptors
Cytosolic RIG-like receptors
Cell surface scavenger receptors
q.p: Step 1 (Localize internalized microbial nucleic acids to the endosomal compartment) -> Step 2 (Identify endosomal Toll-like receptors as the sensors of ingested microbial nucleic acids)

r.A: Cell surface lectin receptors bind extracellular microbial polysaccharides rather than internalized nucleic acids.
r.C: Cytosolic NOD-like receptors detect intracellular bacterial peptidoglycans and products of damaged cells in the cytoplasm.
r.D: Cytosolic RIG-like receptors recognize viral RNA located free within the host cell cytoplasm.
r.E: Cell surface scavenger receptors mediate the initial recognition and attachment of extracellular microbes for phagocytosis.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 10: Pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs, TLRs)

q.v: During the immune response to an intracellular bacterial infection, T cells and natural killer cells secrete a cytokine that binds to receptors on tissue macrophages to enhance their antimicrobial killing capacity and support intracellular pathogen control. Which of the following cytokines is responsible for this macrophage activation?
o: IL-10
CXCL8 (IL-8)
G-CSF
IFN-γ
Type I interferons
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the process of cytokine-mediated macrophage activation for intracellular pathogen control) -> Step 2 (Match this function to IFN-γ)

r.A: IL-10 acts as an anti-inflammatory brake that limits inflammatory activation and may reduce microbial clearance.
r.B: CXCL8 (IL-8) is a chemokine that directs neutrophil chemotaxis to the site of infection.
r.C: G-CSF stimulates bone marrow neutrophil production and is used clinically to accelerate neutrophil recovery.
r.E: Type I interferons establish an antiviral state in nearby cells rather than directly activating macrophage phagolysosomal killing.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 11: Macrophage activation & Slide 20: Step-1-relevant Cytokines and their functions

q.v: A 58-year-old woman undergoing myelosuppressive chemotherapy for breast cancer develops severe neutropenia. To reduce her risk of life-threatening bacterial infections, her oncologist administers a recombinant cytokine that stimulates the bone marrow to accelerate neutrophil recovery. Which of the following mediators is being administered?
o: IL-1
IL-6
G-CSF
IL-12
TNF
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize clinical need to stimulate neutrophil production following chemotherapy) -> Step 2 (Identify G-CSF as the cytokine that drives neutrophil production)

r.A: IL-1 induces fever, acute-phase inflammation, and endothelial activation rather than selective neutrophil recovery.
r.B: IL-6 drives fever and hepatic acute-phase responses and is a target for blockade in pathologic inflammation.
r.D: IL-12 enhances natural killer cell activity and shapes adaptive immunity rather than accelerating bone marrow neutrophil production.
r.E: TNF promotes endothelial activation and leukocyte recruitment, and its blockade is used to reduce inflammatory tissue injury.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 20: Step-1-relevant Cytokines and their functions

q.v: A 47-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with acute bacterial pneumonia. Activated alveolar macrophages at the site of infection secrete TNF and IL-1, which travel through the bloodstream to the liver and brain to induce acute-phase protein synthesis and fever. Which of the following terms best describes this mode of cytokine signaling?
o: Autocrine
Paracrine
Endocrine
Juxtacrine
Chemotactic
q.p: Step 1 (Identify cytokines traveling through the circulation to act on distant organs like the liver and brain) -> Step 2 (Classify distant signaling via circulation as endocrine)

r.A: Autocrine signaling occurs when a secreted cytokine acts directly back on the same cell that secreted it.
r.B: Paracrine signaling occurs when a cytokine acts locally on nearby cells in the immediate tissue environment.
r.D: Juxtacrine signaling requires direct cell-to-cell contact via membrane-bound molecules rather than soluble circulating factors.
r.E: Chemotactic signaling refers specifically to chemical gradients that guide leukocyte migration into tissues.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 18 & 19: Innate Functions 6: Cytokine signaling – local or systemic

q.v: During an acute bacterial skin infection, resident macrophages release TNF and IL-1 to activate the local vascular endothelium, initiating the recruitment of circulating neutrophils. What is the correct sequence of leukocyte-endothelial interactions that allows neutrophils to exit the bloodstream?
o: Selectin-mediated rolling -> chemokine-mediated integrin activation -> integrin-mediated stable adhesion -> migration through endothelium
Integrin-mediated rolling -> selectin-mediated activation -> chemokine-mediated stable adhesion -> migration through endothelium
Chemokine-mediated rolling -> selectin-mediated stable adhesion -> integrin activation -> migration through endothelium
Selectin-mediated stable adhesion -> integrin-mediated rolling -> chemokine activation -> migration through endothelium
Migration through endothelium -> selectin-mediated rolling -> integrin activation -> stable adhesion
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the multistep leukocyte extravasation cascade) -> Step 2 (Order events: selectin rolling, chemokine activation of integrins to high-affinity state, integrin stable adhesion, transendothelial migration)

r.B: Selectins mediate initial rolling while integrins mediate stable adhesion, not the reverse.
r.C: Rolling is mediated by selectin-selectin ligand interactions rather than chemokines, and precedes stable adhesion.
r.D: Selectins mediate low-affinity rolling, whereas high-affinity integrins are required for firm, stable adhesion.
r.E: Migration through the endothelium is the final step of extravasation, occurring after rolling and firm adhesion.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 14: Checkpoint! (Leukocyte recruitment)

q.v:
A researcher isolates two populations of host epithelial cells from a patient with a viral respiratory infection. Flow cytometry is performed to measure surface receptor ligands, and the cells are then co-cultured with healthy natural killer (NK) cells:
  Population 1: Expresses activating ligands; normal surface HLA class I expression
  Population 2: Expresses activating ligands; markedly reduced surface HLA class I expression
Which of the following outcomes is most likely to be observed in this co-culture experiment?
o: Both Population 1 and Population 2 will be killed by cytotoxic granules
Neither Population 1 nor Population 2 will be killed
Population 1 will be killed; Population 2 will be spared
Population 1 will be spared; Population 2 will be killed
Population 1 will undergo complement lysis; Population 2 will undergo phagocytosis
q.p: Step 1 (Evaluate balance of activating and HLA class I inhibitory signals on both cell populations) -> Step 2 (Predict that normal HLA class I spares Population 1 while reduced HLA class I leads to killing of Population 2)

r.A: Population 1 expresses normal levels of self HLA class I, which engages inhibitory receptors on NK cells to prevent killing.
r.B: Population 2 has reduced HLA class I expression, removing the inhibitory signal and allowing activating signals to trigger NK cell killing.
r.C: HLA class I delivers an inhibitory 'self' signal that spares healthy cells, so Population 1 is protected while Population 2 is eliminated.
r.E: NK cells kill target cells directly by releasing cytotoxic granules and producing IFN-γ, not via complement lysis or phagocytosis.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 15 & 16: Innate Functions 4: NK cells killing unwanted cells

q.v: A 2-year-old boy is hospitalized with bacteremia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. In the bloodstream, mannose-binding lectin (MBL) recognizes and binds to mannose residues on the bacterial carbohydrate surface, activating MASP-1/2 to cleave C4 and C2. Generation of C3 convertase in this pathway directly results in which of the following?
o: Cleavage of C3 into C3b for opsonization and C3a for inflammation
Direct assembly of the C5b–C9 pore without C5 cleavage
Stabilization of the C4b2a complex by properdin
Neutralization of TNF activity on vascular endothelium
Downregulation of HLA class I on bacterial surfaces
q.p: Step 1 (Identify lectin pathway convergence at C3 convertase) -> Step 2 (Determine that C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3b to coat/opsonize microbes and C3a to promote inflammation)

r.B: Assembly of the C5b–C9 membrane attack complex requires prior formation of C5 convertase and cleavage of C5 into C5a and C5b.
r.C: Properdin stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), not the classical/lectin C3 convertase (C4b2a).
r.D: Complement activation amplifies inflammation rather than neutralizing TNF activity.
r.E: Bacteria do not express host HLA class I molecules, which are involved in regulating NK cell responses to host cells.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 24 & 25: Three pathways, different triggers & Convergence at C3

q.v:
A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for a history of recurrent sinopulmonary and invasive bloodstream infections with encapsulated bacteria. Functional complement screening and component assays are performed:
  Serum IgG, IgA, IgM: normal
  CH50: markedly decreased
  AH50: markedly decreased
  Terminal components (C5–C9): normal
A genetic deficiency in which of the following complement proteins best explains this patient's laboratory pattern?
o: C1q
C2
C3
C4
Factor B
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret low CH50 and low AH50 as a defect in the shared terminal pathway or C3) -> Step 2 (Rule out C5–C9 with normal terminal component levels to identify C3 deficiency)

r.A: A deficiency in C1q impairs only the classical pathway, resulting in a low CH50 but a normal AH50.
r.B: A deficiency in C2 impairs the classical and lectin pathways while leaving the alternative pathway intact, yielding a normal AH50.
r.D: Because C4 is shared by the classical and lectin pathways but not the alternative pathway, C4 deficiency produces a low CH50 with a normal AH50.
r.E: Factor B is specific to the alternative pathway, so its deficiency causes a low AH50 while CH50 remains normal.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 30 & 31: Complement testing: use the pattern

q.v: A 16-year-old boy presents to the clinic for an immunology evaluation after recovering from his second episode of Neisseria meningitidis bacteremia. Laboratory testing shows normal serum immunoglobulin levels, a normal CH50, and a markedly reduced AH50. A deficiency in which of the following proteins is the most likely cause of this patient's recurrent infections?
o: C2
C4
C8
Properdin
Mannose-binding lectin
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize recurrent Neisseria infection with normal CH50 and low AH50 as an alternative pathway defect) -> Step 2 (Identify properdin deficiency, which destabilizes C3bBb and predisposes to Neisseria)

r.A: C2 deficiency affects the classical and lectin pathways, which would present with an extremely low CH50 and a normal AH50.
r.B: C4 is required for the classical and lectin pathways, so its deficiency causes a reduced CH50 rather than an isolated reduction in AH50.
r.C: C8 is a terminal complement component shared by all pathways, so C8 deficiency causes both CH50 and AH50 to be markedly reduced.
r.E: Mannose-binding lectin initiates the lectin pathway and does not affect either the CH50 or the AH50 functional screening assays.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 31 & 32: Complement testing: use the pattern & Complement: key takeaways
