q.v:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain radiating to her back and recurrent vomiting. Physical examination reveals clusters of small, yellowish papules over her back and extensor surfaces that are biopsied and found to contain lipid-laden foam cells. Her parents are healthy and have normal lipid profiles. Laboratory studies show:
  Plasma triglycerides: 2,850 mg/dL
  Plasma total cholesterol: 195 mg/dL
  Serum amylase and lipase: markedly elevated
Which of the following lipoproteins is most likely accumulating in this patient's plasma?
o: Chylomicrons
Low-density lipoproteins (LDL)
Intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL)
Very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) only
High-density lipoproteins (HDL)
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize autosomal recessive Type I hyperchylomicronemia from childhood acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas with foam cells, and severely elevated triglycerides) -> Step 2 (Identify that a defect in lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II causes isolated accumulation of chylomicrons because VLDLs have an alternative hepatic clearance pathway)

r.B: Low-density lipoproteins (LDL) accumulate in Type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia, which presents with tendon xanthomas and elevated plasma cholesterol with normal triglycerides.
r.C: Intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL) and chylomicron remnants accumulate in Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia due to a defect in apolipoprotein E.
r.D: Isolated elevation of VLDL is characteristic of Type IV hypertriglyceridemia rather than Type I hyperchylomicronemia.
r.E: High-density lipoproteins (HDL) participate in reverse cholesterol transport and do not cause eruptive xanthomas or hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 5: Hyperlipidemias: Type I

q.v:
A 28-year-old woman presents for a routine cardiovascular evaluation because her mother had a myocardial infarction at age 38. Physical examination reveals hard, nodular masses on her Achilles tendons and the extensor tendons of both hands. A fasting lipid panel shows:
  Total cholesterol: 410 mg/dL
  LDL cholesterol: 330 mg/dL
  Triglycerides: 110 mg/dL
Which of the following best describes the primary molecular defect and inheritance pattern of this patient's condition?
o: Apolipoprotein E defect / Autosomal recessive
LDL receptor defect / Autosomal dominant
Lipoprotein lipase defect / Autosomal recessive
Apolipoprotein C-II defect / Autosomal recessive
OCTN2 transporter defect / Autosomal recessive
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia from tendon xanthomas, premature family history of cardiovascular disease, and isolated elevation of LDL and total cholesterol with normal triglycerides) -> Step 2 (Match Type IIa hyperlipidemia to an autosomal dominant defect in the LDL receptor)

r.A: An autosomal recessive defect in apolipoprotein E causes Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia, which presents with palmar xanthomas and elevations in both cholesterol and triglycerides.
r.C: An autosomal recessive defect in lipoprotein lipase causes Type I hyperchylomicronemia, presenting in childhood with eruptive xanthomas, massive hypertriglyceridemia, and pancreatitis.
r.D: An autosomal recessive defect in apolipoprotein C-II also causes Type I hyperchylomicronemia by failing to activate lipoprotein lipase.
r.E: An OCTN2 transporter defect causes primary carnitine deficiency, which presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia and cardiomyopathy rather than hypercholesterolemia.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 6: Hyperlipidemias Type IIA and Type IIB

q.v:
A 48-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic for evaluation of premature coronary artery disease. On physical examination, yellowish-orange lipid deposits are noted within the palmar creases of both hands. A fasting lipid profile shows:
  Total cholesterol: 360 mg/dL
  Triglycerides: 380 mg/dL
  Lipoprotein electrophoresis: elevated IDL and chylomicron remnants
A defect in apolipoprotein E is confirmed. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic and dietary treatment regimen for this patient?
o: High-carbohydrate diet and avoidance of fasting
Oral carnitine supplementation
Diet modification, statins, and fibrates
Cortisone to inhibit phospholipase A2
Low-dose aspirin therapy alone
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia from unique palmar xanthomas, elevated IDL and chylomicron remnants, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, and an APOE defect) -> Step 2 (Select the recommended treatment of diet modification plus statins for high cholesterol and fibrates for high triglycerides)

r.A: A high-carbohydrate diet and avoidance of fasting is the treatment for medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency, not Type III hyperlipidemia.
r.B: Oral carnitine supplementation is the specific therapy for primary carnitine deficiency due to an OCTN2 transporter defect.
r.D: Cortisone inhibits phospholipase A2 to reduce eicosanoid synthesis in inflammatory states and does not treat dysbetalipoproteinemia.
r.E: Low-dose aspirin inhibits platelet COX-1 to reduce thromboxane A2 formation, but it does not correct the underlying hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 9: Hyperlipidemias: Type III

q.v: A 56-year-old woman with elevated LDL cholesterol is started on a combination of a statin and a bile salt-binding resin. The physician explains that both medications ultimately lower plasma LDL levels through a shared cellular response in hepatocytes. Which of the following best describes how lowering intracellular hepatic cholesterol reduces plasma LDL levels?
o: Decreased intestinal packaging of dietary lipids into chylomicrons
Increased expression of hepatic LDL receptors and enhanced LDL uptake
Direct activation of hormone-sensitive lipase in peripheral adipocytes
Inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I on the outer mitochondrial membrane
Increased hepatic overproduction and secretion of apolipoprotein B-100
q.p: Step 1 (Recall that statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and bile salt-binding resins deplete bile acids, both lowering intracellular hepatocyte cholesterol) -> Step 2 (Connect reduced intracellular cholesterol to the compensatory increase in LDL receptor number on hepatocytes, increasing LDL uptake from plasma)

r.A: Chylomicrons package dietary triglycerides and cholesterol in intestinal enterocytes and are not the target of statins or hepatic LDL receptor upregulation.
r.C: Hormone-sensitive lipase is activated during fasting to mobilize stored triglycerides from adipose tissue and does not clear plasma LDL.
r.D: Inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) by malonyl-CoA blocks long-chain fatty acid transport into mitochondria for beta-oxidation.
r.E: Overproduction of apolipoprotein B-100 causes accumulation of LDL and VLDL in Type IIb familial combined hyperlipidemia rather than lowering plasma LDL.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 8: Multiple Therapies Lower LDL Cholesterol: Increase LDLR Number and LDL Uptake

q.v:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for progressive skeletal muscle weakness and exercise intolerance over the past several months. Echocardiography reveals dilated cardiomyopathy. A fasted blood sample obtained after strenuous activity shows:
  Serum glucose: 38 mg/dL
  Urine ketones: undetectable
  Plasma triglycerides: elevated
A skeletal muscle biopsy demonstrates prominent lipid vacuoles. Tandem mass spectrometry of plasma and muscle shows:
  Free carnitine (C0): 1% of normal (↓↓↓)
  Acylcarnitines (all species): markedly decreased (↓)
Which of the following is the most likely defective protein and most appropriate treatment for this patient?
o: MCAD / Avoid fasting and high-carbohydrate diet
CPT-I / Avoid fasting
OCTN2 transporter / Carnitine supplementation
CPT-II / Avoid triggers and dietary therapy
Apolipoprotein C-II / Diet, lifestyle, and fibrates
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the acylcarnitine profile showing extremely reduced free carnitine [C0] at 1-2% of normal and decreased acylcarnitines of all species, alongside cardiomyopathy, muscle lipid vacuoles, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia) -> Step 2 (Identify primary carnitine deficiency caused by defective OCTN2 cellular uptake and renal reabsorption, treated with carnitine supplementation)

r.A: MCAD deficiency presents with normal or decreased free carnitine and elevated medium-chain (C8) acylcarnitines, and does not cause severe depletion of all acylcarnitine species.
r.B: CPT-I deficiency prevents conversion of long-chain fatty acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine, resulting in elevated free carnitine (C0) and decreased long-chain acylcarnitines.
r.D: CPT-II deficiency impairs regeneration of acyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, leading to elevated long-chain (C16, C18:1) acylcarnitines.
r.E: Apolipoprotein C-II deficiency impairs lipoprotein lipase activity in Type I hyperlipidemia and does not cause hypoketotic hypoglycemia or carnitine depletion.

q.s: SLO 2, Slides 11 & 15: Carnitine Deficiencies

q.v:
A 7-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with lethargy and vomiting after a viral gastroenteritis caused her to miss overnight feedings. Physical examination shows hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation reveals:
  Serum glucose: 32 mg/dL
  Urine ketones: absent
  Liver transaminases: elevated
A plasma acylcarnitine profile is obtained and compared against reference patterns for fatty acid oxidation disorders:
  Free carnitine (C0): elevated (↑)
  Long-chain acylcarnitines (C16, C18:1): decreased (↓)
  Medium-chain acylcarnitines (C8): normal
Which of the following enzymes or transporters is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD)
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I)
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT-II)
Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase (CACT)
Organic cation/carnitine transporter 2 (OCTN2)
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize hypoketotic hypoglycemia and liver dysfunction with an acylcarnitine profile showing increased free carnitine [C0] and decreased long-chain acylcarnitines) -> Step 2 (Map this profile to a defect in CPT-I on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which fails to form long-chain acylcarnitines from free carnitine and fatty acyl-CoA)

r.A: MCAD deficiency causes an elevation in medium-chain (C8) blood acylcarnitines with normal or decreased free carnitine.
r.C: CPT-II deficiency results in elevated long-chain (C16, C18:1) blood acylcarnitines with normal or decreased free carnitine.
r.D: CACT deficiency impairs transport of acylcarnitines into the mitochondrial matrix, producing decreased free carnitine and elevated long-chain (C16, C18:1) acylcarnitines.
r.E: OCTN2 deficiency causes primary carnitine deficiency, characterized by severely decreased free carnitine (↓↓↓) and decreased levels of all acylcarnitine species.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 15: Carnitine Shuttle & MCAD Comparison Table

q.v:
A 6-month-old boy who is exclusively fed breast milk is brought to the emergency department after becoming unresponsive following a 10-hour overnight fast. Laboratory studies show:
  Blood glucose: 30 mg/dL
  Urine ketones: absent
  Plasma free fatty acids: elevated
  Plasma octanoylcarnitine (C8): markedly elevated
Which of the following biochemical reactions is directly catalyzed by the enzyme deficient in this infant?
o: Carboxylation of propionyl-CoA to D-methylmalonyl-CoA
Conversion of L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
Transfer of carnitine to long-chain fatty acyl-CoA on the outer mitochondrial membrane
First step of beta-oxidation of C8 and C10 fatty acyl-CoAs producing FADH2
Carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA in the cytosol
q.p: Step 1 (Identify MCAD deficiency from infant fasting intolerance on milk rich in MCFAs, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, and elevated C8 medium-chain acylcarnitines) -> Step 2 (Identify the biochemical role of MCAD as catalyzing the FAD-dependent first step of beta-oxidation for medium-length [C8 and C10] fatty acids)

r.A: Carboxylation of propionyl-CoA is catalyzed by biotin-dependent propionyl-CoA carboxylase during the oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids.
r.B: Conversion of L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA is catalyzed by vitamin B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in odd-chain fatty acid oxidation.
r.C: Transfer of carnitine to long-chain fatty acyl-CoA on the outer mitochondrial membrane is catalyzed by CPT-I, whereas medium-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria independent of the carnitine shuttle.
r.E: Carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA is catalyzed by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the regulated first step in cytosolic fatty acid synthesis.

q.s: SLO 2, Slides 12–14: MCAD Deficiency

q.v: In a state of high glucose availability and low energy demand, hepatic glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate, which enters the mitochondrion to form acetyl-CoA. Which of the following correctly pairs the molecule that transports this acetyl-CoA out of the mitochondrion into the cytosol with the positive allosteric effect that molecule exerts on the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis?
o: Malonyl-CoA / Activates carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
Citrate / Activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Oxaloacetate / Activates hormone-sensitive lipase
Palmitoyl-CoA / Activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Acetoacetate / Activates lipoprotein lipase
q.p: Step 1 (Recall that mitochondrial acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate, which is transported into the cytosol and cleaved back to acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis) -> Step 2 (Identify that high cytosolic citrate allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, converting inactive dimers into active polymers)

r.A: Malonyl-CoA is the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase in the cytosol and acts to inhibit, not activate, carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I).
r.C: Oxaloacetate does not cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly to carry acetyl groups, and hormone-sensitive lipase is activated during fasting by glucagon and epinephrine.
r.D: Long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs such as palmitoyl-CoA negatively regulate (inhibit) acetyl-CoA carboxylase rather than activating it.
r.E: Acetoacetate is a ketone body produced by the liver during fasting and does not transport acetyl groups for fatty acid synthesis or regulate lipoprotein lipase.

q.s: SLO 3, Slides 26, 29–31: Carbohydrates to fats & Fatty acid synthesis

q.v: During the catabolism of odd-chain fatty acids, beta-oxidation proceeds until a three-carbon propionyl-CoA residue remains, which is subsequently converted into the TCA cycle intermediate succinyl-CoA. Which of the following correctly pairs the two enzymes in this pathway with their required vitamin cofactors?
o: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (Vitamin B12) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (Biotin)
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (Biotin) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (Vitamin B12)
Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (Biotin) and enoyl-CoA hydratase (Vitamin B12)
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Vitamin B12) and CPT-I (Biotin)
HMG-CoA reductase (Biotin) and thiophorase (Vitamin B12)
q.p: Step 1 (Trace the conversion of propionyl-CoA to D-methylmalonyl-CoA by propionyl-CoA carboxylase, and L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase) -> Step 2 (Match propionyl-CoA carboxylase to its biotin [B7] cofactor and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase to its vitamin B12 [deoxyadenosylcobalamin] cofactor)

r.A: This option reverses the cofactors; biotin is required for the carboxylation of propionyl-CoA, whereas vitamin B12 is required for the mutase reaction.
r.C: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase requires FAD as a cofactor in standard beta-oxidation, and enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water without requiring biotin or B12.
r.D: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses biotin for fatty acid synthesis, and CPT-I does not require either biotin or vitamin B12.
r.E: HMG-CoA reductase and thiophorase are involved in cholesterol synthesis and ketone body utilization, respectively, and require neither biotin nor vitamin B12.

q.s: SLO 3, Slides 14, 26, & 27: Beta oxidation of odd chained fatty acids

q.v: A 64-year-old man with severe osteoarthritis and a history of peptic ulcer disease is evaluated for pain management. His physician avoids prescribing a selective COX-2 inhibitor due to the patient's history of coronary artery disease and instead discusses the vascular balance of eicosanoids. Which of the following best explains why selective COX-2 inhibitors increase the risk of myocardial infarction whereas low-dose aspirin is antithrombotic?
o: Selective COX-2 inhibitors block prostacyclin (PGI2) without inhibiting platelet COX-1-derived thromboxane A2 (TXA2)
Selective COX-2 inhibitors shunt arachidonic acid into the 5-lipoxygenase pathway to overproduce thromboxane A2
Anucleate platelets rapidly synthesize new COX-2 enzyme after exposure to low-dose aspirin
Selective COX-2 inhibitors directly activate phospholipase A2 in vascular endothelial cells
Low-dose aspirin selectively inhibits COX-2 in platelets while sparing endothelial COX-1
q.p: Step 1 (Recall that prothrombotic TXA2 is synthesized by COX-1 in anucleate platelets that cannot regenerate the enzyme, whereas antithrombotic PGI2 is produced by COX-1/COX-2) -> Step 2 (Explain that selective COX-2 inhibitors reduce PGI2 without blocking TXA2, disrupting the antithrombotic balance and increasing heart attack risk)

r.B: Shunting of arachidonic acid to the 5-lipoxygenase pathway produces leukotrienes that cause bronchoconstriction in aspirin-induced asthma, not thromboxane A2.
r.C: Platelets lack nuclei and therefore cannot synthesize new COX-1 enzyme to replace the enzyme irreversibly inhibited by aspirin.
r.D: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids and is inhibited by cortisone, not activated by selective COX-2 inhibitors.
r.E: Aspirin inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2, and its antithrombotic effect relies on irreversibly inhibiting COX-1 in anucleate platelets to block TXA2 formation.

q.s: SLO 4, Slides 34–36: Practice Questions 13–15 & Eicosanoid Metabolism

q.v: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with acute-onset severe epigastric pain and vomiting. Physical examination reveals numerous small yellowish papules over his buttocks and knees, which biopsy confirms to be accumulations of cutaneous foam cells. Laboratory evaluation shows markedly elevated plasma triglycerides and an accumulation of chylomicrons, while VLDL levels remain within the normal range. Which of the following best describes the primary pharmacological class indicated for this patient's disorder?
o: Statins
Fibrates
Bile salt-binding resins
Cortisone
Carnitine supplementation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Type I hyperchylomicronemia from childhood pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, and isolated chylomicron elevation) -> Step 2 (Select fibrates alongside diet and lifestyle as the recommended treatment)

r.A: Statins are the primary pharmacological treatment for hypercholesterolemias such as Type IIa and Type IIb, rather than isolated chylomicronemia.
r.C: Bile salt-binding resins are used to deplete hepatic bile acids and upregulate LDL receptors to lower plasma LDL cholesterol.
r.D: Cortisone is a glucocorticoid that inhibits phospholipase A2 to block eicosanoid synthesis and has no role in lowering triglycerides.
r.E: Carnitine supplementation is the specific therapy for primary carnitine deficiency (OCTN2 defect), not hyperlipidemias.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 5: Hyperlipidemias: Type I

q.v: A 34-year-old man presents for a routine health maintenance exam. His father and paternal aunt both suffered myocardial infarctions in their early 40s. Physical examination reveals hard, nodular masses on his Achilles tendons and the extensor tendons of his hands. Lipoprotein analysis demonstrates elevated plasma concentrations of both LDL and VLDL particles. Which of the following is the most likely underlying molecular defect in this patient?
o: Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase
Defective apolipoprotein E
Overproduction of apolipoprotein B-100
Deficiency of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
Mutation in the OCTN2 transporter
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Type IIb familial combined hyperlipidemia from tendon xanthomas, premature CAD family history, and combined LDL + VLDL elevation) -> Step 2 (Identify Apo B-100 overproduction as the underlying defect)

r.A: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes Type I hyperchylomicronemia, characterized by chylomicron accumulation and eruptive xanthomas.
r.B: Defective apolipoprotein E causes Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia, which leads to elevated IDL and chylomicron remnants and palmar xanthomas.
r.D: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I deficiency impairs long-chain fatty acid transport into mitochondria, causing hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
r.E: Mutations in the OCTN2 transporter cause primary carnitine deficiency, presenting with cardiomyopathy and extremely reduced plasma carnitine.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 6: Hyperlipidemias Type IIA and Type IIB

q.v:
A 45-year-old man is evaluated at a lipid clinic for abnormal laboratory results obtained during a life insurance screening. He has no family history of premature coronary artery disease, and physical examination shows no tendon or palmar xanthomas. His fasting lipid panel and lipoprotein electrophoresis show:
  Total cholesterol: 210 mg/dL
  Triglycerides: 680 mg/dL
  Chylomicrons: absent
  VLDL: markedly increased
  LDL: normal
Which of the following clinical complications is most strongly associated with this patient's disorder if his lipid abnormality becomes severe?
o: Acute pancreatitis
Rhabdomyolysis
Dilated cardiomyopathy
Bronchospasm
Sudden infant death syndrome
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret lipid panel showing isolated VLDL and triglyceride elevation without strong atherosclerosis association as Type IV hypertriglyceridemia) -> Step 2 (Predict acute pancreatitis as the major complication of severe hypertriglyceridemia)

r.B: Rhabdomyolysis is a characteristic clinical finding of CPT II deficiency rather than Type IV hypertriglyceridemia.
r.C: Dilated cardiomyopathy is a classic complication of primary carnitine deficiency and CACT deficiency due to energy-deprived cardiac muscle.
r.D: Bronchospasm is a complication of NSAID ingestion in patients with aspirin-induced asthma due to leukotriene overproduction.
r.E: Sudden infant death syndrome is associated with beta-oxidation defects such as MCAD deficiency in fasting infants.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 10: Hyperlipidemias: Type IV and V

q.v:
A 9-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with lethargy and poor feeding following a 12-hour febrile illness. She has no evidence of cardiomyopathy on cardiac evaluation. Laboratory studies obtained prior to intravenous dextrose administration show:
  Blood glucose: 32 mg/dL
  Urine ketones: undetectable
  Liver transaminases: elevated
  Plasma free carnitine (C0): elevated
  Plasma long-chain acylcarnitines: decreased
Which of the following proteins is most likely defective in this patient?
o: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD)
OCTN2 carnitine transporter
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I)
Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase (CACT)
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT II)
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze acylcarnitine profile showing elevated free carnitine and decreased long-chain acylcarnitines alongside hypoketotic hypoglycemia and liver dysfunction) -> Step 2 (Map defect to CPT I, which converts long-chain acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine)

r.A: MCAD deficiency presents with normal or decreased free carnitine and elevated medium-chain (C8) acylcarnitines.
r.B: OCTN2 transporter defects (primary carnitine deficiency) cause severely reduced free carnitine and decreased levels of all acylcarnitine species.
r.D: CACT deficiency results in decreased free carnitine, elevated long-chain (C16, C18:1) acylcarnitines, and cardiomyopathy.
r.E: CPT II deficiency presents with normal or decreased free carnitine and elevated long-chain (C16, C18:1) acylcarnitines.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 15: Carnitine Shuttle and MCAD Comparison Table

q.v: A 19-year-old man presents to the clinic with severe muscle pain and dark, reddish-brown urine following a prolonged endurance run in cold weather. He reports similar episodes of muscle cramping after fasting or viral illnesses. Laboratory evaluation reveals markedly elevated serum creatine kinase and myoglobinuria. A plasma acylcarnitine profile shows normal free carnitine (C0) levels and significantly elevated C16 and C18:1 acylcarnitine species. Which of the following functions is directly impaired in this patient?
o: Cellular uptake and renal reabsorption of carnitine
Formation of long-chain acylcarnitines at the outer mitochondrial membrane
Regeneration of acyl-CoA from acylcarnitine in the mitochondrial matrix
Dehydrogenation of C8 and C10 fatty acyl-CoAs in the mitochondrial matrix
Preliminary beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids in the peroxisome
q.p: Step 1 (Identify CPT II deficiency from exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis, normal/low C0, and elevated C16/C18:1 long-chain acylcarnitines) -> Step 2 (Determine the biochemical function of CPT II as regenerating acyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix)

r.A: Cellular uptake and renal reabsorption of carnitine is the function of OCTN2, which is defective in primary carnitine deficiency.
r.B: Formation of long-chain acylcarnitines at the outer mitochondrial membrane is catalyzed by CPT I, whose deficiency lowers long-chain acylcarnitines.
r.D: Dehydrogenation of C8 and C10 fatty acyl-CoAs is performed by MCAD, which leads to elevated C8 acylcarnitines when defective.
r.E: Preliminary beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (>22 carbons) occurs in peroxisomes and does not cause isolated C16/C18:1 acylcarnitine elevation.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 15: Carnitine Shuttle and MCAD Comparison Table

q.v: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the pediatrician after a prolonged episode of lethargy that occurred when he slept through his overnight feeding. He is exclusively fed breast milk, which is rich in medium-chain fatty acids. Diagnostic testing confirms a deficiency in the enzyme that catalyzes the first step of mitochondrial beta-oxidation for C8 and C10 fatty acids. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term dietary management for this patient?
o: High-carbohydrate diet and avoidance of fasting
High-fat, ketogenic diet with medium-chain triglycerides
Complete restriction of dietary cholesterol
Oral L-carnitine supplementation
Substitution of dietary fats with odd-chain fatty acids
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize MCAD deficiency from infant fed milk rich in MCFA presenting with fasting lethargy and C8/C10 beta-oxidation defect) -> Step 2 (Select high-carbohydrate diet and avoidance of fasting as the recommended treatment)

r.B: A ketogenic diet or medium-chain triglyceride supplementation is contraindicated because the patient cannot oxidize medium-chain fatty acids or synthesize ketones.
r.C: Restriction of dietary cholesterol is used in managing hypercholesterolemias such as Type IIa, not fatty acid oxidation defects.
r.D: Oral L-carnitine supplementation is the primary treatment for OCTN2 deficiency (primary carnitine deficiency).
r.E: Odd-chain fatty acids still require beta-oxidation to reach the final propionyl-CoA residue and would not bypass an MCAD block.

q.s: SLO 2, Slides 13 and 15: MCAD Deficiency

q.v: Following a carbohydrate-rich meal, elevated plasma insulin levels promote the storage of energy as triacylglycerols in adipose tissue and stimulate de novo fatty acid synthesis in the liver. Which of the following correctly pairs the enzyme stimulated by insulin on capillary endothelial cells with the rate-limiting enzyme activated by insulin in hepatic fatty acid synthesis?
o: Hormone-sensitive lipase / Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
Hormone-sensitive lipase / Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Lipoprotein lipase / Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Lipoprotein lipase / HMG-CoA reductase
Pancreatic lipase / Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify lipoprotein lipase as the endothelial enzyme stimulated by insulin to promote fatty acid uptake into adipocytes) -> Step 2 (Identify acetyl-CoA carboxylase as the first step of fatty acid synthesis activated by insulin and citrate)

r.A: Hormone-sensitive lipase is activated during fasting by cAMP/PKA to mobilize fatty acids, and CPT I is inhibited during the fed state by malonyl-CoA.
r.B: Hormone-sensitive lipase is inhibited by insulin in the fed state, whereas lipoprotein lipase is stimulated.
r.D: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis rather than fatty acid synthesis.
r.E: Pancreatic lipase digests dietary triacylglycerols in the gut lumen, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is involved in odd-chain fatty acid oxidation.

q.s: SLO 3, Slides 17, 21, and 30: Practice Questions and Lipid Storage

q.v: In the liver, palmitate (16:0) synthesized in the cytosol can be further modified to generate longer-chain fatty acids such as stearate (18:0), and essential dietary linoleic acid can be converted into arachidonic acid through the introduction of double bonds. In which of the following cellular compartments do these elongation and desaturation reactions take place?
o: Mitochondrial matrix
Peroxisome
Endoplasmic reticulum
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
q.p: Step 1 (Recall that fatty acid elongation beyond 16 carbons and desaturation occur in a specific organelle) -> Step 2 (Identify the endoplasmic reticulum as the site of elongation and desaturation)

r.A: The mitochondrial matrix is the site of beta-oxidation of short-, medium-, and long-chain fatty acids and ketogenesis.
r.B: The peroxisome is responsible for the preliminary beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (>22 carbons) and alpha-oxidation of branched-chain phytanic acid.
r.D: The Golgi apparatus processes proteins such as the newly synthesized LDL receptor during its transport to the cell surface.
r.E: The lysosome degrades internalized LDL particles to release free cholesterol and amino acids while the LDL receptor is recycled.

q.s: SLO 3, Slides 30 and 33: Elongation and Desaturation

q.v: A 60-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery stent placement is prescribed daily low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention of myocardial infarction. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which decreases the synthesis of both prothrombotic thromboxane A2 (TXA2) and antithrombotic prostacyclin (PGI2). Which of the following best explains why low-dose aspirin produces a net antithrombotic effect despite inhibiting both pathways?
o: Platelets lack nuclei and cannot synthesize new COX-1 enzyme to restore TXA2 production
Aspirin selectively activates lipoxygenase in platelets to generate vasodilatory leukotrienes
Endothelial cells express only COX-2, which is completely resistant to aspirin inhibition
Aspirin inhibits phospholipase A2 exclusively in megakaryocytes and circulating platelets
TXA2 is synthesized via COX-2, whereas PGI2 is synthesized exclusively via COX-1
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that aspirin inhibits both TXA2 via COX-1 and PGI2 via COX-1/2) -> Step 2 (Identify that anucleate platelets cannot synthesize replacement COX-1 enzyme, resulting in sustained suppression of platelet aggregation)

r.B: Shunting of arachidonic acid to the lipoxygenase pathway produces leukotrienes, which cause bronchoconstriction and inflammation rather than antithrombotic vasodilation.
r.C: Aspirin inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2, and PGI2 is formed by COX-1/2 in nucleated endothelial cells that can regenerate the enzymes.
r.D: Cortisone, rather than aspirin, inhibits phospholipase A2 to block the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids.
r.E: TXA2 is formed by COX-1 in platelets, while PGI2 is formed by COX-1 and COX-2, which is why selective COX-2 inhibitors spare TXA2 and increase heart attack risk.

q.s: SLO 4, Slide 34: Practice Questions (Eicosanoid Metabolism)

q.v: A 38-year-old woman presents to the clinic with an acute flare of rheumatoid arthritis. To rapidly suppress joint inflammation, her physician administers an intra-articular injection of cortisone, which blocks the production of both prostaglandins and leukotrienes. Which of the following enzymes is directly inhibited by this medication?
o: Cyclooxygenase-1
Cyclooxygenase-2
5-Lipoxygenase
Phospholipase A2
Acyl-CoA synthetase
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that cortisone prevents the synthesis of both COX-derived prostaglandins and LOX-derived leukotrienes) -> Step 2 (Identify phospholipase A2 as the upstream enzyme inhibited by cortisone that releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids)

r.A: Cyclooxygenase-1 is inhibited by NSAIDs and aspirin, which blocks prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis but spares leukotriene production.
r.B: Cyclooxygenase-2 is inhibited by NSAIDs and selective COX-2 inhibitors, which does not prevent arachidonic acid from entering the lipoxygenase pathway.
r.C: 5-Lipoxygenase converts arachidonic acid into 5-HPETE and leukotrienes, and its inhibition would not block prostaglandin formation.
r.E: Acyl-CoA synthetase activates fatty acids by attaching CoA at the outer mitochondrial membrane and endoplasmic reticulum, unrelated to steroid anti-inflammatory action.

q.s: SLO 4, Slide 35: Eicosanoid Metabolism / Cortisone Mechanism

q.v: A 26-year-old woman begins a strict, unfortified vegan diet that excludes all meat, poultry, fish, eggs, and dairy products, while maintaining high daily intake of leafy green vegetables, beans, and fresh citrus fruits. Assuming normal gastrointestinal function and no supplementation, which of the following vitamins has the largest hepatic storage capacity, delaying clinical signs of deficiency for 3 to 5 years?
o: Thiamine (B1)
Riboflavin (B2)
Biotin (B7)
Folate (B9)
Cobalamin (B12)
q.p: Step 1 (Elimination of animal products removes dietary Vitamin B12) -> Step 2 (Extensive hepatic storage of B12 delays clinical deficiency for 3-5 years)

r.A: Thiamine (B1) has very limited storage in the body, lasting only approximately 2.5 weeks.
r.B: Riboflavin (B2) is stored in limited quantities for approximately 4 weeks and is also present in whole grains and nuts.
r.C: Biotin (B7) is not stored in significant quantities and is rapidly excreted by the kidneys.
r.D: Folate (B9) is the other water-soluble vitamin with notable storage in the liver, but its stores last only 3 to 4 months and it is abundant in vegetables and legumes.

q.s: SLO 1; Slide 4 (Some Sources) and Slide 8 (Storage and Excretion)

q.v: A 38-year-old man with a history of chronic pancreatitis and severe exocrine pancreatic insufficiency presents with progressive fatigue and paresthesias in his feet. His diet includes adequate amounts of meat and dairy, and his gastric parietal cell function is intact. Impaired secretion of pancreatic proteases in the duodenum directly prevents which of the following steps in vitamin absorption?
o: Cleavage of haptocorrin from cobalamin
Binding of intrinsic factor in the stomach
Release of cobalamin from food protein
Active transport via the SVCT1 carrier
Secretion of haptocorrin by salivary glands
q.p: Step 1 (Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency decreases duodenal protease levels) -> Step 2 (Failure to cleave haptocorrin from B12 in the duodenum prevents B12 from binding intrinsic factor for absorption in the terminal ileum)

r.B: Intrinsic factor is secreted by gastric parietal cells, and B12 binds to it in the duodenum only after haptocorrin is cleaved by pancreatic proteases.
r.C: Release of cobalamin from food protein occurs in the stomach via the action of gastric HCl and pepsin.
r.D: The SVCT1 transporter mediates the active intestinal uptake of vitamin C (ascorbic acid), not vitamin B12.
r.E: Haptocorrin is secreted by the salivary glands in the mouth prior to food reaching the stomach or duodenum.

q.s: SLO 1; Slide 7 (Vit B12 Absorption)

q.v: Which of the following pairs of water-soluble vitamins has intestinal absorption directly impaired by chronic ethanol consumption through downregulation or inhibition of intestinal transport?
o: Thiamine (B1) and Folate (B9)
Riboflavin (B2) and Pantothenic acid (B5)
Niacin (B3) and Pyridoxine (B6)
Pyridoxine (B6) and Biotin (B7)
Biotin (B7) and Cobalamin (B12)
q.p: Step 1 (Chronic ethanol exposure in the small intestine) -> Step 2 (Downregulation of thiamine transporters and inhibition of folate transport reduce absorption of B1 and B9)

r.B: Riboflavin (B2) and pantothenic acid (B5) are not the primary targets of ethanol-mediated intestinal transporter downregulation shown on the absorption slides.
r.C: Niacin (B3) is decreased in Hartnup disease and carcinoid syndrome, while pyridoxine (B6) is depleted by isoniazid.
r.D: Pyridoxine (B6) activity is inhibited by isoniazid, and biotin (B7) absorption is prevented by avidin in raw egg whites.
r.E: Biotin (B7) is bound by avidin in raw egg whites, and cobalamin (B12) absorption depends on gastric HCl, pancreatic proteases, and intrinsic factor.

q.s: SLO 1; Slide 5 (Water Soluble Vitamin Absorption) and Slide 6 (Absorption Complications)

q.v: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with worsening shortness of breath, orthopnea, and bilateral lower extremity swelling. He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use and lives primarily on polished white rice and alcohol. Physical examination reveals jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, and 3+ pitting edema in both legs, along with decreased sensation in his feet. Which of the following sets of pathways is directly impaired by his underlying vitamin deficiency?
o: Pentose phosphate pathway, pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, and TCA cycle
Gluconeogenesis from pyruvate, fatty acid synthesis, and VOMIT pathway
Urea cycle, glycogenolysis, and heme synthesis
Purine synthesis, thymidylate synthesis, and homocysteine remethylation
Collagen crosslinking, carnitine synthesis, and norepinephrine synthesis
q.p: Step 1 (Diet of polished rice and heavy alcohol use causes Thiamine/B1 deficiency presenting as wet and dry beriberi) -> Step 2 (Impaired coenzyme activity in the pentose phosphate pathway, pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, TCA cycle, and VOMIT pathway)

r.B: Carboxylation reactions in gluconeogenesis from pyruvate, lipogenesis, and the VOMIT pathway require biotin (B7).
r.C: Glycogenolysis, amino acid metabolism, and heme synthesis require pyridoxine (B6 / PLP).
r.D: Purine synthesis, thymidylate synthesis, and homocysteine remethylation require folate (B9).
r.E: Collagen crosslinking, carnitine synthesis, and norepinephrine synthesis require vitamin C (ascorbic acid).

q.s: SLO 2 and SLO 3; Slide 3 (Studies of Beriberi disease) and Slide 10 (B1: PPP, PDC, TCA, VOMIT pathway)

q.v: A 58-year-old woman with a metastatic neuroendocrine tumor of the ileum presents with episodic flushing, chronic watery diarrhea, and a new symmetric, hyperpigmented, scaly rash around her neck that worsens with sun exposure. Her family also notes increasing confusion and memory loss over the past month. Diversion of a dietary amino acid precursor by her tumor has resulted in a deficiency of which of the following coenzymes?
o: Thiamine pyrophosphate
Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)
Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)
Tetrahydrofolate (THF)
q.p: Step 1 (Carcinoid syndrome increases tryptophan utilization, decreasing Niacin/B3 synthesis and causing pellagra) -> Step 2 (Deficiency of NAD+ and NADP+ impairs catabolic pathways and DNA repair)

r.A: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the active form of vitamin B1; its deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome rather than Casal necklace dermatitis.
r.B: Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) is derived from riboflavin (B2), which is not synthesized from tryptophan.
r.D: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the active coenzyme of vitamin B6; deficiency is associated with isoniazid therapy and causes sideroblastic anemia and neuropathy.
r.E: Tetrahydrofolate (THF) is derived from folate (B9); deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia without photosensitive dermatitis or dementia.

q.s: SLO 1, SLO 2, and SLO 3; Slide 6 (Absorption Complications) and Slide 12 (B3: NAD and NADP precursor)

q.v: A 42-year-old man is being treated with multi-drug therapy including isoniazid for active pulmonary tuberculosis. Six months into therapy, he develops fatigue, pallor, and numbness and tingling in his fingers and toes. Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia due to impaired heme synthesis. Which of the following enzymes is directly dependent on the vitamin depleted by his medication?
o: Xanthine oxidase
Pyruvate carboxylase
Glutathione reductase
Cystathionine synthase
Thymidylate synthase
q.p: Step 1 (Isoniazid increases excretion and inhibits activity of Vitamin B6/PLP) -> Step 2 (Decreased activity of PLP-dependent enzymes including delta-aminolevulinate synthase and cystathionine synthase)

r.A: Xanthine oxidase requires riboflavin (B2) in the purine degradation pathway.
r.B: Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin (B7)-dependent enzyme in gluconeogenesis.
r.C: Glutathione reductase utilizes NADPH derived from niacin (B3) and FAD from riboflavin (B2).
r.E: Thymidylate synthase requires 5,10-methylene-THF, a derivative of folate (B9), for dTMP synthesis.

q.s: SLO 1 and SLO 2; Slide 6 (Absorption Complications) and Slide 15 (B6)

q.v:
A 6-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department for lethargy, poor feeding, and a generalized seizure. Physical examination reveals marked hypotonia, patchy alopecia, and a scaly erythematous rash around the eyes, nose, and mouth. Arterial blood gas and metabolic panel results are shown below:
  Arterial pH: 7.26
  Serum bicarbonate: 14 mEq/L
  Serum lactate: elevated
  Serum pyruvate: elevated
  Urine propionyl-CoA metabolites: elevated
A defect in the utilization of which of the following vitamins best explains these findings?
o: Thiamine (B1)
Riboflavin (B2)
Pantothenic acid (B5)
Pyridoxine (B6)
Biotin (B7)
q.p: Step 1 (Infant presents with scaly dermatitis, alopecia, hypotonia, seizures, and lactic/pyruvate acidosis) -> Step 2 (Biotin/B7 deficiency impairs pyruvate carboxylase and propionyl-CoA carboxylase)

r.A: Thiamine (B1) deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and does not typically present with alopecia and periorificial scaly dermatitis in newborn screening disorders.
r.B: Riboflavin (B2) deficiency is very rare and does not impair carboxylation reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase.
r.C: Pantothenic acid (B5) is required for CoA synthesis; deficiency is extremely rare and does not cause the classic triad of scaly dermatitis, alopecia, and hypotonia.
r.D: Pyridoxine (B6) deficiency causes sideroblastic anemia, dermatitis, and seizures, but does not directly block pyruvate carboxylase or propionyl-CoA carboxylase.

q.s: SLO 2 and SLO 3; Slide 16 (B7)

q.v:
A 64-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use disorder presents to the clinic with progressive fatigue and a sore, red, smooth tongue. Detailed neurologic examination shows intact vibration and position sense in the lower extremities and normal ankle reflexes. Laboratory studies show:
  Hemoglobin: 8.6 g/dL
  MCV: 116 fL
  Peripheral smear: macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils
  Serum homocysteine: elevated
  Serum methylmalonic acid: normal
Impaired synthesis of which of the following compounds is directly responsible for his hematologic abnormalities?
o: Heme
Deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP)
Succinyl-CoA
Collagen
Acetyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Macrocytic anemia with elevated homocysteine, normal MMA, and no neurologic deficits indicates Folate/B9 deficiency) -> Step 2 (Lack of 5,10-methylene-THF impairs conversion of dUMP to dTMP by thymidylate synthase, disrupting DNA synthesis)

r.A: Impaired heme synthesis occurs in vitamin B6 deficiency and causes microcytic sideroblastic anemia rather than megaloblastic anemia.
r.C: Impaired conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA occurs in vitamin B12 deficiency, which would elevate serum methylmalonic acid and cause neurologic deficits.
r.D: Impaired collagen crosslinking occurs in vitamin C deficiency and causes scurvy (bleeding gums, petechiae) with normal MCV.
r.E: Impaired acetyl-CoA formation from pyruvate occurs in deficiencies of B1, B2, B3, or B5, which do not cause megaloblastic anemia.

q.s: SLO 2 and SLO 3; Slide 17 (B9 B12)

q.v: A 7-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder is brought to the pediatric clinic because of gingival bleeding, easy bruising, and leg pain. His parents report an extremely selective diet consisting exclusively of plain white pasta, chicken nuggets, and water for the past year. Physical examination reveals swollen, bleeding gums and perifollicular petechiae on both lower legs. In addition to impaired connective tissue crosslinking, this patient has decreased enzymatic synthesis of which of the following pairs of molecules?
o: Norepinephrine and carnitine
Dopamine and serotonin
Purines and pyrimidines
Methionine and cysteine
Fatty acids and cholesterol
q.p: Step 1 (Restrictive diet in a child with ASD leads to Vitamin C deficiency/scurvy) -> Step 2 (Decreased vitamin C impairs collagen crosslinking as well as norepinephrine and carnitine synthesis)

r.B: Dopamine synthesis from DOPA requires vitamin B6 (PLP) as a cofactor for DOPA decarboxylase.
r.C: De novo purine and pyrimidine (dTMP) synthesis requires folate (B9) derivatives.
r.D: Methionine regeneration requires B9 and B12, while conversion of homocysteine to cysteine requires B6.
r.E: Fatty acid synthesis requires biotin (B7) for acetyl-CoA carboxylase and NADPH from niacin (B3).

q.s: SLO 2 and SLO 3; Slide 18 (Vitamin C)

q.v: Which of the following set of four B-complex vitamins is required for the shared enzymatic machinery of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, and the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex (VOMIT pathway)?
o: B1, B2, B3, and B5
B1, B2, B6, and B12
B2, B3, B6, and B7
B3, B5, B7, and B9
B5, B6, B9, and B12
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the three alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes: PDC, TCA alpha-KGDH, and VOMIT BCKDH) -> Step 2 (All three complexes require coenzymes derived from Thiamine/B1, Riboflavin/B2, Niacin/B3, and Pantothenic acid/B5)

r.B: Vitamins B6 and B12 are involved in amino acid and methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism, respectively, rather than the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
r.C: Vitamins B6 and B7 are required for transamination/decarboxylation and carboxylation reactions, respectively, not the dehydrogenase complexes.
r.D: Biotin (B7) is a carboxylation cofactor (propionyl-CoA carboxylase in the VOMIT pathway) and folate (B9) is for one-carbon transfers, neither of which is part of PDC.
r.E: Vitamins B6, B9, and B12 are involved in homocysteine metabolism rather than the pyruvate or alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes.

q.s: SLO 2; Slides 10, 11, 12, and 14 (B1, B2, B3, and B5 pathway diagrams)

q.v: A 41-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus and a long history of heavy smoking presents to the clinic with fatigue, easy bruising, and bleeding gums when brushing her teeth. Her diet consists mainly of fast food and sweetened beverages. In addition to low dietary intake, her persistent hyperglycemia directly impairs the cellular uptake of the oxidized form of the deficient vitamin by competing for which of the following transporters?
o: Sodium-dependent vitamin C transporter 1 (SVCT1)
Glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1)
Intrinsic factor receptor
Haptocorrin
Thiamine transporter
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize scurvy / Vitamin C deficiency in a patient with hyperglycemia) -> Step 2 (Identify that oxidized vitamin C uses GLUT1/GLUT3 channels and competes with high glucose for cellular uptake)

r.A: SVCT1 is the primary active transport protein for reduced ascorbic acid in the intestine and exhibits dose saturation, rather than direct competition with glucose for oxidized vitamin C uptake.
r.C: The intrinsic factor receptor in the terminal ileum mediates the absorption of the vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complex.
r.D: Haptocorrin is a salivary gland protein that binds vitamin B12 in the stomach before being cleaved by pancreatic proteases in the duodenum.
r.E: The thiamine transporter mediates vitamin B1 absorption in the small intestine and is downregulated by chronic alcohol consumption.

q.s: SLO1, Slide 5 (Water Soluble Vitamin Absorption), Slide 6 (Absorption Complications), and Slide 18 (Vitamin C)

q.v: Unlike most water-soluble vitamins that are rapidly excreted in the urine when consumed in excess, two water-soluble vitamins are stored in significant quantities in the liver, delaying the onset of clinical deficiency for several months or years. Which of the following correctly pairs these two vitamins with their typical duration of hepatic storage?
o: Thiamine (B1: 3-4 months) and Riboflavin (B2: 3-5 years)
Pyridoxine (B6: 3-4 months) and Biotin (B7: 3-5 years)
Folate (B9: 3-4 months) and Cobalamin (B12: 3-5 years)
Vitamin C (3-4 months) and Niacin (B3: 3-5 years)
Pantothenic acid (B5: 3-4 months) and Cobalamin (B12: 3-5 years)
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the two major exceptions to limited hepatic storage among water-soluble vitamins) -> Step 2 (Match Folate [B9] to 3-4 months and Cobalamin [B12] to 3-5 years)

r.A: Thiamine (B1) is stored for only about 2.5 weeks and riboflavin (B2) for about 4 weeks.
r.B: Pyridoxine (B6) is stored for weeks to months, while biotin (B7) is rapidly excreted.
r.D: Vitamin C is stored for only about 1 month (1-2 grams total body pool) and niacin (B3) is rapidly excreted.
r.E: Pantothenic acid (B5) is retained for only a few days rather than months.

q.s: SLO1, Slide 8 (Storage and Excretion) and Slide 9 (SLO1 Study Questions)

q.v: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after being found confused and wandering in a park. He has a known history of severe alcohol use disorder and malnutrition. Physical examination shows disorientation to time and place, bilateral abducens nerve palsies, horizontal nystagmus, and a wide-based, unsteady gait. An emergency medicine resident orders an immediate intravenous infusion of 50% dextrose before administering any vitamins. Which of the following enzyme activities is most likely to acutely stall and worsen his neurological condition following this infusion?
o: Xanthine oxidase
Pyruvate carboxylase
Methionine synthase
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome triggered/worsened by a glucose bolus without thiamine [B1]) -> Step 2 (Identify the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex [PDC] as a B1-dependent enzyme that stalls under a glucose load)

r.A: Xanthine oxidase requires riboflavin (B2) as a cofactor in purine degradation to uric acid.
r.B: Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin (B7) to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate during gluconeogenesis.
r.C: Methionine synthase requires cobalamin (B12) to transfer a methyl group from 5-methyl-THF to homocysteine.
r.E: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires cobalamin (B12) to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the VOMIT pathway.

q.s: SLO2 and SLO3, Slide 10 (B1: PPP, PDC, TCA, VOMIT pathway) and Slide 19 (SLO2 Study Questions)

q.v: A 2-day-old newborn in the neonatal intensive care unit is undergoing intensive blue-light phototherapy for severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The neonatologist orders supplementation of a specific water-soluble vitamin that is degraded by light exposure and serves as a direct precursor to the coenzymes required by succinate dehydrogenase and xanthine oxidase. Which of the following vitamins is being supplemented?
o: Thiamine (B1)
Riboflavin (B2)
Niacin (B3)
Pantothenic acid (B5)
Pyridoxine (B6)
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the vitamin deficiency associated with infants undergoing phototherapy and needed for xanthine oxidase and TCA cycle [succinate dehydrogenase]) -> Step 2 (Match FAD/FADH2 precursor to Riboflavin [B2])

r.A: Thiamine (B1) is required for transketolase and alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenases, not xanthine oxidase or succinate dehydrogenase.
r.C: Niacin (B3) is the precursor to NAD+ and NADP+, rather than FAD/FADH2.
r.D: Pantothenic acid (B5) is a component of CoA used in the PDC, TCA cycle, and lipid metabolism, not xanthine oxidase.
r.E: Pyridoxine (B6) is converted to PLP for transamination, glycogenolysis, and heme synthesis.

q.s: SLO2, Slide 11 (B2: XO, PDC, TCA, VOMIT pathway)

q.v: A 14-year-old boy is evaluated in the clinic for a recurrent, symmetric, hyperpigmented, scaly rash on his neck, forearms, and dorsal hands that worsens every summer. His parents also note that he has had intermittent watery diarrhea and recent difficulty concentrating in school. Laboratory evaluation reveals aminoaciduria caused by a genetic defect in the intestinal and renal transport of neutral amino acids, leading to markedly decreased plasma tryptophan levels. The photosensitive skin lesions in this patient are most directly linked to impaired maintenance of which of the following cellular processes?
o: Collagen fibril crosslinking
DNA repair and cell signaling
Heme biosynthesis
Fatty acid beta-oxidation
Glycogen phosphorolysis
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Hartnup disease causing tryptophan deficiency and secondary Niacin [B3] deficiency / pellagra) -> Step 2 (Connect pellagra dermatitis to impaired NAD+ substrate role in DNA repair and signaling)

r.A: Collagen fibril crosslinking requires vitamin C, and its impairment causes scurvy rather than photosensitive dermatitis.
r.C: Heme biosynthesis requires vitamin B5 (succinyl-CoA) and vitamin B6 (PLP), and its impairment causes anemia.
r.D: Fatty acid beta-oxidation utilizes NAD+ catabolically, whereas the slide table explicitly connects pellagra dermatitis to the maintenance role of NAD+ as a substrate in DNA repair.
r.E: Glycogenolysis requires vitamin B6 (PLP) as a cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase.

q.s: SLO2 and SLO3, Slide 6 (Absorption Complications), Slide 12 (B3: NAD and NADP precursor), and Slide 20 (SLO3 Study Questions)

q.v: A 31-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician complaining of progressive numbness, tingling, and burning pain in her feet and hands over the past two months. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no prescription medications, but she reports taking high-dose over-the-counter nutritional supplements daily for the past year to manage severe premenstrual syndrome. Physical examination reveals decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in a stocking-glove distribution. Which of the following enzyme pathways relies on the active coenzyme form of the vitamin causing her toxicity?
o: Conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine
Carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA
Conversion of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA
Reduction of oxidized glutathione
Decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Vitamin B6 [pyridoxine] overdose toxicity presenting as sensory peripheral neuropathy in a patient self-treating premenstrual syndrome) -> Step 2 (Identify cystathionine synthase / cystathionase in homocysteine metabolism as a B6/PLP-dependent pathway)

r.B: Carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA in lipogenesis requires biotin (B7).
r.C: Carboxylation of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA in the VOMIT pathway requires biotin (B7).
r.D: Reduction of oxidized glutathione by glutathione reductase requires NADPH derived from niacin (B3).
r.E: Decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex requires vitamins B1, B2, B3, and B5, not B6.

q.s: SLO2 and SLO3, Slide 15 (B6 PLP)

q.v: Which of the following enzymes requires both folate (as 5,10-methylene-THF) and vitamin B6 (indirectly via one-carbon metabolism) to catalyze the synthesis of dTMP from dUMP for DNA synthesis?
o: Dihydrofolate reductase
Methionine synthase
Thymidylate synthase
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
Cystathionine synthase
q.p: Step 1 (Locate the pyrimidine metabolism pathway converting dUMP to dTMP on the B9/B12 slide) -> Step 2 (Identify thymidylate synthase as the enzyme utilizing 5,10-methylene-THF to produce dTMP and DHF)

r.A: Dihydrofolate reductase reduces DHF back to THF rather than directly methylating dUMP to dTMP.
r.B: Methionine synthase uses vitamin B12 and 5-methyl-THF to convert homocysteine to methionine.
r.D: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses vitamin B12 to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA.
r.E: Cystathionine synthase uses vitamin B6 (PLP) to convert homocysteine to cystathionine.

q.s: SLO2, Slide 17 (B9 B12) and Slide 19 (SLO2 Study Questions)

q.v: A 47-year-old man with a history of Crohn disease who underwent a surgical resection of 100 cm of his terminal ileum four years ago presents with progressive fatigue and paresthesias in his toes. He has not followed up with his gastroenterologist since the surgery. Which of the following laboratory profiles is most likely to be seen in this patient?
o: MCV: 72 fL | Serum homocysteine: normal | Serum methylmalonic acid: normal
MCV: 112 fL | Serum homocysteine: elevated | Serum methylmalonic acid: normal
MCV: 114 fL | Serum homocysteine: elevated | Serum methylmalonic acid: elevated
MCV: 88 fL | Serum homocysteine: normal | Serum methylmalonic acid: elevated
MCV: 110 fL | Serum homocysteine: normal | Serum methylmalonic acid: normal
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize terminal ileum resection causes Vitamin B12 malabsorption, leading to megaloblastic anemia and neurological symptoms) -> Step 2 (Identify elevated MCV, elevated homocysteine, and elevated methylmalonic acid as the lab profile of B12 deficiency)

r.A: Microcytic anemia (low MCV) with normal metabolites is seen in iron or B6 deficiency, not B12 malabsorption.
r.B: Elevated MCV with elevated homocysteine and normal methylmalonic acid is characteristic of isolated folate (B9) deficiency, which does not cause neurologic deficits.
r.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs both methionine synthase (raising homocysteine) and DNA synthesis (raising MCV), so neither would be normal.
r.E: Megaloblastic anemia from B12 deficiency is accompanied by elevations in both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid.

q.s: SLO1 and SLO3, Slide 7 (Vit B12 Absorption), Slide 17 (B9 B12), and Slide 20 (SLO3 Study Questions)

q.v:
A 33-year-old man is brought to the clinic for evaluation of fatigue, muscle cramps, and numbness and tingling in his lower legs. He lives in a remote area and subsists almost entirely on unfortified white polished rice and tea. On physical examination, he has symmetrical distal sensory loss and diminished ankle jerk reflexes, but his lungs are clear to auscultation, jugular venous pressure is normal, and there is no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum pyruvate: elevated
  Serum lactate: elevated
  Erythrocyte transketolase activity: decreased
Which of the following conditions best describes this patient's presentation?
o: Wet beriberi
Dry beriberi
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
Pellagra
Subacute combined degeneration
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret labs showing decreased transketolase and elevated pyruvate/lactate in a patient eating polished rice as Thiamine [B1] deficiency) -> Step 2 (Distinguish Dry beriberi [peripheral neuropathy without heart failure/edema] from Wet beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff)

r.A: Wet beriberi presents with cardiovascular involvement, including high-output heart failure and peripheral edema.
r.C: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is a central nervous system manifestation of B1 deficiency characterized by ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, confusion, and confabulation.
r.D: Pellagra is caused by niacin (B3) deficiency and presents with dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.
r.E: Subacute combined degeneration is the neurologic manifestation of vitamin B12 deficiency, characterized by elevated methylmalonic acid rather than decreased transketolase.

q.s: SLO1 and SLO3, Slide 3 (Beriberi), Slide 10 (B1: PPP, PDC, TCA, VOMIT pathway), and Slide 20 (SLO3 Study Questions)

q.v:
A 29-year-old man is brought to the clinic due to worsening lethargy, muscle aches, a scaly erythematous rash around his mouth and eyes, and patchy hair loss. He is an amateur bodybuilder who has consumed a daily shake containing a dozen raw egg whites for the past 8 months. Laboratory studies show:
  Arterial pH: 7.30
  Serum bicarbonate: 17 mEq/L
  Serum pyruvate: elevated
  Urine propionic acid: elevated
Impaired conversion of pyruvate to which of the following intermediates best explains the accumulation of pyruvate and lactic acidosis in this patient?
o: Acetyl-CoA
Oxaloacetate
Lactate
Alanine
Phosphoenolpyruvate
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize raw egg white [avidin] ingestion causing Biotin [B7] deficiency with dermatitis, alopecia, metabolic acidosis, and elevated pyruvate/propionate) -> Step 2 (Identify that B7 is required for pyruvate carboxylase, which converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in gluconeogenesis)

r.A: Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is catalyzed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which requires vitamins B1, B2, B3, and B5, not biotin (B7).
r.C: Conversion of pyruvate to lactate is catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase using NADH (vitamin B3), which remains intact and drives lactic acidosis when pyruvate accumulates.
r.D: Conversion of pyruvate to alanine is a transamination reaction requiring vitamin B6 (PLP).
r.E: Phosphoenolpyruvate is formed from oxaloacetate by PEPCK using GTP, a step downstream of the biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase reaction.

q.s: SLO2 and SLO3, Slide 6 (Absorption Complications), Slide 16 (B7), and Slide 19 (SLO2 Study Questions)
