slides.name: MAD Adaptive Immunology 2026 final with quiz questions for canvas.pdf

practice.name: CYK5_ Adaptive Immunity_ Metabolism and Defense - MS2030.WS.pdf

q.v:
A 26-year-old man steps on a rusty nail while gardening and develops redness, warmth, and swelling around the puncture wound within 3 hours. Tissue-resident macrophages and recruited neutrophils immediately begin phagocytosing bacteria at the site. Meanwhile, dendritic cells capture bacterial antigens and migrate to the regional lymph node to initiate a lymphocyte response that will take several days to develop.

Which of the following best distinguishes the immediate response in the foot from the delayed response developing in the lymph node?
o: Recognition of conserved microbial patterns by pre-existing effectors
Clonal expansion of rare lymphocytes with distinct receptor specificities
HLA-restricted recognition of processed peptides on cell surfaces
Generation of long-lived memory cells for faster recall responses
Secretion of antigen-specific immunoglobulins by differentiated plasma cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the immediate 3-hour response mediated by macrophages and neutrophils as innate immunity) -> Step 2 (Match innate immunity to its defining operating mode: detection of conserved PAMPs/DAMPs by pre-existing effectors)

r.B: Clonal expansion of rare antigen-specific lymphocytes is a hallmark of the adaptive immune response that develops over days.
r.C: HLA-restricted peptide recognition is a feature of T-cell receptors in the adaptive immune system, not innate phagocytes.
r.D: Immunologic memory is generated by adaptive B and T lymphocytes rather than innate neutrophils and macrophages.
r.E: Antigen-specific antibodies are secreted by plasma cells during the humoral phase of adaptive immunity.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 5: From innate detection to adaptive precision

q.v:
A 45-year-old woman presents with fever and a productive cough for 4 days. Sputum cultures grow an extracellular encapsulated bacterium. Within her draining mediastinal lymph nodes, naïve B lymphocytes directly bind components of the bacterial capsule, while naïve T lymphocytes require dendritic cells to process and present bacterial proteins before they can respond.

Which of the following best explains why the naïve B cells and naïve T cells recognize this pathogen differently?
o: B-cell receptors bind peptide-HLA complexes; T-cell receptors bind intact native antigen
B-cell receptors bind intact native antigen; T-cell receptors bind peptide-HLA complexes
B-cell receptors bind conserved PAMPs; T-cell receptors bind soluble cytokines
B-cell receptors bind costimulatory molecules; T-cell receptors bind complement fragments
B-cell receptors bind intracellular peptides; T-cell receptors bind free extracellular microbes
q.p: Step 1 (Compare the antigen recognition mechanisms of B cells and T cells) -> Step 2 (Identify that membrane-bound immunoglobulin/BCR binds intact native antigen directly, whereas TCR is HLA-restricted and recognizes processed peptide displayed by HLA)

r.A: This reverses the recognition systems; B cells recognize intact antigen while T cells recognize peptide-HLA complexes.
r.C: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) of the innate immune system bind conserved PAMPs, whereas BCRs and TCRs recognize specific antigens.
r.D: Costimulatory molecules provide Signal 2 and complement is an innate effector mechanism; neither is the primary antigen target of BCRs or TCRs.
r.E: B-cell receptors recognize intact antigens in body fluids or tissues, whereas T cells cannot recognize free intact microbes.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 6 & 7: Two recognition systems

q.v: Which of the following best describes the primary role of Signal 3 during the activation of a naïve T cell by an antigen-presenting cell?
o: Recognition of a specific peptide displayed by an HLA molecule
Engagement of CD28 by CD80/CD86 to confirm the presence of danger
Cytokine signaling that shapes clonal expansion and functional differentiation
Transport of captured antigen from peripheral tissue to the draining lymph node
Direct lysis of infected host cells expressing intracellular viral proteins
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the three-signal model required for full activation of a naïve T cell by an APC) -> Step 2 (Identify Signal 3 as cytokines, such as IL-2 and IL-12, binding cytokine receptors to guide proliferation and functional differentiation)

r.A: Recognition of a specific peptide-HLA complex by the T-cell receptor represents Signal 1, which defines target specificity.
r.B: Binding of CD80/CD86 on the APC to CD28 on the T cell represents Signal 2 (costimulation), which licenses activation.
r.D: Antigen capture and migration to the draining lymph node by dendritic cells occurs prior to the three-signal T-cell activation synapse.
r.E: Direct killing of infected host cells is the downstream effector function of differentiated CD8 cytotoxic T cells, not an activation signal.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 11: T-cell activation is a decision

q.v:
A 28-year-old man is evaluated for an acute viral respiratory infection. A biopsy of a cervical lymph node shows activated dendritic cells presenting viral antigens to naïve T cells. In a separate laboratory assay, one subset of these naïve T cells is exposed to artificial membranes containing only peptide-HLA complexes without CD80 or CD86 molecules.

Laboratory assay findings:
  Signal 1 (TCR engagement of peptide-HLA): present
  Signal 2 (CD80/CD86 binding to CD28): absent
  Signal 3 (IL-2 and IL-12 cytokines): absent

Which of the following is the most likely outcome for the naïve T cells in the laboratory assay?
o: Immediate differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells
Robust clonal proliferation and migration to the infected lung
Conversion into innate phagocytes that detect microbial patterns
Induction of functional unresponsiveness (anergy)
Direct cytotoxic killing of the antigen-presenting cells
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab data showing presence of Signal 1/peptide-HLA recognition in the absence of Signal 2/costimulation) -> Step 2 (Predict the outcome of TCR engagement without costimulation in a naïve T cell, which is anergy)

r.A: Plasma cells differentiate from activated B lymphocytes, not T lymphocytes.
r.B: Productive clonal expansion and effector deployment require all three coordinated activation signals, including costimulation.
r.C: Lymphocytes do not convert into innate phagocytes; they maintain their lineage and receptor specificity.
r.E: Naïve T cells cannot perform cytotoxic killing without first undergoing full activation, clonal expansion, and differentiation.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 11 & 13: T-cell activation is a decision / Checkpoint

q.v:
A 31-year-old woman sustains a cat scratch on her left forearm and develops tender left epitrochlear and axillary lymphadenopathy 5 days later. Within the enlarged lymph nodes, rare antigen-specific lymphocytes that continuously recirculate through secondary lymphoid organs encounter their cognate antigen and begin to proliferate before leaving for the bloodstream.

Which anatomical feature of secondary lymphoid organs most directly facilitates the initial encounter between these rare naïve lymphocytes and the captured antigen?
o: Direct opening of peripheral blood capillaries into the infected skin site
Organized cell zones that concentrate antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes
Continuous secretion of complement proteins by medullary sinus macrophages
Absence of costimulatory molecules on resident follicular dendritic cells
Immediate retention of all innate neutrophils within the efferent lymphatics
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the 'needle in a haystack' problem of matching rare naïve lymphocyte clones to captured tissue antigen) -> Step 2 (Recognize that secondary lymphoid organs solve this via organized cell zones, such as the paracortex and follicles, through which naïve cells recirculate)

r.A: Naïve lymphocytes are activated in secondary lymphoid organs like draining lymph nodes rather than directly at the peripheral site of infection.
r.C: Complement secretion is an innate effector mechanism and does not solve the spatial problem of bringing rare naïve clones to APCs.
r.D: Productive activation of naïve T cells in the lymph node requires the presence, not absence, of costimulatory molecules on APCs.
r.E: Efferent lymphatics serve as the exit route for expanded adaptive effector lymphocytes leaving the lymph node for blood and tissue.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 8: Where adaptive activation happens

q.v:
A 19-year-old man presents with fever, pharyngitis, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Blood studies confirm an acute intracellular viral infection of his pharyngeal epithelial cells, while a throat swab also reveals secondary colonization by extracellular bacteria in the mucosal fluid.

Which of the following correctly matches the adaptive immune effector to its primary role in clearing these two distinct threats?
o: Plasma cell antibodies: lyse virally infected epithelial cells via HLA class I recognition
CD8 cytotoxic T cells: secrete immunoglobulins to opsonize extracellular bacteria
CD4 helper T cells: bind intact extracellular bacteria via membrane-bound immunoglobulin
B-cell effectors: neutralize and opsonize extracellular bacteria and activate complement
Naïve T cells: immediately phagocytose intracellular viruses at the mucosal barrier
q.p: Step 1 (Distinguish between the intracellular viral threat inside host cells and the extracellular bacterial threat in mucosal fluids) -> Step 2 (Match B-cell derived antibodies to extracellular neutralization, opsonization, and complement activation)

r.A: Antibodies bind intact extracellular antigens and cannot recognize intracellular viral peptides presented on HLA class I.
r.B: CD8 cytotoxic T cells directly kill infected host cells displaying peptide-HLA class I; plasma cells secrete immunoglobulins.
r.C: CD4 helper T cells recognize peptide-HLA class II to coordinate immunity, whereas B cells express membrane-bound immunoglobulin.
r.E: Naïve T cells are not phagocytic and must first be activated and expanded in secondary lymphoid organs before deploying as effectors.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 5 & 7: From innate detection to adaptive precision / Two recognition systems

q.v:
A 7-year-old girl is exposed to a novel respiratory virus for the first time. Serial blood and lymph node samples are analyzed over a 21-day period to track her primary adaptive immune response:

  Day 1: Viral replication at respiratory mucosa; dendritic cells capture antigen
  Day 4: Antigen-specific clones selected and proliferating in draining lymph nodes
  Day 8: Peak circulating antigen-specific effector T cells
  Day 12: Peak serum antigen-specific antibody titer; viral clearance achieved
  Day 21: Sharp decline in circulating effector lymphocytes; small persistent pool of antigen-specific cells

Which of the following best explains the change observed between Day 12 and Day 21?
o: Failure of costimulation leading to complete deletion of all antigen-specific clones
Contraction of short-lived effectors with preservation of long-lived memory B and T cells
Conversion of differentiated plasma cells back into naïve recirculating T lymphocytes
Exhaustion of the innate immune system due to loss of pattern recognition receptors
Migration of all remaining effector lymphocytes into the thymus for negative selection
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the time-course data showing pathogen elimination by Day 12 followed by a drop in effector numbers by Day 21) -> Step 2 (Identify the final phases of a typical adaptive response: contraction of short-lived effectors and retention of a subset as long-lived memory B and T cells)

r.A: Costimulation succeeded earlier in the timeline, as evidenced by clonal expansion, peak effector counts, and viral clearance.
r.C: Differentiated plasma cells do not de-differentiate into naïve T cells; a selected subset of activated B and T clones persists as memory cells.
r.D: The decline in lymphocyte numbers after pathogen clearance represents normal homeostatic contraction, not innate receptor exhaustion.
r.E: After contraction, memory B and T cells persist in the periphery and lymphoid organs to provide long-term protection, rather than returning to the thymus.

q.s: LO3 & LO5 / Slide 10 & 14: A typical adaptive response / Primary versus secondary responses

q.v: Which of the following statements best describes the functional relationship between innate and adaptive immunity during an active infection?
o: Adaptive immunity completely replaces innate immunity once clonal expansion is complete
Innate immunity requires HLA-restricted peptide presentation to initiate inflammation
Adaptive effectors depend on innate activation signals and redirect innate clearance mechanisms
Innate phagocytes undergo somatic receptor rearrangement to generate immunologic memory
Adaptive memory responses occur instantaneously without requiring antigen recognition
q.p: Step 1 (Evaluate common misconceptions regarding how innate and adaptive immunity interact) -> Step 2 (Recognize that innate immunity provides the danger context/costimulation to initiate adaptive responses, and adaptive effectors like antibodies and CD4 cytokines redirect innate mechanisms like phagocytosis and complement)

r.A: Adaptive immunity does not replace innate immunity; rather, it builds upon and directs innate effector mechanisms.
r.B: Innate cells detect conserved microbial patterns via PRRs, whereas HLA restriction is a specific property of T-cell receptors.
r.D: Only adaptive lymphocytes express distinct clonal receptors and form long-lived immunologic memory.
r.E: Although memory recall responses are faster and larger than primary responses, they still require antigen recognition, activation, and deployment.

q.s: LO1 & LO4 / Slide 5 & 17: From innate detection to adaptive precision / Common traps

q.v:
A 24-year-old medical student receives a first dose of a subunit vaccine containing a purified recombinant viral surface glycoprotein mixed with a chemical adjuvant. Four months later, she receives a second booster dose of the same vaccine. Her serum antibody titers and antigen-specific lymphocyte counts rise much more rapidly and reach a significantly higher peak after the second dose compared to the first.

Which of the following best explains the accelerated kinetics observed after the second vaccine dose?
o: The adjuvant in the second dose bypasses the need for B- and T-cell receptor binding
Activation of an expanded pool of primed memory B and T cells persisted from the first dose
Immediate transformation of tissue neutrophils into antibody-secreting plasma cells
Elimination of the requirement for lymphocyte activation and effector deployment
Direct binding of the intact viral glycoprotein to HLA class I molecules on naïve CD8 T cells
q.p: Step 1 (Compare the primary response to the first vaccine dose with the secondary recall response to the booster dose) -> Step 2 (Attribute the faster, larger secondary response to the persistence of a larger pool of primed memory B and T cells following primary expansion and contraction)

r.A: Even during a memory recall response or in the presence of an adjuvant, specific antigen recognition by lymphocyte receptors is still required.
r.C: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes and cannot transform into lymphoid plasma cells.
r.D: Memory recall is faster and stronger, but it still requires antigen recognition, cellular activation, and effector deployment.
r.E: T cells cannot bind intact glycoproteins directly; their receptors only recognize processed peptides displayed by HLA molecules.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 14, 15, & 17: Primary versus secondary responses / Vaccination rehearses the response

q.v:
A pharmaceutical company is developing a new vaccine against an extracellular bacterial toxin. In a Phase 1 clinical trial, healthy volunteers are randomized to receive either Formulation X (purified detoxified toxin protein alone in saline) or Formulation Y (the same purified detoxified toxin protein combined with an adjuvant that stimulates innate pattern recognition receptors).

Clinical trial results at Day 28:
  Formulation X group: minimal serum anti-toxin IgG; negligible memory T-cell pool
  Formulation Y group: high serum anti-toxin IgG; robust memory B- and T-cell pools

Which of the following actions of the adjuvant best accounts for the superior response in the Formulation Y group?
o: Cleaving the intact toxin so naïve B-cell receptors can bind it via HLA class II
Supplying a danger signal that activates APCs to express costimulatory molecules
Allowing naïve T cells to proliferate in peripheral tissue without entering lymph nodes
Inducing antigen-independent polyclonal expansion of all circulating lymphocyte clones
Replacing specific TCR-peptide recognition with nonspecific cytokine receptor binding
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the trial data showing that purified protein antigen alone yields weak activation, whereas adding an adjuvant yields robust immunity) -> Step 2 (Connect the adjuvant to the 'Danger Signal' step of vaccination, which activates APCs and upregulates costimulation/Signal 2 required for productive clonal expansion and memory)

r.A: B-cell receptors recognize intact native antigen directly and do not require HLA presentation.
r.C: Naïve T-cell activation still occurs in draining secondary lymphoid organs after dendritic cells capture antigen and migrate there.
r.D: Clonal selection and expansion remain strictly antigen-specific; only clones whose receptors match the presented toxin antigen expand.
r.E: Signal 3 (cytokines) shapes differentiation, but cannot replace Signal 1 (specific TCR recognition of peptide-HLA).

q.s: LO5 / Slide 15 & 16: Vaccination rehearses the response / Checkpoint

q.v: A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department 4 hours after scraping his knee on a playground. Physical examination reveals localized erythema and edema around the abrasion. A wound fluid aspirate shows abundant neutrophils and macrophages actively engulfing bacteria, with no detectable pathogen-specific antibodies or antigen-specific T cells. Which of the following receptor systems is primarily responsible for pathogen recognition during this initial phase of the host response?
o: Pattern recognition receptors detecting conserved microbial patterns
Membrane-bound immunoglobulins binding intact native antigens
T-cell receptors recognizing peptides displayed by HLA class I
T-cell receptors recognizing peptides displayed by HLA class II
Costimulatory CD28 receptors binding directly to microbial toxins
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize an early response occurring within hours of exposure mediated by neutrophils and macrophages as innate immunity) -> Step 2 (Identify that innate immune cells detect microbes using pattern recognition receptors [PRRs] that recognize conserved PAMPs/DAMPs)

r.B: Membrane-bound immunoglobulins (B-cell receptors) mediate adaptive recognition of specific intact antigens and require days to expand upon first exposure.
r.C: T-cell receptors recognizing peptide-HLA class I complexes are part of the adaptive immune response, which develops over days rather than hours.
r.D: T-cell receptors recognizing peptide-HLA class II complexes mediate adaptive CD4 T-cell activation in secondary lymphoid organs rather than immediate innate phagocytosis.
r.E: CD28 is a T-cell costimulatory receptor that binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells to provide Signal 2, not a microbial pattern receptor.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 5: From innate detection to adaptive precision

q.v: Which of the following correctly contrasts the site and mechanism of antigen recognition between B-cell receptors (BCRs) and T-cell receptors (TCRs)?
o: BCRs bind peptide-HLA in lymph nodes; TCRs bind intact antigen in body fluids
BCRs bind intact antigen in body fluids or tissues; TCRs bind peptide-HLA on cell surfaces
BCRs bind conserved PAMPs on microbes; TCRs bind soluble cytokines in blood
BCRs bind processed peptides on dendritic cells; TCRs bind native viral coats in plasma
BCRs and TCRs both bind intact native antigens solely within the bloodstream
q.p: Step 1 (Compare B-cell and T-cell antigen recognition requirements) -> Step 2 (Match BCR to intact native antigen recognition in body fluids, tissue, or lymphoid organs, and TCR to peptide-HLA recognition on the surface of another cell)

r.A: This reverses the recognition mechanisms; BCRs recognize intact native antigen whereas TCRs are restricted to peptide-HLA complexes.
r.C: Conserved microbial patterns (PAMPs) are recognized by innate pattern recognition receptors, not by antigen-specific BCRs.
r.D: BCRs recognize intact native three-dimensional antigens rather than processed linear peptides bound to HLA molecules.
r.E: TCRs cannot bind soluble intact native antigens in the bloodstream and strictly require peptide presentation by HLA molecules on a cell surface.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 7: Two recognition systems

q.v: A 52-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic for a 3-day history of painful swelling in his right groin following a bacterial skin infection on his right lower leg. Physical examination reveals a tender, enlarged right inguinal lymph node. Prior to this infection, the patient had only a minuscule fraction of naïve lymphocytes capable of recognizing this specific bacterium. Which of the following features of secondary lymphoid organs most directly solves the challenge of bringing these rare naïve lymphocytes together with their cognate antigen?
o: Continuous recirculation of naïve lymphocytes through organized cell zones where captured antigen is concentrated
Direct conversion of tissue-resident macrophages into antigen-specific antibody-secreting plasma cells
Spontaneous mutation of all circulating neutrophils into T lymphocytes within the infected skin
Immediate release of preformed high-affinity antibodies from the bone marrow prior to antigen capture
Restriction of naïve B- and T-cell trafficking exclusively to peripheral non-lymphoid barrier tissues
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the 'needle in a haystack' problem of rare antigen-specific naïve lymphocyte clones) -> Step 2 (Recognize that secondary lymphoid organs solve this by concentrating tissue-captured antigen and guiding continuously recirculating naïve B and T cells through organized cell zones)

r.B: Macrophages are innate phagocytes and cannot transdifferentiate into antigen-specific B-lineage plasma cells.
r.C: Neutrophils are terminally differentiated innate effector cells and do not convert into antigen-specific T lymphocytes.
r.D: Adaptive antibody production requires clonal selection, expansion, and differentiation of B cells over several days rather than immediate preformed release.
r.E: Naïve B and T cells continuously recirculate through secondary lymphoid organs like lymph nodes, whereas activated effector cells leave for infected peripheral tissues.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 8: Where adaptive activation happens

q.v: A 38-year-old woman presents with a localized cellulitis of her left hand after a rose thorn puncture. Within the affected subcutaneous tissue, resident dendritic cells engulf bacterial proteins, detect microbial danger signals, and migrate via afferent lymphatics to the draining epitrochlear lymph node. To successfully initiate a primary T-cell response, which of the following pairs of molecules must these dendritic cells express on their plasma membrane to deliver both Signal 1 and Signal 2 to naïve T lymphocytes?
o: Membrane-bound IgM and secreted interleukin-2
Peptide-HLA complexes and CD80/CD86 costimulatory molecules
CD28 receptors and intact native bacterial polysaccharides
Pattern recognition receptors and soluble complement fragments
T-cell receptors and cytotoxic granules
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the requirements for full activation of a naïve T cell by an APC) -> Step 2 (Match Signal 1 to peptide displayed by an HLA molecule and Signal 2 to CD80/CD86 costimulatory molecules on the APC binding CD28 on the T cell)

r.A: Membrane-bound IgM serves as the B-cell receptor on naïve B cells, whereas dendritic cells present antigen via HLA molecules.
r.C: CD28 is the costimulatory receptor expressed on the T cell (not the dendritic cell), and T cells cannot recognize intact polysaccharides.
r.D: Pattern recognition receptors detect microbes in peripheral tissue, and complement fragments are innate effectors rather than T-cell Signal 1 and 2 ligands.
r.E: T-cell receptors and cytotoxic granules are expressed by T lymphocytes rather than antigen-presenting dendritic cells.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 11: T-cell activation is a decision

q.v: A 16-year-old girl presents to her pediatrician with fever, malaise, and cervical lymphadenopathy. A rapid molecular panel from a nasopharyngeal swab is positive for an acute viral infection that replicates within the cytosol of respiratory epithelial cells. Seven days into her illness, antigen-specific adaptive effector cells enter the respiratory mucosa and directly induce apoptosis of the virus-infected epithelial cells. Which of the following best describes the adaptive lymphocyte population performing this effector function?
o: Plasma cells secreting soluble antibodies that diffuse across the host cell membrane
Naïve B cells binding intact viral particles inside the epithelial cell nucleus
CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognizing viral peptides bound to HLA class I
CD4 helper T lymphocytes recognizing intact viral capsids free in the mucus
Memory dendritic cells phagocytosing whole infected epithelial cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify viral replication in the cytosol of nucleated host cells as an intracellular threat) -> Step 2 (Match direct elimination of infected cells to CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognizing viral peptide displayed by HLA class I)

r.A: Antibodies act against extracellular targets in body fluids and tissues and cannot cross intact plasma membranes to eliminate intracellular cytosolic viruses.
r.B: B cells recognize extracellular intact antigens and do not enter host cell nuclei to clear intracellular pathogens.
r.D: CD4 helper T cells recognize processed peptides bound to HLA class II on APCs and coordinate immune responses rather than binding free intact viral capsids.
r.E: Dendritic cells are innate-bridge antigen-presenting cells that lack antigen-specific memory and do not function as adaptive cytotoxic effectors.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 12: Checkpoint! (Intracellular viral replication and CD8 T cells)

q.v: A 62-year-old man is hospitalized with bacteremia caused by an extracellular toxin-producing bacterium. Ten days after symptom onset, his clinical condition improves significantly as high titers of pathogen-specific IgG antibodies appear in his serum. Which of the following sets of effector mechanisms is most directly mediated by these secreted antibodies to clear the extracellular threat?
o: Direct lysis of infected host hepatocytes and secretion of interleukin-12
Neutralization of bacterial toxins, opsonization for phagocytes, and complement activation
Presentation of processed peptides on HLA class II to naive CD8 T cells
Upregulation of CD80/CD86 on erythrocytes and induction of T-cell anergy
Transport of intact bacteria through afferent lymphatics to the thymic cortex
q.p: Step 1 (Identify secreted antibodies from plasma cells as the primary humoral effector against extracellular bacteria and toxins) -> Step 2 (Recall the three primary effector values of antibodies: neutralization, opsonization, and complement activation)

r.A: Direct killing of infected host cells is mediated by CD8 cytotoxic T cells, and IL-12 is a Signal 3 cytokine produced by APCs.
r.C: Antibodies bind intact native antigen and do not present processed peptides on HLA molecules.
r.D: Erythrocytes do not act as professional APCs expressing CD80/CD86, and antibodies promote pathogen clearance rather than T-cell anergy.
r.E: Antigen capture and transport to draining lymph nodes via lymphatics is performed by dendritic cells, not secreted antibodies.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 7: Two recognition systems & Slide 5: From innate detection to adaptive precision

q.v:
In an immunology research laboratory, a suspension of peripheral blood mononuclear cells containing millions of distinct naïve B- and T-cell clones is incubated with a single purified viral protein antigen under optimal activating conditions. Flow cytometry is performed over 7 days to quantify lymphocyte subsets:

  Day 0: Clones specific for the viral antigen represent < 0.001% of total lymphocytes
  Day 5: Clones specific for the viral antigen represent 12% of total lymphocytes
  Day 5: Clones specific for unrelated antigens remain at < 0.001% of total lymphocytes

Which of the following fundamental principles of adaptive immunity is best demonstrated by these laboratory findings?
o: Innate pattern recognition by all circulating leukocytes
Clonal selection and expansion of lymphocytes with complementary receptors
Induction of functional anergy due to absence of Signal 1
Random receptor mutation in all lymphocyte clones after antigen contact
Immediate contraction of the entire naïve lymphocyte repertoire
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the data table showing massive proliferation exclusively in the rare lymphocyte clones specific for the introduced viral antigen) -> Step 2 (Identify this process as clonal selection and clonal expansion of lymphocytes carrying complementary antigen-specific receptors)

r.A: Innate pattern recognition uses conserved receptors shared by many cells rather than expanding a rare 0.001% clone of antigen-specific lymphocytes.
r.C: Anergy results in unresponsiveness and failure to proliferate, whereas these antigen-specific clones expanded dramatically.
r.D: Each naïve lymphocyte clone carries a distinct receptor generated before antigen exposure, and only the matching clones are selected to proliferate.
r.E: Contraction occurs after pathogen elimination to reduce effector numbers, whereas Day 0 to Day 5 demonstrates clonal expansion.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 4: The defining feature: specificity & Slide 13: Selection and Expansion

q.v:
A 29-year-old healthy volunteer participates in a study evaluating peripheral T-cell tolerance. Researchers isolate a clone of naïve CD4 T cells from her blood and culture them with artificial cell membranes expressing the exact cognate peptide-HLA class II complex. Five days later, the T cells are harvested and restimulated with fully activated dendritic cells. A functional assay reveals the following results:

  TCR binding to peptide-HLA during initial culture: Present
  CD28 engagement by CD80/CD86 during initial culture: Absent
  Clonal proliferation (cell divisions): 0
  Interleukin-2 production upon restimulation: Undetectable

Which of the following best explains the state of these T cells at the end of the experiment?
o: Differentiation into long-lived memory T cells
Activation-induced differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells
Induction of anergy due to antigen recognition without costimulation
Successful licensing of the T cells to kill intracellular bacteria
Spontaneous class-switching of the T-cell receptor to HLA class I
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab data showing Signal 1 [TCR binding peptide-HLA] present without Signal 2 [CD80/CD86-CD28 costimulation], resulting in zero proliferation and unresponsiveness) -> Step 2 (Identify the outcome of Signal 1 without Signal 2 in a naïve T cell as the induction of anergy)

r.A: Memory T-cell formation requires productive activation through all three signals (antigen, costimulation, and cytokines) followed by clonal expansion.
r.B: Only B lymphocytes differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells; T cells never produce antibodies.
r.D: Licensing requires danger signals that upregulate costimulation on APCs; absence of Signal 2 prevents effector T-cell activation.
r.E: T-cell receptors do not undergo immunoglobulin class-switching and remain restricted to their original HLA specificity.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 11: T-cell activation is a decision & Slide 13: Checkpoint! (Anergy)

q.v: A 6-year-old boy stepped on a splinter in his backyard. He had completed his primary childhood vaccination series against tetanus toxoid at age 18 months and received a booster at age 4 years. Because of his prior immunization, his adaptive immune system mounts a protective recall response that prevents clinical disease. Compared with a primary adaptive response in an unvaccinated individual, which of the following accurately characterizes this child's secondary response?
o: It is instantaneous and eliminates the toxin without requiring antigen recognition or clonal activation
It relies exclusively on innate neutrophils because adaptive memory cells are lost during contraction
It is slower and smaller because memory lymphocytes must first de-differentiate into naïve cells
It is faster and larger because a persistent pool of primed memory B and T cells is activated
It bypasses the need for HLA restriction, allowing memory T cells to bind intact free toxin
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize a repeat antigen exposure following prior vaccination as a secondary/recall immune response) -> Step 2 (Identify that persistent memory B and T cells form a larger primed pool that activates more rapidly and generates a greater magnitude response than rare naïve clones)

r.A: Memory recall is faster and larger than a primary response, but it is not instantaneous and still requires antigen recognition, activation, and deployment.
r.B: While most effectors die during contraction, a selected subset of antigen-specific memory B and T cells persists long-term.
r.C: Memory responses are faster and larger—not slower—and memory cells do not revert to a naïve state prior to activation.
r.E: Memory T cells remain strictly HLA-restricted and still recognize processed peptide bound to HLA molecules rather than intact toxin.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 14: Primary versus secondary responses & Slide 17: Common traps

q.v: During the resolution phase of an acute bacterial pneumonia, after the pathogen has been successfully cleared by antibodies and phagocytes, the vast majority of antigen-specific effector lymphocytes are eliminated through contraction. Which of the following best describes the lymphocyte population that survives this contraction phase?
o: Short-lived polymorphonuclear neutrophils that retain rearranged immunoglobulin genes
Long-lived antigen-specific memory B and T cells that provide faster recall on re-exposure
Naïve T-cell clones that have permanently lost their T-cell receptors to prevent autoimmunity
Tissue-resident dendritic cells that continuously secrete high-affinity antibodies into the blood
Unspecified innate natural killer cells that acquire HLA-restricted peptide receptors
q.p: Step 1 (Locate the post-elimination contraction phase in the sequence of a typical adaptive immune response) -> Step 2 (Identify that after contraction of short-lived effectors, a subset of selected clones persists as long-lived memory B and T cells)

r.A: Neutrophils are innate granulocytes that neither rearrange immunoglobulin genes nor form immunologic memory.
r.C: Surviving memory lymphocytes retain their specific antigen receptors (BCRs or TCRs) so they can recognize the pathogen upon repeat exposure.
r.D: Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells and do not secrete antibodies, which are produced exclusively by B-lineage plasma cells.
r.E: Natural killer cells are innate effectors that do not express rearranged, HLA-restricted T-cell receptors or form adaptive clonal memory.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 10: A typical adaptive response & Slide 14: Primary versus secondary responses

add.cloze: Nascent polypeptides enter the ER lumen through the {{c1::translocon}}
add.extra: Sec61 complex; the SRP receptor docks the ribosome at the translocon

add.cloze: Signal {{c1::peptidase}} cleaves the signal sequence in the ER lumen
add.extra: Preproinsulin → proinsulin. B&B says the signal peptide is cleaved but never names the enzyme

add.cloze: {{c1::Disulfide}} bonds between cysteine residues form in the rough ER
add.extra: Rough ER events: signal cleavage, membrane insertion, folding, disulfide bonds, N-linked glycosylation

add.cloze: C-peptide has a {{c1::longer}} half-life than insulin
add.extra: Secreted equimolar with insulin and little is removed by the liver on first pass, so it is a steadier marker of endogenous insulin; low with exogenous insulin

add.cloze: {{c1::SNARE}} proteins mediate vesicle fusion with the target membrane
add.extra: Cleaved by botulinum and tetanus toxins

add.cloze: Vesicle v-SNAREs pair with {{c1::t-SNAREs}} on the target membrane
add.extra: Pairing gives specificity and drives membrane fusion

add.cloze: {{c1::Constitutive}} secretion releases proteins continuously without a signal
add.extra: vs regulated secretion: cargo stored in vesicles until a signal

add.cloze: Insulin is released by {{c1::regulated}} secretion
add.extra: Stored in secretory granules and released on a signal (glucose)

add.cloze: {{c1::E3}} ubiquitin ligases transfer ubiquitin to the specific substrate
add.extra: E1 activates (1), E2 conjugates (~30), E3 ligates and gives substrate specificity (~600)

add.cloze: Proteasomal degradation needs a chain of at least {{c1::4}} ubiquitins
add.extra: Ubiquitin is attached to substrate lysine side chains, then to lysines of ubiquitin itself → polyubiquitin chain

add.cloze: The proteasome 19S cap uses {{c1::ATP}} hydrolysis to unfold substrates
add.extra: Unfolded polypeptide is threaded into the 20S catalytic core

add.cloze: Proteasomes cut proteins into peptides {{c1::7-9}} residues long
add.extra: Right length for MHC I binding

add.cloze: Proteasome-derived peptides are displayed on MHC class {{c1::I}}
add.extra: All nucleated cells; recognized by T cells

add.cloze: {{c1::Mannose-6-phosphate}} added in the Golgi targets acid hydrolases to lysosomes
add.extra: Carried by the M6P receptor to endosomes → lysosomes; defective tagging = I-cell disease

add.cloze: Lysosomal degradation of a cell's own organelles is called {{c1::autophagy}}
add.extra: Autophagosome engulfs cargo, then fuses with a lysosome; bulk autophagy in starvation recycles building blocks

add.cloze: Selective autophagy of damaged mitochondria is called {{c1::mitophagy}}
add.extra: Quality-control form of autophagy

add.cloze: CFTR {{c1::correctors}} improve folding and trafficking to the cell surface
add.extra: e.g., lumacaftor, for ΔF508. Potentiators (ivacaftor) instead raise channel open probability

add.cloze: Hurler syndrome is caused by {{c1::α-L-iduronidase}} deficiency
add.extra: Heparan and dermatan sulfate accumulate; AR; corneal clouding

q.v: Which of the following combinations of vesicle coat protein and motor protein is responsible for retrograde transport of luminal proteins containing a K/HDEL retrieval signal from the Golgi apparatus back to the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
o: COPI coat and kinesin motor
COPI coat and dynein motor
COPII coat and dynein motor
COPII coat and kinesin motor
Clathrin coat and dynein motor
q.p: Step 1 (Luminal ER proteins that escape to the Golgi bind K/HDEL receptors and are packaged into COPI-coated vesicles) -> Step 2 (COPI vesicles associate with kinesin motors to move away from the MTOC toward the ER for uncoating and fusion)

r.B: COPI coats mediate retrograde Golgi-to-ER transport, but dynein moves vesicles toward the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) near the Golgi rather than toward the ER.
r.C: COPII coats and dynein motors work together to mediate anterograde transport from the rough ER toward the Golgi apparatus.
r.D: COPII coats mediate anterograde budding from the ER, whereas kinesin drives movement away from the MTOC toward the ER or plasma membrane.
r.E: Clathrin coats are involved in building endocytic vesicles at the plasma membrane and transport vesicles from the trans-Golgi network rather than ER-Golgi retrieval.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 8: Golgi-ER trafficking

q.v: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe muscle spasms and rigidity one week after stepping on a rusty nail in her garden. She has not received any booster vaccinations in over 20 years. The physician suspects intoxication with a clostridial neurotoxin that acts as an intracellular protease. Cleavage of target proteins by this toxin most directly prevents which of the following cellular processes?
o: Cleavage of the N-terminal signal sequence in the rough ER
Recognition of the nascent polypeptide by the signal recognition particle
Fusion of docked synaptic vesicles with the plasma membrane
Internal cleavage of pro-peptides within Golgi secretory vesicles
Formation of clathrin-coated pits during receptor-mediated endocytosis
q.p: Step 1 (Clostridial neurotoxins such as tetanus and botulinum toxins enter neurons and act as proteases that cleave SNARE proteins) -> Step 2 (Loss of functional v-SNARE and t-SNARE complexes prevents synaptic vesicle exocytosis and neurotransmitter release)

r.A: Signal peptidase cleaves the signal sequence in the rough ER lumen and is not targeted by clostridial neurotoxins.
r.B: The signal recognition particle (SRP) directs ribosomes translating secreted proteins to the ER translocon and is unaffected by tetanus toxin.
r.D: Internal cleavage of pro-hormones (such as pro-insulin to insulin and C-peptide) occurs in Golgi-derived secretory vesicles prior to docking.
r.E: Clathrin and AP-2 mediate receptor-mediated endocytosis at the plasma membrane, whereas SNAREs mediate membrane fusion during exocytosis.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 12: Clostridial neurotoxins and SNAREs

q.v: In the ubiquitylation system, a sequential cascade of three enzymes attaches ubiquitin to lysine sidechains on a target protein. Which of the following best describes the specific role of the E1 enzyme and the typical length of peptide products generated when the polyubiquitinated protein is subsequently degraded by the 26S proteasome?
o: Activates ubiquitin using ATP / 7 to 9 amino acid residues
Conjugates ubiquitin to the substrate / 7 to 9 amino acid residues
Lligates ubiquitin to lysine residues / 20 to 30 amino acid residues
Activates ubiquitin using ATP / 20 to 30 amino acid residues
Recognizes specific protein substrates / 2 to 4 amino acid residues
q.p: Step 1 (E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme uses ATP to form a thioester bond with ubiquitin before transferring it to E2 and E3) -> Step 2 (The 26S proteasome unfolds the polyubiquitinated protein and cleaves it into 7–9 residue peptides suitable for MHC Class I presentation)

r.B: E2 is the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme and E3 is the ligase that attaches ubiquitin to the substrate, whereas E1 is the ubiquitin-activating enzyme.
r.C: Ligation to lysine sidechains is catalyzed by E3 (~600 types), and the proteasome yields 7–9 residue peptides rather than 20–30 residue fragments.
r.D: Although E1 activates ubiquitin using ATP, the 26S proteasome consistently generates smaller fragments of 7–9 residues for HLA-1/MHC-1 display.
r.E: Selective recognition of protein substrates is performed by E3 ubiquitin ligases, and proteasomal degradation products fall in a narrow range of 7–9 residues.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 18 & 20: The Ubiquitylation System and Proteasome structure

q.v: A 19-year-old man is hospitalized in the intensive care unit following a severe motor vehicle collision and remains NPO (nothing by mouth) for several days. During this period of prolonged fasting and severe injury, his hepatocytes significantly upregulate bulk protein and RNA recycling as well as the removal of entire damaged mitochondria. Which of the following cellular structures directly encloses these intracellular substrates to deliver them for degradation?
o: 26S proteasome
Autophagosome
Clathrin-coated pit
COPII-coated vesicle
Sec61 translocon
q.p: Step 1 (During starvation or cellular injury, intracellular substrates and damaged organelles like mitochondria are enclosed by autophagosomes) -> Step 2 (The autophagosome fuses with a lysosome, where acid hydrolases digest proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids)

r.A: The 26S proteasome degrades unfolded, polyubiquitinated polypeptides in the cytosol and nucleus, but cannot enclose whole organelles like mitochondria.
r.C: Clathrin-coated pits invaginate from the plasma membrane to internalize extracellular ligands via receptor-mediated endocytosis.
r.D: COPII-coated vesicles bud from the rough ER to transport newly synthesized cargo proteins to the Golgi apparatus.
r.E: The Sec61 complex is the ER translocon channel through which nascent polypeptides enter the rough ER lumen during translation.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slide 21: Endocytic system, autophagy, and lysosomes

q.v: A 9-year-old girl with a history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections and pancreatic insufficiency undergoes sweat chloride testing, which shows a chloride concentration of 88 mmol/L (normal < 30 mmol/L). Genetic testing reveals homozygosity for the ΔF508 mutation in the CFTR gene. She is started on a combination therapy consisting of a CFTR corrector and a CFTR potentiator. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the CFTR corrector component?
o: Increases the channel-open probability of CFTR at the cell surface
Facilitates folding and trafficking of CFTR to the plasma membrane
Inhibits clathrin-mediated endocytosis of CFTR from the apical membrane
Promotes read-through of premature termination codons in CFTR mRNA
Converts CFTR from a passive chloride channel into an active ATPase pump
q.p: Step 1 (The ΔF508 deletion of a phenylalanine residue causes CFTR misfolding in the ER and degradation by the proteasome) -> Step 2 (CFTR correctors facilitate proper folding, processing, and trafficking to increase the quantity of CFTR reaching the cell surface)

r.A: Increasing the channel-open probability (channel gating) of CFTR at the cell surface is the mechanism of action of CFTR potentiators, not correctors.
r.C: Increased endocytosis and accelerated turnover at the plasma membrane is the defect in Class VI CFTR mutations, which is not the target of correctors.
r.D: Premature termination codons such as G542X cause Class I synthesis defects, whereas ΔF508 is a Class II processing and folding defect.
r.E: Although CFTR is gated by ATP binding and regulatory domain phosphorylation, it always functions as a passive channel rather than an active ion pump.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 28, 30, & 34: CFTR Mutations and Potentiators/Correctors

q.v: A 14-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis is evaluated in the pulmonology clinic for a chronic productive cough and worsening dyspnea. Bronchoscopy reveals thick, sticky mucus plugging the bronchioles. Which of the following combinations of epithelial ion transport changes directly causes the dehydration and thickening of airway mucus in this patient?
o: Decreased chloride secretion and increased sodium absorption
Increased chloride secretion and increased sodium absorption
Decreased chloride secretion and decreased sodium absorption
Increased chloride secretion and decreased sodium absorption
Active chloride pumping into the cell and passive sodium efflux
q.p: Step 1 (Defective or deficient CFTR channels at the apical airway epithelium result in decreased passive chloride secretion into the lumen and loss of inhibition of sodium channels, causing increased sodium absorption/retention) -> Step 2 (Because water follows salt, water is drawn out of the airway lumen, resulting in dehydrated, viscous mucus and bronchial obstruction)

r.B: CFTR deficiency impairs apical chloride exit into the airway lumen, leading to decreased rather than increased chloride secretion.
r.C: Normal CFTR regulates sodium channels to limit sodium absorption; when CFTR is defective, sodium absorption and retention are increased rather than decreased.
r.D: This pattern describes the exact opposite of cystic fibrosis pathogenesis and would lead to excess fluid in the airway lumen rather than dehydrated mucus.
r.E: CFTR is an ATP-gated channel that allows passive movement of chloride down its concentration gradient, not an active ion pump.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 27, 30, & 33: Lung Pathogenesis Summary

q.v:
A 7-month-old girl is brought to the pediatrician due to progressive weakness and loss of previously attained motor milestones. Her parents also report that she startles excessively at normal household noises. Fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral cherry-red spots on the macula. Physical examination shows generalized hypotonia. A peripheral blood smear and bone marrow aspirate are performed, and laboratory findings show:
  Hepatosplenomegaly: present
  Bone marrow macrophages: foamy cytoplasm filled with lipid vacuoles
  Leukocyte hexosaminidase A activity: normal
Which of the following substrates is accumulating within the lysosomes of this patient's cells?
o: GM2 ganglioside
Glucocerebroside
Sphingomyelin
Galactocerebroside
Ceramide trihexoside
q.p: Step 1 (Infant with neurodegeneration, cherry-red macula, foamy macrophages, and hepatosplenomegaly has Niemann-Pick disease type A rather than Tay-Sachs) -> Step 2 (Deficiency of acid sphingomyelinase causes lysosomal accumulation of sphingomyelin)

r.A: GM2 ganglioside accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency), which presents with a cherry-red spot and onion-skin lysosomes but no hepatosplenomegaly.
r.B: Glucocerebroside accumulates in Gaucher disease, which causes hepatosplenomegaly and crumpled tissue paper macrophages rather than foamy macrophages and a cherry-red macula.
r.D: Galactocerebroside accumulates in Krabbe disease, which presents at 6 months with vision loss and multinucleated globoid cells in white matter without hepatosplenomegaly.
r.E: Ceramide trihexoside accumulates in Fabry disease, an X-linked recessive disorder presenting with angiokeratomas and acroparesthesias without hepatosplenomegaly.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 39 & 46: Niemann-Pick Disease

q.v: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric neurology clinic because she has begun stumbling frequently and falling over the past four months. She previously walked and spoke in short sentences at 18 months of age, but her speech has recently regressed and she appears increasingly confused. Physical examination shows lower extremity weakness and gait ataxia. Ophthalmologic examination is normal, and the liver and spleen are not palpable. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Galactocerebrosidase
Arylsulfatase A
Glucocerebrosidase
Alpha-L-iduronidase
Hexosaminidase A
q.p: Step 1 (Later onset at 2+ years with ataxia in a child old enough to walk, speech regression, dementia, and no hepatosplenomegaly indicates Metachromatic Leukodystrophy) -> Step 2 (Metachromatic Leukodystrophy is caused by an autosomal recessive deficiency of arylsulfatase A, leading to cerebroside sulfate accumulation)

r.A: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes Krabbe disease, which presents earlier (around 6 months) before a child learns to walk or talk.
r.C: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, which is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bone fractures.
r.D: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome, which presents with coarse facial features, corneal clouding, and hepatosplenomegaly.
r.E: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, which presents in infancy with a cherry-red macula, exaggerated startle, and loss of motor skills.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 41 & 46: Metachromatic Leukodystrophy

q.v: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay, noisy breathing, and increasingly aggressive behavior at school. Physical examination shows coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, and joint stiffness. Slit-lamp examination reveals clear corneas bilaterally. Biochemical testing of his urine shows elevated excretion of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Which of the following best pairs the deficient enzyme with the inheritance pattern of this patient's disorder?
o: Iduronate-2-sulfatase / X-linked recessive
Iduronate-2-sulfatase / Autosomal recessive
Alpha-L-iduronidase / Autosomal recessive
Alpha-L-iduronidase / X-linked recessive
Alpha-galactosidase A / X-linked recessive
q.p: Step 1 (Coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, heparan/dermatan sulfate accumulation, aggressive behavior, and absence of corneal clouding distinguish Hunter syndrome from Hurler syndrome) -> Step 2 (Hunter syndrome is an X-linked recessive mucopolysaccharidosis caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency)

r.B: Hunter syndrome is caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, but it is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner rather than autosomal recessive.
r.C: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome (autosomal recessive), which is more severe and features prominent corneal clouding.
r.D: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes autosomal recessive Hurler syndrome, not X-linked recessive Hunter syndrome.
r.E: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency is also X-linked recessive (Fabry disease), but it causes accumulation of ceramide trihexoside and presents with angiokeratomas and burning pain in the hands and feet.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 44, 46, & 47: Hunter/Hurler disease

q.v:
An 8-month-old girl is evaluated for failure to thrive, developmental delay, and restricted joint movement. Physical examination reveals coarse facial features, bilateral corneal clouding, and hepatosplenomegaly. Phase-contrast microscopy of cultured fibroblasts shows numerous dark cytoplasmic inclusion bodies. Laboratory assays of lysosomal hydrolases are performed on both plasma and isolated fibroblast lysosomes:
  Plasma beta-hexosaminidase: markedly elevated
  Plasma iduronate-2-sulfatase: markedly elevated
  Plasma arylsulfatase A: markedly elevated
  Intralysosomal hydrolase activities: severely decreased
Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Signal peptidase
Ubiquitin protein ligase (E3)
Mannose-6-phosphate receptor
Alpha-L-iduronidase
N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase
q.p: Step 1 (Coarse facies, corneal clouding, inclusion bodies, and multiple lysosomal enzymes high in plasma but absent from lysosomes indicate I-cell disease / Mucolipidosis II) -> Step 2 (Deficiency of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase prevents mannose-6-phosphate tagging in the Golgi, causing hydrolases to be secreted into plasma rather than trafficked to lysosomes)

r.A: Signal peptidase cleaves the N-terminal signal sequence in the rough ER lumen; its loss would prevent normal ER processing rather than selectively abolishing M6P tagging in the Golgi.
r.B: Ubiquitin protein ligase (E3) attaches ubiquitin to cytosolic proteins for proteasomal degradation and does not play a role in trafficking acid hydrolases to lysosomes.
r.C: In I-cell disease, the mutation prevents the enzymatic attachment of the mannose-6-phosphate tag itself (by N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase), rather than a primary deficiency of the M6P receptor.
r.D: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome, which presents with similar clinical features but involves isolated deficiency of a single enzyme rather than high plasma levels of multiple hydrolases.

q.s: SLO 2 & SLO 4 / Slides 24, 45, & 46: I-cell disease and M6P trafficking

q.v: During the synthesis and maturation of insulin in pancreatic beta cells, preproinsulin undergoes sequential modifications as it transits from the rough endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus and into secretory vesicles. Which of the following best describes the compartments in which cleavage of the N-terminal signal sequence and internal cleavage releasing C-peptide occur, respectively?
o: Rough endoplasmic reticulum / Golgi apparatus and secretory vesicles
Golgi apparatus and secretory vesicles / Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Cytosol / Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Rough endoplasmic reticulum / Cytosol
Trans-Golgi network / Early endosomes
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that preproinsulin has its signal sequence cleaved by signal peptidase upon entering the rough ER lumen to form proinsulin) -> Step 2 (Identify that proinsulin undergoes internal cleavage in the Golgi and secretory vesicles to yield mature insulin and C-peptide)

r.B: This reverses the order of events; the signal sequence is cleaved in the ER before the protein reaches the Golgi apparatus.
r.C: Signal peptidase is located in the ER membrane rather than free in the cytosol, and C-peptide cleavage occurs later in the Golgi and secretory vesicles.
r.D: While signal sequence cleavage occurs in the rough ER, internal cleavage of proinsulin occurs within the Golgi and secretory vesicles, not the cytosol.
r.E: Preproinsulin signal cleavage occurs in the rough ER rather than the trans-Golgi network, and insulin maturation occurs in secretory vesicles rather than endosomes.

q.s: SLO 1, Slides 3, 5, 6, and 7: Translation on the ER and Golgi and Vesicles

q.v: A researcher isolates pancreatic beta-cell fractions corresponding to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (containing proinsulin) and mature secretory granules (containing mature insulin and C-peptide). Both fractions are treated with a reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds and are then analyzed by denaturing gel electrophoresis. How many distinct polypeptide bands of different lengths will be observed in the rough ER fraction compared to the mature secretory granule fraction?
o: 1 band in the rough ER fraction / 2 bands in the secretory granule fraction
1 band in the rough ER fraction / 3 bands in the secretory granule fraction
2 bands in the rough ER fraction / 3 bands in the secretory granule fraction
3 bands in the rough ER fraction / 1 band in the secretory granule fraction
2 bands in the rough ER fraction / 2 bands in the secretory granule fraction
q.p: Step 1 (Determine that proinsulin in the ER is a single uncleaved polypeptide chain containing the A, B, and C domains after signal peptide removal) -> Step 2 (Determine that internal cleavage in secretory vesicles produces the A chain, B chain, and C-peptide, which separate into 3 bands when disulfide bonds are broken)

r.A: Two bands would be seen in the secretory granule fraction only if disulfide bonds between the A and B chains remained intact or if C-peptide were lost.
r.C: In the rough ER, proinsulin is still a single continuous polypeptide chain with intrachain disulfide bonds, yielding only 1 band after reduction.
r.D: Proinsulin is a single polypeptide chain in the ER, and cleavage into separate chains occurs later in the Golgi and secretory vesicles.
r.E: Proinsulin in the ER has not yet undergone internal cleavage, and mature granules contain three distinct chains (A chain, B chain, and C-peptide) once disulfide bonds are reduced.

q.s: SLO 1, Slides 7 and 9: Golgi and Vesicles / Bonus Question

q.v: Which of the following best contrasts the degradation of endogenous viral proteins with the degradation of phagocytosed extracellular bacteria in antigen-presenting cells?
o: Endogenous viral proteins are degraded by the 26S proteasome / Extracellular bacteria are degraded by lysosomal hydrolases
Endogenous viral proteins are degraded by lysosomal hydrolases / Extracellular bacteria are degraded by the 26S proteasome
Endogenous viral proteins are enclosed in autophagosomes / Extracellular bacteria are tagged with polyubiquitin chains
Endogenous viral proteins are cleaved by signal peptidase / Extracellular bacteria are cleaved by E3 ubiquitin ligases
Endogenous viral proteins are targeted by mannose-6-phosphate / Extracellular bacteria are targeted by clathrin coats
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that endogenous intracellular proteins are degraded into 7-9 residue peptides by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway for MHC Class I display) -> Step 2 (Identify that extracellular antigens taken up by phagocytosis are degraded by acid hydrolases in lysosomes)

r.B: This reverses the two pathways; proteasomes degrade endogenous cytosolic and nuclear proteins, whereas lysosomes degrade phagocytosed extracellular cargo.
r.C: Endogenous viral proteins are targeted to the proteasome via polyubiquitination, while extracellular bacteria enter via phagosomes rather than autophagosomes.
r.D: Signal peptidase cleaves N-terminal ER signal sequences and E3 ligases attach ubiquitin to intracellular substrates, neither of which directly degrades bacteria.
r.E: Mannose-6-phosphate targets newly synthesized acid hydrolases from the Golgi to the lysosome, not endogenous viral proteins.

q.s: SLO 2, Slides 16, 17, 20, and 21: Why degrade proteins? / Endocytic system, autophagy, and lysosomes

q.v: A 16-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis is evaluated at a follow-up visit. Genetic testing previously showed that he is homozygous for the ΔF508 mutation in the CFTR gene. He is prescribed a combination medication containing both a CFTR corrector and a CFTR potentiator. Why is a single potentiator drug alone insufficient to treat this patient's underlying molecular defect?
o: The mutant protein is truncated early by a nonsense codon and lacks nucleotide-binding domains
The mutant protein misfolds and is degraded by the proteasome before reaching the cell surface
The mutant protein is excessively endocytosed from the apical membrane and degraded in lysosomes
The mutant protein lacks a mannose-6-phosphate tag and is secreted into the extracellular space
The mutant protein forms insoluble aggregates inside the lumen of the trans-Golgi network
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that the ΔF508 mutation is a Class II processing defect that causes CFTR misfolding and proteasomal degradation, preventing trafficking to the cell surface) -> Step 2 (Conclude that a corrector is required to facilitate folding and trafficking to the plasma membrane so that a potentiator has surface channels to act upon)

r.A: Early truncation due to a premature termination codon describes Class I mutations such as G542X, whereas ΔF508 is a three-base deletion causing a missing phenylalanine.
r.C: Increased endocytosis and accelerated turnover at the plasma membrane describe Class VI CFTR mutations rather than the Class II ΔF508 mutation.
r.D: Mannose-6-phosphate tagging is used to traffic soluble acid hydrolases to the lysosome and is defective in I-cell disease, not cystic fibrosis.
r.E: The ΔF508 CFTR protein is arrested in the endoplasmic reticulum and degraded by the cytosolic proteasome rather than aggregating in the trans-Golgi network.

q.s: SLO 3, Slides 28, 31, and 34: Examples of CFTR Mutations / Correctors and Potentiators

q.v: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the pediatrician for poor feeding, failure to thrive, and progressive muscle weakness. His parents are of Ashkenazi Jewish descent. Physical examination reveals hypotonia, marked hepatosplenomegaly, and a cherry-red spot on the macula bilaterally. A bone marrow aspirate demonstrates large macrophages packed with lipid-laden vacuoles giving the cytoplasm a foamy appearance. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Hexosaminidase A
Galactocerebrosidase
Glucocerebrosidase
Sphingomyelinase
Arylsulfatase A
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Niemann-Pick disease Type A from the combination of infantile neurodegeneration, cherry-red macula, hepatosplenomegaly, and foamy macrophages) -> Step 2 (Match Niemann-Pick disease to a deficiency of lysosomal sphingomyelinase)

r.A: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, which also presents with a cherry-red spot and neurodegeneration but does not cause hepatosplenomegaly.
r.B: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes Krabbe disease, which presents with vision loss and globoid cells in white matter without hepatosplenomegaly or a cherry-red macula.
r.C: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, which features hepatosplenomegaly and crumpled tissue paper macrophages rather than foamy macrophages and a cherry-red macula.
r.E: Arylsulfatase A deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy, which presents after age 2 with ataxia and speech regression and lacks hepatosplenomegaly.

q.s: SLO 4, Slides 39 and 46: Niemann-Pick Disease / LSD Comparison Table

q.v: A 6-month-old girl is brought to the clinic for progressive stiffness in her extremities, weakness, and unexplained crying episodes. Her parents report that she no longer tracks faces or toys with her eyes. Physical examination shows spasticity, optic atrophy, and a normal liver and spleen span. Brain biopsy of the subcortical white matter reveals demyelination and abnormal multinucleated macrophages (globoid cells). Which of the following substrates is accumulating within the lysosomes of this patient's cells?
o: GM2 ganglioside
Galactocerebroside
Cerebroside sulfate
Glucocerebroside
Ceramide trihexoside
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose Krabbe disease based on onset at 6 months, purely neurologic symptoms with vision loss, absence of hepatosplenomegaly, and globoid cells in white matter) -> Step 2 (Identify galactocerebroside as the accumulated substrate due to galactocerebrosidase deficiency)

r.A: GM2 ganglioside accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease, which is characterized by a cherry-red macula, exaggerated startle reflex, and onion-skin lysosomes.
r.C: Cerebroside sulfate (sulfatides) accumulates in metachromatic leukodystrophy, which presents later in childhood (2+ years) with ataxia, dementia, and speech regression.
r.D: Glucocerebroside accumulates in Gaucher disease, which presents with hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, bone fractures, and crumpled tissue paper macrophages.
r.E: Ceramide trihexoside accumulates in Fabry disease, an X-linked recessive disorder presenting with angiokeratomas, burning pain in the extremities, and hypohidrosis.

q.s: SLO 4, Slides 37, 40, and 46: Krabbe disease / LSD Comparison Table

q.v:
A 19-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for increasing fatigue, easy bruising, and deep aching pain in her femurs over the past year. She recently sustained a pathologic fracture of her distal radius after a minor fall. Physical examination shows pallor and massive splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:
  Hemoglobin: 9.2 g/dL
  Platelet count: 65,000/mm³
  Bone marrow biopsy: enlarged macrophages with striated cytoplasm resembling crumpled tissue paper
Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: α-Galactosidase A
Sphingomyelinase
Glucocerebrosidase
α-L-Iduronidase
Iduronate-2-sulfatase
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Gaucher disease from the triad of hepatosplenomegaly, bone fractures/pain, and anemia/thrombocytopenia along with crumpled tissue paper macrophages) -> Step 2 (Identify glucocerebrosidase [β-glucosidase] as the deficient lysosomal enzyme)

r.A: α-Galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease, which presents with angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, and renal failure without hepatosplenomegaly.
r.B: Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease, which produces lipid-laden foamy macrophages rather than crumpled tissue paper macrophages.
r.D: α-L-Iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome, a mucopolysaccharidosis presenting in early childhood with coarse facial features, corneal clouding, and developmental delay.
r.E: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency causes Hunter syndrome, an X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis presenting with coarse facial features, developmental delay, and aggressive behavior.

q.s: SLO 4, Slides 42 and 46: Gaucher disease / LSD Comparison Table

q.v: A 24-year-old man is evaluated in the nephrology clinic for newly detected proteinuria and progressive renal insufficiency. Since late childhood, he has experienced episodes of severe burning pain in his palms and soles triggered by exercise and hot weather, and he notes that he rarely sweats. Physical examination reveals clusters of small, dark red papules over his lower abdomen and groin, as well as bilateral corneal opacities on slit-lamp exam. His liver and spleen are normal in size. Which of the following treatments is specifically indicated for this patient's condition?
o: Lumacaftor and ivacaftor combination therapy
Enzyme replacement with agalsidase-α/β or chaperone therapy with migalastat
Purified hexosaminidase A supplementation targeted via clathrin receptors
Oral chenodeoxycholic acid to inhibit ceramide synthesis
High-dose pyridoxine and betaine supplementation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Fabry disease from X-linked presentation in a young adult male with acroparesthesias, hypohidrosis, angiokeratomas, corneal opacities, renal failure, and no hepatosplenomegaly) -> Step 2 (Select enzyme replacement therapy with agalsidase-α/β or chaperone therapy with migalastat as the specific treatment taught for Fabry disease)

r.A: Combination therapy with a CFTR corrector and potentiator is used to treat cystic fibrosis caused by the ΔF508 mutation.
r.C: Hexosaminidase A is the deficient enzyme in Tay-Sachs disease, and lysosomal enzyme replacement therapies are targeted via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor.
r.D: Fabry disease is caused by accumulation of ceramide trihexoside from α-galactosidase A deficiency and is treated with agalsidase or migalastat.
r.E: Pyridoxine and betaine are cofactors used in amino acid metabolism disorders rather than lysosomal storage diseases.

q.s: SLO 4, Slides 43 and 46: Fabry disease

q.v: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric genetics clinic for evaluation of developmental delay, coarse facial features, and noisy breathing. Physical examination shows hepatosplenomegaly, restricted joint mobility, and bilateral corneal clouding. Her 6-year-old male cousin on her mother's side also has coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, and developmental delay, but his corneas are clear and he exhibits severe aggressive behavior. Which of the following correctly pairs the accumulated substrates common to both children with the enzyme deficient in the 4-year-old girl?
o: Heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate / α-L-Iduronidase
Heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate / Iduronate-2-sulfatase
Ceramide trihexoside and glucocerebroside / α-Galactosidase A
Cerebroside sulfate and galactocerebroside / Arylsulfatase A
GM2 ganglioside and sphingomyelin / Hexosaminidase A
q.p: Step 1 (Differentiate Hurler syndrome in the 4-year-old girl [autosomal recessive, corneal clouding present] from Hunter syndrome in the male cousin [X-linked, no corneal clouding, aggressive behavior]) -> Step 2 (Identify heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate as the accumulated mucopolysaccharides in both conditions, and α-L-iduronidase as the enzyme deficient in Hurler syndrome)

r.B: While heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate accumulate in both disorders, iduronate-2-sulfatase is deficient in the cousin with Hunter syndrome rather than the girl with Hurler syndrome.
r.C: Ceramide trihexoside accumulates in Fabry disease (α-galactosidase A deficiency) and glucocerebroside accumulates in Gaucher disease.
r.D: Cerebroside sulfate accumulates in metachromatic leukodystrophy (arylsulfatase A deficiency) and galactocerebroside accumulates in Krabbe disease.
r.E: GM2 ganglioside accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency) and sphingomyelin accumulates in Niemann-Pick disease.

q.s: SLO 4, Slides 44 and 46: Hunter/Hurler disease / LSD Comparison Table

q.v:
A 10-month-old boy is evaluated for failure to thrive, developmental delay, coarse facial features, corneal clouding, and hepatosplenomegaly. Biochemical assays are performed on the patient's plasma and cultured fibroblasts to measure the activities of several lysosomal enzymes:
  Plasma hexosaminidase A activity: 850% of normal
  Plasma iduronate-2-sulfatase activity: 920% of normal
  Plasma arylsulfatase A activity: 780% of normal
  Intralysosomal activity of all three enzymes in fibroblasts: < 5% of normal
A defect in which of the following cellular processes best explains this patient's laboratory findings?
o: Cleavage of the N-terminal signal sequence by signal peptidase in the rough ER
Addition of mannose-6-phosphate to carbohydrate chains on hydrolases in the Golgi
Binding of polyubiquitin chains to misfolded hydrolases by E3 ubiquitin ligases
Unfolding and translocation of hydrolases into the central cavity of the 26S proteasome
Retrieval of K/HDEL-containing luminal proteins from the Golgi via COPI vesicles
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab panel showing high plasma levels and absent intralysosomal levels of multiple lysosomal enzymes, along with coarse facies and corneal clouding, as I-cell disease [mucolipidosis II]) -> Step 2 (Connect I-cell disease to a mutation in N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase that prevents mannose-6-phosphate [M6P] tagging in the Golgi, causing secretion of hydrolases into plasma instead of delivery to lysosomes)

r.A: A defect in signal peptidase would prevent proteins from being properly released into the rough ER lumen rather than causing extracellular secretion of multiple Golgi-processed lysosomal enzymes.
r.C: Polyubiquitination targets cytosolic and misfolded ER proteins for proteasomal destruction and is not responsible for sorting acid hydrolases to the lysosome.
r.D: The 26S proteasome degrades ubiquitin-tagged polypeptides into small peptides in the cytosol and nucleus; it does not traffic lysosomal enzymes.
r.E: COPI-mediated K/HDEL retrieval returns escaped ER resident proteins from the Golgi to the rough ER, whereas lysosomal hydrolases require mannose-6-phosphate receptors for transport to endosomes and lysosomes.

q.s: SLO 2 and SLO 4, Slides 24, 45, and 46: Mannose-6-phosphate receptor / I-cell disease

myLectures.name: Antigen Processing and Presentation
myLectures.note: David Mullins, 2026-11-09. 15 B&B notes (MHC I/II expression, CD8/CD4 pairing, β2-microglobulin, invariant chain, acidified-endosome loading, HLA loci and codominance, signal 1, ubiquitin-proteasome, CD8 killing) plus 45 one-word clozes covering every one of your 35 cards that B&B doesn't fully cover (TAP, ER loading, CLIP, HLA-DM, cross-presentation, DC priming, pathway defects). No previous lecture JSONs were supplied, so cross-lecture duplicates weren't checked; the ubiquitin-proteasome note may already be unsuspended by a cell bio lecture. Left out: 1486952664370 (MHC II 'APCs only') and 1489970516941 (IFN-γ MHC II 'on all cells'), which conflict with the lecture; NK/MHC I, superantigen, bare lymphocyte syndrome, HLA disease associations, Langerhans cells and anergy, which aren't taught. Card 35 clozes follow the lecture's five moves instead of the card's list.

add.extra: Inducible on some nonprofessional cells by IFN-γ

add.extra: Express both HLA I and HLA II; DCs are best at priming naive T cells

add.extra: They also do not synthesize intracellular proteins to present

add.extra: In the cytosol; proteins are often tagged first by ubiquitination (slide 6)

add.cloze: HLA class I is loaded with peptide in the {{c1::ER}}

add.extra: Also receptor-mediated uptake

add.cloze: Extracellular proteins are degraded for HLA II in {{c1::acidified}} endosomes and lysosomes

add.extra: Invariant chain is trimmed to CLIP before HLA-DM swaps in antigen peptide

add.extra: Contrast: HLA class I is loaded in the ER

add.extra: Cross-presentation + costimulation + cytokines

add.extra: Also more peptide–HLA display and cytokines
