q.v: A 34-year-old woman presents with fever, cough, and myalgias during an winter respiratory outbreak. A respiratory virus infects her bronchial epithelial cells, leading to the synthesis of viral nucleoproteins directly within the host cell cytosol. If these proteins remain strictly within the cytosolic compartment of the infected epithelial cells, which of the following best describes their expected processing and presentation route?
o: Endosomal proteolysis -> acidified vesicle loading -> HLA class II -> CD4 T cell
Proteasomal degradation -> TAP transport -> HLA class I -> CD8 T cell
Proteasomal degradation -> invariant-chain binding -> HLA class II -> CD8 T cell
Endosomal proteolysis -> TAP transport -> HLA class I -> CD4 T cell
Vesicular proteolysis -> HLA-DM editing -> HLA class I -> CD8 T cell
q.p: Cytosolic viral protein -> ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation -> TAP transport into ER -> HLA class I loading -> CD8 T-cell recognition

r.A: Endosomal proteolysis and HLA class II loading are used for exogenous proteins captured into vesicles, not cytosolic proteins in epithelial cells.
r.C: Invariant-chain binding is part of the HLA class II assembly pathway, which presents peptides to CD4 T cells rather than CD8 T cells.
r.D: Endosomal proteolysis does not feed into TAP transport for conventional presentation, and HLA class I presents to CD8 T cells rather than CD4 T cells.
r.E: Vesicular proteolysis and HLA-DM editing belong to the exogenous HLA class II pathway rather than the HLA class I pathway.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 4: HLA class I and class II solve different surveillance problems; Slide 6: HLA class I: sample the cytosol

q.v: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated in the immunology clinic for recurrent sinopulmonary viral infections. Genetic sequencing identifies an autosomal recessive loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP). Flow cytometry of his peripheral blood mononuclear cells demonstrates markedly decreased cell-surface HLA class I expression. Which of the following intracellular steps is most directly impaired in this patient?
o: Degradation of ubiquitinated proteins into short peptides in the cytosol
Translocation of cytosol-derived peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum
Blockade of the HLA class II peptide-binding groove in the endoplasmic reticulum
Removal of CLIP from the peptide-binding groove in acidified vesicles
Proteolysis of phagocytosed extracellular proteins within endolysosomes
q.p: TAP deficiency -> failure to transport proteasome-generated cytosolic peptides into the ER -> impaired HLA class I peptide loading -> reduced surface HLA class I display

r.A: Degradation of ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins into peptides is performed by the proteasome prior to TAP transport.
r.C: Blockade of the HLA class II peptide-binding groove in the endoplasmic reticulum is performed by the invariant chain.
r.D: Removal of CLIP and peptide editing in acidified vesicles are mediated by HLA-DM in the HLA class II pathway.
r.E: Proteolysis of phagocytosed proteins in acidified vesicles is mediated by endosomal and lysosomal proteases.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 6: HLA class I: sample the cytosol; Slide 16: Checkpoint! Predict the consequence when a pathway component fails

q.v: A 4-year-old girl with a history of recurrent bacterial infections undergoes immunologic evaluation. Laboratory studies of her peripheral blood B lymphocytes and macrophages show normal total cell-surface HLA class II levels, but specialized staining reveals that the vast majority of these surface HLA class II molecules have their peptide-binding grooves occupied by CLIP. A deficiency in which of the following proteins best explains these laboratory findings?
o: TAP
Proteasome
Invariant chain
HLA-DM
Beta-2-microglobulin
q.p: HLA-DM deficiency -> failure to remove CLIP and edit peptides in acidified vesicles -> HLA class II reaches cell surface with CLIP retained in the groove

r.A: TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum for HLA class I loading and does not interact with CLIP.
r.B: The proteasome degrades ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins for the HLA class I pathway.
r.C: Invariant chain occupies the HLA class II groove in the ER and is degraded to leave CLIP; its deficiency would cause premature ER peptide binding rather than CLIP retention.
r.E: Beta-2-microglobulin stabilizes the HLA class I heavy chain and plays no role in HLA class II peptide editing.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 9: Why invariant chain and HLA-DM matter; Slide 16: Checkpoint! Predict the consequence when a pathway component fails

q.v: A 68-year-old man with multiple myeloma is started on a targeted therapy that inhibits the catalytic activity of the proteasome. In addition to its direct antitumor effects, this medication alters antigen processing in his nucleated cells. Which of the following is the most immediate consequence of this drug on antigen presentation?
o: Impaired removal of CLIP from HLA class II in acidified vesicles
Premature binding of endoplasmic reticulum peptides to HLA class II
Reduced generation of peptides from ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins
Inability of invariant chain to direct HLA class II toward endosomes
Enhanced transport of exogenous peptides through TAP into the Golgi
q.p: Proteasome inhibition -> decreased cleavage of ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins -> reduced generation of cytosolic peptides for the HLA class I pathway

r.A: CLIP removal from HLA class II in acidified vesicles depends on HLA-DM rather than the proteasome.
r.B: Preventing premature binding of endoplasmic reticulum peptides to HLA class II is the function of the invariant chain.
r.D: Directing HLA class II toward endosomal vesicles is mediated by the invariant chain, which is unaffected by proteasome inhibition.
r.E: TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum, not exogenous peptides into the Golgi.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 6: HLA class I: sample the cytosol; Slide 16: Checkpoint! Predict the consequence when a pathway component fails

q.v: During a localized viral infection of the skin, viral particles exclusively infect keratinocytes and do not infect local dendritic cells. However, dendritic cells in the dermis capture viral proteins released from dying keratinocytes, migrate to the draining lymph node, and successfully prime naive virus-specific CD8 T cells. Which of the following mechanisms allows the dendritic cells to activate these naive CD8 T cells?
o: Routing of captured exogenous viral antigen into the HLA class I pathway
Direct recognition of intact extracellular viral proteins by the CD8 T-cell receptor
Presentation of endocytosed viral peptides on HLA class II to CD8 T cells
Spontaneous conversion of cell-surface HLA class II molecules into HLA class I
Activation of naive CD8 T cells by infected keratinocytes lacking costimulation
q.p: Extracellular viral antigen uptake by dendritic cell -> cross-presentation routing into the HLA class I pathway -> display of peptide-HLA class I plus costimulation -> priming of naive CD8 T cells

r.B: T-cell receptors do not inspect intact proteins; they only recognize processed peptides bound to HLA molecules.
r.C: CD8 T cells recognize peptides bound to HLA class I, whereas HLA class II presents peptides to CD4 T cells.
r.D: HLA class I and HLA class II are distinct gene products and do not convert into one another.
r.E: Naive T-cell priming requires peptide-HLA plus costimulation and cytokines from professional APCs such as dendritic cells, which keratinocytes do not provide.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 7: One pathway, two biological contexts; Slide 12: Cross-presentation: the purposeful exception

q.v: A 59-year-old man with metastatic melanoma undergoes a biopsy of a rapidly growing subcutaneous nodule that has stopped responding to T-cell-based immunotherapy. Pathologic analysis shows abundant infiltrating effector CD8 T cells surrounding the tumor cells, but the tumor cells are not being lysed. Molecular profiling of the malignant cells reveals a biallelic loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding beta-2-microglobulin. Which of the following best explains how this mutation promotes tumor immune evasion?
o: Tumor cells can no longer degrade extracellular proteins in acidified vesicles
HLA class I complexes become unstable and fail to display tumor peptides to CD8 T cells
HLA class II molecules bind endoplasmic reticulum peptides too early in the secretory pathway
Dendritic cells in the lymph node can no longer provide costimulatory signals to naive T cells
Tumor cells overexpress CLIP within the peptide-binding groove of HLA class I
q.p: Beta-2-microglobulin loss in tumor cells -> unstable HLA class I complex -> loss of surface peptide-HLA class I display -> evasion of effector CD8 T-cell recognition

r.A: Degradation of extracellular proteins in acidified vesicles is part of the exogenous HLA class II pathway and does not require beta-2-microglobulin.
r.C: Preventing early binding of endoplasmic reticulum peptides to HLA class II is the role of the invariant chain.
r.D: A somatic mutation within the tumor cells affects target recognition by effector T cells, not dendritic cell costimulation in the lymph node.
r.E: CLIP occupies the groove of HLA class II during vesicular trafficking and is not a component of HLA class I assembly.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 16: Checkpoint! Predict the consequence when a pathway component fails; Slide 17: Clinical connections: the same framework keeps recurring

q.v: Which of the following best distinguishes the recognition of peptide-HLA class I complexes by naive CD8 T cells in lymphoid tissue from recognition by effector CD8 T cells in peripheral tissues?
o: Naive CD8 T cells recognize peptide-HLA class II, whereas effector CD8 T cells recognize peptide-HLA class I
Naive CD8 T cells can be primed by any nucleated cell, whereas effector CD8 T cells only recognize dendritic cells
Naive CD8 T-cell priming requires costimulation and cytokines from a dendritic cell, whereas effector CD8 T-cell recognition of target cells does not
Naive CD8 T cells inspect intact proteins on cell surfaces, whereas effector CD8 T cells inspect processed peptides in the groove
Naive CD8 T cells require HLA-DM editing for target recognition, whereas effector CD8 T cells require invariant-chain cleavage
q.p: Dendritic cell displays peptide-HLA class I + costimulation + cytokines -> primes naive CD8 T cell -> differentiated effector CD8 T cell recognizes peptide-HLA class I on any infected/malignant nucleated cell without requiring priming costimulation

r.A: Both naive and effector CD8 T cells recognize peptides displayed on HLA class I molecules.
r.B: Naive CD8 T cells are primed by professional APCs like dendritic cells in lymphoid tissue, whereas effector CD8 T cells survey any nucleated cell in tissues.
r.D: Neither naive nor effector T cells inspect intact proteins; all TCRs inspect peptide-HLA complexes at cell surfaces.
r.E: HLA-DM editing and invariant-chain cleavage are components of the HLA class II pathway for CD4 T cells.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 7: One pathway, two biological contexts

q.v: During the synthesis and assembly of HLA class II molecules in a macrophage, how is the peptide-binding groove prevented from binding endogenous peptides present in the endoplasmic reticulum?
o: TAP actively pumps peptides out of the endoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol
Closed ends of the HLA class II groove sterically block endoplasmic reticulum peptides
Beta-2-microglobulin caps the HLA class II groove until it reaches the Golgi apparatus
The invariant chain occupies the groove in the endoplasmic reticulum and directs HLA class II to vesicles
HLA-DM remains bound to the groove in the endoplasmic reticulum until acidification occurs
q.p: HLA class II synthesized in ER -> invariant chain binds and occupies the peptide-binding groove -> blocks ER peptides and directs HLA class II to acidified vesicles

r.A: TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum, not out of it.
r.B: HLA class II molecules have open groove ends, not closed ends.
r.C: Beta-2-microglobulin associates with HLA class I heavy chains and does not cap the HLA class II groove.
r.E: HLA-DM acts in acidified vesicles to remove CLIP and promote stable peptide loading, not to block the groove in the endoplasmic reticulum.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 8: HLA class II: report material captured into vesicles; Slide 9: Why invariant chain and HLA-DM matter

q.v:
A research laboratory elutes naturally bound peptides from purified cell-surface HLA molecules on human B lymphocytes and characterizes their properties. The results are shown in the table below:

  Sample 1: Peptide length 9 amino acids; groove has closed ends; anchor residues fit allele-specific pockets
  Sample 2: Peptide length 16 amino acids; groove has open ends; binding core is nested within a longer peptide

Which of the following correctly pairs Sample 1 and Sample 2 with the loading compartment and responding T-cell subset?
o: Sample 1: Acidified vesicle, CD4 T cell / Sample 2: Endoplasmic reticulum, CD8 T cell
Sample 1: Endoplasmic reticulum, CD8 T cell / Sample 2: Acidified vesicle, CD4 T cell
Sample 1: Endoplasmic reticulum, CD4 T cell / Sample 2: Acidified vesicle, CD8 T cell
Sample 1: Cytosol, CD8 T cell / Sample 2: Endoplasmic reticulum, CD4 T cell
Sample 1: Acidified vesicle, CD8 T cell / Sample 2: Endoplasmic reticulum, CD4 T cell
q.p: Sample 1 (8-10 aa, closed groove = HLA class I) -> loaded in ER -> recognized by CD8 T cells; Sample 2 (13-18 aa, open groove = HLA class II) -> loaded in acidified vesicle -> recognized by CD4 T cells

r.A: This option reverses the loading sites and responding T-cell subsets for HLA class I (Sample 1) and HLA class II (Sample 2).
r.C: Sample 1 represents HLA class I, which presents to CD8 T cells, whereas Sample 2 represents HLA class II, which presents to CD4 T cells.
r.D: HLA class I peptide loading occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than the cytosol, and HLA class II loading occurs in acidified vesicles rather than the endoplasmic reticulum.
r.E: Sample 1 (HLA class I) is loaded in the endoplasmic reticulum, while Sample 2 (HLA class II) is loaded in acidified vesicles.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 4: HLA class I and class II solve different surveillance problems; Slide 11: Peptide-binding grooves shape what can be displayed

q.v:
A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus undergoes flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood cells and inflamed tissue biopsy specimens. The expression profiles of classical HLA molecules across four purified cell populations are shown below:

  Population W: Expresses HLA class I only
  Population X: Expresses both HLA class I and HLA class II constitutively
  Population Y: Expresses neither HLA class I nor HLA class II
  Population Z: Nonprofessional APC that expresses HLA class II after exposure to IFN-gamma

Which of the following correctly identifies Populations W, X, Y, and Z?
o: W: Mature erythrocyte / X: Dendritic cell / Y: Hepatocyte / Z: B lymphocyte
W: Hepatocyte / X: Mature erythrocyte / Y: Macrophage / Z: Inflamed tissue cell
W: Hepatocyte / X: Dendritic cell / Y: Mature erythrocyte / Z: Inflamed nonprofessional cell
W: Macrophage / X: Hepatocyte / Y: Mature erythrocyte / Z: Dendritic cell
W: B lymphocyte / X: Macrophage / Y: Inflamed tissue cell / Z: Mature erythrocyte
q.p: Nucleated non-APC (hepatocyte) = HLA I only; Professional APC (dendritic cell) = HLA I + HLA II; Anucleate cell (mature erythrocyte) = neither HLA I nor II; Nonprofessional cell exposed to IFN-gamma = inducible HLA II

r.A: Mature erythrocytes lack nuclei and express neither HLA class I nor class II, whereas hepatocytes are nucleated cells that express HLA class I.
r.B: Mature erythrocytes do not express HLA molecules, whereas macrophages are professional APCs that express both HLA class I and class II.
r.D: Macrophages express both HLA class I and class II, whereas hepatocytes constitutively express only HLA class I.
r.E: B lymphocytes are professional APCs that express both HLA class I and class II, and mature erythrocytes express neither.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 4: HLA class I and class II solve different surveillance problems; Slide 13: Expression determines who can report what

q.v: A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever, purulent sputum, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Sputum culture grows an extracellular encapsulated bacterium. In the alveoli, resident macrophages engulf the extracellular bacterial proteins into endocytic vesicles, where the proteins remain confined within the vesicular system. Which of the following sequences best describes the conventional processing and presentation of these bacterial antigens?
o: Vesicular proteolysis -> loading onto HLA class II -> recognition by CD4 T cells
Proteasomal degradation -> TAP transport -> recognition by CD8 T cells
Vesicular proteolysis -> TAP transport -> recognition by CD4 T cells
Proteasomal degradation -> invariant-chain binding -> recognition by CD8 T cells
Direct binding of intact protein to HLA class II -> recognition by CD4 T cells
q.p: Step 1 (Extracellular protein is endocytosed/phagocytosed into acidified vesicles) -> Step 2 (Vesicular proteases generate peptides that load onto HLA class II for CD4 T-cell recognition)

r.B: Proteasomal degradation and TAP transport into the endoplasmic reticulum are steps of the endogenous HLA class I pathway used for cytosolic proteins.
r.C: TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum for HLA class I loading, not vesicular peptides for HLA class II loading.
r.D: Proteasomal degradation and CD8 T-cell recognition belong to the HLA class I pathway, whereas the invariant chain functions in the HLA class II pathway.
r.E: T-cell receptors do not recognize intact proteins; antigens must first be proteolytically processed into peptides and loaded onto HLA molecules.

q.s: LO1, LO2 / Slide 8: HLA class II: report material captured into vesicles

q.v: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is started on a medication that accumulates within intracellular vesicles and blocks endosomal acidification in antigen-presenting cells. Which of the following antigen-processing steps is most directly impaired in her macrophages as a result of this drug's mechanism?
o: Ubiquitination of cytosolic viral proteins
Transport of peptides across the endoplasmic reticulum membrane
Proteolysis of captured exogenous proteins in vesicles
Stabilization of HLA class I heavy chains in the endoplasmic reticulum
Trafficking of peptide-HLA class I complexes through the Golgi apparatus
q.p: Step 1 (Endosomal acidification is blocked) -> Step 2 (Acid-dependent vesicular proteases cannot efficiently degrade captured exogenous proteins for the HLA class II pathway)

r.A: Ubiquitination occurs in the cytosol to tag endogenous proteins for proteasomal degradation in the HLA class I pathway.
r.B: Peptide transport across the endoplasmic reticulum membrane is mediated by TAP in the cytosolic HLA class I pathway and does not depend on endosomal acidification.
r.D: Stabilization of the HLA class I heavy chain in the endoplasmic reticulum is mediated by beta-2-microglobulin, not by acidified vesicles.
r.E: Golgi trafficking of assembled peptide-HLA class I complexes is part of the endogenous pathway and is not the direct target of endosomal acidification blockade.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 8 & Slide 16: Predict the consequence when a pathway component fails

q.v: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic colon adenocarcinoma shows disease progression despite high numbers of tumor-infiltrating cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Molecular profiling of the resistant tumor cells reveals a biallelic loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding beta-2-microglobulin, while TAP and proteasome subunit expression remain normal. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this mutation in the tumor cells?
o: Premature binding of endoplasmic reticulum peptides to HLA class II
Impaired removal of CLIP from the peptide-binding groove
Failure of peptides to be cleaved from ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins
Instability of the HLA class I complex and loss of surface display
Inability to acidify endosomal and lysosomal compartments
q.p: Step 1 (Loss of beta-2-microglobulin in tumor cells) -> Step 2 (HLA class I heavy chain complex is unstable in the ER and cannot be displayed on the cell surface for CD8 T-cell recognition)

r.A: Prevention of premature peptide binding to HLA class II in the endoplasmic reticulum is the function of the invariant chain, not beta-2-microglobulin.
r.B: Removal of CLIP from the HLA class II groove is mediated by HLA-DM in acidified vesicles.
r.C: Cleavage of ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins into peptides is performed by the proteasome, which is intact in this patient's tumor.
r.E: Endosomal acidification is required for exogenous protein proteolysis in the HLA class II pathway and is independent of beta-2-microglobulin.

q.s: LO2, LO3 / Slide 6, Slide 16, & Slide 17: Clinical connections (Cancer)

q.v: A 26-year-old man receives an intramuscular subunit vaccine containing a purified recombinant viral surface protein and an adjuvant. Although the vaccine protein is extracellular and cannot replicate or synthesize proteins within host cells, the patient successfully generates a population of virus-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Which of the following cellular mechanisms in lymphoid tissue is required to initiate this response?
o: Recognition of peptide-HLA class I on mature erythrocytes without costimulation
Presentation of peptide-HLA class I with costimulation and cytokines by dendritic cells
Direct binding of intact recombinant protein to naive CD8 T-cell receptors
Presentation of peptide-HLA class II by nonprofessional nucleated cells
Conversion of cell-surface HLA class II molecules into HLA class I molecules
q.p: Step 1 (Dendritic cells cross-present captured extracellular vaccine antigen on HLA class I) -> Step 2 (Dendritic cells provide peptide-HLA I plus costimulation and cytokines to prime naive CD8 T cells)

r.A: Mature erythrocytes lack a nucleus and do not express classical HLA class I or class II molecules.
r.C: T-cell receptors cannot inspect intact proteins; they only recognize processed peptides bound to HLA molecules on cell surfaces.
r.D: HLA class II molecules present peptides to CD4 T cells, not CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
r.E: HLA class II molecules do not convert into HLA class I molecules; instead, cross-presentation routes extracellular antigen into the HLA class I pathway.

q.s: LO3, LO4 / Slide 7 & Slide 12: One pathway, two biological contexts & Cross-presentation

q.v:
A 52-year-old man is being evaluated for a living-related kidney transplant. Tissue typing by DNA sequencing and flow cytometry is performed on peripheral blood leukocytes from the patient and his family members: 
  Father's genotype: HLA-A1, A11; HLA-B7, B8; HLA-DR3, DR4
  Mother's genotype: HLA-A2, A5; HLA-B14, B35; HLA-DR1, DR7
  Patient's cell-surface expression: HLA-A1, A2, B7, B14, DR1, DR3
Which of the following sets of properties best explains why this patient's cells simultaneously express six different classical HLA molecules from these loci on every antigen-presenting cell?
o: Polygenic loci and codominant expression
Somatic recombination and allelic exclusion
Isotype switching and affinity maturation
Closed groove ends and anchor residue pockets
Cross-presentation and interferon-gamma induction
q.p: Step 1 (Presence of multiple classical loci [HLA-A, -B, -DR] reflects polygeny) -> Step 2 (Simultaneous surface expression of both maternal and paternal alleles at each locus reflects codominance)

r.B: HLA genes do not undergo somatic recombination or allelic exclusion; both parental alleles are expressed on each cell.
r.C: Isotype switching and affinity maturation are processes that occur in B-cell immunoglobulin genes, not HLA molecules.
r.D: Groove end structure and anchor residue pockets describe the peptide-binding cleft architecture rather than the genetic inheritance and expression of multiple loci.
r.E: Cross-presentation and cytokine induction regulate antigen routing and inducible HLA class II levels, not the baseline simultaneous expression of parental HLA haplotypes.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 14 & Slide 15: HLA diversity: polygenic, polymorphic, and codominant

q.v: A 31-year-old woman presents with a localized cutaneous viral infection caused by a virus that strictly infects epidermal keratinocytes and cannot enter or replicate within hematopoietic cells. Despite this restriction, naive virus-specific CD8 T cells in the draining lymph node become primed and differentiate into effector cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Once these effector CD8 T cells migrate back to the infected skin, how do they identify and kill the infected keratinocytes?
o: By recognizing viral peptide-HLA class I on keratinocytes without requiring priming costimulation
By recognizing viral peptide-HLA class II induced on keratinocytes by invariant chain
By requiring dendritic cells to fuse with keratinocytes to provide costimulatory signals
By binding intact viral capsid proteins budding from the keratinocyte plasma membrane
By recognizing CLIP-HLA class I complexes transported via the endosomal pathway
q.p: Step 1 (Dendritic cells cross-present viral antigen to prime naive CD8 T cells in lymphoid tissue) -> Step 2 (Differentiated effector CD8 T cells recognize peptide-HLA class I on infected nucleated target cells in tissue without requiring priming costimulation)

r.B: CD8 T cells recognize peptides bound to HLA class I, whereas HLA class II molecules are recognized by CD4 T cells.
r.C: Once primed in lymphoid tissue, effector CD8 T cells do not require priming costimulation from dendritic cells to recognize infected target cells in peripheral tissues.
r.D: T-cell receptors only inspect peptide-HLA complexes at the cell surface and do not recognize intact viral proteins.
r.E: CLIP is a fragment of the invariant chain that temporarily occupies the HLA class II groove, not HLA class I.

q.s: LO3, LO4 / Slide 7 & Slide 12: One pathway, two biological contexts

q.v: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent bacterial and viral infections. Immunologic testing of his dendritic cells reveals a selective defect in the synthesis of the invariant chain, while HLA class I heavy chain, beta-2-microglobulin, and TAP are normal. Which of the following abnormalities is most likely to occur within his antigen-presenting cells?
o: HLA class II molecules can bind peptides prematurely in the endoplasmic reticulum and have disrupted vesicular routing
Cytosolic viral peptides fail to be transported across the endoplasmic reticulum membrane
HLA class I molecules are trapped in acidified vesicles and degraded by lysosomal proteases
Extracellular proteins cannot be internalized by endocytosis or phagocytosis
Proteasomes fail to cleave ubiquitinated endogenous proteins in the cytosol
q.p: Step 1 (Deficiency of invariant chain during HLA class II synthesis in the ER) -> Step 2 (Loss of groove protection allows premature binding of ER peptides and disrupts routing of HLA class II to acidified vesicles)

r.B: Transport of cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum is mediated by TAP in the HLA class I pathway, which is normal in this patient.
r.C: The invariant chain binds and directs HLA class II molecules, not HLA class I molecules.
r.D: Endocytosis and phagocytosis of extracellular proteins occur at the plasma membrane prior to and independently of invariant chain function in the endoplasmic reticulum.
r.E: Proteasomal degradation of ubiquitinated cytosolic proteins is part of the HLA class I pathway and does not involve the invariant chain.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 9 & Slide 16: Why invariant chain and HLA-DM matter

q.v: An immunogenetics laboratory analyzes the peptide repertoires bound to HLA-DR molecules isolated from two unrelated healthy blood donors. Donor 1 is homozygous for HLA-DRB1*01:01, and Donor 2 is homozygous for HLA-DRB1*04:01. Mass spectrometry shows that the HLA-DR molecules from the two donors bind overlapping but distinct sets of pathogen-derived peptides. Which of the following features of the HLA system best accounts for this difference between the two donors?
o: Polymorphic residues lining the peptide-binding groove create allele-specific pockets
Open ends of the HLA class I groove allow peptides to bind in multiple registers
Differential splicing of beta-2-microglobulin alters the floor of the HLA-DR cleft
Editing by TAP selectively pumps different peptides into endocytic vesicles
Somatic hypermutation of HLA-DR genes occurs following pathogen exposure
q.p: Step 1 (HLA loci are highly polymorphic in the population) -> Step 2 (Polymorphic amino acid residues line the peptide-binding groove, creating allele-specific pockets that interact with distinct peptide anchor residues)

r.B: Open groove ends and multiple binding registers are features of HLA class II, not HLA class I, and do not explain the difference between two distinct alleles.
r.C: Beta-2-microglobulin is a structural component of HLA class I molecules, whereas HLA-DR is an HLA class II molecule composed of alpha and beta chains.
r.D: TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum for HLA class I loading; peptide editing for HLA class II in vesicles is performed by HLA-DM.
r.E: HLA genes are germline-encoded and do not undergo somatic hypermutation after antigen exposure.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 11 & Slide 15: Peptide-binding grooves shape what can be displayed

q.v: Which of the following best describes the primary role of HLA-DM during the processing and presentation of exogenous antigens?
o: It removes CLIP from the HLA class II groove and favors the loading of stable peptides
It transports proteasome-generated peptides from the cytosol into the endoplasmic reticulum
It occupies the HLA class II cleft in the endoplasmic reticulum to block endogenous peptide binding
It pairs with the HLA class I heavy chain to stabilize the peptide-binding complex
It ubiquitinates cytosolic proteins to target them for proteasomal degradation
q.p: Step 1 (Invariant chain is degraded in acidified vesicles, leaving CLIP in the HLA class II groove) -> Step 2 (HLA-DM removes CLIP and edits peptides to favor stable peptide-HLA class II loading)

r.B: Transport of proteasome-generated peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum is performed by TAP.
r.C: Occupying the HLA class II groove in the endoplasmic reticulum and directing vesicle trafficking is the function of the invariant chain.
r.D: Pairing with and stabilizing the HLA class I heavy chain is the role of beta-2-microglobulin.
r.E: Ubiquitination tags cytosolic proteins for degradation by the proteasome in the HLA class I pathway and is unrelated to HLA-DM.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 8 & Slide 9: Why invariant chain and HLA-DM matter

q.v: Why is the structural architecture of the HLA class II peptide-binding groove able to accommodate longer peptides (typically 13-18 amino acids) compared with the shorter peptides (typically 8-10 amino acids) bound by HLA class I?
o: The HLA class II groove has open ends that allow a binding core to be nested within a longer peptide
The HLA class II groove is formed by a single heavy chain paired with beta-2-microglobulin
The HLA class II groove covalently cross-links the N- and C-termini of intact proteins
The HLA class II groove is assembled inside the proteasome before peptide trimming is complete
The HLA class II groove requires TAP to stretch the cleft during endoplasmic reticulum loading
q.p: Step 1 (HLA class II peptide-binding groove has open ends, unlike the closed ends of HLA class I) -> Step 2 (Peptide ends can extend beyond the cleft, allowing a binding core to sit within a longer 13-18 aa peptide)

r.B: A single alpha heavy chain paired with beta-2-microglobulin describes the structure of HLA class I, whereas HLA class II consists of alpha and beta chains.
r.C: HLA molecules noncovalently bind processed peptide fragments via anchor residues and pockets, not intact proteins.
r.D: HLA class II molecules are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum and loaded in acidified vesicles, not assembled inside the proteasome.
r.E: TAP is involved in endoplasmic reticulum transport for HLA class I, whereas HLA class II loads peptides in acidified vesicles via HLA-DM.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 4 & Slide 11: Peptide-binding grooves shape what can be displayed

myLectures.name: T Cells and TCR
myLectures.note: Mullins, 11/10/2026. Unsuspends 23 B&B AnKing notes and adds 46 new cloze cards covering all five SLOs: αβ TCR structure and CD3/ζ signaling, V(D)J recombination and junctional diversity, CD4/HLA II vs CD8/HLA I restriction, the three-signal model with anergy and checkpoints, and superantigens. B&B has almost nothing on TCR chain architecture, ITAMs, V(D)J segment usage for TCR (its V(D)J cards are immunoglobulin heavy chain), the immunological synapse, the NFAT/NF-κB/AP-1 arms, or CTLA-4 and PD-1, so most of those facts are new clozes. Left out: thymic cortex/medulla locations, AIRE, SCID and RAG-deficiency cards, HLA-A/B/C and DP/DQ/DR loci, invariant chain, Fas/FasL killing, LAD-1, sirolimus and calcineurin-inhibitor side effects — none were taught here. Three B&B superantigen notes (1500581779802, 1500581596511, 1487117356804) were deliberately excluded because they call superantigen activation nonspecific or say it activates any CD4+ T cell, which the lecture explicitly lists as an incorrect mental model; a cloze teaches the Vβ-restricted version instead. No previous lecture JSONs were supplied, so duplicate checking is within this file only.

add.cloze: The {{c1::variable}} domains of the TCR α and β chains contact the peptide–HLA complex
add.extra: Constant domains anchor the receptor in the membrane.

add.cloze: The αβ TCR has short {{c1::cytoplasmic}} tails and cannot signal efficiently by itself
add.extra: Signaling depends on the associated CD3 and ζ chains.

add.cloze: The αβ TCR associates with CD3 {{c1::γε}} and CD3 δε dimers
add.extra: Plus a ζζ homodimer.

add.cloze: Besides the CD3 dimers, the TCR associates with a {{c1::ζζ}} homodimer
add.extra: Multiple ITAMs amplify the activation signal.

add.cloze: ITAMs sit in the cytoplasmic tails of {{c1::CD3}} and ζ chains
add.extra: ITAM = immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif.

add.cloze: ITAMs are phosphorylated on {{c1::tyrosine}} residues to initiate TCR signaling
add.extra: This creates docking sites for proximal signaling proteins.

add.cloze: The ζζ homodimer amplifies signaling because it carries multiple {{c1::ITAMs}}
add.extra: Several phosphorylation and docking sites per receptor.

add.cloze: With defective CD3, a T cell keeps peptide–HLA {{c1::binding}} but cannot transmit the signal
add.extra: Recognition is preserved; signal transduction fails.

add.cloze: The TCR β chain variable region is built from V, {{c1::D}} and J segments
add.extra: The α chain uses V and J only.

add.cloze: The TCR α chain variable region is built from V and {{c1::J}} segments only
add.extra: No D segment in the α chain.

add.cloze: TCR V(D)J recombination is initiated by {{c1::RAG1}} and RAG2
add.extra: RAG1/2 assemble the variable-region genes.

add.cloze: Junctional diversity comes from addition and {{c1::deletion}} of nucleotides at gene-segment joins
add.extra: Falls in the region contacting peptide–HLA.

add.cloze: The largest single increment to TCR diversity comes from {{c1::junctional}} diversity
add.extra: Greater than combinatorial segment choice alone.

add.cloze: Independent pairing of rearranged α and β chains {{c1::multiplies}} the TCR repertoire
add.extra: Combinatorial pairing on top of segment and junctional diversity.

add.cloze: TCR rearrangement happens {{c1::before}} antigen exposure and is not directed by infection
add.extra: Antigen later selects a matching pre-existing clone.

add.cloze: HLA restriction means the TCR sees peptide only when presented by {{c1::self}}-HLA
add.extra: The recognition unit is peptide plus HLA, not peptide alone.

add.cloze: The TCR recognizes a {{c1::composite}} surface of peptide plus HLA, not free antigen
add.extra: Explains both peptide specificity and HLA restriction.

add.cloze: CD4 and CD8 recruit the kinase {{c1::Lck}} to the engaged TCR complex
add.extra: Lck phosphorylates the CD3 and ζ ITAMs.

add.cloze: The immunological {{c1::synapse}} is the organized interface between a T cell and an APC
add.extra: Coordinates recognition, adhesion, signaling and directed secretion.

add.cloze: At the synapse periphery, {{c1::LFA-1}} on the T cell binds {{c2::ICAM-1}} on the APC
add.extra: Adhesion stabilizes contact and sustains signaling.

add.cloze: The synapse focuses granules or cytokines onto the target by {{c1::directed}} secretion
add.extra: Polarized cytoskeleton and secretory machinery.

add.cloze: The calcium arm of TCR signaling activates {{c1::NFAT}}
add.extra: PLC-γ raises cytosolic calcium, activating calcineurin.

add.cloze: The DAG–PKC arm of TCR signaling activates {{c1::NF-κB}}
add.extra: One of the three converging transcriptional arms.

add.cloze: The Ras–MAPK arm of TCR signaling activates {{c1::AP-1}}
add.extra: One of the three converging transcriptional arms.

add.cloze: Calcium activates {{c1::calcineurin}}, which dephosphorylates NFAT and lets it enter the nucleus
add.extra: Target of cyclosporine and tacrolimus.

add.cloze: AP-1 is formed by {{c1::Fos}} and Jun downstream of Ras–MAPK signaling
add.extra: Supports IL-2 transcription, proliferation and differentiation.

add.cloze: NFAT, NF-κB and AP-1 cooperate to support {{c1::IL-2}} production
add.extra: IL-2 drives T-cell survival and proliferation.

add.cloze: {{c1::ZAP-70}} docks on phosphorylated ITAMs and is activated by Lck
add.extra: Links the receptor to downstream pathways.

add.cloze: Phosphorylated {{c1::LAT}} is the scaffold that assembles TCR signaling complexes
add.extra: Recruits Grb2, Gads and PLC-γ1.

add.cloze: PLC-γ1 cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and {{c1::DAG}} downstream of the TCR
add.extra: IP3 raises calcium; DAG activates PKC.

add.cloze: CTLA-4 competes with {{c1::CD28}} for B7 molecules and limits costimulation
add.extra: Higher affinity for B7 than CD28.

add.cloze: CTLA-4 acts mainly during {{c1::early}} activation in lymphoid tissues
add.extra: PD-1 acts later, in peripheral tissues.

add.cloze: PD-1 is engaged by {{c1::PD-L1}} or PD-L2 and reduces TCR-associated signaling
add.extra: Dampens activation during ongoing responses.

add.cloze: PD-1 restrains T cells mainly during {{c1::persistent}} stimulation in tissues
add.extra: Tumors often upregulate PD-L1 to exploit this.

add.cloze: Checkpoint blockade can cause immune-related {{c1::adverse}} events by weakening peripheral tolerance
add.extra: Greater immune activity can injure healthy tissue.

add.cloze: Checkpoint blockade removes a {{c1::brake}} rather than supplying a new antigen receptor
add.extra: It does not change TCR specificity.

add.cloze: Staphylococcal {{c1::enterotoxins}} and TSST-1 are the superantigen examples in this session
add.extra: Both are bacterial superantigens.

add.cloze: Superantigens activate T cells carrying particular TCR {{c1::Vβ}} families, not every T cell
add.extra: Polyclonal but Vβ-restricted activation.

add.extra: Also IL-35.

q.v: A 4-month-old boy presents to the immunology clinic with recurrent severe viral and fungal infections. Immunophenotyping and molecular studies of his peripheral blood lymphocytes reveal T cells that express intact, clonotypic αβ T-cell receptor heterodimers on their surface, which bind normally to peptide-HLA tetramers in vitro. However, the cells fail to phosphorylate ZAP-70 or flux calcium after receptor cross-linking. Which of the following components is most likely defective in this patient's T cells?
o: CD28 costimulatory receptor
CD3 γε, δε, and ζζ signaling dimers
LFA-1 integrin adhesion molecule
RAG1 and RAG2 recombinase complex
TCR α and β variable domains
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that intact peptide-HLA binding with absent proximal ZAP-70 phosphorylation indicates a defect in the TCR signaling module rather than the recognition module) -> Step 2 (Identify CD3 γε, δε, and ζζ dimers as the ITAM-containing subunits required to transmit and amplify the TCR signal)

r.A: CD28 provides Signal 2 costimulatory permission by binding B7, rather than initiating proximal ZAP-70 phosphorylation via ITAMs.
r.C: LFA-1 binds ICAM-1 in the periphery of the immunological synapse to stabilize cell-cell adhesion.
r.D: RAG1/2 mediates V(D)J gene recombination during T-cell development; a defect here would prevent expression of intact αβ TCRs.
r.E: The TCR α and β variable domains contact peptide-HLA to provide specificity, which is preserved in this patient.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 5: The αβ TCR is the recognition module

q.v: During thymic development, each conventional T cell generates a unique clonotypic receptor before encountering foreign antigen. Which mechanism contributes the single largest increment of diversity to the peptide-contacting regions of the αβ T-cell receptor repertoire?
o: Combinatorial selection of V, D, and J segments
Junctional nucleotide addition and deletion at segment joins
Pairing of rearranged α chains with β chains
Somatic hypermutation following peripheral antigen exposure
Alternative splicing of constant region gene segments
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the mechanisms of V(D)J recombination that generate clonotypic TCR diversity) -> Step 2 (Identify junctional diversity at the V-D, D-J, and V-J joins as the largest diversity increment)

r.A: Random selection of V, D, and J gene segments provides combinatorial diversity, but adds less total diversity than junctional modifications.
r.C: Pairing of α and β chains multiplies the repertoire, but junctional diversity adds the largest single diversity increment.
r.D: TCR specificity is created before antigen exposure and does not undergo somatic hypermutation after activation.
r.E: Constant domains anchor the receptor to the membrane and do not generate clonotypic diversity via alternative splicing.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 8: One clone, one clonotypic receptor

q.v:
A 6-month-old girl is evaluated in the inpatient ward for chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and recurrent opportunistic pneumonia. A diagnostic gene sequencing panel and flow cytometry analysis are performed on thymic precursors:
  RAG1 enzymatic activity: absent
  TCR β chain V-D-J rearrangement: undetectable
  TCR α chain V-J rearrangement: undetectable
  Surface CD3+ αβ T cells: <1% of normal
Which of the following processes is directly blocked by the enzyme deficiency in this infant?
o: Phosphorylation of CD3 and ζ chain ITAMs by Lck
Cleavage and joining of V, D, and J gene segments
Loading of cytosolic peptides onto HLA class I molecules
Dephosphorylation of NFAT by calcium-activated calcineurin
Cross-linking of ICAM-1 on antigen-presenting cells
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab panel showing absent RAG1 activity and absent V(D)J rearrangement) -> Step 2 (Connect RAG1/2 function directly to the sequential selection and joining of V, D, and J gene segments to assemble variable-region genes)

r.A: Lck phosphorylates CD3 and ζ chain ITAMs during mature T-cell signaling, after TCR expression is already established.
r.C: Peptide loading onto HLA class I occurs in nucleated cells for antigen presentation, independent of RAG1/2.
r.D: Calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT downstream of PLC-γ1 and calcium flux in activated mature T cells.
r.E: LFA-1 on the T cell binds ICAM-1 on the APC to form the peripheral adhesive ring of the immunological synapse.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 8: One clone, one clonotypic receptor

q.v: A 34-year-old man presents to the clinic with fever, fatigue, cervical lymphadenopathy, and pharyngitis caused by an acute intracellular viral infection of his B lymphocytes. Viral proteins synthesized inside the cytosol of the infected cells are degraded into peptides and presented on the cell surface. Which of the following molecular interactions is directly responsible for stabilizing recognition of these infected cells to trigger their apoptosis via perforin and granzymes?
o: CD4 binding to the β2 domain of HLA class II
CD8 binding to the α3 domain of HLA class I
CD28 binding to B7-1 and B7-2 costimulatory molecules
TCR αβ binding directly to intact soluble viral proteins
CTLA-4 binding to PD-L1 on the infected cell surface
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that cytosolic viral proteins in nucleated cells are presented on HLA class I to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells) -> Step 2 (Match the CD8 coreceptor to the α3 domain of HLA class I)

r.A: CD4 binds the invariant β2 domain of HLA class II to help coordinate immune responses rather than directly killing cells via perforin and granzymes.
r.C: CD28 binds B7 (CD80/CD86) on professional APCs to provide Signal 2 permission during naive T-cell priming.
r.D: Conventional αβ TCRs recognize a composite surface of peptide plus HLA and cannot bind free, intact soluble proteins.
r.E: CTLA-4 competes for B7 ligands, while PD-1 binds PD-L1; both deliver inhibitory signals rather than triggering target cell apoptosis.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 6: What does a TCR actually recognize?

q.v:
A 48-year-old woman undergoes a cadaveric renal transplant for end-stage kidney disease and is started on tacrolimus to prevent acute cellular rejection. Two weeks later, an assay of her peripheral blood T lymphocytes is performed to monitor immunosuppressive efficacy:
  Intracellular FKBP-drug complex: present
  Cytosolic calcium influx after TCR ligation: normal
  Calcineurin phosphatase activity: markedly decreased
  Nuclear translocation of NFAT: decreased
Which of the following T-cell processes is most directly reduced as a consequence of these findings?
o: Transcription of IL-2 and T-cell clonal expansion
Phosphorylation of LAT scaffold proteins by ZAP-70
Activation of AP-1 via the Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK cascade
Degradation of IκB by the CARMA1-Bcl10-MALT1 complex
Adhesion of LFA-1 to ICAM-1 in the peripheral synapse
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab panel showing tacrolimus binding FKBP to inhibit calcineurin and block NFAT nuclear entry) -> Step 2 (Connect decreased NFAT activation to reduced IL-2 transcription and impaired T-cell proliferation)

r.B: ZAP-70 phosphorylation of LAT is a proximal signaling event upstream of PLC-γ1 and calcium mobilization, which remains intact.
r.C: AP-1 (Fos/Jun) is activated through the Grb2-SOS and Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK MAP kinase arm, not by calcineurin.
r.D: IκB degradation and NF-κB activation occur through the DAG and PKCθ-CARMA1-Bcl10-MALT1 pathway.
r.E: LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1 stabilizes the immunological synapse periphery upstream of transcriptional activation.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 12: Three major transcriptional arms converge

q.v: A 55-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis refractory to methotrexate is started on abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig) therapy. Within two months, her joint swelling and morning stiffness improve significantly. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how this medication limits pathogenic T-cell activation in this patient?
o: Binds B7 molecules with high affinity to block CD28 costimulation
Engages PD-L1 on peripheral tissues to reduce TCR Signal 1
Inhibits calcineurin to block NFAT nuclear translocation
Prevents LFA-1 from binding ICAM-1 at the immunological synapse
Neutralizes APC-derived instructive cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-4
q.p: Step 1 (Identify abatacept as CTLA-4-Ig used in autoimmune disease like rheumatoid arthritis) -> Step 2 (Explain that CTLA-4 competes with CD28 by binding B7 [CD80/CD86] with higher affinity, blocking Signal 2 costimulation)

r.B: PD-1 binds PD-L1 or PD-L2 in peripheral tissues, whereas CTLA-4-Ig targets B7 (CD80/CD86) costimulation.
r.C: Cyclosporine and tacrolimus inhibit calcineurin, whereas CTLA-4-Ig blocks extracellular CD28-B7 costimulation.
r.D: Abatacept blocks central B7-CD28 costimulatory interactions rather than peripheral LFA-1/ICAM-1 adhesion.
r.E: Instructive cytokines provide Signal 3 context, whereas CTLA-4-Ig specifically blocks Signal 2 permission.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 14: Brakes on T-cell activation

q.v: A 67-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma receives pembrolizumab (an anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody). Six weeks after starting therapy, restaging CT scans show a marked reduction in his pulmonary tumor burden, but he develops severe autoimmune pneumonitis and hepatitis. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism of action of this therapy?
o: Generates new TCR variable domains specific for tumor neoantigens
Cross-links HLA class II directly to polyclonal TCR Vβ families
Releases inhibitory brakes on pre-existing effector T cells in tissues
Upregulates FOXP3 expression to expand regulatory T-cell populations
Provides exogenous B7 ligands to bypass the need for TCR Signal 1
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize pembrolizumab as an anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor causing both tumor regression and immune-related adverse events) -> Step 2 (Identify its mechanism as blocking PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitory signaling to restore effector T-cell activity in peripheral tissues and tumors)

r.A: Checkpoint blockade removes an inhibitory brake from existing T-cell responses; it does not create new TCR specificity.
r.B: Cross-linking HLA class II to TCR Vβ families outside the groove is the mechanism of bacterial superantigens.
r.D: CD4+ FOXP3+ regulatory T cells suppress immune responses via IL-10 and TGF-β, which would inhibit rather than increase antitumor and autoimmune activity.
r.E: T-cell activation always requires TCR recognition of peptide-HLA (Signal 1) for specificity; PD-1 blockade restores attenuated TCR signaling.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 14: Brakes on T-cell activation

q.v: During the priming of a naive CD4+ T cell by a dendritic cell in a draining lymph node, the T cell receives Signal 1 (TCR engagement with peptide-HLA class II) and Signal 2 (CD28 engagement with B7). The dendritic cell simultaneously secretes high levels of IL-12 into the immunological synapse. Which of the following differentiated T-cell fates and primary functions will most likely result from this Signal 3 context?
o: Th1 cells that secrete IFN-γ to activate macrophages
Th2 cells that secrete IL-4 and IL-5 to activate eosinophils
Th17 cells that secrete IL-17 to recruit neutrophils
Tfh cells that secrete IL-21 to help B cells make antibodies
Treg cells that secrete IL-10 and TGF-β to suppress APCs
q.p: Step 1 (Identify APC-derived cytokines as Signal 3, which directs naive CD4+ T-cell differentiation into specialized subsets) -> Step 2 (Match instructive cytokine context to the Th1 subset producing IFN-γ for macrophage activation)

r.B: Th2 differentiation is driven by cytokines such as IL-4 and leads to IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 secretion for eosinophil and IgE responses.
r.C: Th17 cells produce IL-17 to mediate neutrophil recruitment rather than IFN-γ-mediated macrophage activation.
r.D: Follicular helper T (Tfh) cells produce IL-21 to provide B-cell help and support antibody responses.
r.E: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are FOXP3+ cells that produce IL-10, TGF-β, and IL-35 to maintain self-tolerance and limit immune responses.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 4 & Slide 13: T cells: one lineage, multiple jobs / Naive T-cell activation uses a three-signal model

q.v: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department 4 days after nasal packing for severe epistaxis with a high fever, blood pressure of 82/48 mm Hg, diffuse erythematous rash, and confusion. Blood cultures grow a bacterium that secretes toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1). Which of the following mechanisms best explains the massive cytokine release (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) observed in this patient?
o: Endogenous processing of toxin peptides onto HLA class I molecules
Outside-the-groove cross-linking of HLA class II and TCR Vβ regions
Clonal expansion of a single rare T-cell clone specific for the toxin
Direct phosphorylation of ZAP-70 without APC or HLA involvement
Competitive inhibition of CTLA-4 binding to B7-1 and B7-2 molecules
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize TSST-1 as a bacterial superantigen causing toxic shock syndrome) -> Step 2 (Identify its mechanism as binding outside the peptide-binding groove to cross-link HLA class II on APCs with particular TCR Vβ families, driving polyclonal T-cell activation)

r.A: Superantigens do not require intracellular proteolysis or peptide loading into the HLA class I or II groove.
r.C: Conventional peptide antigens activate rare matching clones, whereas superantigens cause polyclonal activation of all T cells sharing the targeted Vβ family.
r.D: Superantigens require an APC expressing HLA class II to cross-link the TCR and cannot activate T cells without HLA molecules.
r.E: Blocking CTLA-4 is a checkpoint mechanism; superantigens bypass conventional Signal 1 specificity by bridging HLA class II and TCR Vβ.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 16: Superantigens bypass conventional specificity

q.v:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with acute-onset vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and hypotension 4 hours after eating contaminated food at a picnic. An immunological assay comparing her T-cell response to the causative bacterial enterotoxin (Patient A) versus a healthy control responding to a standard tetanus toxoid booster vaccine (Patient B) shows:
  Patient A: Intracellular APC proteolysis not required; 20% of peripheral CD4+ T cells activated; single TCR Vβ family expanded
  Patient B: Intracellular APC proteolysis required; 0.001% of peripheral CD4+ T cells activated; restricted clonotypic TCR αβ expanded
Which of the following best explains the findings in Patient A compared to Patient B?
o: The enterotoxin binds inside the peptide groove of HLA class I molecules
The enterotoxin activates T cells without requiring any TCR engagement
The enterotoxin bridges HLA class II and the TCR Vβ domain without peptide processing
The enterotoxin induces RAG1/2 expression in mature peripheral T cells
The enterotoxin blocks CD28-B7 interaction to induce widespread T-cell anergy
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the data table contrasting Patient A's polyclonal, Vβ-specific, processing-independent response with Patient B's rare clonotypic, processing-dependent response) -> Step 2 (Conclude that Patient A's staphylococcal enterotoxin acts as a superantigen that cross-links HLA class II and TCR Vβ outside the groove without requiring peptide processing)

r.A: Conventional peptides bind inside the HLA groove, whereas staphylococcal enterotoxins bind outside the groove of HLA class II.
r.B: Superantigens strictly require engagement of the TCR Vβ region to trigger intracellular T-cell signaling.
r.D: V(D)J recombination by RAG1/2 occurs only in developing thymocytes prior to antigen exposure, not in mature peripheral T cells.
r.E: Blocking CD28-B7 induces unresponsiveness (anergy), whereas the data show massive polyclonal T-cell activation (20% of T cells).

q.s: LO5 / Slide 16: Superantigens bypass conventional specificity

q.v:
An 8-month-old girl is brought to the pediatric immunology clinic for evaluation of recurrent oral candidiasis and severe viral bronchiolitis. Flow cytometry of her peripheral blood shows a normal number of T cells that express intact αβ T-cell receptors, CD3 γε dimers, and CD3 δε dimers on their surface. However, when her T cells are stimulated with peptide-presenting dendritic cells in vitro, intracellular signaling amplification is severely blunted. Molecular analysis reveals a selective defect in the homodimeric component of the TCR signaling complex that contains multiple immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs).

Which of the following proteins is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: TCR α chain
CD4 coreceptor
CD28 receptor
ζ (zeta) chain
β2-microglobulin
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize intact αβ TCR and CD3 γε/δε dimers with blunted signal amplification due to a missing homodimer containing multiple ITAMs) -> Step 2 (Identify the ζζ homodimer as the component that provides multiple ITAMs to amplify the TCR activation signal)

r.A: The TCR α chain pairs with the TCR β chain to form the variable antigen-binding heterodimer with short cytoplasmic tails that cannot signal on its own.
r.B: The CD4 coreceptor is a monomeric glycoprotein that binds the invariant β2 domain of HLA class II molecules and recruits Lck rather than forming an ITAM-containing homodimer.
r.C: CD28 is a costimulatory receptor on T cells that binds B7 (CD80/CD86) on antigen-presenting cells to provide Signal 2 permission.
r.E: β2-microglobulin is an invariant extracellular protein that associates with the HLA class I α chain and does not participate in intracellular ITAM signaling.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 5: The αβ TCR is the recognition module

q.v: During thymocyte development on chromosome 14, the gene segments encoding the variable domain of the T-cell receptor α (TCR α) chain undergo RAG1/2-mediated somatic rearrangement prior to antigen exposure. Which of the following combinations of gene segments is joined to form the rearranged variable-region gene of the TCR α chain?
o: V and J segments
V, D, and J segments
D and J segments
V and C segments
D and C segments
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the locus undergoing rearrangement as the TCR α chain on chromosome 14) -> Step 2 (Recall that the TCR α chain variable region is generated by V-J joining only, unlike the β chain which uses V, D, and J segments)

r.B: V, D, and J segments are rearranged sequentially on chromosome 7 to assemble the variable region of the TCR β chain, not the TCR α chain.
r.C: D and J joining is the initial step in TCR β chain rearrangement, whereas the TCR α locus lacks D segments entirely.
r.D: The constant (C) region is joined to the rearranged V-J transcript by RNA splicing after transcription, not by RAG1/2-mediated DNA recombination.
r.E: Neither D segments nor C segments undergo direct DNA recombination to form the variable domain of the TCR α chain.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 8: One clone, one clonotypic receptor

q.v:
A 14-year-old boy presents to the clinic with a 3-day history of productive cough, fever, and purulent nasal discharge. Sputum cultures grow an extracellular bacterium. In the draining cervical lymph nodes, macrophages and dendritic cells internalize the extracellular bacterial proteins, degrade them within endocytic vesicles, and display the resulting peptides on their cell surface to naive helper T cells. 

Which of the following molecular interactions directly stabilizes the T-cell coreceptor with the antigen-presenting molecule in this response?
o: CD8 binding to the α3 domain of HLA class I
CD4 binding to the β2 domain of HLA class II
CD28 binding to the peptide-binding groove of HLA class II
LFA-1 binding to the invariant region of HLA class I
TCR αβ binding directly to free bacterial protein
q.p: Step 1 (Determine that captured extracellular proteins are presented by professional APCs on HLA class II to CD4+ helper T cells) -> Step 2 (Identify that the CD4 coreceptor binds to the invariant β2 domain of HLA class II to stabilize recognition)

r.A: CD8 binds to the α3 domain of HLA class I molecules to stabilize recognition of cytosolic peptides on nucleated cells by cytotoxic T cells.
r.C: CD28 binds to B7 (CD80/CD86) molecules on the APC to provide costimulation (Signal 2), not to the peptide-binding groove of HLA class II.
r.D: LFA-1 is an integrin on the T cell that binds ICAM-1 on the APC in the periphery of the immunological synapse to stabilize cell-cell adhesion.
r.E: Conventional αβ TCRs cannot bind free soluble proteins and instead require a composite surface formed by a processed peptide bound to an HLA molecule.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 6: What does a TCR actually recognize?

q.v:
A 52-year-old man who underwent a heart transplant 3 months ago is maintained on a calcineurin inhibitor to prevent acute cellular rejection. A peripheral blood T-cell signaling assay is performed to evaluate the three major transcriptional arms downstream of T-cell receptor (TCR) ligation:
  TCR + peptide-HLA engagement: normal
  CD3 and ζ ITAM phosphorylation by Lck: normal
  ZAP-70 and LAT scaffold phosphorylation: normal
  Nuclear translocation of NF-κB: normal
  Nuclear translocation of AP-1 (Fos/Jun): normal
  Nuclear translocation of NFAT: markedly decreased

If this patient is taking cyclosporine rather than tacrolimus, which of the following intracellular proteins does his medication directly bind to form the complex that inhibits calcineurin?
o: FKBP
Cyclophilin
PKCθ
Calmodulin
CARMA1
q.p: Step 1 (Confirm from the lab panel that the calcium/calcineurin/NFAT arm is selectively blocked while proximal signaling, NF-κB, and AP-1 arms remain intact) -> Step 2 (Differentiate cyclosporine from tacrolimus by identifying cyclophilin as the direct intracellular binding partner of cyclosporine)

r.A: FKBP (FK506-binding protein) is bound by tacrolimus, not cyclosporine, to form a complex that inhibits calcineurin.
r.C: PKCθ is activated by diacylglycerol (DAG) downstream of PLC-γ1 to drive the NF-κB transcriptional pathway, which is unaffected in this patient.
r.D: Calmodulin is a calcium-binding protein involved in physiological calcium signaling, not the immunophilin bound by cyclosporine.
r.E: CARMA1 forms a complex with Bcl10 and MALT1 downstream of PKCθ to activate IKK and promote NF-κB nuclear translocation.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 12: Three major transcriptional arms converge

q.v:
A 3-year-old boy is evaluated in the immunology clinic for recurrent bacterial skin abscesses and delayed umbilical cord separation. Special functional assays of his T lymphocytes are performed using fluorescence microscopy to track immunological synapse formation with antigen-presenting cells (APCs) over 60 minutes. Although his TCRs transiently engage peptide-HLA complexes in the center of the contact zone, his T cells fail to form a stable peripheral adhesion ring, resulting in premature detachment and weak T-cell activation. 

Defective binding between which of the following pairs of molecules in the periphery of the immunological synapse best explains these findings?
o: TCR αβ and peptide-HLA
CD28 and B7 (CD80/CD86)
LFA-1 and ICAM-1
CTLA-4 and B7 (CD80/CD86)
PD-1 and PD-L1
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that the defect involves the peripheral adhesive zone of the immunological synapse required to stabilize T cell-APC contact) -> Step 2 (Identify LFA-1 on the T cell binding ICAM-1 on the APC as the principal peripheral adhesion interaction)

r.A: TCR αβ and peptide-HLA interactions localize to the center of the immunological synapse to provide antigen specificity (Signal 1).
r.B: CD28 and B7 interactions localize to the center of the immunological synapse to provide costimulatory permission (Signal 2).
r.D: CTLA-4 binds B7 with high affinity to competitively inhibit costimulation during early T-cell priming in lymphoid tissues.
r.E: PD-1 binds PD-L1 or PD-L2 in peripheral tissues to deliver an inhibitory signal that reduces TCR signaling and effector function.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 9: The immunological synapse organizes the conversation

q.v: During the activation of a naive T cell by an antigen-presenting cell, diacylglycerol (DAG) activates PKCθ, which promotes assembly of the CARMA1-Bcl10-MALT1 (CBM) complex and subsequent degradation of IκB. Which of the following transcription factors is directly activated by this specific signaling arm to support pro-survival and cytokine gene transcription?
o: NFAT
NF-κB
AP-1
FOXP3
RAG1
q.p: Step 1 (Trace the signaling pathway from DAG -> PKCθ -> CARMA1-Bcl10-MALT1 complex -> IKK -> IκB degradation) -> Step 2 (Identify NF-κB as the transcription factor released by IκB degradation to drive pro-survival and inflammatory cytokine genes)

r.A: NFAT is activated via the inositol trisphosphate (IP3)-mediated increase in cytosolic calcium and subsequent dephosphorylation by calcineurin.
r.C: AP-1 (Fos/Jun) is activated through the Grb2-SOS and Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase signaling arm.
r.D: FOXP3 is a lineage-defining transcription factor expressed by regulatory T cells (Tregs) that maintain self-tolerance and suppress immune responses.
r.E: RAG1 is a recombinase enzyme that mediates V(D)J gene rearrangement during thymocyte development prior to antigen exposure.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 11: Three major transcriptional arms converge

q.v:
A 25-year-old woman volunteers for a clinical study investigating T-cell responses to a novel peptide antigen. In an in vitro experiment, naive CD4+ T cells isolated from her peripheral blood are cultured with engineered antigen-presenting cells under three different conditions:
  Condition 1 (Peptide-HLA II only): No IL-2 production; T cells become unresponsive to subsequent stimulation
  Condition 2 (Peptide-HLA II + B7 + IL-12): High IL-2 production; T cells proliferate and differentiate into IFN-γ-producing cells
  Condition 3 (Peptide-HLA II + B7 + IL-4): High IL-2 production; T cells proliferate and differentiate into IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13-producing cells

Which of the following best describes the functional state induced in the T cells in Condition 1 and the specific effector subset generated in Condition 3?
o: Apoptosis in Condition 1 / Th1 subset in Condition 3
Anergy in Condition 1 / Th2 subset in Condition 3
Clonal expansion in Condition 1 / Th17 subset in Condition 3
Anergy in Condition 1 / Tfh subset in Condition 3
Polyclonal activation in Condition 1 / Treg subset in Condition 3
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret Condition 1: Signal 1 alone without Signal 2 [B7] induces T-cell anergy/functional unresponsiveness) -> Step 2 (Interpret Condition 3: Signals 1 and 2 plus instructive cytokine IL-4 drives differentiation into the Th2 subset producing IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13)

r.A: Signal 1 without costimulation classically induces functional unresponsiveness (anergy), and Th1 differentiation is driven by IL-12 (as seen in Condition 2) to produce IFN-γ.
r.C: Clonal expansion requires Signals 1 and 2 to drive IL-2 production, and Th17 differentiation is driven by IL-6 and TGF-β to produce IL-17 for neutrophil recruitment.
r.D: Although Condition 1 induces anergy, T follicular helper (Tfh) cells produce IL-21 to assist B-cell antibody responses rather than secreting IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13.
r.E: Polyclonal activation occurs with bacterial superantigens rather than Signal 1 alone, and regulatory T cells (Tregs) produce inhibitory cytokines such as IL-10, TGF-β, and IL-35.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 13: Naive T-cell activation uses a three-signal model

q.v:
A 61-year-old woman with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer is treated with atezolizumab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1). Biopsy of her tumor prior to treatment showed abundant infiltrating CD8+ T cells and high surface expression of PD-L1 on the malignant cells. Following treatment, her tumor regresses significantly. 

Which of the following mechanisms best explains how blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway restores antitumor immunity in this patient?
o: It competes with CD28 for B7 binding in secondary lymphoid organs
It relieves inhibition of TCR signaling and effector function in peripheral tissues
It induces RAG1/2 expression to generate new tumor-specific TCRs
It cross-links HLA class II to TCR Vβ domains outside the peptide groove
It prevents Lck from phosphorylating ITAMs on the CD3 complex
q.p: Step 1 (Identify atezolizumab as an anti-PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor acting on tumor-infiltrating effector/exhausted T cells in peripheral tissues) -> Step 2 (Recognize that blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interaction removes the inhibitory signal that dampens TCR signaling, IL-2 production, and cytotoxicity)

r.A: Competing with CD28 for B7 (CD80/CD86) binding in secondary lymphoid organs during initial priming is the mechanism of CTLA-4, not PD-1/PD-L1.
r.C: Checkpoint blockade removes an inhibitory brake from pre-existing T-cell responses and does not induce V(D)J recombination or create new TCR specificity.
r.D: Cross-linking HLA class II to TCR Vβ domains outside the peptide-binding groove is the mechanism of bacterial superantigens such as TSST-1.
r.E: Preventing Lck from phosphorylating CD3 ITAMs would inhibit T-cell activation, whereas anti-PD-L1 therapy restores proximal TCR signaling.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 14: Brakes on T-cell activation

q.v:
A 31-year-old man receives a booster dose of a tetanus toxoid vaccine 10 years after his primary immunization series. Within 3 days, he mounts a rapid, high-magnitude T-cell response that requires much lower antigen levels than his initial priming response a decade earlier. 

Which of the following characteristics best describes the T-cell population responsible for this rapid recall response?
o: Short-lived effector cells that die during the contraction phase
Naive T cells undergoing de novo V(D)J recombination in the lymph node
Long-lived descendants of previously activated CD4+ or CD8+ T cells
FOXP3-expressing cells that secrete IL-10 and TGF-β
Cells that recognize intact toxoid protein independently of HLA molecules
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize the rapid, enhanced response at lower antigen levels upon re-exposure as a memory T-cell recall response) -> Step 2 (Identify memory T cells as a long-lived, self-renewing population descended from previously activated antigen-specific CD4+ or CD8+ T cells)

r.A: Short-lived effector T cells execute immediate pathogen clearance and undergo apoptosis during the contraction phase once antigen levels decline.
r.B: Naive T cells complete V(D)J recombination in the thymus before antigen exposure and respond more slowly and with a higher activation threshold than memory cells.
r.D: FOXP3-expressing cells that secrete IL-10, TGF-β, and IL-35 are regulatory T cells (Tregs) that suppress immune responses and maintain self-tolerance.
r.E: Memory T cells retain their original clonotypic αβ TCR and still require peptide presentation by an appropriate HLA molecule for activation.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 4 & 15: T cells: one lineage, multiple jobs / From one clone to an immune response

q.v:
A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with high fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension (BP 78/42 mm Hg), and multiorgan dysfunction 3 days after sustaining a deep skin wound that became infected with Staphylococcus aureus. Laboratory studies show markedly elevated serum levels of TNF, IL-1, and IL-6. The bacterial toxin responsible for his presentation activates a large fraction of his peripheral T-cell repertoire without requiring intracellular antigen processing.

Which of the following combinations of molecules on the antigen-presenting cell and the T cell is directly cross-linked by this bacterial toxin?
o: HLA class I α3 domain and TCR Vα domain
HLA class II (outside the peptide groove) and TCR Vβ region
B7-1 (CD80) and CD28 costimulatory receptor
ICAM-1 and LFA-1 integrin
Peptide-binding groove of HLA class I and CD8 coreceptor
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize toxic shock syndrome caused by a staphylococcal superantigen bypassing conventional antigen processing to trigger polyclonal T-cell activation and cytokine storm) -> Step 2 (Identify the binding mechanism as cross-linking HLA class II outside the peptide-binding groove to particular TCR Vβ families)

r.A: Bacterial superantigens bind to HLA class II molecules and the variable beta (Vβ) region of the TCR, rather than HLA class I and TCR Vα.
r.C: B7-1 and CD28 interact during physiological costimulation (Signal 2) and are not the cross-linking targets of bacterial superantigens.
r.D: ICAM-1 and LFA-1 mediate cell-cell adhesion in the periphery of the immunological synapse rather than superantigen-induced polyclonal activation.
r.E: The peptide-binding groove of HLA class I presents cytosolic peptides to the TCR of CD8+ T cells, whereas superantigens bind outside the peptide groove on HLA class II.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 16: Superantigens bypass conventional specificity
