add.cloze: Amino acid catabolism yields an α-ketoacid plus {{c1::ammonium}}
add.extra: Carbon skeleton → energy, glucose or ketones; NH4+ → urea (liver) or renal excretion

add.cloze: All amino acids except leucine and lysine are {{c1::glucogenic}}
add.extra: Glucogenic skeletons enter as pyruvate or TCA intermediates

add.cloze: Purely ketogenic amino acids enter metabolism as acetyl-CoA or {{c1::acetoacetyl-CoA}}
add.extra: Cannot make net glucose

add.cloze: Leucine is a major source of ketone bodies during {{c1::starvation}}
add.extra: Leucine is a large share of muscle protein; proteolysis releases it

add.cloze: Valine, isoleucine, threonine and methionine enter the TCA cycle as {{c1::succinyl-CoA}}
add.extra: VITM; relevant to B12 deficiency (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase)

add.cloze: Branched-chain amino acids make up most free amino acids in {{c1::plasma}}
add.extra: Also a large component of skeletal muscle; oxidized by most tissues

add.cloze: MSUD can result from mutations in any of {{c1::four}} genes for the BCKD complex
add.extra: Slide 8 says four; the SLO1 answer key says three. Autosomal recessive

add.cloze: MSUD urine odor comes from accumulated branched-chain {{c1::α-ketoacids}}
add.extra: Plus the BCAAs themselves (Ile, Leu, Val); also neurotoxic

add.cloze: MSUD symptoms usually begin about one {{c1::week}} after birth
add.extra: Lethargy and poor suckling first; then weight loss, neuro signs, ketosis, burnt-sugar odor

add.cloze: Untreated MSUD causes {{c1::white}} matter disease
add.extra: Delayed myelination, cerebral edema, neuron death; the brain relies heavily on BCAAs

add.cloze: MSUD diets often use {{c1::gelatin}} as the protein source
add.extra: Plus synthetic formulas and high-dose thiamine

add.cloze: BCAAs cannot be eliminated from the MSUD diet because they are {{c1::essential}}
add.extra: Needed for growth; the goal is to normalize levels, not remove them

add.cloze: MSUD is far more common in {{c1::Mennonite}} communities
add.extra: ~1:300 (Pennsylvania) vs ~1:150,000 in the general population

add.cloze: Transamination usually moves an amino group onto {{c1::α-ketoglutarate}}
add.extra: Forming glutamate, the central nitrogen collector

add.cloze: Transamination reactions are {{c1::reversible}}
add.extra: The same aminotransferase makes or breaks the amino acid

add.cloze: ALT converts alanine + α-ketoglutarate into {{c1::pyruvate}} + {{c2::glutamate}}
add.extra: Alanine aminotransferase

add.cloze: AST converts aspartate + α-ketoglutarate into {{c1::oxaloacetate}} + glutamate
add.extra: Run in reverse, AST makes aspartate for the urea cycle

add.cloze: Transamination of oxaloacetate yields {{c1::aspartate}}
add.extra: Pyruvate → alanine; α-KG → glutamate

add.cloze: Transamination of α-ketoglutarate yields {{c1::glutamate}}
add.extra: Glutamate → glutamine, proline, arginine

add.cloze: ALT and AST leak into the blood when {{c1::hepatocytes}} are damaged
add.extra: Both are abundant inside liver cells

add.cloze: {{c1::ALT}} is the more liver-specific aminotransferase
add.extra: AST is also in heart, skeletal muscle and RBCs

add.cloze: AST is found in liver, heart, skeletal muscle and {{c1::RBCs}}
add.extra: So AST rises with liver, heart or muscle damage

add.cloze: Cysteine is synthesized from the essential amino acid {{c1::methionine}}
add.extra: Serine donates the carbon skeleton

add.cloze: Tyrosine and cysteine become conditionally {{c1::essential}} when Phe or Met is lacking
add.extra: Or when the converting enzyme is defective (e.g., PAH in PKU)

add.cloze: Most ammonia is produced by gut {{c1::microbes}}
add.extra: Other sources include amino acid breakdown

add.cloze: Glutamine {{c1::synthetase}} adds free ammonia to glutamate
add.extra: Uses ATP; makes glutamine for transport to the liver

add.cloze: In the liver, glutaminase releases NH4+ from glutamine for the {{c1::urea}} cycle
add.extra: Also active in the kidney

add.cloze: Glutamine carries {{c1::two}} nitrogens to the liver; alanine carries one
add.extra: Glutamine: glutamine synthetase. Alanine: ALT (muscle)

add.cloze: Glutamine is a safer nitrogen carrier because free ammonia is {{c1::neurotoxic}}
add.extra: Glutamine moves nitrogen without raising free NH3 or disturbing pH

add.cloze: Only the {{c1::liver}} expresses arginase, so only it completes the urea cycle
add.extra: Other tissues use the cycle enzymes to make arginine

add.cloze: Short-term urea cycle regulation: arginine stimulates N-acetylglutamate {{c1::synthase}}
add.extra: Arginine rises after a protein-rich meal; NAG activates CPS-I

add.cloze: N-acetylglutamate is made from glutamate and {{c1::acetyl-CoA}}
add.extra: Obligate allosteric activator of CPS-I

add.cloze: Long-term, a high-protein diet raises {{c1::glucagon}}, inducing urea cycle enzymes
add.extra: Postnatal life also activates transcription of urea cycle genes

add.cloze: Making one urea costs {{c1::3}} ATP
add.extra: 2 ATP at CPS-I + 1 ATP (→ AMP + PPi) at argininosuccinate synthase

add.cloze: Citrulline is exported from the {{c1::mitochondria}} to the cytosol
add.extra: Ornithine is imported back; CPS-I and OTC are mitochondrial

add.cloze: Urea cycle fumarate re-enters the {{c1::TCA}} cycle
add.extra: Fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate → aspartate via AST

add.cloze: Hyperammonemia raises astrocyte {{c1::glutamine}}, causing osmotic swelling
add.extra: → cerebral edema and ↑ intracranial pressure

add.cloze: Hyperammonemia lowers brain {{c1::GABA}}
add.extra: α-KG is pulled toward glutamate/glutamine; contributes to encephalopathy

add.cloze: Rising plasma {{c1::glutamine}} warns of a coming hyperammonemic crisis
add.extra: Monitor in urea cycle disorders

add.cloze: Overly low-protein diets in infants with UCDs can cause {{c1::growth}} retardation
add.extra: Treat with enough protein, arginine and energy

add.cloze: Urea cycle defects in infants present with vomiting, poor feeding and {{c1::lethargy}}
add.extra: In the first days of life

add.cloze: CPS-I, NAGS and OTC deficiencies all show {{c1::decreased}} citrulline
add.extra: Plus ↑ ammonia

add.cloze: NAGS deficiency has the same lab pattern as {{c1::CPS-I}} deficiency
add.extra: ↑ NH3, ↓ citrulline, low orotic acid; autosomal recessive

add.cloze: Argininosuccinate synthase deficiency causes massively elevated {{c1::citrulline}}
add.extra: Citrullinemia type I; ↑ ammonia

add.cloze: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency elevates {{c1::argininosuccinate}}
add.extra: Argininosuccinic aciduria; ↑ ammonia

add.cloze: Arginase deficiency causes high {{c1::arginine}}
add.extra: Ammonia is often near normal

add.cloze: Serotonin is converted to {{c1::melatonin}} in the pineal gland
add.extra: By acetylation and methylation; tryptophan → 5-HTP → serotonin

add.cloze: Histamine is synthesized from {{c1::histidine}}
add.extra: By decarboxylation (B6); immune responses and gastric acid secretion

add.cloze: Histidine is converted to histamine by {{c1::decarboxylation}}
add.extra: Removes CO2

add.cloze: GABA is made from glutamate by glutamate {{c1::decarboxylase}}
add.extra: GAD; requires B6

add.cloze: Nitric oxide made from arginine is a {{c1::vasodilator}}
add.extra: Regulates vascular tone; citrulline is the co-product

add.cloze: Glycine is the amino acid precursor for {{c1::porphyrins}}
add.extra: Porphyrin → heme

add.cloze: Glutamate is a precursor of the antioxidant {{c1::glutathione}}
add.extra: Redox balance

add.cloze: Carnitine is synthesized from protein-bound {{c1::lysine}}
add.extra: Lysine side chain is trimethylated; needs SAM, vitamin C and PLP

add.cloze: Carnitine deficiency can present in children with {{c1::cardiomyopathy}}
add.extra: Heart relies on fatty acid oxidation; LVH, ↓ EF, lipid droplets; reversed by carnitine

add.cloze: Creatine kinase phosphorylates creatine to {{c1::phosphocreatine}}
add.extra: A high-energy phosphate buffer for muscle ATP

add.cloze: Creatinine is the spontaneous breakdown product of {{c1::creatine}}
add.extra: Cleared by the kidney; high creatinine suggests loss of kidney function

add.cloze: Cystatin {{c1::C}} is an alternative to creatinine for measuring kidney function
add.extra: Gives consistent results across populations (e.g., GATM alleles affect creatinine)

add.cloze: PKU is inherited in an autosomal {{c1::recessive}} pattern
add.extra: ~1 in 50 people in the USA are carriers

add.cloze: Untreated PKU can cause {{c1::self-mutilation}}
add.extra: Plus hypopigmentation, eczema, light hair and eyes

add.cloze: In PKU, excess Phe blocks brain uptake of other amino acids at a shared {{c1::transporter}}
add.extra: L-type large neutral amino acid transporter at the blood-brain barrier

add.cloze: PKU brain deficiency of {{c1::tyrosine}} reduces dopamine, NE and epinephrine
add.extra: Phe ~1000 µM vs ~60 µM normal outcompetes Tyr

add.cloze: PKU brain deficiency of {{c1::tryptophan}} reduces serotonin
add.extra: Trp also competes for the same transporter

add.cloze: Alkaptonuria is caused by deficient homogentisate {{c1::1,2-dioxygenase}}
add.extra: HGD; homogentisic acid accumulates

add.cloze: Blue-black pigmentation of sclera and ear cartilage in alkaptonuria is called {{c1::ochronosis}}
add.extra: Homogentisic acid deposits in connective tissue

add.cloze: Alkaptonuria arthritis usually begins around age {{c1::30}}
add.extra: Spine, hips and knees; severe and progressive

add.cloze: Alkaptonuria is inherited in a {{c1::recessive}} pattern
add.extra: Very rare

q.v: A 6-day-old female newborn is brought to the emergency department due to progressive lethargy, poor suckling, and weight loss after appearing normal at birth. Physical examination shows signs of brain edema, and the infant's urine has a distinct odor of burnt sugar. The physician suspects an autosomal recessive defect in the enzyme complex that catalyzes the committed step of branched-chain amino acid catabolism. High-dose supplementation with which of the following vitamins is most appropriate as part of this patient's treatment?
o: Thiamine (B1)
Riboflavin (B2)
Pyridoxine (B6)
Ascorbic acid (C)
Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Maple Syrup Urine Disease from lethargy, poor suckling, burnt sugar urine odor, and cerebral edema in a 1-week-old newborn) -> Step 2 (Identify that branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase requires thiamine [B1] as a cofactor and high-dose thiamine is used in treatment)

r.B: Riboflavin (B2) is required alongside vitamin B6 for the conversion of tryptophan to niacin, not for the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex.
r.C: Pyridoxine (B6) is converted to pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) to serve as the cofactor for transaminases and decarboxylases, rather than the dehydrogenase complex impaired in Maple Syrup Urine Disease.
r.D: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is required for the synthesis of carnitine from lysine and the conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine, not branched-chain amino acid oxidation.
r.E: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is the cofactor required for the hydroxylation of phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan, and is not involved in branched-chain amino acid catabolism.

q.s: SLO1 / Slides 8, 10: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD)

q.v: During prolonged starvation, the carbon skeletons of catabolized muscle amino acids are converted into central metabolic intermediates to support fuel homeostasis. Which of the following sets of amino acids are both glucogenic and ketogenic?
o: Leucine and lysine
Alanine, cysteine, glycine, and serine
Arginine, glutamine, histidine, and proline
Methionine and valine
Phenylalanine, isoleucine, tyrosine, threonine, and tryptophan
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the classification of amino acid carbon skeletons into purely glucogenic, purely ketogenic, and mixed) -> Step 2 (Identify the PITTT / WIFTY group—phenylalanine, isoleucine, tyrosine, threonine, and tryptophan—as both gluconeogenic and ketogenic)

r.A: Leucine and lysine yield only acetyl-CoA or acetoacetyl-CoA and are the two purely ketogenic amino acids.
r.B: Alanine, cysteine, glycine, and serine are purely glucogenic amino acids that enter central metabolism via pyruvate.
r.C: Arginine, glutamine, histidine, and proline are purely glucogenic amino acids that are converted into glutamate and enter the TCA cycle as alpha-ketoglutarate.
r.D: Methionine and valine are purely glucogenic amino acids whose carbon skeletons enter the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA.

q.s: SLO1 / Slide 6: How Do We Convert Amino Acids to Ketone Bodies?

q.v: A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for progressive fatigue and scleral icterus due to acute viral hepatitis. Serum laboratory studies show markedly elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). In healthy hepatocytes, these two enzymes work sequentially to channel amino acid nitrogen into the immediate precursor that donates the second nitrogen atom to the urea cycle. Which of the following alpha-ketoacids accepts an amino group from glutamate via AST to form this immediate urea cycle donor?
o: Pyruvate
Alpha-ketoglutarate
Oxaloacetate
Fumarate
Succinyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that aspartate provides the second nitrogen of urea and is formed via AST) -> Step 2 (Recognize that AST transfers the amino group from glutamate to oxaloacetate to generate aspartate and alpha-ketoglutarate)

r.A: Pyruvate accepts an amino group from glutamate via alanine aminotransferase (ALT) to form alanine, which transports nitrogen from muscle to the liver.
r.B: Alpha-ketoglutarate is the universal amino group acceptor in the first step of amino acid catabolism, forming glutamate rather than aspartate.
r.D: Fumarate is released in the cytosol by argininosuccinate lyase and must first be hydrated to malate and oxidized to oxaloacetate before undergoing transamination.
r.E: Succinyl-CoA is a TCA cycle intermediate derived from the catabolism of isoleucine, methionine, threonine, and valine, and does not participate in AST-mediated transamination.

q.s: SLO2 / Slides 21, 35: Transaminases move nitrogen around to get it in the form of aspartate

q.v: Once glutamine from peripheral tissues reaches the liver, which of the following pairs of enzymes sequentially liberates its two nitrogen atoms as free ammonia while generating alpha-ketoglutarate?
o: Glutamine synthetase and alanine aminotransferase
Glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase
Aspartate aminotransferase and argininosuccinate synthase
Argininosuccinate lyase and arginase
q.p: Step 1 (Trace glutamine arrival in the liver where glutaminase hydrolyzes glutamine to glutamate and NH4+) -> Step 2 (Trace glutamate conversion by glutamate dehydrogenase [GDH] to alpha-ketoglutarate and a second NH4+ molecule)

r.A: Glutamine synthetase adds free ammonia to glutamate in peripheral tissues to form glutamine, and alanine aminotransferase transfers an amino group between alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate.
r.C: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase are mitochondrial urea cycle enzymes that incorporate free ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate and citrulline.
r.D: Aspartate aminotransferase transfers nitrogen from glutamate to oxaloacetate to form aspartate, which argininosuccinate synthase then ligates to citrulline.
r.E: Argininosuccinate lyase cleaves argininosuccinate into fumarate and arginine, and arginase cleaves arginine into urea and ornithine.

q.s: SLO2 / Slides 19, 20, 22: Glutamate, Glutamine Are Central to Nitrogen Metabolism

q.v:
A 3-day-old male infant is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for poor feeding, vomiting, and progressive lethargy. Family history reveals that a maternal uncle died in the neonatal period after a similar presentation. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum ammonia: 480 µmol/L (markedly elevated)
  Plasma glutamine: elevated
  Plasma citrulline: decreased
  Urine orotic acid: elevated
Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of this patient's condition?
o: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose ornithine transcarbamylase [OTC] deficiency from neonatal hyperammonemia, decreased citrulline, and elevated orotic acid) -> Step 2 (Identify the inheritance pattern of OTC deficiency as X-linked recessive, the only X-linked urea cycle disorder)

r.A: None of the classic urea cycle enzyme deficiencies taught in this block follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
r.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance is characteristic of all other urea cycle disorders—including CPS-I, NAGS, argininosuccinate synthase, argininosuccinate lyase, and arginase deficiencies—which do not match the combination of low citrulline and high orotic acid.
r.D: OTC deficiency is inherited as an X-linked recessive disorder that affects males more severely, rather than an X-linked dominant condition.
r.E: Although the OTC enzyme is located inside the mitochondrial matrix, the OTC gene is encoded on the X chromosome rather than mitochondrial DNA.

q.s: SLO3 / Slides 28, 34, 38: UREA CYCLE Disorder Summary

q.v:
A 2-day-old female neonate develops severe lethargy, hypothermia, and vomiting shortly after starting formula feeds. Laboratory evaluation is performed to determine the cause of her acute encephalopathy:
  Serum ammonia: 610 µmol/L (markedly elevated)
  Plasma citrulline: < 2 µmol/L (markedly decreased)
  Urine orotic acid: decreased
Administration of carglumic acid (a synthetic analog of N-acetylglutamate) rapidly normalizes her serum ammonia and plasma citrulline levels. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
N-acetylglutamate synthase
Ornithine transcarbamylase
Argininosuccinate synthase 1
Argininosuccinate lyase
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab panel: hyperammonemia with low citrulline and low orotic acid narrows the defect to CPS-I or NAGS deficiency) -> Step 2 (Recognize that correction with carglumic acid is diagnostic of N-acetylglutamate synthase [NAGS] deficiency, because supplying the missing allosteric activator restores CPS-I activity)

r.A: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) deficiency also presents with elevated ammonia, low citrulline, and low orotic acid, but it does not respond to carglumic acid because the CPS-I enzyme itself is defective.
r.C: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency presents with elevated urine orotic acid due to carbamoyl phosphate buildup, rather than decreased orotic acid.
r.D: Argininosuccinate synthase 1 deficiency (Citrullinemia Type I) presents with massively elevated plasma citrulline rather than decreased citrulline.
r.E: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency presents with elevated argininosuccinate and citrulline, along with trichorrhexis nodosa (brittle hair).

q.s: SLO3 / Slides 30, 38: UREA CYCLE Disorder Summary

q.v: A 58-year-old man with a history of alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department for slurred speech, blurred vision, and somnolence after eating a high-protein meal. Physical examination shows a flapping tremor of his outstretched hands (asterixis). Laboratory studies reveal a markedly elevated serum ammonia level. To reduce his serum ammonia by invoking an alternative pathway for nitrogen waste disposal, the physician administers sodium phenylacetate. This medication lowers ammonia levels by conjugating with which of the following molecules to form a water-soluble product excreted by the kidneys?
o: Ornithine
Citrulline
Glutamine
Argininosuccinate
Fumarate
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize acquired hyperammonemia / hepatic encephalopathy from cirrhosis, asterixis, slurred speech, and somnolence) -> Step 2 (Identify that phenylacetate conjugates with glutamine to form phenylacetylglutamine, which is excreted renally as an alternative nitrogen waste disposal pathway)

r.A: Ornithine is a urea cycle intermediate regenerated by arginase and transported into the mitochondrion, not the target of phenylacetate conjugation.
r.B: Citrulline is a urea cycle intermediate formed in the mitochondrion by OTC and transported into the cytosol, not a substrate for phenylacetate.
r.D: Argininosuccinate is a cytosolic urea cycle intermediate cleaved into arginine and fumarate, and does not react with phenylacetate.
r.E: Fumarate is a carbon skeleton intermediate that links the urea cycle to the TCA cycle and contains no nitrogen atoms for disposal.

q.s: SLO3 / Slides 24, 25: HYPERAMMONEMIA

q.v: A 6-year-old girl who recently immigrated with her family is evaluated in the pediatric clinic for severe intellectual disability, self-mutilation behaviors, and an eczematous rash. Physical examination shows fair skin, blonde hair, and blue eyes, which contrast sharply with the dark hair and brown eyes of her parents. Her urine has a classic musty or "mousy" odor. Laboratory testing shows a plasma phenylalanine level of 1,050 µM (normal: 60 µM). Which of the following mechanisms best explains how elevated phenylalanine impairs neurotransmitter synthesis in this patient's central nervous system?
o: Inhibition of pyridoxal phosphate synthesis in astrocytes
Depletion of alpha-ketoglutarate from the neuronal TCA cycle
Accumulation of homogentisic acid in cerebral connective tissue
Competition with tryptophan and tyrosine for the blood-brain barrier transporter
Direct allosteric inhibition of glutamic acid decarboxylase
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose untreated phenylketonuria [PKU] from mousy urine odor, hypopigmentation, eczema, self-mutilation, and Phe > 1000 µM) -> Step 2 (Identify the CNS pathophysiology: excess blood phenylalanine saturates the large neutral amino acid transporter at the blood-brain barrier, competing away tryptophan, tyrosine, and BCAAs from entering the brain)

r.A: Pyridoxal phosphate (active vitamin B6) is a cofactor for neurotransmitter synthesis, but its production is not inhibited by phenylalanine in PKU.
r.B: Depletion of alpha-ketoglutarate and glutamine-induced osmotic shifts are the mechanisms of CNS toxicity in hyperammonemia, not PKU.
r.C: Accumulation of homogentisic acid occurs in alkaptonuria and causes blue-black pigmentation of cartilage and sclerae (ochronosis), not CNS neurotransmitter deficiency.
r.E: Glutamic acid decarboxylase converts glutamate to GABA using vitamin B6, and is not the target of phenylalanine toxicity in PKU.

q.s: SLO4 & SLO5 / Slides 49, 50, 51, 53: Excess Phenylalanine Competes Away Other Amino Acids

q.v:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician for progressive generalized muscle weakness and exercise intolerance over the past 8 months. Physical examination reveals a displaced apical impulse, and echocardiography shows left ventricular hypertrophy with a reduced ejection fraction. Muscle biopsy demonstrates prominent intracellular lipid droplets. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum AST: 115 U/L (elevated)
  Serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK): 940 U/L (elevated)
  Plasma total carnitine: 3 µM (normal: 25–50 µM)
Supplementation with oral carnitine leads to rapid clinical improvement. In healthy individuals, endogenous biosynthesis of the deficient molecule requires protein-bound lysine residues and which of the following sets of cofactors/substrates?
o: S-adenosylmethionine, vitamin C, and pyridoxal phosphate
Tetrahydrobiopterin, vitamin B12, and folate
Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, and NAD+
Biotin, ATP, and bicarbonate
N-acetylglutamate, ornithine, and carbamoyl phosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize primary carnitine deficiency from cardiomyopathy, muscle weakness, lipid droplets in muscle, elevated CPK/AST, and plasma carnitine < 5 µM) -> Step 2 (Identify that endogenous carnitine biosynthesis from protein lysine residues requires S-adenosylmethionine [SAM], vitamin C, and pyridoxal phosphate [PLP])

r.B: Tetrahydrobiopterin is used by amino acid hydroxylases, whereas vitamin B12 and folate are involved in one-carbon and homocysteine metabolism, not carnitine synthesis.
r.C: Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, and NAD+ are cofactors for alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes such as branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase.
r.D: Biotin, ATP, and bicarbonate are required for carboxylase reactions, rather than the methylation and hydroxylation of lysine to form carnitine.
r.E: N-acetylglutamate, ornithine, and carbamoyl phosphate are mitochondrial components of the urea cycle and do not participate in carnitine synthesis.

q.s: SLO5 / Slides 42, 43: Protein Lysine Residues Serve As The Substrate for Carnitine Biosynthesis

q.v: A 36-year-old woman presents to the clinic with progressive stiffness and pain in her lower back, hips, and knees over the past 3 years. She also mentions that her urine turns dark black when left standing in the toilet bowl. Physical examination reveals blue-black pigmentation of her ear cartilage and the sclerae of both eyes. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Phenylalanine hydroxylase
Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase
Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase
Argininosuccinate lyase
Glutamic acid decarboxylase
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose alkaptonuria from urine turning black on air exposure, ochronosis of ear cartilage and sclerae, and large-joint arthritis starting around age 30) -> Step 2 (Identify the underlying autosomal recessive enzyme defect in phenylalanine/tyrosine catabolism as homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase [HGD])

r.A: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes phenylketonuria, which presents with hypopigmentation, eczema, intellectual disability, and a mousy urine odor.
r.B: Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes Maple Syrup Urine Disease, presenting in neonates with lethargy, ketosis, and a burnt sugar urine odor.
r.D: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causes argininosuccinic aciduria, a urea cycle disorder characterized by hyperammonemia, liver fibrosis, and brittle hair (trichorrhexis nodosa).
r.E: Glutamic acid decarboxylase synthesizes the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA from glutamate and is not involved in tyrosine degradation.

q.s: SLO5 / Slide 52: Breakdown of Phenylalanine and Tyrosine Deficiency - Alkaptonuria (AKU)

q.v: A 10-day-old male infant from a Pennsylvania Mennonite community is brought to the clinic for poor feeding, weight loss, and progressive lethargy after appearing healthy at birth. Physical examination shows increased muscle tone, and his diaper has an odor resembling burnt sugar. In addition to restricting branched-chain amino acids in the diet, high-dose supplementation with which of the following vitamins is most appropriate for this patient?
o: Thiamine (B1)
Riboflavin (B2)
Pyridoxine (B6)
Cobalamin (B12)
Ascorbic acid (C)
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Maple Syrup Urine Disease from lethargy, burnt sugar urine odor, and Mennonite heritage) -> Step 2 (Identify thiamine [vitamin B1] as the required cofactor for the deficient branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex)

r.B: Riboflavin (B2) is required along with vitamin B6 for the synthesis of niacin from tryptophan, not for the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex.
r.C: Pyridoxine (B6), in its active form pyridoxal phosphate, serves as the essential cofactor for aminotransferases and decarboxylases rather than branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase.
r.D: Cobalamin (B12) is not a cofactor for the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex and is not used to treat Maple Syrup Urine Disease.
r.E: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is a cofactor required for converting dopamine to norepinephrine and synthesizing carnitine from lysine, not for catabolizing branched-chain amino acids.

q.s: SLO1 / Slide 8: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) and Slide 10: MSUD is a Disorder of BCAA Catabolism

q.v: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being stranded in the wilderness for 5 days without food. To provide energy for his brain during prolonged starvation, his liver synthesizes ketone bodies from the carbon skeletons of catabolized muscle protein. Which of the following amino acids serves as a major source of ketone bodies in starvation without contributing to net glucose synthesis?
o: Alanine
Isoleucine
Leucine
Phenylalanine
Valine
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that purely ketogenic amino acids produce acetyl-CoA or acetoacetyl-CoA without contributing to gluconeogenesis) -> Step 2 (Select leucine as a purely ketogenic amino acid that makes up a major percentage of body protein)

r.A: Alanine is a purely glucogenic amino acid that is transaminated to pyruvate to serve as a substrate for gluconeogenesis.
r.B: Isoleucine is both glucogenic and ketogenic, yielding succinyl-CoA for gluconeogenesis in addition to acetyl-CoA.
r.D: Phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic, yielding fumarate for glucose synthesis as well as acetoacetyl-CoA.
r.E: Valine is a glucogenic branched-chain amino acid whose catabolism yields succinyl-CoA, a TCA cycle intermediate used for gluconeogenesis.

q.s: SLO1 / Slide 6: How Do We Convert Amino Acids to Ketone Bodies? and Slide 7: Summary: The Catabolic Fate of the Carbon Skeletons

q.v: During the synthesis of non-essential amino acids in the liver, transaminases transfer an amino group from glutamate to specific glycolytic or TCA cycle intermediates. Which of the following correctly pairs the central metabolic intermediate with the non-essential amino acid formed directly from its transamination?
o: Pyruvate -> Aspartate
Oxaloacetate -> Alanine
Succinyl-CoA -> Cysteine
Alpha-ketoglutarate -> Serine
Oxaloacetate -> Aspartate
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the reversible transamination reactions that synthesize non-essential amino acids from glycolytic and TCA intermediates) -> Step 2 (Match oxaloacetate with aspartate via aspartate aminotransferase [AST])

r.A: Transamination of pyruvate via alanine aminotransferase (ALT) directly produces alanine, not aspartate.
r.B: Oxaloacetate is transaminated to form aspartate, whereas pyruvate is the glycolytic intermediate transaminated to form alanine.
r.C: Cysteine is synthesized from the essential amino acid methionine and non-essential serine, not by the transamination of succinyl-CoA.
r.D: Transamination of alpha-ketoglutarate produces glutamate, which is the precursor for glutamine, proline, and arginine, rather than serine.

q.s: SLO2 / Slide 16: Transamination Is Key to Non-Essential Amino Acid Synthesis and Slide 21: Transaminases move nitrogen around to get it in the form of aspartate

q.v: A 52-year-old woman with a history of chronic viral hepatitis presents to the emergency department with confusion, slurred speech, and a flapping tremor of her outstretched hands. Her symptoms are attributed to the accumulation of ammonia in the central nervous system. Which of the following mechanisms directly contributes to central nervous system toxicity and cerebral edema in this patient's condition?
o: Accumulation of homogentisic acid and oxidation in neural tissue
Depletion of alpha-ketoglutarate and glutamine-induced osmotic shifts
Overflow of carbamoyl phosphate into the cytosolic pyrimidine pathway
Competition by excess phenylalanine at the blood-brain barrier transporter
Impaired transport of long-chain fatty acids into neuronal mitochondria
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize hyperammonemia/hepatic encephalopathy from liver disease, confusion, slurred speech, and asterixis) -> Step 2 (Identify that excess NH3 depletes alpha-ketoglutarate to inhibit the TCA cycle and increases glutamine, causing osmotic shifts and cerebral edema)

r.A: Accumulation and oxidation of homogentisic acid occurs in alkaptonuria, causing dark urine, ochronosis, and arthritis rather than cerebral edema.
r.C: Overflow of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate into the cytosol increases orotic acid in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, which is not the mechanism of ammonia neurotoxicity.
r.D: Competition at the blood-brain barrier amino acid transporter by excess phenylalanine is the mechanism of neurological injury in untreated phenylketonuria.
r.E: Impaired transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria occurs in carnitine deficiency, which presents with cardiomegaly and muscle weakness.

q.s: SLO2 & SLO3 / Slide 24: Hyperammonemia and Slide 39: SLO3 Review

q.v: Following a protein-rich meal, increased amino acid catabolism in the liver requires rapid upregulation of the urea cycle to prevent hyperammonemia. Which of the following best describes the short-term regulation of the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle under these conditions?
o: Glucagon-mediated phosphorylation of ornithine transcarbamylase
Allosteric inhibition of arginase by elevated cytosolic ornithine
Transcriptional repression of argininosuccinate lyase by insulin
Allosteric activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I by N-acetylglutamate
Competitive inhibition of glutamate dehydrogenase by alpha-ketoglutarate
q.p: Step 1 (Identify carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I [CPS-I] as the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle) -> Step 2 (Recognize that high arginine levels after a protein meal stimulate N-acetylglutamate synthase to produce N-acetylglutamate, the essential allosteric activator of CPS-I)

r.A: Elevated serum glucagon from a high-protein diet provides long-term regulation by stimulating the transcription of urea cycle enzymes, not short-term phosphorylation of ornithine transcarbamylase.
r.B: Arginase cleaves arginine to produce urea and regenerate ornithine in the liver and is not the site of short-term allosteric regulation after a meal.
r.C: A high-protein diet activates the transcription of genes encoding urea cycle enzymes for long-term regulation rather than repressing argininosuccinate lyase.
r.E: Short-term regulation of the urea cycle occurs via N-acetylglutamate activating CPS-I rather than competitive inhibition of glutamate dehydrogenase.

q.s: SLO3 / Slide 30: The Urea Cycle and Its Connection to the TCA Cycle and Slide 33: Urea Cycle Regulation Reminder

q.v:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric neurology clinic for evaluation of developmental delay and difficulty walking. His birth history was unremarkable, and he had no neonatal episodes of coma or severe vomiting. Physical examination reveals stiff, spastic lower extremities (spastic diplegia) with brisk deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum ammonia: 45 µmol/L (normal: 15–45 µmol/L)
  Plasma arginine: 680 µmol/L (normal: 40–120 µmol/L)
  Urine orotic acid: normal
Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
N-acetylglutamate synthase
Ornithine transcarbamylase
Argininosuccinate synthase 1
Arginase
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab panel showing markedly elevated plasma arginine with near-normal serum ammonia alongside spastic diplegia) -> Step 2 (Identify arginase deficiency as the urea cycle disorder with this unique clinical and biochemical profile)

r.A: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency presents with severe neonatal hyperammonemia, decreased citrulline, and low orotic acid.
r.B: N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency presents identically to CPS-I deficiency with severe neonatal hyperammonemia and low citrulline, and it responds to carglumic acid.
r.C: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is X-linked and presents with hyperammonemia, decreased citrulline, and elevated orotic acid.
r.D: Argininosuccinate synthase 1 deficiency (Citrullinemia Type I) presents with hyperammonemia and massively elevated plasma citrulline rather than high arginine.

q.s: SLO3 / Slide 38: Urea Cycle Disorder Summary

q.v:
A 14-month-old girl is evaluated in the genetics clinic for poor growth, developmental delay, and unusual hair that breaks easily. Physical examination shows hepatomegaly and coarse, brittle hair (trichorrhexis nodosa). A liver biopsy demonstrates early hepatic fibrosis. Laboratory evaluation shows:
  Serum ammonia: 190 µmol/L (normal: 15–45 µmol/L)
  Plasma argininosuccinate: markedly elevated
  Plasma citrulline: elevated
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Citrullinemia Type I
Argininosuccinic aciduria
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
Alkaptonuria
Maple syrup urine disease
q.p: Step 1 (Correlate the unique clinical features of brittle hair [trichorrhexis nodosa] and liver fibrosis with hyperammonemia and elevated argininosuccinate) -> Step 2 (Diagnose argininosuccinic aciduria caused by argininosuccinate lyase deficiency)

r.A: Citrullinemia Type I is caused by argininosuccinate synthase 1 deficiency and features massively high citrulline without argininosuccinate accumulation or brittle hair.
r.C: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency causes hyperammonemia with decreased citrulline and high orotic acid, and is not associated with trichorrhexis nodosa.
r.D: Alkaptonuria is a defect in tyrosine degradation causing dark urine, ochronosis, and arthritis in adulthood, not hyperammonemia or brittle hair.
r.E: Maple syrup urine disease is a defect in branched-chain amino acid catabolism presenting with ketosis and burnt sugar-smelling urine rather than hyperammonemia and elevated argininosuccinate.

q.s: SLO3 / Slide 38: Urea Cycle Disorder Summary

q.v: A 4-year-old boy with an untreated inborn error of metabolism is evaluated for severe intellectual disability, hyperactivity, and seizures. He has fair skin, blonde hair, blue eyes, and an eczematous rash on his flexor surfaces, and his urine has a musty, 'mousy' odor. Plasma amino acid analysis shows a phenylalanine level of 1100 µM (normal: 60 µM). Which of the following mechanisms best explains the profound neurological dysfunction in this patient?
o: Accumulation of glutamine in astrocytes leading to intracellular osmotic swelling
Depletion of thiamine pyrophosphate impairing alpha-ketoacid decarboxylation
Excess phenylalanine competing away other large neutral amino acids at the blood-brain barrier transporter
Precipitation of oxidized homogentisic acid polymers within cerebral white matter
Defective synthesis of carnitine resulting in impaired neuronal beta-oxidation
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize untreated phenylketonuria [PKU] from hypopigmentation, eczema, mousy urine odor, and Phe > 1000 µM) -> Step 2 (Identify that excess phenylalanine saturates the blood-brain barrier transporter, competing away tryptophan, tyrosine, valine, isoleucine, and leucine needed for brain protein and neurotransmitter synthesis)

r.A: Astrocytic glutamine accumulation and osmotic swelling is the mechanism of cerebral edema in hyperammonemia due to urea cycle disorders or cirrhosis.
r.B: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex affected in Maple Syrup Urine Disease, not phenylketonuria.
r.D: Oxidation of homogentisic acid causes ochronosis in connective tissues such as sclerae and ear cartilage in alkaptonuria, not cerebral white matter disease in PKU.
r.E: Carnitine is synthesized from protein lysine residues and its deficiency causes cardiomyopathy and skeletal muscle weakness rather than the neurological phenotype of PKU.

q.s: SLO5 / Slide 49: Phenylketonuria, Slide 51: Excess Phenylalanine Competes Away Other Amino Acids, and Slide 53: SLO4 & SLO5 Review

q.v: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician for progressive generalized muscle weakness and poor exercise tolerance. Echocardiography reveals cardiomegaly with left ventricular hypertrophy and a reduced ejection fraction. Muscle biopsy shows prominent lipid droplets, and laboratory studies reveal a plasma carnitine level of 3 µM (normal: 25–50 µM). In healthy individuals, the molecule deficient in this patient is synthesized from protein lysine residues using which of the following sets of cofactors and substrates?
o: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) and riboflavin (B2)
S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), vitamin C, and pyridoxal phosphate (B6)
Thiamine (B1), CoA-SH, and NAD+
N-acetylglutamate, bicarbonate, and ATP
Folate (B9), cobalamin (B12), and serine
q.p: Step 1 (Identify primary carnitine deficiency from cardiomegaly, lipid droplets in muscle, and low plasma carnitine, and recall that carnitine is synthesized from protein lysine residues) -> Step 2 (Select S-adenosylmethionine, vitamin C, and pyridoxal phosphate as the required cofactors/substrates for carnitine biosynthesis)

r.A: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is required for the hydroxylation of phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan, while riboflavin (B2) is used in converting tryptophan to niacin.
r.C: Thiamine (B1), CoA-SH, and NAD+ are required by the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex for catabolizing leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
r.D: N-acetylglutamate, bicarbonate, and ATP are required by mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the first step of the urea cycle.
r.E: Serine condenses with methionine derivatives to form cysteine, and folate and cobalamin are not the cofactors used to convert lysine residues into carnitine.

q.s: SLO5 / Slide 41: Amino Acid Derivative Overview, Slide 42: Protein Lysine Residues Serve As The Substrate for Carnitine Biosynthesis, and Slide 43: Carnitine: Case Study

q.v: Amino acids serve as precursors for numerous specialized biomolecules and neurotransmitters that regulate vascular tone, energy buffering, and neurotransmission. Which of the following correctly pairs a specialized physiological product with both its amino acid precursor and its required cofactor?
o: GABA — Glutamate — Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)
Histamine — Tryptophan — Pyridoxal phosphate (B6)
Nitric oxide — Arginine — Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)
Epinephrine — Tyrosine — Ascorbic acid (C) only
Creatine — Lysine — S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)
q.p: Step 1 (Evaluate the amino acid derivative synthesis pathways and their specific cofactors) -> Step 2 (Confirm that arginine is converted to nitric oxide [a vasodilator] using tetrahydrobiopterin [BH4] as a cofactor)

r.A: GABA is synthesized from glutamate via glutamic acid decarboxylase, which requires vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate), not tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).
r.B: Histamine is synthesized via the decarboxylation of histidine using vitamin B6, whereas tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin, melatonin, and niacin.
r.D: The conversion of tyrosine to epinephrine requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), vitamin B6, vitamin C, and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) across sequential steps, not vitamin C alone.
r.E: Creatine is synthesized from arginine to serve as a high-energy phosphate donor in muscle, whereas carnitine is synthesized from lysine.

q.s: SLO4 & SLO5 / Slide 41: Amino Acid Derivative Overview, Slide 44: Arginine -> Creatine, and Slide 47: Amino Acid Neurotransmitters
