q.v: A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 4-day history of fever, myalgias, and a nonproductive cough caused by an acute respiratory viral infection. Antigen-specific T cells are activated in her draining lymph nodes and undergo differentiation into effector cells before migrating to the infected lung tissue. Which of the following changes in surface receptor expression most directly prepares these activated effector T cells to exit the lymph node and home to inflamed peripheral tissue?
o: Downregulation of CD62L and CCR7; upregulation of S1P1 and LFA-1
Upregulation of CD62L and CCR7; downregulation of S1P1 and VLA-4
Downregulation of CXCR3 and CCR5; upregulation of CD62L and CCR7
Upregulation of CTLA-4 and CD25; downregulation of LFA-1 and VLA-4
Downregulation of S1P1 and ICAM-1; upregulation of PECAM-1 and CCR7
q.p: Step 1 (T cell activation in lymph node) -> Step 2 (Downregulation of L-selectin/CD62L and CCR7, and upregulation of S1P1, chemokine receptors, and integrins LFA-1/VLA-4 to exit lymph node and enter inflamed tissue)

r.B: Naive T cells, rather than activated effector T cells, express high levels of CD62L and CCR7 to enter and recirculate through lymph nodes via high endothelial venules.
r.C: Effector T cells upregulate inflammatory chemokine receptors such as CXCR3 and CCR5 while downregulating lymph node homing receptors CD62L and CCR7.
r.D: High expression of CTLA-4 and CD25 characterizes regulatory T cells, and effector cells upregulate rather than downregulate integrins LFA-1 and VLA-4.
r.E: Activated T cells upregulate S1P1 to follow the sphingosine-1-phosphate gradient out of the lymph node into the efferent lymphatics.

q.s: LO1 / Slides 7-8: Effector CD8 T cells traffic to inflamed tissues; Naive and effector T cells use different homing programs

q.v: A 6-month-old boy is evaluated in the immunology clinic for severe, early-onset autoimmune enteropathy, dermatitis, and endocrinopathy. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood mononuclear cells shows a normal total CD4+ T-cell count, but a subset of cells normally responsible for maintaining self-tolerance is absent. In healthy individuals, which of the following combinations of lineage-defining transcription factor, surface markers, and secreted cytokines best characterizes this missing T-cell population?
o: T-bet; CXCR3 and CD40L; IFN-γ and TNF
FOXP3; CD25 and CTLA-4; IL-10 and TGF-β
GATA-3; CCR4 and ICOS; IL-4 and IL-5
RORγt; CCR6 and LFA-1; IL-17 and IL-22
STAT4; CD28 and CD62L; IL-12 and IL-21
q.p: Step 1 (Loss of self-tolerance/autoimmunity indicates regulatory T cell defect) -> Step 2 (Identify Treg profile: FOXP3+, high CD25, CTLA-4, secreting suppressive IL-10 and TGF-β)

r.A: T-bet, CD40L, IFN-γ, and TNF are characteristic of Th1 cells that activate macrophages against intracellular pathogens.
r.C: GATA-3, IL-4, and IL-5 define Th2 cells, which coordinate immunity against helminths and drive immediate hypersensitivity.
r.D: RORγt, IL-17, and IL-22 characterize Th17 cells, which recruit neutrophils to defend barrier tissues against extracellular bacteria and fungi.
r.E: STAT4 and IL-12 are involved in Th1 differentiation, whereas IL-21 is a signature cytokine of Tfh and Th17 cells.

q.s: LO1, LO3, LO5 / Slide 14: Treg: restrain immune responses and preserve tolerance

q.v: Which of the following correctly pairs the instructive cytokine environment (Signal 3) with the intracellular signaling pathway and master transcription factor that commits a naive CD4+ T cell to the Th17 lineage?
o: IL-12 activating STAT4 and T-bet
IL-4 activating STAT6 and GATA-3
IL-1, IL-6, and TGF-β activating STAT3 and RORγt
IL-2 and TGF-β activating FADD and FOXP3
IFN-γ and TNF activating STAT1 and ICOS
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Th17 polarization) -> Step 2 (Match inducing cytokines IL-1, IL-6, and TGF-β to signaling via STAT3 and lineage-defining factor RORγt)

r.A: IL-12 signals through STAT4 to induce T-bet, which commits naive CD4+ T cells to the Th1 lineage.
r.B: IL-4 signals through STAT6 to induce GATA-3, which drives Th2 differentiation.
r.D: TGF-β promotes Treg development via FOXP3, while FADD is an adaptor protein in the Fas apoptosis pathway.
r.E: IFN-γ and TNF are effector outputs of Th1 cells, and ICOS is a costimulatory receptor utilized by Tfh cells.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 12: Th17: reinforce barriers and recruit neutrophils

q.v: A 45-year-old man who recently immigrated from a rural region presents with chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats. Sputum examination and chest imaging confirm an infection with an intracellular bacterium that persists inside macrophage phagosomes. In the draining lymph nodes, dendritic cells present bacterial peptides on HLA class II molecules and secrete IL-12. This cytokine environment induces responding CD4+ T cells to express T-bet and differentiate into effector cells. Which of the following effector combinations will these differentiated T cells use to help clear the infection?
o: IL-4 and IL-13 to induce alternative (M2) macrophage activation
IL-17 and IL-22 to stimulate epithelial antimicrobial peptide production
Perforin and granzymes to directly lyse the infected macrophages
IFN-γ and CD40L to induce classical (M1) macrophage activation
CTLA-4 and IL-10 to remove B7 molecules from the macrophage surface
q.p: Step 1 (Intracellular phagosomal microbe induces IL-12/T-bet/Th1 response) -> Step 2 (Th1 cells deliver IFN-γ and engage CD40 via CD40L to trigger classical M1 macrophage activation and microbicidal killing)

r.A: IL-4 and IL-13 are produced by Th2 cells and drive alternative (M2) macrophage activation for tissue repair and fibrosis.
r.B: IL-17 and IL-22 are produced by Th17 cells to recruit neutrophils and strengthen mucosal barrier defenses against extracellular pathogens.
r.C: Th1 cells do not kill infected cells directly via perforin and granzymes; instead, they activate macrophages to enhance phagolysosomal killing.
r.E: CTLA-4 and IL-10 are used by regulatory T cells to suppress immune responses and condition APCs to a tolerogenic state.

q.s: LO2, LO3, LO5 / Slide 10: Th1: activate macrophages against intracellular microbes

q.v: A 19-year-old woman presents with seasonal wheezing, nasal congestion, and watery eyes upon exposure to tree pollen. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis shows increased numbers of eosinophils, degranulated mast cells, and abundant mucus. Cytokine profiling of her airway CD4+ T cells reveals elevated levels of IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. Which of the following best describes the specific effector roles of IL-5 and IL-13 in this patient's presentation?
o: IL-5 drives B-cell class switching to IgG; IL-13 recruits neutrophils to the airway
IL-5 activates classical M1 macrophages; IL-13 upregulates endothelial E-selectin
IL-5 induces T-cell proliferation; IL-13 stimulates bone marrow G-CSF production
IL-5 promotes germinal center formation; IL-13 induces epithelial defensin secretion
IL-5 promotes eosinophil growth and activation; IL-13 stimulates mucus and smooth muscle responses
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Th2-mediated allergic response with IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) -> Step 2 (Match IL-5 to eosinophil recruitment/activation and IL-13 to mucus hypersecretion, smooth muscle responses, and M2 macrophage polarization)

r.A: Class switching to IgE and IgG4 is driven by IL-4 and IL-13, whereas neutrophil recruitment is driven by IL-17.
r.B: Classical M1 macrophage activation is driven by Th1-derived IFN-γ, whereas IL-13 promotes alternative M2 macrophage polarization.
r.C: IL-2 drives T-cell clonal proliferation, and G-CSF production is stimulated by Th17-derived IL-17.
r.D: Germinal center formation is supported by Tfh cells producing IL-21 and CXCL13, and epithelial defensins are induced by Th17-derived IL-22.

q.s: LO3, LO5 / Slide 11: Th2: expel helminths and drive immediate hypersensitivity

q.v:
A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections. Immunologic workup reveals normal numbers of circulating B cells and T cells, but lymph node biopsy following vaccination shows poorly formed germinal centers and an absence of long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells. Laboratory studies of her serum immunoglobulins show:
  Serum IgM: normal
  Serum IgG: markedly decreased
  Serum IgA: markedly decreased
  Serum IgE: markedly decreased
  Antigen-specific antibody affinity: low
Impaired function of which of the following T-cell subsets and its key effector molecules best explains these laboratory findings?
o: Tfh cells utilizing ICOS, CD40L, and IL-21
Th17 cells utilizing LFA-1, IL-17A, and GM-CSF
Treg cells utilizing CTLA-4, CD25, and TGF-β
Th1 cells utilizing STAT4, IFN-γ, and TNF
CD8+ CTLs utilizing FasL, perforin, and granzymes
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret lab data: normal IgM with low IgG/IgA/IgE and low affinity indicates failed class switch recombination and affinity maturation in germinal centers) -> Step 2 (Identify Tfh cells, which migrate via CXCR5 and use ICOS, CD40L, and IL-21 to help germinal center B cells)

r.B: Th17 cells produce IL-17A and GM-CSF to recruit neutrophils and enhance myeloid inflammation at mucosal barriers.
r.C: Treg cells use CTLA-4, CD25, and TGF-β to suppress B-cell and T-cell activation rather than promote germinal center antibody maturation.
r.D: Th1 cells use IFN-γ and TNF to enhance macrophage phagocytosis and microbicidal activity against intracellular pathogens.
r.E: CD8+ CTLs use FasL, perforin, and granzymes to induce apoptosis in virus-infected or malignant nucleated cells.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 13: Tfh: provide cognate help to germinal-center B cells

q.v: How does the FasL–Fas mechanism of CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) killing differ from the perforin–granzyme pathway?
o: FasL–Fas killing relies on soluble antibodies rather than direct cell-to-cell contact
FasL–Fas signaling recruits FADD and procaspase-8 via death domains and contributes to lymphocyte homeostasis
FasL–Fas requires target cell expression of HLA class II molecules to trigger granule exocytosis
FasL–Fas induces necrosis by forming osmotic pores directly in the target cell plasma membrane
FasL–Fas is the primary mechanism used by Th1 cells to destroy bacteria inside phagosomes
q.p: Step 1 (Compare CD8 cytotoxicity mechanisms) -> Step 2 (Perforin-granzyme uses polarized granule exocytosis; FasL-Fas uses trimerization of Fas/CD95, FADD adaptor recruitment, and procaspase-8 activation for regulated death and lymphocyte homeostasis)

r.A: Both perforin–granzyme and FasL–Fas pathways are antigen-specific, contact-dependent mechanisms that act across an immunological synapse.
r.C: CD8+ CTLs recognize peptide presented on HLA class I, and granule exocytosis is the mechanism of the perforin–granzyme pathway.
r.D: Both CTL killing pathways induce programmed cell death (apoptosis) via caspase cascades to limit collateral tissue injury, rather than osmotic necrosis.
r.E: Th1 cells activate macrophages via IFN-γ and CD40L and do not directly kill target cells using CTL cytotoxicity pathways.

q.s: LO4 / Slides 5-6: CD8 cytotoxic T cells induce apoptosis

q.v: A 34-year-old man presents with acute hepatomegaly, fever, and elevated serum transaminases due to an intracellular viral infection of his hepatocytes. A liver biopsy demonstrates CD8+ lymphocytes closely apposed to infected hepatocytes, with histological evidence of hepatocyte apoptosis and minimal damage to adjacent uninfected liver cells. In addition to FasL–Fas engagement, which of the following mechanisms is most likely being used by these lymphocytes to eliminate the reservoir of infection?
o: Secretion of IL-17 and IL-22 to induce hepatocyte defensin production
Engagement of CD28 by B7 to remove costimulatory molecules via transendocytosis
Recognition of peptide–HLA class I followed by polarized exocytosis of perforin and granzymes
Release of IL-5 to recruit eosinophils that degranulate major basic protein onto hepatocytes
Secretion of CXCL13 to organize germinal centers within the hepatic parenchyma
q.p: Step 1 (Identify cytosolic viral infection in nucleated hepatocytes targeted by CD8+ CTLs) -> Step 2 (CTLs recognize peptide-HLA I and release perforin and granzymes across the immunological synapse to activate caspases and induce apoptosis)

r.A: IL-17 and IL-22 are secreted by Th17 cells to stimulate epithelial cells and recruit neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi.
r.B: Removal of B7 molecules from APCs via transendocytosis is mediated by CTLA-4 on regulatory T cells to inhibit T-cell priming.
r.D: IL-5 and eosinophil release of toxic granule proteins such as major basic protein are Th2 effector mechanisms against helminths.
r.E: CXCL13 is produced by follicular stromal cells and Tfh cells to organize B cells and Tfh cells within lymphoid follicles.

q.s: LO4, LO5 / Slides 5, 16: CD8 cytotoxic T cells induce apoptosis; Choose the response by pathogen location

q.v:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a 2-week history of abdominal discomfort and fatigue after visiting a rural farming community. Stool examination reveals ova of an intestinal helminth. A complete blood count with differential and serum immunology panel are obtained:
  Total leukocyte count: 11,500/µL
  Neutrophils: 48%
  Lymphocytes: 30%
  Eosinophils: 18% (markedly elevated)
  Serum IgE: 1,450 IU/mL (markedly elevated)
  Duodenal biopsy: goblet cell hyperplasia and increased mucin
Which of the following transcription factors is most directly responsible for polarizing the CD4+ T-cell subset driving these findings?
o: T-bet
RORγt
FOXP3
GATA-3
STAT4
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret labs: helminth infection with marked eosinophilia, elevated IgE, and mucus hyperplasia indicates a Th2 response) -> Step 2 (Identify GATA-3, induced by IL-4 via STAT6, as the master transcription factor for Th2 differentiation)

r.A: T-bet is the master transcription factor for Th1 cells, which produce IFN-γ to activate macrophages against intracellular microbes.
r.B: RORγt is the lineage-defining transcription factor for Th17 cells, which recruit neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi.
r.C: FOXP3 is the master transcription factor for regulatory T cells, which suppress immune activation and maintain self-tolerance.
r.E: STAT4 is activated by IL-12 during Th1 commitment, whereas Th2 differentiation utilizes STAT6 to induce GATA-3.

q.s: LO2, LO3, LO5 / Slides 11, 16, 17: Th2: expel helminths and drive immediate hypersensitivity

q.v: A 52-year-old woman receiving biological therapy for an autoimmune skin disorder develops recurrent, severe staphylococcal skin abscesses and oral candidiasis. Analysis of biopsy specimens from the infected skin lesions shows abundant extracellular bacteria and fungal hyphae, reduced levels of epithelial beta-defensins, and a marked paucity of neutrophils despite normal bone marrow granulocyte precursors. Blockade of which of the following cytokine pairs best explains this patient's susceptibility to infection?
o: IL-4 and IL-5
IL-10 and TGF-β
IFN-γ and TNF
IL-12 and IL-2
IL-17 and IL-22
q.p: Step 1 (Extracellular bacteria/fungi with impaired neutrophil recruitment and reduced epithelial defensins indicates a Th17 pathway defect) -> Step 2 (Identify IL-17, which induces chemokines and G-CSF for neutrophils, and IL-22, which induces epithelial antimicrobial peptides and barrier repair)

r.A: IL-4 and IL-5 are Th2 cytokines that mediate IgE class switching and eosinophil activation in response to helminths and allergens.
r.B: IL-10 and TGF-β are suppressive cytokines produced by regulatory T cells to dampen inflammation and maintain tolerance.
r.C: IFN-γ and TNF are Th1 cytokines that activate macrophages to kill intracellular pathogens persisting inside phagosomes.
r.D: IL-12 induces Th1 polarization and IL-2 drives T-cell clonal expansion, neither of which directly mediates epithelial defensin production and neutrophil recruitment.

q.s: LO3, LO5 / Slides 12, 15, 16: Th17: reinforce barriers and recruit neutrophils

q.v:
A 26-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of sore throat and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of an enlarged cervical lymph node demonstrates circulating T lymphocytes entering the node directly from the bloodstream across specialized postcapillary venules before scanning dendritic cells for antigen. Flow cytometry of these entering T cells is performed:

  CD62L (L-selectin): high
  CCR7: high
  CXCR3: undetectable
  CCR5: undetectable

Which of the following endothelial ligands do these T cells bind to enter the lymph node?
o: PNAd and CCL19/CCL21 on high endothelial venules
ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 on inflamed capillary endothelium
PECAM-1 (CD31) at interendothelial junctions
CXCL13 secreted by follicular stromal cells
CXCL1 and CXCL8 on mucosal epithelial cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify naive T cells by high CD62L and CCR7 expression) -> Step 2 (Match naive T-cell homing receptors to their ligands PNAd and CCL19/CCL21 on high endothelial venules)

r.B: ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 bind high-affinity integrins (LFA-1 and VLA-4) on activated effector T cells to mediate firm adhesion in inflamed peripheral tissues.
r.C: PECAM-1 (CD31) is involved in diapedesis (transendothelial migration) of effector T cells into inflamed tissues rather than initial lymph node entry.
r.D: CXCL13 is the chemokine produced by follicular stromal cells that attracts CXCR5+ Tfh cells into B-cell follicles.
r.E: CXCL1 and CXCL8 are chemokines induced by IL-17 to recruit neutrophils to mucosal and barrier surfaces.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 8: Naive and effector T cells use different homing programs

q.v: A 41-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent pulmonary infections with an intracellular mycobacterium that survives within macrophage phagosomes. In vitro stimulation of her peripheral blood mononuclear cells with mycobacterial antigen shows normal dendritic cell production of IL-12, but her responding CD4+ T cells fail to differentiate into IFN-γ–producing effector cells. Which of the following intracellular signaling pathways is most likely defective in her CD4+ T cells?
o: STAT6 activation and GATA3 induction
STAT4 activation and T-bet induction
STAT3 activation and RORγt induction
FOXP3 expression and TGF-β signaling
FADD recruitment and procaspase-8 cleavage
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize impaired Th1 polarization in response to dendritic cell-derived IL-12) -> Step 2 (Identify STAT4 and T-bet as the committing transcription factor pathway downstream of IL-12)

r.A: STAT6 and GATA3 are induced by IL-4 to drive Th2 differentiation in response to helminths and allergens.
r.C: STAT3 and RORγt are induced by TGF-β and IL-6 (with IL-1 and IL-23) to drive Th17 differentiation against extracellular bacteria and fungi.
r.D: FOXP3 is the lineage-defining transcription factor for regulatory T cells that restrain immune responses and preserve self-tolerance.
r.E: FADD recruitment and procaspase-8 activation mediate target-cell apoptosis downstream of FasL–Fas engagement by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.

q.s: LO2 / Slide 10: Th1: activate macrophages against intracellular microbes

q.v: Which of the following combinations of signals is delivered by differentiated CD4+ Th1 cells to drive classical (M1) macrophage activation and enhance phagosomal killing of intracellular microbes?
o: IFN-γ and CD40L
IL-4 and IL-13
IL-17A and GM-CSF
IL-10 and CTLA-4
Perforin and granzyme B
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the effector function of Th1 cells as classical M1 macrophage activation) -> Step 2 (Match Th1 execution to IFN-γ secretion and CD40L-CD40 engagement)

r.B: IL-4 and IL-13 are secreted by Th2 cells to drive alternative (M2) macrophage activation for tissue repair and fibrosis.
r.C: IL-17A and GM-CSF are produced by Th17 cells to recruit neutrophils and enhance myeloid inflammatory responses against extracellular pathogens.
r.D: IL-10 and CTLA-4 are used by regulatory T cells to suppress macrophage activation and remove costimulatory B7 molecules from antigen-presenting cells.
r.E: Perforin and granzymes are released by CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes to induce apoptosis in virus-infected or malignant target cells.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 10: Th1: activate macrophages against intracellular microbes

q.v: A 30-year-old man presents with chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea 3 months after a camping trip in a tropical region. Stool examination confirms a chronic intestinal helminth infection. Colonic biopsy shows mucosal fibrosis, smooth muscle hypercontractility, goblet cell hyperplasia, and numerous macrophages with an alternatively activated (M2) phenotype. Which of the following cytokines are most directly responsible for inducing this M2 macrophage polarization and tissue remodeling?
o: IL-12 and TNF
IL-17F and IL-22
IL-4 and IL-13
IL-2 and IFN-γ
IL-1 and IL-6
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize the Th2 response to a helminth with alternative M2 macrophage activation, mucus production, and fibrosis) -> Step 2 (Identify IL-4 and IL-13 as the Th2 cytokines driving M2 polarization and smooth muscle/mucus responses)

r.A: IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation, and TNF acts with IFN-γ to promote classical (M1) macrophage activation and inflammation.
r.B: IL-17F and IL-22 are Th17 cytokines that recruit neutrophils and stimulate epithelial antimicrobial peptide production.
r.D: IL-2 drives T-cell clonal proliferation, while IFN-γ induces classical (M1) microbicidal activity in macrophages.
r.E: IL-1 and IL-6 act with TGF-β as instructive cytokines that polarize naive CD4+ T cells toward the Th17 lineage.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 11: Th2: expel helminths and drive immediate hypersensitivity

q.v: A 16-year-old girl with a history of recurrent skin and mucosal fungal infections is evaluated in the immunodeficiency clinic. Superficial skin scrapings grow *Candida albicans*. Biopsy of an infected mucosal lesion reveals intact numbers of resident macrophages and T cells, but a marked deficiency of beta-defensins and other epithelial antimicrobial peptides, along with poor mucosal barrier repair. Decreased production of which of the following T-cell cytokines best explains the impaired epithelial antimicrobial defense in this patient?
o: IL-5
IL-10
IL-21
IL-22
IFN-γ
q.p: Step 1 (Connect mucocutaneous fungal infection and defective epithelial antimicrobial peptide/defensin production to the Th17 pathway) -> Step 2 (Identify IL-22 as the specific Th17 cytokine that acts on barrier epithelial cells to induce defensins and barrier repair)

r.A: IL-5 is a Th2 cytokine that promotes eosinophil growth, recruitment, and activation against helminths.
r.B: IL-10 is an immunosuppressive cytokine produced by regulatory T cells to decrease inflammatory cytokine production by macrophages and dendritic cells.
r.C: IL-21 is primarily secreted by Tfh and Th17 cells to support B-cell activation, germinal center reactions, and mucosal IgA class switching.
r.E: IFN-γ is the signature Th1 cytokine that activates macrophages to kill phagosomal microbes via reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 12: Th17: reinforce barriers and recruit neutrophils

q.v: A 10-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections. Immunologic evaluation shows normal total lymphocyte counts, but serum levels of IgG and IgA are markedly decreased while IgM is normal. Lymph node biopsy performed after tetanus toxoid booster vaccination demonstrates that antigen-activated CD4+ T cells fail to migrate into B-cell follicles, and germinal centers are absent. Upregulation of which of the following chemokine receptors is required for these helper T cells to localize to the B-cell follicle?
o: CCR4
CCR5
CCR7
CXCR3
CXCR5
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize failure of T follicular helper [Tfh] cells to migrate into B-cell follicles to form germinal centers) -> Step 2 (Identify CXCR5 as the chemokine receptor upregulated on Tfh cells to migrate toward follicular CXCL13)

r.A: CCR4 is a chemokine receptor used by regulatory T cells to home to secondary lymphoid organs and inflamed tissues.
r.B: CCR5 is upregulated on activated effector T cells to guide migration along inflammatory chemokine gradients into peripheral tissues.
r.C: CCR7 is expressed on naive T cells and subsets of Tregs to enter lymph nodes via high endothelial venules in response to CCL19 and CCL21.
r.D: CXCR3 is expressed on effector T cells to direct migration toward CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11 in acutely inflamed peripheral tissues.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 13: Tfh: provide cognate help to germinal-center B cells

q.v: An 18-month-old boy presents with severe autoimmune enteropathy, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and eczematous dermatitis. Genetic testing identifies a loss-of-function mutation in the transcription factor FOXP3. In a healthy individual, FOXP3+ T cells directly remove B7 (CD80/CD86) costimulatory molecules from the surface of antigen-presenting cells via transendocytosis to limit T-cell priming. Which of the following surface molecules mediates this specific regulatory mechanism?
o: CD25 (IL-2Rα)
CD28
CD40L (CD154)
CTLA-4
ICOS
q.p: Step 1 (Identify FOXP3+ cells as regulatory T cells [Tregs] that restrain immune responses) -> Step 2 (Match the mechanism of competing with CD28 and removing B7 from APCs via transendocytosis to the inhibitory receptor CTLA-4)

r.A: CD25 is the high-affinity IL-2 receptor alpha chain on Tregs that consumes IL-2 to limit its availability to effector T cells.
r.B: CD28 is the costimulatory receptor on naive T cells that binds B7 on antigen-presenting cells to deliver Signal 2 for activation.
r.C: CD40L (CD154) is expressed on Th1 and Tfh cells to activate macrophages and germinal-center B cells via CD40 engagement.
r.E: ICOS is a costimulatory receptor expressed on Tfh cells that binds ICOSL on germinal-center B cells to support affinity maturation.

q.s: LO3 / Slide 14: Treg: restrain immune responses and preserve tolerance

q.v:
A researcher isolates CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) from a patient recovering from an acute viral infection and co-cultures them with peptide-pulsed target cells. The researcher adds a pharmacological inhibitor that completely blocks polarized granule exocytosis, yet the CTLs still induce apoptosis in a subset of target cells over several hours. Quantitative analysis of the target cells reveals the following:

  Target cell surface CD95 (Fas): high
  Intracellular FADD adaptor recruitment: increased
  Cleaved caspase-8: increased
  Pore formation in target membrane: absent

In addition to killing virus-infected cells, which of the following physiological roles is specifically attributed to this granule-independent cytotoxic pathway?
o: Enhancing macrophage phagolysosomal fusion
Contributing to lymphocyte homeostasis
Converting leukocyte rolling into firm adhesion
Driving B-cell somatic hypermutation
Stimulating bone marrow neutrophil production
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the FasL–Fas [CD95L–CD95] death-domain signaling pathway from FADD and caspase-8 activation) -> Step 2 (Connect the FasL–Fas pathway to its role in repeated/regulated death signaling and lymphocyte homeostasis)

r.A: Enhancing macrophage microbicidal activity and phagosomal killing is mediated by Th1-derived IFN-γ and CD40L.
r.C: Converting rolling leukocytes into firm adhesion on vascular endothelium is mediated by chemokine signaling activating integrins.
r.D: Driving B-cell affinity maturation and class switching in germinal centers is mediated by Tfh cells via IL-21 and CD40L.
r.E: Stimulating neutrophil production via G-CSF and chemokines is an effector function of Th17-derived IL-17.

q.s: LO4 / Slide 6: CD8 cytotoxic T cells induce apoptosis

q.v: During an acute viral myocarditis, activated CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes exit the draining mediastinal lymph node and traffic through the bloodstream to the inflamed myocardium. Which of the following pairs of molecules mediates the transient tethering and rolling of these effector T cells along the activated vascular endothelium prior to firm adhesion?
o: S1P1 on T cells binding sphingosine-1-phosphate in lymph
LFA-1 on T cells binding ICAM-1 on endothelial cells
VLA-4 on T cells binding VCAM-1 on endothelial cells
Sialyl Lewis X on T cells binding E-selectin and P-selectin on endothelial cells
TCR on T cells binding peptide-HLA class I on target cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Step 3 of effector T-cell migration to inflamed tissue as selectin-mediated rolling) -> Step 2 (Match the carbohydrate ligand sialyl Lewis X on T cells to E-selectin and P-selectin on activated endothelium)

r.A: S1P1 binding to the sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) gradient mediates egress of T cells from the lymph node into efferent lymphatics.
r.B: LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1 mediates chemokine-activated firm adhesion of effector T cells to the endothelium, not initial rolling.
r.C: VLA-4 binding to VCAM-1 mediates high-affinity integrin-dependent firm adhesion following chemokine activation.
r.E: TCR recognition of peptide-HLA class I occurs inside the tissue on infected target cells to trigger cytotoxicity after migration is complete.

q.s: LO1 / Slide 7: Effector CD8 T cells traffic to inflamed tissues

q.v:
A 58-year-old man is hospitalized with severe bacterial pneumonia caused by an extracellular encapsulated bacterium. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid is obtained and analyzed alongside a peripheral blood sample:

  Bronchoalveolar lavage predominant cell: neutrophils (88%)
  Bronchoalveolar lavage CXCL8 (IL-8): markedly elevated
  Bronchoalveolar lavage G-CSF: markedly elevated
  Bronchoalveolar lavage eosinophils: <1%

Secretion of which of the following cytokines by antigen-specific CD4+ T cells in the lung parenchyma most directly drives this local chemokine and growth factor profile?
o: IFN-γ
IL-4
IL-5
IL-10
IL-17
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the lab panel as robust neutrophil recruitment driven by CXCL8 and G-CSF in response to an extracellular bacterium) -> Step 2 (Identify Th17-derived IL-17 as the cytokine that stimulates chemokines [CXCL1, CXCL8] and G-CSF)

r.A: IFN-γ is produced by Th1 cells to activate macrophages and increase reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide production.
r.B: IL-4 is produced by Th2 cells to induce B-cell class switching to IgE and promote alternative macrophage activation.
r.C: IL-5 is produced by Th2 cells to drive eosinophil recruitment, activation, and survival rather than neutrophil recruitment.
r.D: IL-10 is a suppressive cytokine released by Tregs that inhibits inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production.

q.s: LO5 / Slide 12: Th17: reinforce barriers and recruit neutrophils

myLectures.name: B Cells and B Cell Activation
myLectures.note: Mullins (David W. Mullins, PhD), 11/11/2026, M&D B Cells and B Cell Activation. 44 B&B AnKing notes unsuspended and 28 new clozes (card check: 8 Yes, 13 Partly, 9 No). Sources: slides incl. all figures, your 30 cards, and the ScholarRx brick 'B-Cell Activation and Differentiation' (used for conjugate vs polysaccharide vaccine and TD/TI notes). No previous lecture JSONs were provided, so the cross-lecture duplicate check was skipped; MHC II/invariant chain, splenectomy vaccine and CVID notes may overlap with other lectures. Left out because B&B contradicts the lecture's framing (lecture: TI responses are 'primarily IgM, minimal class switching' with 'limited memory'): 1487117025756 (IgM is the ONLY Ig to TI antigens) and 1487117018684 (TI antigens give NO memory). Also left out (not taught): follicular lymphoma/BCL-2 SHM notes, XLA notes, CVID IVIG, sickle-cell autosplenectomy, post-splenectomy target cells, Hib diphtheria-toxoid carrier, IgA switching (IL-5/TGF-β), splenic IgM, IgM pentamer/monomer, and the ScholarRx antibody effector-function list (neutralization, opsonization, ADCC, etc.). Slide errors: LO4/LO5 and the summary's RECOGNIZE/REFINE lines are about T-cell states and CD8 killing (copied from the T-cell lecture); speaker notes on slides 4-16 describe TCR/CD3 and T-cell subsets; slide 11 lists CD40L as a cytokine.
myLectures.deck: Mullins - B Cells and B Cell Activation

add.cloze: After binding antigen, the BCR both initiates intracellular {{c1::signaling}} and {{c1::internalizes}} the antigen for presentation on HLA class II
add.extra: Igα/Igβ (CD79a/b) transmit the signal; uptake is by receptor-mediated (clathrin) endocytosis

add.cloze: A B cell and CD4 T cell can share a protein antigen because the BCR binds {{c1::intact native}} antigen, while the TCR sees a {{c2::processed peptide}} on HLA class {{c2::II}}
add.extra: They usually recognize different epitopes of the same protein

add.cloze: Linked recognition: the B cell presents a {{c1::peptide}} from the {{c1::same}} protein its BCR bound and gets help from a {{c2::CD4}} T cell specific for that peptide–HLA II
add.extra: T-dependent B-cell response

add.cloze: Antigen-activated B cells first meet cognate helper T cells at the {{c1::T-cell–B-cell border}} of a secondary lymphoid organ
add.extra: B cells ↑CCR7 → move toward T zone (CCL19/CCL21); Tfh ↑CXCR5 → move toward follicle (CXCL13)

add.cloze: CD40 signaling in an activated B cell enables robust {{c1::proliferation}} and {{c1::germinal-center}} formation
add.extra: CD40 on B cell binds CD40L (CD154) on Tfh

add.cloze: CD40 signaling in an activated B cell enables {{c1::class-switch recombination}}, {{c1::affinity maturation}}, and {{c1::memory}} development
add.extra: Loss of CD40–CD40L → hyper-IgM

add.cloze: The extrafollicular B-cell response is {{c1::rapid}} and makes mainly short-lived {{c1::plasmablasts}} with {{c1::lower-affinity}} antibody
add.extra: Mostly IgM; buys time before the germinal center matures

add.cloze: The germinal-center response is {{c1::slower}} and yields {{c1::affinity-matured}}, often {{c1::class-switched memory}} B cells and {{c1::long-lived}} plasma cells
add.extra: vs. rapid extrafollicular plasmablasts

add.cloze: {{c1::cytidine deaminase}} initiates both somatic hypermutation and class-switch recombination
add.extra: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID); expressed in activated germinal-center B cells

add.cloze: Somatic hypermutation alters the {{c1::variable}} region DNA of immunoglobulin genes
add.extra: Creates BCR variants with different antigen affinity

add.cloze: Class-switch recombination changes the immunoglobulin {{c1::heavy}} chain {{c1::constant}} region
add.extra: This sets the isotype (IgM → IgG, IgA, IgE)

add.cloze: Class switching changes antibody function but not specificity because the {{c1::constant}} region changes while the {{c1::variable}} region is retained
add.extra: Variable region = antigen-binding site

add.cloze: In the germinal-center dark zone, {{c1::centroblasts proliferate}}
add.extra: Rapid clonal expansion

add.cloze: In the germinal-center dark zone, AID introduces random {{c1::mutations}} into immunoglobulin {{c1::variable}} region genes
add.extra: Somatic hypermutation; mutations may raise, lower, or keep affinity

add.cloze: In the germinal-center light zone, B cells {{c1::compete}} for antigen on {{c2::follicular dendritic}} cells and for survival signals from {{c3::Tfh}} cells
add.extra: Selection step of affinity maturation

add.cloze: Higher-affinity germinal-center B cells capture more {{c1::antigen}}, so they present more {{c2::peptide–HLA}} II and win more Tfh help
add.extra: Competition for cognate Tfh signals

add.cloze: Affinity maturation is selection: AID makes {{c1::random}} variants, and {{c2::competition}} for antigen and Tfh help preserves clones with better binding
add.extra: Not directed improvement; mutations can increase, decrease, or preserve affinity

add.cloze: Germinal-center B cells that compete poorly for antigen and Tfh help undergo {{c1::apoptosis}}
add.extra: Light-zone selection

add.cloze: Plasma cells are specialized for antibody {{c1::secretion}}, whereas memory B cells retain surface {{c2::BCR}} and respond {{c2::rapidly}} to re-exposure
add.extra: Mature plasma cells have reduced surface BCR

add.cloze: Serum antibody can persist without continued antigen exposure because {{c1::long-lived plasma}} cells keep secreting it
add.extra: Reside in bone-marrow survival niches

add.cloze: Compared with a primary response, a secondary humoral response has a {{c1::shorter}} lag, {{c1::greater}} magnitude, {{c1::higher}} affinity, and often {{c1::class-switched}} antibody
add.extra: Driven by memory B cells; booster vaccine example

add.cloze: T-independent B-cell responses are less durable because they get limited {{c1::T-cell}} help
add.extra: No CD40L or Tfh cytokines

add.cloze: Limited T help in T-independent responses means little {{c1::germinal-center}} activity, {{c1::affinity maturation}}, {{c1::class switching}}, and {{c1::memory}}
add.extra: Mainly short-lived plasma cells making IgM

add.cloze: T-independent B-cell responses are commonly triggered by {{c1::repetitive nonprotein}} antigens such as bacterial {{c1::polysaccharides}}
add.extra: e.g., bacterial capsule; also lipids, nucleic acids

add.cloze: Repetitive T-independent antigens strongly {{c1::cross-link}} BCRs and may also provide {{c2::innate}} signals
add.extra: Innate signals: TLR ligands (LPS), complement C3d via CR2 (CD21), BAFF

add.cloze: CD40L deficiency also causes opportunistic infections because CD40L is needed for {{c1::macrophage}} activation, not just B-cell class switching
add.extra: Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium, Toxoplasma; encapsulated bacteria come from the class-switch defect

add.cloze: Biallelic AID deficiency causes an autosomal-recessive {{c1::hyper-IgM}} antibody phenotype
add.extra: vs. X-linked hyper-IgM from CD40L deficiency

add.cloze: Biallelic AID deficiency gives a hyper-IgM phenotype with defective {{c1::class-switch recombination}} and {{c1::somatic hypermutation}}
add.extra: Both processes need AID

myLectures.name: Planetary Health
myLectures.note: Lecturer: David W. Mullins, Ph.D.; 11/11/2026 (Metabolism and Defense 2026). 9 B&B notes unsuspended and 19 cloze cards added from 13 of your cards (0 Yes, 6 Partly, 7 No). No previous lecture JSONs were provided, so the cross-lecture duplicate check was skipped; general notes (PRRs, IgE class switching, asthma PFTs) may already be owned by an earlier immunology/pulm lecture. B&B notes cover barrier/innate sensing (inflammasome, PRRs), allergic asthma (IgE, IL-4/IL-13 class switching, leukotriene effects, reversible bronchoconstriction, FEV1/FVC with bronchodilator response) and Lyme geography; one ScholarRx brick note (lead poisoning in children). B&B has no notes for alarmins (TSLP/IL-25/IL-33), ILC2, IL-5 → eosinophils, the biodiversity/microbiome hypothesis, West Nile clinical features, social/structural risk or environmental history. Left out as not taught: Lyme staging, Ixodes vector and treatment notes; anti-IL-5/anti-IgE drugs; major basic protein, Charcot-Leyden crystals; the Th2 IL-4/IL-10 asthma note (1473628103469), which names IL-10 rather than the lecture's IL-4/IL-13/IL-5; heat stroke, cholera mechanism, and brick-only topics (planetary boundaries, SDGs, Doughnut Model). Slide notes: slide 6 checkpoint repeats option D as E; slide 14 is titled 'Pollution burden' but its map legend shows 'Crude Prevalence %', so it looks like a disease (likely asthma) prevalence map rather than a pollution measure.

add.cloze: A planetary {{c1::driver}} leads to {{c2::exposure}}, which triggers an {{c3::immune response}} and then a {{c4::clinical outcome}}
add.extra: Planetary-health framework (slide 4): e.g., wildfire → inhaled smoke → barrier injury/Th2 → asthma exacerbation

add.cloze: Smoke and air pollution start airway inflammation by injuring airway {{c1::epithelial}} cells, disrupting the {{c2::barrier}}, and releasing {{c3::danger signals}}
add.extra: Oxidative (ROS) injury, impaired cilia, altered tight junctions; DAMPs activate PRRs and the inflammasome (slides 5–6)

add.cloze: Epithelial alarmins {{c1::TSLP}}, {{c1::IL-25}}, and {{c1::IL-33}} promote type 2 inflammation
add.extra: Released from injured airway epithelium; amplify ILC2/Th2 signaling (slide 7)

add.cloze: In allergic asthma, pollution damages the epithelial {{c1::barrier}}, while allergens provide the specific {{c2::antigen}}
add.extra: Pollution lowers the inflammatory threshold; allergen (pollen/mold proteins) provides immune specificity (slide 7)

add.cloze: The innate lymphoid cell that promotes type 2 inflammation is the {{c1::ILC2}}
add.extra: Activated by the alarmins TSLP, IL-25, IL-33 (slide 7)

add.cloze: Type 2 cytokines {{c1::IL-4}} and {{c1::IL-13}} promote IgE and mucus
add.extra: Slide 7: amplified type 2 effectors

add.cloze: The type 2 cytokine {{c1::IL-5}} promotes eosinophils
add.extra: Slide 7: amplified type 2 effectors

add.cloze: Elevated {{c1::eosinophils}} and {{c1::IgE}} with compatible allergic features support type 2 asthma
add.extra: Jayden case: eosinophils and IgE elevated; reversible obstruction (slides 8–9)

add.cloze: Mast cells worsen allergic asthma by releasing mediators that cause {{c1::bronchoconstriction}}, {{c1::mucus}}, and {{c1::edema}}
add.extra: Slide 7. B&B's matching note names leukotrienes C4/D4/E4 as the mediators

add.cloze: The same exposure affects patients differently because risk also depends on {{c1::age}} and underlying {{c1::health}}
add.extra: Host factors

add.cloze: The same exposure affects patients differently because risk also depends on {{c1::housing}}, {{c1::occupation}}, {{c1::neighborhood}}, and {{c1::access to resources}}
add.extra: Structural factors; Jayden lives in subsidized housing within 500 m of an interstate (slides 10–16)

add.cloze: Planetary-health care asks: what can I {{c1::treat}} now, what {{c2::exposure}} can be reduced, and what requires help {{c3::beyond the individual visit}}?
add.extra: Jayden case (slides 17–19): treat today, avoid/mitigate, what he can't simply choose to avoid

add.cloze: Biodiversity loss may affect immunity by reducing environmental {{c1::microbial}} inputs
add.extra: Environmental, skin, airway, and gut microbial exposures shape immune education (slide 20)

add.cloze: Fewer environmental microbial inputs may alter the {{c1::microbiome}}, immune {{c1::regulation}}, {{c1::barrier}} function, and {{c1::tolerance}}
add.extra: Treg function, barrier integrity, tolerogenic signaling (slide 20). Caution: not every exposure is beneficial

add.cloze: Changing vector ecology should update the {{c1::pretest probability}} of vector-borne disease, not be used to assume a diagnosis
add.extra: Slide 21: clinical move when familiar diseases appear in new places or seasons

add.cloze: To update pretest probability for vector-borne disease, use local {{c1::geography}}, {{c1::season}}, {{c1::activities}}, and {{c1::vector exposure}}
add.extra: e.g., Lyme disease expanding range 1995 → 2023 (slide 22)

add.extra: Plus housing, occupation, food/water, travel, outdoor activity, vectors, symptom timing

quizSettings.prompt:
You are writing practice questions for a second-year medical student preparing for a weekly timed, open-book course quiz in a pre-clinical biochemistry/genetics/metabolism block. The questions you write must look, read, and feel like that course quiz.

INPUTS
1. LECTURE MATERIALS (slide deck PDF): the ONLY source of tested content.
2. READINESS QUIZ and PRACTICE QUIZ: written by the course faculty. They show what the instructor considers high-yield and how the instructor phrases questions. Use them to calibrate style and emphasis.

======================================================
STEP 1: BUILD A TEST BLUEPRINT (internal; do not output)
======================================================
- List the lecture's Session Learning Objectives (SLOs), its instructor-written study questions, any end-of-lecture practice cases, and any comparison tables (e.g., "be able to differentiate...").
- Treat these as the highest-yield signals. Also high-yield: content emphasized in red/bold, content repeated across slides, and concepts tested in the reference quizzes.
- SKIP: slides labeled trivia, history of discovery, epidemiology percentages, cartoons, "Other Resources," and anything the instructor marks as beyond scope.
- Allocate 10 questions across the SLOs in proportion to their emphasis. Every SLO gets at least 1 question. Heavily emphasized comparison topics may get 2-3.
- No two questions may share the same correct answer or test the same fact.

======================================================
STEP 2: QUESTION MIX
======================================================
- 6 clinical vignette questions
- 2 short conceptual questions (one- or two-sentence stem, no patient). Examples of the format: "Which compound regulates both X and Y?" or "Which of the following is true regarding the regulation of X?"
- 2 data-interpretation questions. The vignette or stem gives a lab panel, lipid panel, acylcarnitine profile, ABG, or small data table, and the student must interpret it. Use whichever data type the lecture actually teaches.

======================================================
STEP 3: HOUSE STYLE FOR EACH QUESTION
======================================================
VIGNETTES
- Open with "A [age]-year-old [man/woman/infant/boy/girl]..." Include the setting, relevant history (diet, alcohol, medications, surgery, family history), symptoms, and exam findings, using the classic descriptors the lecture uses.
- When labs matter, list them one per line with values and units, e.g.:
    Hemoglobin: 9.0 g/dL
    MCV: 110 fL
    Serum methylmalonic acid: elevated
- Length: 3-6 sentences plus any lab list.
- All clues point to the same answer. Do not plant trick red herrings and do not write riddles. Difficulty should come from telling apart closely related conditions the lecture teaches, not from obscure wording.
- Do not name the disorder in the stem when recognizing it is the point of the question.
- The lead-in is a separate final sentence, phrased like the course quiz:
    "Which of the following is most likely deficient in this patient?"
    "Which of the following enzyme activities is most likely decreased in this patient?"
    "Which of the following best explains...?"
    "Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of this patient's condition?"
    "Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?"

REASONING DEPTH
- One or two steps. The typical two-step pattern is: recognize the disorder or deficiency from the vignette, then name its enzyme, cofactor, inheritance pattern, expected lab finding, mechanism, or treatment.
- Do not add a contrived extra step (embryology, distant downstream consequences, unrelated organ systems).

ANSWER OPTIONS
- Exactly 5 options (A-E), single best answer.
- Options must be short and concrete: a vitamin, enzyme, lipoprotein, transporter, disorder name, inheritance pattern, organelle, drug, or lab change. Use a short phrase (15 words or fewer) only when the answer is a mechanism.
- Do not use abstract genetics or biochemistry jargon that does not appear on the slides.
- All 5 options must come from the same category, and the distractors must be drawn from the lecture itself (e.g., other vitamins covered, other hyperlipidemia types, other carnitine-shuttle defects). The best distractors are the conditions the lecture explicitly asks students to differentiate.
- Keep options parallel in length and grammar. The correct answer must not be the longest or most specific option.
- Combination options are encouraged when the lecture teaches a contrast. Examples: "Free carnitine decreased / long-chain acylcarnitines increased"; "Vitamin C, folate (B9), and cobalamin (B12)".
- Never use "all of the above," "none of the above," or EXCEPT/NOT stems.
- Distribute correct answers across A-E. No letter may be correct more than 3 times in the quiz.

======================================================
SOURCE RULES
======================================================
- Every fact in the stem, correct answer, distractors, and explanation must be stated or directly derivable from the lecture slides. If a classic board fact is not in the lecture, do not use it.
- You MAY test the same core concepts the reference quizzes and lecture cases test, because the real exam does this. You must write a NEW patient (different age, sex, setting, and history). Where possible, ask a different question about the concept (e.g., if the reference asks "which vitamin," ask "which enzyme" or "which lab finding").
- Never copy or lightly reword a reference-quiz or lecture-case stem.
- If a slide appears to conflict with standard references, do not build a question on that point.
- Do not test ATP-yield arithmetic or exact prevalence numbers.

======================================================
STYLE EXEMPLARS
======================================================
These come from a DIFFERENT lecture. They show format only. Never reuse their content.

Example A (vignette with labs):
A 22-year-old man presents with fatigue, jaundice, and dark urine two days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Laboratory studies show:
  Hemoglobin: 8.5 g/dL
  Reticulocyte count: elevated
  Haptoglobin: decreased
  Peripheral smear: bite cells
Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of this patient's underlying condition?
A. Autosomal dominant  B. Autosomal recessive  C. X-linked recessive  D. X-linked dominant  E. Mitochondrial

Example B (short conceptual):
Which compound regulates both the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and the TCA cycle?
A. NADH  B. NADPH  C. FADH2  D. Malonyl-CoA  E. Acetyl-CoA

======================================================
OUTPUT FORMAT (repeat for each question)
======================================================
**Question [N]**
[Stem and lead-in]

A. ...
B. ...
C. ...
D. ...
E. ...

**Correct Answer:** [Letter]. [Text]
**Explanation:** 2-4 sentences in the voice of a course answer key, explaining why the answer is correct using the mechanism taught on the slides.
**Why the others are wrong:**
- [Letter]: one sentence
- [Letter]: one sentence
- [Letter]: one sentence
- [Letter]: one sentence
**SLO / Slide Source:** [SLO number and slide title]
